docs.title: Reactions
docs.text:
Define the reactions and reaction networks that several fields share.

A reaction moves units between states, and a reaction network builds one element per species and one reaction per row of its table.

docs.title: ReactionInteraction(label, *, target=None, reactants=None, products=None, k=1.0, propensity=None, modifiers=None, mode='rate', form='symbolic', phase=None, schedule='synchronous')
docs.text:
Bases: JumpInteraction

An interaction that moves units from its reactants to its products.

A reactant, a product, or a modifier is a pair of the path of an element and the name of its state, mapped to its stoichiometric coefficient, the number of units the reaction takes or gives. So S + I -> 2 I has the reactants {('S', 'n'): 1, ('I', 'n'): 1} and the products {('I', 'n'): 2}. A coefficient is a positive number or a function of the namespace. A species may also be the name of a state of target alone, such as {'u': 1, 'v': 2}, and a target that is a group or a field reacts in every member. A subclass may bind its species under roles of its own, such as susceptible and infected, and return its entries from _get_reactants, _get_products, and _get_modifiers.

The propensity is the rate constant k times the product of the reactant and modifier amounts, each raised to its coefficient, or the expression that propensity returns. Fields name this product their own way: mass action in chemistry, homogeneous mixing in epidemiology, the encounter term of Lotka and Volterra in ecology. The mode says how the reaction runs:

  • 'rate': a rate equation.
  • 'jump': a random event at the propensity that moves the units of the coefficients.
  • 'langevin': the chemical Langevin equation, the rate equation with a noise of amplitude the square root of the propensity.

In the agent form every member of an agent group reacts on its own states at every step, by schedule.

Unlike JumpInteraction, which it extends, it builds the changes from a stoichiometric vector and the propensity from mass action, and it can also run as a rate or a Langevin equation. Choose it when a model is written as reactions between species.

It appears in many fields. Molecules react in a cell, people pass from susceptible to infected in an epidemic, predators eat prey, and enzymes bind their substrates.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the reaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str | None, RoleSpec(elements=(ANY,), states=(reactants, products, modifiers))]

The path of the element, group, or field whose states the species named by a state alone are, or None.

None reactants Annotated[Stoichiometry | None, RoleSpec(variadic=True, elements=(ANY,))]

The coefficients of the reactants, or None for a source.

None products Annotated[Stoichiometry | None, RoleSpec(variadic=True, elements=(ANY,))]

The coefficients of the products, or None for a sink.

None k Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=closed_open(0, oo))]

The rate constant.

1.0 propensity Callable[..., object] | None

A function of the namespace of the reaction that returns the propensity, or None for the product propensity. The namespace holds the tuples reactants, products, and modifiers of the namespaces of the elements their pairs bind, in the order of their entries, target, the namespace of the target or of one of its members, and the symbol k. In the agent form, a function propensity(agent, system) that returns a number.

None modifiers Annotated[Stoichiometry | None, RoleSpec(variadic=True, elements=(ANY,))]

The coefficients of the modifiers, whose states the propensity reads but the reaction does not change, or None.

None mode str

The form of the laws, 'rate', 'jump', or 'langevin'.

'rate' form str

'symbolic' for the laws of the states, or 'agent' for a rule in which every member of an agent group reacts on its own states.

'symbolic' phase str | None

The phase of the step the agent form runs in, or None for the default phase.

None schedule str

The order of the members in the agent form, 'synchronous', 'sequential', 'random-sequential', or 'member'.

'synchronous'

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The mode, the form, or the schedule is unknown, the symbolic form is not synchronous, the reaction has neither reactants nor products, an entry is neither a pair of a path and a state name nor a state name of a given target, a coefficient is neither a positive number nor a function, or the agent form has no target, has an entry that is a pair, or has the mode 'langevin'.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import NonnegativeElement
>>> from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionInteraction
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> infection = ReactionInteraction(
...     'infection', reactants={('S', 'x'): 1, ('I', 'x'): 1}, products={('I', 'x'): 2}, k=0.0005
... )
>>> recovery = ReactionInteraction('recovery', reactants={('I', 'x'): 1}, products={('R', 'x'): 1}, k=0.1)
>>> system = CompositeSystem(
...     elements=[NonnegativeElement('S', x=990), NonnegativeElement('I', x=10), NonnegativeElement('R')],
...     interactions=[infection, recovery],
... )
>>> states = simulate(system, until=50, dt=1.0).states
>>> round(float(states[-1].sum()), 6)
1000.0

The decay x -> 0 at every site of a field, at the rate k x of the site:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import FieldElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
>>> decay = ReactionInteraction('decay', target='cells', reactants={'x': 1}, k=1.0)
>>> values = {'x': np.arange(3.0)}
>>> cells = FieldElement('cells', element=NonnegativeElement, space=LatticeSpace((3,)), values=values)
>>> trajectory = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[cells], interactions=[decay]), until=1, dt=1.0)
>>> np.round(trajectory.get_lattice('cells.x')[-1], 3).tolist()
[0.0, 0.368, 0.736]

A coefficient that is a parameter, the decay at the rate x that removes 1 / epsilon units per event:

>>> from typing import Annotated
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
>>> from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec
>>> class ScaledElement(Element):
...     def __init__(
...         self,
...         label,
...         x: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0,
...         epsilon: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.5,
...     ):
...         super().__init__(label)
...         self.x = x
...         self.epsilon = epsilon
>>> scaled = ReactionInteraction(
...     'decay', target='box', reactants={'x': lambda s: 1 / s.target.epsilon}, propensity=lambda s: s.target.x
... )
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[ScaledElement('box')], interactions=[scaled])
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=0.5, dt=0.01)
>>> round(float(trajectory.get_values('box.x')[-1]), 3)
0.368

Every agent of a group decays on its own states, by k n in a step of the rate equation:

>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import GroupElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> class CellElement(Element):
...     def __init__(self, label, n: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 3.0):
...         super().__init__(label)
...         self.n = n
>>> cells = GroupElement('cells', element=CellElement, size=2)
>>> decay = ReactionInteraction('decay', target='cells', reactants={'n': 1}, k=0.1, form='agent')
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[cells], interactions=[decay], time=DiscreteTime())
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=2)
>>> np.round(trajectory.get_agents('cells', 2).values['n'], 6).tolist()
[2.43, 2.43]

docs.title: ReactionNetworkSystem(species=None, reactions=None, *, mode='rate', label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem[CompositeSystem]

A system of amounts and the reactions between them, written as a table.

Every species is a NonnegativeElement named after it, whose state x holds its amount. Every reaction is a ReactionInteraction with a coefficient for each reactant and product and a rate constant k. Its propensity is k times the product of the reactant amounts, each raised to its coefficient. So S + I -> 2 I at the rate constant beta has the reactants {'S': 1, 'I': 1}, the products {'I': 2}, and the propensity beta S I. A species that is both a reactant and a product with one coefficient, such as a catalyst, enters the propensity and does not change.

In the mode 'rate' the reactions are rate equations, in the mode 'jump' the random events of a Markov chain in continuous time, run by the algorithm of Gillespie, and in the mode 'langevin' the chemical Langevin equations. A subclass takes the parameters of its model under its own names and gives its species, reactions, and mode from the hooks _get_species, _get_reactions, and _get_mode, or its reactions as interactions from _get_interactions.

Unlike CompositeSystem, which takes any parts, it builds NonnegativeElement and ReactionInteraction parts from a table of reactions. Choose it when a model is a list of reactions with rate constants.

It appears in many fields. Epidemics of susceptible, infected, and recovered people, enzyme kinetics of Michaelis and Menten, and predator and prey cycles of Lotka and Volterra are reaction networks.

Attributes:

Name Type Description system_ CompositeT

The composite of the species and the reactions built from the parameters at the last prepare.

laws_ Sequence[BasePart]

The laws the system contributes for the namespace of its last run.

Examples:

The reversible isomerization A <-> B, whose amounts relax to k_back / (k_forth + k_back) of the total:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> isomerization = ReactionNetworkSystem(
...     species={'A': 10.0, 'B': 0.0},
...     reactions={'forth': ({'A': 1}, {'B': 1}, 0.3), 'back': ({'B': 1}, {'A': 1}, 0.1)},
... )
>>> [element.label for element in isomerization.prepare().system_.elements]
['A', 'B']
>>> trajectory = simulate(isomerization, until=50.0, dt=1.0)
>>> round(float(trajectory.get_values('A.x')[-1]), 3)
2.5

The same reactions as jumps, whose tags are those of a stochastic system:

>>> tags = isomerization.set_params(mode='jump').get_tags()
>>> sorted(tags.laws), tags.randomness
(['jump'], 'stochastic')

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default species Mapping[str, float] | None

The initial amount of every species, by name, or None for no species.

None reactions ReactionTable | None

The reactants, the products, and the rate constant of every reaction, by label, the reactants and the products as coefficients by species name, empty for a source or a sink, or None for no reactions.

None mode str

The form of the laws of the reactions, 'rate', 'jump', or 'langevin'.

'rate' label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system' Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/general/reactions/_reaction_network.py 
def __init__(
    self,
    species: Mapping[str, float] | None = None,
    reactions: ReactionTable | None = None,
    *,
    mode: str = 'rate',
    label: str = 'system',
) -> None:
    """Store the species, the reactions, the mode, and the label of the system.

    Args:
        species:
            The initial amount of every species, by name, or `None` for no species.

        reactions:
            The reactants, the products, and the rate constant of every reaction, by label, the reactants and the
            products as coefficients by species name, empty for a source or a sink, or `None` for no reactions.

        mode:

docs.title: BakerMapSystem(x=0.2, y=0.3, *, alpha=1 / 3, lambda_a=1 / 3, lambda_b=2 / 3, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The generalized baker map.

The map stretches the unit square along x and stacks the two pieces in y.

The strip x < alpha is stretched by 1 / alpha and squeezed into the bottom band of height lambda_a, and the rest is stretched by 1 / (1 - alpha) and squeezed into the top band of height lambda_b. The map preserves area when lambda_a = alpha and lambda_b = 1 - alpha, and it has a fractal attractor when lambda_a + lambda_b < 1. The system has the states map.x and map.y.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

Hénon's area-preserving quadratic map.

The map is a rotation by 2π nu with a quadratic kick.

The map is x' = a x + b y + b x², y' = -b x + a y + a x² with a = cos 2π nu and b = sin 2π nu (Dilão 2023, Example 3.17 and Exercise 2.8). For nu in (0, 1/2) the origin is a centre surrounded by invariant curves, and (2 tan(π nu), -2 tan²(π nu)) is a saddle whose manifolds bound the region of bounded orbits, the dynamic aperture of accelerator physics. The default nu gives cos 2π nu = 0.24, the case of Hénon (1969). The system has the states map.x and map.y.

docs.title: CubicChaoticMapSystem(n_walkers=100, *, lam=15.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Bertin's cubic chaotic map and the chaotic walk it drives.

The walk spreads like a random walk.

Every walker follows the map x' = λ x (x - 1/2)(x - 1) + x on the unit interval and moves by the step y' = y + 2x - 1. The fixed point x = 1/2 is stable for λ < 8, a period-two cycle follows, and the map is chaotic at λ = 15. The walkers start at y = 0 with values of x spread regularly over the unit interval, so the mean position stays near 0 while the mean square position grows linearly in time, and the invariant density of x is not uniform. The system has the states walkers.x and walkers.y and the observables displacement, the mean position, and square_displacement, the mean square position.

Parameters:

docs.title: DoublingMapSystem(n_points=100, *, x=0.4, spread=0.01, q=DOUBLING_DENOMINATOR, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

An ensemble of the doubling map x' = 2x (mod 1).

The map is iterated exactly on fractions with an odd denominator.

In floating point 2x (mod 1) shifts out one binary digit per step, and every orbit reaches 0 within 53 steps. The system keeps every point on the fractions k / q of an odd denominator q and applies the map to them exactly, k' = 2k (mod q), through the update x' = (2 round(q x) mod q) / q. The orbits are the exact orbits of these fractions. The default q is a prime below 2^50 of which 2 is a primitive root, so every orbit except that of 0 has the period q - 1, about 10^15. The points start in a narrow interval and spread until their histogram matches the uniform invariant density. The system has the states points.x.

Parameters:

The number of points of the ensemble.

100 x float

The left end of the interval of initial points, which are rounded to the nearest fraction k / q.

0.4 spread float

The width of the interval of initial points.

0.01 q float

The odd denominator of the fractions the points stay on, an integer below 2^51.

DOUBLING_DENOMINATOR random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the initial points.

0 label str

docs.title: KoopmanSlowManifoldSystem(x1=1.0, x2=-1.0, *, mu=-0.05, lam=-1.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The quadratic flow x1' = mu x1, x2' = lam (x2 - x1^2).

The flow has a slow manifold and a linear embedding.

For lam < mu < 0 the fast direction contracts onto the slow manifold x2 = x1^2, and the state then slides along it to the origin. With the observable x1^2, the coordinates (x1, x2, x1^2) span a Koopman-invariant subspace in which the flow is linear, with the eigenvalues mu, lam, and 2 mu. The Koopman eigenfunctions phi_mu = x1 and phi_lam = x2 - b x1^2 with b = lam / (lam - 2 mu) decay exactly as exp(mu t) and exp(lam t), so trajectories follow the parabolas x2 = b x1^2 + C |x1|^(lam / mu). The system has the states flow.x1 and flow.x2.

Parameters:

Bases: BaseSystem

The Rössler flow driven through its bifurcations.

A slow Ornstein-Uhlenbeck control parameter drives the flow.

The flow is x' = -y - z, y' = x + a y + eta, z' = b + z (x - c), Eq. 13 of Cestnik and Martens, and the control follows eta' = (-eta + rho xi) / tau with white noise xi. The control is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with the correlation time tau and the stationary variance rho^2 / (2 tau). A control that varies slowly against the period of the flow sweeps it through the period doublings and chaotic bands of its bifurcation diagram. The system has the states rossler.x, rossler.y, rossler.z, and the control rossler.eta.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

An ensemble of the skew tent map.

Its density relaxes to the uniform invariant density for any a.

The map is x' = x / a for x < a and x' = (1 - x) / (1 - a) otherwise. Every value has one preimage on each branch, with slopes 1 / a and 1 / (1 - a), so the uniform density is invariant. The points start in a narrow interval and spread over the unit interval until their histogram is flat. For a = 1/2 both slopes are 2, and in floating point every orbit reaches 0 within about 55 steps, so a should differ from 1/2. The system has the states points.x.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The subcritical Hopf normal form.

A stable focus coexists with a stable limit cycle.

The complex amplitude z = x + iy follows z' = (alpha + iω) z + (1 + iq) |z|² z - (gamma + is) |z|⁴ z, so its modulus follows r' = alpha r + r³ - gamma r⁵. The focus z = 0 is stable for alpha < 0. The stable limit cycle of radius r² = (1 + √(1 + 4 alpha gamma)) / (2 gamma) exists for alpha > -1 / (4 gamma), and an unstable cycle separates the two attractors while alpha < 0. A slow sweep of alpha up and down therefore jumps to the cycle at alpha = 0 and falls back to the focus at alpha = -1 / (4 gamma), a hysteresis loop. The system has the states form.x and form.y.

Bases: DynamicalSystem

The Thomas flow x' = -a x + sin y with its cyclic permutations.

Bases: BaseSystem

Points that draw the attractor of an iterated function system by the chaos game.

At every step each point moves by one of the affine maps of the system, drawn with probabilities proportional to the weights. The maps contract, so after a few steps the cloud of points covers the attractor, the unique compact set that the union of the maps leaves unchanged. docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The random function system z -> ±√(z - omega).

Its points settle on the Julia set of z² + omega.

At every step each point moves to the positive square root of z - omega with probability p and to the negative one otherwise (Dilão 2023, Exercise 5.8). Both branches invert the quadratic map z -> z² + omega, which repels its Julia set, so the inverse branches attract the points onto the Julia set, drawn by the chaos game with weights p and 1 - p. docs.title: BarabasiAlbertSystem(n_nodes=303, *, edges=2, seed_nodes=3, fitness=False, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Barabási-Albert growth.

By preferential attachment the degrees follow a power law P(k) ~ k^-3.

The network starts complete on seed_nodes nodes, and every step one node joins with edges edges to nodes drawn with probability proportional to their degree, until it holds n_nodes nodes.

With fitness, every node draws a fitness eta uniformly in [0, 1] and new edges join nodes with probability proportional to eta k, the model of Bianconi and Barabási (2001) that Raman (2021, section 3.2.4) describes. The degree of a node then grows as t^beta(eta) with an exponent that rises with its fitness, so a fit late node overtakes older ones. The system has the groups nodes and links and the arrival growth, and with fitness the state nodes.fitness.

Parameters:

The number of nodes the network holds room for.

303 edges int

The number of edges of every new node.

2 seed_nodes int

The number of nodes of the complete seed network.

3 fitness bool

Whether the nodes draw a fitness that scales their attachment, the Bianconi-Barabási model.

False random_state int | Generator | None

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.networks import BarabasiAlbertSystem
>>> trajectory = simulate(BarabasiAlbertSystem(13), until=10, random_state=0)
>>> int(trajectory.get_network(-1).sources.size)

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The configuration model.

It is the maximally random network of a given degree sequence.

Every node gets as many half-links as its degree, and pairs of half-links drawn uniformly at random become links (Jensen 2023, section 8.5.1, and Thurner et al. 2018, section 4.5.1). Without a degree sequence the degrees are drawn from the power law P(k) ~ k^-exponent for k >= min_degree, cut at sqrt(n_nodes), and one half-link is added to a random node when their sum is odd. The pairing leaves self-loops and multilinks, which the rewiring of Thurner et al. removes while it keeps every degree. A neighbour has the mean degree <k²> / <k>, above the mean degree, the friendship paradox. The system has the group nodes and their states degree and clustering.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default degrees Sequence[int] | None

The degree of every node, or None for degrees drawn from the power law.

The number of nodes of the drawn degrees.

The exponent of the power law of the drawn degrees.

docs.title: DavidsenEbelBornholdtSystem(n_nodes=200, *, turnover=0.1, links=None, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Davidsen-Ebel-Bornholdt network.

Its triadic closure and node turnover give high clustering.

The network starts as an Erdős-Rényi graph of n_nodes nodes and links links, n_nodes by default. Every step a node drawn uniformly joins two of its neighbours that are not yet joined, or, without such a pair, joins a node drawn uniformly. Then, with probability turnover, a node drawn uniformly leaves with its links and a new node takes its place with one link to a node drawn uniformly (Thurner et al. 2018, section 4.5.4.6). A closure always adds one link, and a turnover removes a node of mean degree k and adds one link, so the steady state has the mean degree k = 1 + 1 / turnover. Closing triangles keeps the clustering high, and since a node lies near many others in proportion to its degree, closure attaches preferentially, so hubs emerge as the turnover falls. The system has the groups nodes and links, the closure closure, and the turnover turnover.

Parameters:

The number of nodes.

The probability that a node is replaced at a step.

docs.title: DuplicationDeletionSystem(n_nodes=100, *, kill=1.0, inherit=0.5, parent=0.5, new=0.01, density=0.05, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The steady-state duplication-deletion network of Jensen.

Its connectance settles at Eq. 8.84.

The network starts as an Erdős-Rényi graph of n_nodes nodes and the link probability density. Every step a node drawn uniformly leaves with its links with probability kill, and a parent drawn uniformly among the nodes left is duplicated: the offspring inherits each link of the parent with probability inherit, joins the parent with probability parent, and joins every node the parent does not join with probability new (Jensen 2023, section 8.5.1). With kill = 1 the network keeps N nodes, and its connectance converges to C = (new (N - 2) + parent) / (N - 1 + (new - inherit) (N - 2)), Eq. 8.84. Accurate duplication, with inherit near 1 and new near 0, turns the binomial degrees of noisy duplication into a cut-off power law. With kill < 1 the network grows by 1 - kill nodes per step on average, up to twice its initial size.

The system has the groups nodes and links, the deletion death, and the duplication birth.

docs.title: ExplosivePercolationSystem(n_nodes=1000, *, candidates=2, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Explosive percolation.

The Achlioptas product rule delays and sharpens the giant component.

The network starts with n_nodes isolated nodes, and every step adds one edge. It draws candidates edges, each between two distinct nodes not yet joined drawn uniformly, and adds the one whose product of the sizes of the components it joins is smallest, the product rule of Achlioptas, D'Souza, and Spencer (2009). A map reads the size of the component of every node at the start of every step. With one candidate the edges are those of an Erdős-Rényi graph, whose giant component grows continuously from t = 1/2 edges per node. With two candidates the rule suppresses large components until the giant component jumps in a narrow window near t = 0.888. The system has the size of the component of every node nodes.size.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Growth by the arrival of three-node graphlets.

The tree has a degree exponent that rises with alpha.

The network starts from one edge, and every step a graphlet of a central node and two peripheral nodes joined to it arrives and merges one of its nodes with an existing node drawn with probability proportional to its degree: a peripheral node with probability alpha, so the existing node gains the central node, which carries the other peripheral node, and the central node otherwise, so the existing node gains both peripheral nodes (Filkov et al. 2009, as Raman 2021, section 3.2.4.2, describes). Every step adds two nodes and two edges, and the shares of nodes of degree 1 and 2 are 2 (2 - alpha) / 5 and alpha (7 - alpha) / 15. The system has the groups nodes and links and the arrivals growth and graphlet.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The size-biased random walk on a hypergraph, p_j' = sum_i p_i T_ij - p_j.

The walk starts from one node.

A walker at node i moves to node j at rate T_ij = k_ij / sum_l k_il, with k_ij = sum_e (|e| - 1) e_i e_j over the hyperedges e of the incidence matrix, so large hyperedges carry more of the walk, as in Carletti et al. The probability of the walker spreads from the source, keeps its sum of 1, and settles on the stationary distribution p_i = D_i / sum_l D_l, with D_i = sum_e (|e| - 1)^2 e_i the weight of the hyperedges of i. The system has the probabilities nodes.p and the weights nodes.D.

Parameters:

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The cascade of failures of Buldyrev between two interdependent networks.

The cascade is that of Buldyrev et al., and the nodes of the networks depend on each other.

Two Erdős-Rényi networks of the mean degree mean_degree share their nodes, every node of one depending on the node of the same index in the other, so a node is one pair of dependent nodes. An attack leaves every node functional with probability p. At even steps the nodes outside the giant component of the functional nodes of the first network fail, and at odd steps those outside that of the second network, until the cascade stops at the mutual giant component (Buldyrev et al. 2010, as Artime et al. 2025, section 5, Eqs. 9 to 11, review it). Its share S solves S = p (1 - exp(-k S))², which has a solution above 0 only for p above 2.4554 / k, where the networks collapse at once in a discontinuous transition. The system has the functional nodes nodes.active over the graph of the first network and the layer dependent of the second.

Parameters:

The number of nodes of every network.

2000 mean_degree float

The mean degree k of every network.

4.0 p float

The share of nodes the attack leaves functional.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The cascade of overload failures of Motter and Lai after one node is removed.

The load of a node is its betweenness, the number of shortest paths between other pairs of nodes that pass through it, and its capacity is (1 + tolerance) times its load on the intact network (Motter and Lai 2002, as Artime et al. 2025, section 5, review it). The attack removes one node at the first step, the node of the largest load, of the largest degree, or a random node. Every later step the loads are those of the network present, and every node whose load exceeds its capacity fails at once, until no node is overloaded. A heterogeneous network loses most of its largest component after an attack on a node of large load and a low tolerance, and keeps it after a random failure. The system has the nodes nodes, their load, capacity, and the size of the largest component giant, and the links links.

docs.title: NetworkSuperpositionSystem(n_nodes=100, *, n_subgraphs=20, exponent=2.0, low=0.005, high=0.1, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The network superposition model.

It is a union of Erdős-Rényi graphs whose linking probabilities are drawn.

Every one of n_subgraphs subgraphs of n_nodes nodes draws one linking probability p from Q(p) ~ p^-exponent on [low, high] and links each pair of its nodes with probability p, and the network is their union (Thurner et al. 2018, section 4.5.2). Its degrees mix the Poisson laws of the subgraphs, P(k) = ∫ dp P(k | N p) Q(p), Eq. 4.34, so a power law of the probabilities gives a power law of the degrees up to the largest mean degree N high. The book draws p for every attempted link, which gives one Erdős-Rényi graph of the mean probability, so the probability is drawn once per subgraph, the reading of Eq. 4.34, like the cells of superstatistics. The system has the group nodes and their states degree and clustering.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_nodes int

The number of nodes of every subgraph.

100 n_subgraphs int

The number of subgraphs.

20 exponent float

The exponent of the distribution Q(p) of the linking probabilities.

2.0 low float

The smallest linking probability.

0.005 high float

The largest linking probability.

0.1 random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the linking probabilities and the links.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The bounds of the linking probabilities are not 0 < low <= high <= 1.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.networks import NetworkSuperpositionSystem
>>> system = NetworkSuperpositionSystem(10, n_subgraphs=3).prepare().system_
>>> system.elements[0].values['degree'].size
30

docs.title: NodeMergingSystem(n_nodes=500, *, edges=1, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The node-merging network of Kim and coauthors.

Its merging of linked nodes builds hubs without growth.

The network starts as a random tree of n_nodes nodes. Every step a node drawn uniformly merges with one of its neighbours drawn uniformly into one node that keeps the union of their links, and a new node joins edges nodes drawn uniformly, so the network keeps its size (Thurner et al. 2018, section 4.5.4.6). Merging adds the links of the neighbour to the node, so well-linked nodes absorb more links, and the degrees follow a fat-tailed, q-exponential distribution with hubs far above the degrees of a random graph. The system has the groups nodes and links, the merging merging, and the arrival arrival.

docs.title: PopularitySimilarityNetworkSystem(n_nodes=300, *, edges=2, exponent=2.5, temperature=0.2, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Popularity-similarity growth, scale-free and clustered.

Its nodes attach by hyperbolic distance.

Every step a node joins at a uniform angle on the circle and the radius 2 ln t, every other node s moves to the radius b 2 ln s + (1 - b) 2 ln t with b = 1 / (exponent - 1), and the new node joins edges nodes drawn in proportion to the Fermi-Dirac probability of their hyperbolic distance x = r_s + r_t + 2 ln(theta / 2), at the temperature temperature. The degrees follow a power law of the given exponent, and the clustering falls as the temperature rises (Papadopoulos et al. 2012). The system has the groups nodes and links, the arrival growth, and the states nodes.angle, nodes.age, and nodes.degree.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The construction of an Erdős-Rényi or a Watts-Strogatz random graph.

The graph is built one step of new edges at a time.

The Erdős-Rényi graph starts empty and every node adds an edge to a random node with a probability that brings the mean degree to mean_degree after steps steps, so a giant component emerges when the mean degree passes 1. The Watts-Strogatz graph starts as a ring where every node joins its mean_degree nearest nodes, and every edge moves its target to a random node at a rate that rewires a fraction rewiring of the edges after steps steps, which shortens paths while the clustering stays high. The system has the groups nodes and links, the map degree, and the interaction linking or rewiring.

docs.title: SpatialTriadicPercolationSystem(side=4.0, *, density=100.0, c=0.4, positive=0.2, negative=0.2, structural_range=0.25, regulatory_range=0.25, p=0.8, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Spatial triadic percolation.

Nearby signed regulators make the giant component form moving patterns.

The nodes lie uniformly on a square torus of side side with density nodes per unit area, and two nodes at the distance d are linked with probability c exp(-d / structural_range), a Waxman network, Eq. 1 of Millán et al. A node regulates a link positively with probability positive exp(-d / regulatory_range) and negatively with probability negative exp(-d / regulatory_range), never both, from its distance d to the midpoint of the link, Eq. 2. Every step of the paper runs in two phases. In the phase regulation a link is active with probability p when none of its negative regulators is active and one of its positive regulators is, or, for the rare link without positive regulators, when none of its negative regulators is active. In the phase percolation a node is active when it belongs to the giant component of the active links. All nodes and links start active.

The regulation is local, so the giant component forms clusters, stripes, and octopus-like patterns that move, and its size keeps changing instead of settling. At p = 0.8 with positive = negative the patterns blink: a pattern deactivates the links it regulates negatively and the next step activates the region around it, so the active nodes of consecutive steps are anti-correlated. For long ranges the model becomes the triadic percolation of Erdős-Rényi networks with many regulators per link. The system has the activities nodes.active and links.active, and links.negatives and links.positives, the numbers of negative and positive regulators of every link, on a network whose nodes hold their positions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default side float

The side of the square torus.

4.0 density float

The number of nodes per unit area.

100.0 c float

The prefactor of the probability of a structural link.

0.4 positive float

The prefactor of the probability of a positive regulation.

0.2 negative float

The prefactor of the probability of a negative regulation.

0.2 structural_range float

The typical length of the structural links, d0.

0.25 regulatory_range float

The typical length of the regulations, dr.

0.25 p float

The probability that a link the regulation allows is active.

0.8 random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the positions, the links, and the regulators.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.networks import SpatialTriadicPercolationSystem
>>> system = SpatialTriadicPercolationSystem(1.0).prepare().system_
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=2, random_state=0)
>>> giant = trajectory.get_values('nodes.active').mean(axis=1)
>>> bool(giant[0] == 1.0 and giant[1] < 0.1)
True

docs.title: TriadicPercolationSystem(n_nodes=1000, *, mean_degree=4.0, p=0.5, negative=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Triadic percolation.

Regulating nodes switch links on and off from the giant component.

Every link of an Erdős-Rényi graph has one regulating node, drawn at random among the other nodes, which is negative with probability negative and positive otherwise. The link and its regulator form a hyperedge of size three. Every step is a time step of Millán et al. in two phases. In the phase regulation every link is active with probability p when its positive regulator is active or its negative regulator is inactive, and inactive otherwise. In the phase percolation a node is active when it belongs to the giant component of the links the regulation of the same step left active. All nodes and links start active.

With the fraction R of nodes in the giant component, the links are active with probability p_L = p ((1 - negative) R + negative (1 - R)), and R follows the map R' = S(c p_L), where S(m) solves S = 1 - exp(-m S) for the mean degree c. With negative regulators alone the map decreases, so above the percolation point p = 1 / c its fixed point is unstable and R alternates between a large and a small giant component, a cycle of period two. Below it the giant component vanishes. The system has the activities nodes.active and links.active and the signs links.sign.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_nodes int

The number of nodes.

1000 mean_degree float

The mean degree of the Erdős-Rényi graph.

4.0 p float

The probability that a link the regulation allows is active.

0.5 negative float

The probability that the regulator of a link is negative.

1.0 random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the graph, the regulators, and their signs.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.networks import TriadicPercolationSystem
>>> system = TriadicPercolationSystem(200, p=0.8).prepare().system_
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=3, random_state=0)
>>> giant = trajectory.get_values('nodes.active').mean(axis=1)
>>> bool(giant[1] < 0.5 < giant[2])
True

Bases: BaseSystem

Independent M/M/1 queues.

The queues are birth-death processes with constant arrival and service rates.

Customers arrive as a Poisson process of rate lambda and are served one at a time in exponential times of rate mu. For the load rho = lambda / mu < 1 the length of an unbounded queue reaches the stationary geometric distribution (1 - rho) rho^n, of mean rho / (1 - rho) and variance rho / (1 - rho)^2, and for rho > 1 it grows without bound. The system has the lengths queues.n.

@staticmethod
def multiplies(agent: CascadingBallView, system: SystemView) -> int:
    """Return the number of balls a ball becomes.

    The number is `floor(mu)`, and one more with the probability of the rest.

    Args:
        agent:
            The ball.

        system:
            The system.

    Returns:
        count:
            The number of new balls, of mean `mu`.
    """
    whole = math.floor(agent.mu)
    return whole + int(system.rng.random() < agent.mu - whole)

docs.title: CascadingSampleSpaceReducingSystem(n_cascades=100, *, n_states=100, mu=1.5, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Cascading sample-space-reducing processes.

Their visits follow the power law i^(-mu) for any mu.

Every cascade starts with one ball at the top state n_states. At every step each ball above state 1 jumps to a state drawn uniformly below its own and becomes mu balls there, floor(mu) and one more with the probability of the rest, and a ball at state 1 leaves the cascade. Every ball stays one step, so the states of the balls of all frames are the visits, distributed as i^(-mu) (Thurner et al. 2018, section 3.3.5.4). For mu < 1 balls are lost on the way, 1 - mu being the probability of a removal. With a conservation law that makes the states of the new balls sum to the state of their parent, the exponent is 2 whatever mu, the case of FragmentationSystem. The system has the group balls of state level.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_cascades int

The number of independent cascades, run together.

100 n_states int

The number of states.

100 mu float

The multiplication factor, the mean number of balls a ball becomes at every jump.

1.5 label str

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Stochastic on-off intermittency, dx/dt = (epsilon + xi) x - x^3.

The noise xi is Stratonovich white noise.

The noise has the correlation <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 D delta(t - t'). The variable y = ln x diffuses freely while x is small and is pushed back by -exp(2 y) once x grows, so near the bifurcation epsilon = 0 the variable rests close to 0 for long laminar phases, whose durations are distributed as tau^(-3/2), between bursts where x is of order 1. For epsilon > 0 the power law is cut off beyond durations of order D / epsilon^2. The system has the values variables.x.

docs.title: RandomBranchMapSystem(n_orbits=200, *, p1=0.5, mu=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Orbits of a random map of [0, 1].

The map has the two branches (1 + x) / 2 and mu x².

At every step each orbit applies (1 + x) / 2 with probability p1 and mu x² otherwise (Dilão 2023, Exercise 5.10). The first branch pulls towards 1 and the second towards 0, so the orbits settle on a stationary distribution whose shape changes with p1 and mu. For mu = 0 the second branch resets the orbit to 0, and the stationary mean is p1 / (2 - p1). For mu = 1 both branches fix x = 1, which attracts the orbits once p1 > 1/2, since there the first branch halves the distance to 1 and the second doubles it.

The system has the group orbits of state x.

docs.title: ActiveGelsSystem(shape=None, *, order='nematic', spacing=None, a=None, c=None, K=1.0, xi=None, gamma=1.0, eta=1.0, zeta=None, film=False, perturbation=None, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

An active gel.

A nematic tensor or a polarisation is transported in the Stokes flow of its own stresses.

On a periodic lattice with spectral operators, the order parameter follows its co-rotational derivative in the flow, Section III of Marchetti et al. The flow solves the overdamped Stokes equation of the elastic stress and the active stress, -zeta Q for the nematic and -zeta p p for the polar gel, and the elastic energy relaxes the order. An extensile nematic, zeta > 0, is unstable to bend, and a contractile polar gel, zeta < 0, is unstable to splay above a threshold.

The defaults of the nematic are the chaotic state of Giomi et al. 2012, cited by Marchetti et al., whose free energy has the same form: a box of side 10, the critical density 3 pi / 2, the density twice that, which give a and c, the activity 3 times the squared density, and the flow alignment 0.1, in units of the elastic constant, the rotational viscosity, and the viscosity. The density stays uniform here. At these defaults pairs of +1/2 and -1/2 defects move in a chaotic flow, active turbulence.

The nematic starts from the tensor along the first axis at the order sqrt(-2 a / c), and the polar gel from the polarisation along the first axis at the length sqrt(-a / c), both with noise. With film=True the polarisation along the second axis is odd about the sites 0 and shape[1] / 2 of the second axis, and the other one even, which holds the polarisation along the first axis at these two walls, with stress-free flow there. The system has the field gel.Q or gel.p.

The distance between neighbouring sites, or None for a nematic box of side 10 along the first axis and 1 for the polar gel.

None a float | None

The coefficient of the quadratic energy, negative in the ordered phase, or None for -3 pi / 4 for the nematic and -1 for the polar gel.

None c float | None

The coefficient of the quartic energy, or None for 3 pi for the nematic and 1 for the polar gel.

None K float

The elastic constant.

1.0 xi float | None

The flow-alignment parameter, or None for 0.1 for the nematic and 0 for the polar gel.

None gamma float

The rotational viscosity.

1.0 eta float

The viscosity of the flow.

1.0 zeta float | None

The activity, or None for 3 (3 pi)^2 for the nematic and -0.5 for the polar gel.

None film bool

Whether the polar gel lies between walls of fixed polarisation.

False perturbation float | None

The standard deviation of the initial noise of the order parameter, or None for 0.1 for the nematic and 0.01 for the polar gel.

Bases: BaseSystem

The active and passive agents of Charbonneau (2017) in a periodic box.

The system is that of section 10.4.

All agents repel each other within 2 r_0 with the force epsilon (1 - r / (2 r_0))^exponent, and all feel the force mu (v_t - |v|) v / |v|, with the target speed v_t = v0 for an active agent and 0 for a passive one. An active agent also feels the flocking force alpha V / |V|, with V the sum of the velocities of the agents of both kinds within the flocking radius, itself excluded, and a random force. Agents start at uniform random positions with velocity components uniform up to initial_speed. The defaults are those of figure 10.7 at the compactness C = pi N r_0^2 / size^2 = 0.672. The values exponent=2.5, epsilon=100, mu=0.05, radius=1, flocking_radius=4, and v0=1 are those of Silverberg et al. (2013). The system has the group agents that holds the active agents first, the positions agents.x, the velocities agents.x_d1, the marks agents.active, and the observables polarization, active_distance, and passive_distance.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

An active polymer, a Rouse chain of active Brownian beads.

Each bead swims along its own orientation.

Bead i follows r_i' = v0 n_i + k (r_{i+1} + r_{i-1} - 2 r_i) + sqrt(2 D_t) xi_i, with its orientation n_i = (cos theta_i, sin theta_i) diffusing with D_r, and the end beads bonded to one neighbour. The bonds cancel in the motion of the centre of mass, whose mean squared displacement is (4 D_t t + 2 v0² (D_r t - 1 + exp(-D_r t)) / D_r²) / N, that of an active Brownian particle divided by N. The activity swells the chain: a passive chain has the mean squared end-to-end distance 2 D_t (N - 1) / k in the plane, and self-propulsion of persistence time 1 / D_r adds to the bond fluctuations and stretches it further. The beads start on a straight line with unit spacing and random orientations. The system has the coordinates chain.x and chain.y and the orientations chain.theta of the beads.

A conserved scalar field phi phase separates with active currents.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Active System B+, the conserved field theory of the density of active particles.

The density phi follows phi_t = laplacian(mu) - div(zeta laplacian(phi) grad(phi)) + div(sqrt(2 D) eta), with the chemical potential mu = -phi + phi^3 - kappa laplacian(phi) + lam |grad(phi)|^2 and a conserved white noise eta, Equation 4 of Fodor, Jack, and Cates with unit mobility. The terms lam and zeta are the lowest-order active currents that no free energy gives. With zeta = 0 it is Active System B, where lam shifts the coexisting densities and the phases still coarsen. With lam = 1, zeta = 4, and a majority of the dense phase, the Ostwald ripening of the dilute bubbles reverses, so they stop growing at a finite size, a microphase separation. The noise conserves the total of phi, so its mean stays fixed. The lattice has unit spacing, and an explicit step must stay below about 1/32. The system has the field fluid.phi.

Bases: BaseSystem

A one-dimensional active viscoelastic gel.

Contractile cells concentrate by dragging the gel.

On a periodic line, the density c of the cells and the displacement u of a Kelvin-Voigt gel follow

c_t + (v c)_x = D c_xx,    u_t = v,    (gamma - eta d_xx) v = d_x (E u_x + Ta(c)),

with the active stress Ta(c) = T0 c / (c + c_sat). The force balance holds at every step, as the modified Helmholtz inversion of the stress gradient with the screening sqrt(gamma / eta). Without stiffness the uniform state loses stability at long wavelengths above the contractile threshold c Ta'(c) > gamma D, and the density concentrates into peaks. The source leaves the active stress open, and the saturating one keeps the peaks finite. The catalog entry streams the velocity as the observable v. The system has the density gel.c and the displacement gel.u.

Bases: BaseSystem

Active Brownian particles in a periodic box whose headings align.

A particle aligns with its neighbours within d0.

The heading of particle i follows dtheta_i = gamma sum_{|x_j - x_i| < d0} sin(theta_j - theta_i) dt + sqrt(2 D_r) dW, and the particle swims at the constant speed along it. In the mean-field approximation of the Fokker-Planck equation, the disordered state is unstable above the density rho_c = 2 D_r / (gamma pi d0^2), so at a fixed density rho the particles move together when gamma exceeds 2 D_r / (pi d0^2 rho). The polarization |<exp(i theta)>| is near 0 in the disordered state and near 1 in the ordered one. The system has the positions swimmers.x, the headings swimmers.theta, and the observables mean_heading and polarization.

Self-propelled particles that flock through aligning binary collisions.

This is the Bertin-Droz-Grégoire system.

def fly(self, system: SystemView) -> None:
    """Move the particles for one unit of time.

    Every substep has self-diffusion and collisions.

    Args:
        system:
            The system.
    """
    agents = system.get_agents(self.target, FlockerView)
    size = np.asarray(system.dimensions, dtype=float)
    positions = np.array([agent.location for agent in agents], dtype=float)
    headings = np.array([agent.theta for agent in agents], dtype=float)
    speed, lam, sigma, d0 = (system.get_parameter(name) for name in ('speed', 'lam', 'sigma', 'd0'))
    substeps = max(1, round(system.get_parameter('substeps')))
    tau, rng = 1.0 / substeps, system.rng
    touching = KDTree(positions, boxsize=size).query_pairs(d0)
    for _ in range(substeps):
        positions = np.mod(positions + speed * tau * np.column_stack([np.cos(headings), np.sin(headings)]), size)
        kicked = rng.random(len(headings)) < -math.expm1(-lam * tau)
        headings[kicked] += rng.normal(0.0, sigma, int(kicked.sum()))
        now = KDTree(positions, boxsize=size).query_pairs(d0)
        BinaryCollisionsInteraction._collide(headings, sorted(now - touching), sigma, rng)
        touching = now
    for agent, position, heading in zip(agents, positions, np.mod(headings, 2 * math.pi), strict=True):
        agent.move_to(position)
        agent.theta = float(heading)

docs.title: DeformableActiveParticlesSystem(n_particles=20, *, gamma=1.0, a=1.0, b=1.0, kappa=0.5, noise=0.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Deformable self-propelled particles of Ohta and Ohkuma.

The particles move straight or along circles.

Every particle follows x' = v, v' = gamma v - |v|² v - a S v, and S' = -kappa S + b (v v - |v|² I / 2), with the traceless symmetric deformation tensor S. A fast relaxing shape, large kappa, gives straight motion at the speed sqrt(gamma / (1 + a b / (2 kappa))). For a b (gamma - kappa / 2) > kappa² a circular motion exists, at the speed sqrt(gamma - kappa / 2) with the angular velocity sqrt(a b (gamma - kappa / 2) - kappa²) / 2, its elongation turning with its velocity. For the defaults it exists below kappa ≈ 0.78, and particles started from small velocities reach it for kappa <= 0.5, while closer to the threshold straight motion stays stable too. The particles do not interact, and they start at random positions, small random velocities, and no deformation. The system has the positions cells.x, the velocities cells.v, and the deformations cells.S.

Bases: Element

Brownian particle pumped by an internal energy depot.

The particle follows the system of Schweitzer, Ebeling, and Tilch.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A dry active nematic.

A conserved density is coupled to a symmetric traceless alignment tensor.

On a periodic lattice the density and the tensor follow Section II.2 of Marchetti et al.,

rho_t = -div(J),    J = -D grad(rho) - current div(Q),
Q_t = H / gamma + beta (partial_i partial_j rho - delta_ij laplacian(rho) / 2),

with the molecular field H of the Landau-de Gennes energy, whose coefficient a (1 - rho / rho_c) turns negative above the critical density rho_c. The current along div(Q) is the active current, which no free energy gives. The system has the fields nematic.rho and nematic.Q.

The particles order along a common axis but move both ways along it.

At every step particle i takes the direction of sum_j sign(cos(theta_j - theta_i)) exp(i theta_j) over the particles within the unit distance, itself included, so it aligns with the axis of every neighbour on the side nearer its own heading, plus a uniform angle in [-eta pi, eta pi], and moves v0 along it. At low noise the particles share an axis, with as many moving one way as the other: the nematic order parameter |<exp(2 i theta)>| grows towards 1 while the polar order parameter stays small. The system has the positions flock.x, the headings flock.theta, and the observables polarization and nematic_order.

The distance a particle moves in one step.

The seed of the uniform initial positions and headings.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Grégoire-Chaté system.

Aligning particles also attract and repel, forming cohesive flocks.

At every step particle i takes the direction of alpha sum_j exp(i theta_j) + beta sum_j f(r_ij) e_ij + eta n_i xi, over the n_i particles within the unit distance, where e_ij points from i to j, xi is a random unit vector, and the force f is a strong repulsion below r_c = 0.2, zero at the preferred distance r_e = 0.5, and attractive up to r_a = 0.8. The particle then moves v0 along the new heading. At low noise and moderate cohesion the particles gather into cohesive, aligned flocks, and the polar order parameter grows towards 1. A strong cohesion locks them in place, and the order is lost. The system has the positions flock.x, the headings flock.theta, and the observables polarization and nematic_order.

docs.title: HeadingAlignmentInteraction(label, *, target, nematic=False, neighborhood=None, latency=0, memory=5)
docs.text:
Bases: CouplingInteraction

Vicsek alignment.

Every particle turns to the circular mean heading of its neighbours plus noise.

Every step the heading theta of every particle becomes the circular mean of the headings within the unit distance, itself included, plus a uniform angle in [-eta pi, eta pi] with the parameter eta of the particle. With nematic, every heading is flipped to the side nearer the particle's own heading first, as for particles with an axis rather than a direction. It is the map form of coupling with the circular mean over a radius. Another neighbourhood, such as the k nearest particles or a vision cone, replaces the unit disk.

With a positive latency h, every particle reads the headings of its neighbours h steps ago. With a negative latency it reads their headings predicted |h| steps ahead, by a least-squares line through their last memory headings, unwrapped by taking every change between two steps as the smallest angle. A latent alignment needs particles that keep enough past headings, such as DelayedVicsekParticleElement.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the group of particles.

required nematic bool

Whether every heading is flipped to the side nearer the particle's own heading.

False neighborhood BaseNeighborhood | None

The neighbourhood of every particle, itself included, or None for the unit disk.

None latency int

The number of steps by which the headings of the neighbours are read late, or predicted ahead when negative.

0 memory int

The number of past headings a prediction fits, at least 2.

5

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.active_matter import HeadingAlignmentInteraction
>>> HeadingAlignmentInteraction('alignment', target='flock', nematic=True).reduce
'circular-mean'

docs.title: InertialActiveBrownianParticlesSystem(n_particles=200, *, speed=3.0, mass=0.5, moment=0.1, D_t=0.1, D_r=1.0, size=50.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Active Brownian particles with inertia.

The particles lag behind their orientation as they speed up and turn.

With unit friction, every particle follows m x'' = -x' + v0 n + sqrt(2 D_t) xi and J theta'' = -theta' + sqrt(2 D_r) xi_r, the inertial active Brownian particles of macroscopic swimmers, flyers, and vibrated grains. The velocity relaxes over the time m, so it trails the orientation, and the mean projection of the velocity on the orientation falls below v0. With rotational inertia alone, the orientation correlation is exp(-D_r (t - J (1 - exp(-t / J)))), which gives the steady projection v0 / m ∫ exp(-t / m) exp(-D_r (t - J (1 - exp(-t / J)))) dt, and v0 / (1 + m D_r) without rotational inertia. The particles start at rest at uniform positions and orientations. The system has the positions swimmers.x, the velocities swimmers.x_d1, the orientations swimmers.theta, and the angular velocities swimmers.theta_d1.

The moment of inertia J, in units of the rotational friction.

The translational diffusion coefficient.

The rotational diffusion coefficient.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Keller-Segel system of diffusing cells that climb a chemical gradient.

The cells secrete the chemical.

The cell density follows rho_t = D laplacian(rho) - chi div(rho grad(c)) and the chemical c_t = Dc laplacian(c) + rho - k c, on a periodic square. The total number of cells is conserved. The uniform state of density rho_0 is unstable when the chemotactic drive chi rho_0 exceeds D (k + Dc q^2) for the longest wave q = 2 pi / length. The cells then aggregate into dense spots, which in two dimensions collapse in finite time, so a run above the threshold ends before the density blows up. The system has the cell density colony.rho and the chemical colony.c.

docs.title: LandauDeGennesEnergyInteraction(label, *, target, state='Q', a=-1.0, c=2.0, K=1.0, gamma=1.0, quadratic=None)
docs.text:
Bases: GradientInteraction

Landau-de Gennes free energy gradient flow of a symmetric traceless tensor Q.

The free energy is F = integral a tr(Q^2) / 2 + c tr(Q^2)^2 / 4 + K |grad Q|^2 / 2. Its negative functional derivative among symmetric traceless tensors is the molecular field H = -a Q - c tr(Q^2) Q + K laplacian(Q), and the tensor relaxes as Q_t = H / gamma. A uniform tensor S (n n - I / 2) in two dimensions with a < 0 relaxes to the scalar order S = sqrt(-2 a / c).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the field.

required state str

The name of the state of the field that holds the tensor.

'Q' a Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()]

The coefficient of tr(Q^2) / 2, negative in the ordered phase.

-1.0 c Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=open(0, oo))]

The coefficient of tr(Q^2)^2 / 4.

2.0 K Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=closed_open(0, oo))]

The elastic constant.

1.0 gamma Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=open(0, oo))]

The rotational viscosity, which divides the molecular field.

1.0 quadratic Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object] | None

A function of the namespace that returns the coefficient of tr(Q^2) / 2 instead of a, such as an expression of a density, or None for a.

Motile cell of a tissue.

The cell has its position, the heading of its motility, and its force and motility parameters.

The position follows x' = v0 n + mu F, where n is the unit vector of the heading and F the sum of the pair forces. A pair force is F_rep (d - R_eq) / R_eq towards the neighbour below the distance R_eq, and F_adh (d - R_eq) / (R_0 - R_eq) towards it up to the distance R_0, the cell diameter.

A symmetric traceless tensor Q is carried by an overdamped Stokes flow.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Two species of Vicsek movers in a periodic box with nonreciprocal alignment.

The alignment of each species with the other differs between the two.

Half the movers are species A and half species B, each aligning with its own species. With J_ab = J_ba the two species flock together. With J_ab = -J_ba, A aligns with B while B antialigns with A, so neither settles: the mean headings of the species lock at a quarter turn from each other and rotate together, the chiral phase of Fruchart et al. (2021), which breaks the time-reversal symmetry that reciprocal alignment keeps. The system has the mean headings heading_a and heading_b of the two species.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle.

Its propulsion velocity u is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

The laws are dx = u dt + sqrt(2 D_t) dW and tau du = -u dt + sqrt(2 D) dW, so the propulsion keeps its direction for the persistence time tau and the particle diffuses with D + D_t at long times.

docs.text:
Bases: StokesianMobilityInteraction

Slip of spherical squirmers.

The B1 and B2 modes make them swim and stir each other through the mobility.

A squirmer of radius a with the tangential surface slip B1 sin(theta) + B2 sin(theta) cos(theta) about its orientation p (Lighthill 1952, Blake 1971) swims at 2 B1 / 3 along p. Far from it, the slip stirs the fluid as the stresslet 4 pi eta a^2 B2 (p p - I / 3) and the potential dipole B1 a^3 p / 3 (Ishikawa, Simmonds, and Pedley 2006). So beta = B2 / B1 < 0 makes a pusher, which pushes fluid out along its axis, and beta > 0 a puller, which draws it in. The flows of the other squirmers move every squirmer and turn it by half their vorticity, through StokesianMobilityInteraction. A Weeks-Chandler-Andersen repulsion of strength epsilon keeps the spheres apart, within 2^(1/6) diameters of the current radius.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The cells of Szabó et al. (2006) in a periodic box.

The cells move together above a critical density.

A cell moves at x' = v0 n + mu F, where F sums the pair forces of the neighbours within R_0, the diameter of a cell, and its heading turns towards its velocity, theta' = arcsin((n x v / |v|) . e_z) / tau + xi. No cell reads the headings of the others, and adhesion alone orders them. With eta = 0.6 the transition lies at the number density rho_c = 0.18 / R_0^2. The system has the positions cells.x, the headings cells.theta, and the observables mean_heading and polarization.

def run_and_tumble(self, agent: TumblerView, system: SystemView) -> None:
    """Run one step along the direction, then tumble at random.

    Args:
        agent:
            The agent.

        system:
            The system.
    """
    position = np.asarray(agent.location, dtype=float)
    heading = np.array([math.cos(agent.theta), math.sin(agent.theta)])
    agent.move_to(np.mod(position + agent.speed * heading, agent.width))
    if system.rng.random() < -math.expm1(-agent.tumble_rate):
        agent.theta = float(system.rng.uniform(0.0, 2 * math.pi))

docs.title: VicsekSystem(n_particles=400, *, size=10.0, v0=0.5, eta=0.1, seed=0, neighbors=None, vision=None, delay=0, memory=5, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Vicsek system.

Particles move at a constant speed along the mean heading of their neighbours.

At every step particle i takes the direction of the sum of the headings of the particles within the unit distance, itself included, plus a uniform angle in [-eta pi, eta pi], and moves v0 along it in a periodic box. At low noise and high density the particles align into a flock, and the polar order parameter |<exp(i theta)>| grows from about 1 / sqrt(N) to near 1. Raising the noise or lowering the density destroys the order.

Two variants of Argun et al. (2021, Section 8.3) make the interaction non-metric or non-reciprocal. With neighbors, a particle aligns with its neighbors nearest particles and itself at any distance, a topological interaction that need not be reciprocal, and the clusters grow with neighbors. With vision, a particle sees only the particles within the unit distance whose direction from it makes an angle of at most vision with its heading, a vision cone that breaks reciprocity. The two variants do not combine, since the nearest neighbourhood of the core has no cone.

With a positive delay h, the sensory delay of Section 8.2, a particle aligns with the headings its neighbours had h steps ago, theta_j(n + 1) = <theta_k(n - h)> + noise. Argun et al. report that a short delay stabilizes the clusters, and a long delay hinders them. A negative delay is a prediction: the headings of the neighbours |h| steps ahead are extrapolated by a least-squares line through their last memory headings, and it hinders clustering. Every particle then keeps its last 25 headings, so the delay lies in [-25, 25], and before the start they equal the initial heading. The system has the positions flock.x, the headings flock.theta, and the observables polarization and nematic_order.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Keplerian dumbbell.

Two masses on a rigid massless arm orbit a primary under gravity.

The centre of mass of the dumbbell at the cylindrical coordinates (u, theta, v) about the primary and the arm at the spherical angles (phi, psi) move under the dimensionless Lagrangian L = (u'² + u² theta'² + v'²) / 2 + I (psi'² + sin² psi phi'²) / 2 + (1 - delta) / rho12 + delta / rho13, with the moment of inertia I = delta (1 - delta) epsilon² / mu of the arm. The distances of the two masses from the primary are rho12² = u² + v² + delta² epsilon² + 2 delta epsilon P and rho13² = u² + v² + (1 - delta)² epsilon² - 2 (1 - delta) epsilon P, with P = u sin psi cos(theta - phi) + v cos psi. Its Euler-Lagrange equations are the equations of motion of Dilão and Murteira. The gravity gradient across the arm couples the spin to the orbit, the simplest spin-orbit coupling of a rigid body. For epsilon = 0 the orbit is a Kepler orbit, of period 2π at u = 1. The energy and the angular momentum about the normal to the orbital plane are conserved. By default the arm spins three times faster than it orbits, in the orbital plane, and its spin and orbit exchange angular momentum. The system has the coordinates dumbbell.u, dumbbell.theta, dumbbell.v, dumbbell.phi, and dumbbell.psi of order 2, and the observables dumbbell.energy and dumbbell.angular_momentum.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A particle without angular momentum that falls into a spinning mass.

The mass drags the particle around it.

The particle follows a timelike geodesic of the Kerr spacetime KerrSpace in the equatorial plane, in units with G = c = 1, with its proper time as the time of the system. It starts at rest in the radius at r₀, with zero angular momentum L = g_tφ dt/dτ + g_φφ dφ/dτ = 0. A particle without angular momentum around a static mass falls straight in, but the spin drags the frames around it: the particle turns with the angular velocity dφ/dt = -g_tφ / g_φφ = 2 M a / (r³ + a² r + 2 M a²) of the frames at its radius, faster as it falls. The system has the position particle.x = (t, r, theta, phi) and the four-velocity particle.x_d1.

docs.title: KerrSpace(mass=1.0, spin=0.5, *, curvature=False, label='space')
docs.text:
Bases: SpacetimeSpace

Spacetime outside a spinning mass M, the Kerr metric.

The mass has the angular momentum M a, and the metric is in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates.

With Σ = r² + a² cos²θ and Δ = r² - 2 M r + a², the line element in (t, r, theta, phi) is ds² = -(1 - 2Mr/Σ) dt² - (4 M a r sin²θ / Σ) dt dφ + Σ/Δ dr² + Σ dθ² + (r² + a² + 2 M a² r sin²θ / Σ) sin²θ dφ², in units with G = c = 1. The term in dt dφ drags the frames of free particles around the spin axis. The mass and the spin enter the metric as exact rationals, which keeps the symbolic derivation fast.

docs.title: RelativisticOrbitSystem(u=1.5, du=0.0, *, alpha=1.0, epsilon=0.05, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

Einstein's orbit equation u'' + u = alpha + epsilon u² of a planet.

The perihelion of the planet precesses.

The inverse radius u = 1 / r of the planet is a function of its polar angle, which the simulation time stands for, so the orbit in the plane is (cos t / u, sin t / u). For epsilon = 0 the orbit is a closed Newtonian ellipse of eccentricity |u(0) / alpha - 1| for u'(0) = 0. The term epsilon u² is the first relativistic correction, and with it the orbit is a rosette whose perihelion advances by about 2π epsilon alpha every revolution. The equation has two fixed points, the roots (1 ∓ sqrt(1 - 4 alpha epsilon)) / (2 epsilon) of epsilon u² - u + alpha. The smaller one, close to alpha, is a centre, the stable circular orbit, and the larger one is a saddle, the unstable circular orbit close to the black hole, beyond which a planet falls in. The system has the inverse radius planet.u of order 2 along the angle and its derivative planet.u_d1.

Parameters:

The initial inverse radius.

1.5 du float

The initial derivative of the inverse radius along the angle.

The Newtonian inverse semi-latus rectum.

1.0 epsilon float

The strength of the relativistic correction.

Examples:

docs.title: RestrictedThreeBodySystem(x=0.5, y=0.0, vx=0.0, vy=1.15, *, mu=0.01215, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A light body moving in the plane of two primaries on circular orbits.

The body moves in the frame that rotates with the primaries.

The primaries of masses 1 - μ and μ sit at (-μ, 0) and (1 - μ, 0), and the light body moves under the Hamiltonian H = (px² + py²) / 2 + y px - x py - (1 - μ) / r1 - μ / r2 of the rotating frame, with the momenta px = x' - y and py = y' + x. Its terms y px - x py couple the coordinates and the momenta, so the Hamiltonian is not separable. It equals minus half the Jacobi constant x² + y² + 2 (1 - μ) / r1 + 2 μ / r2 - x'² - y'², which is conserved. The default μ is that of the Earth and the Moon.

The default start has the Jacobi constant 2.835, below that of the neck towards the Moon, and its orbit is chaotic: it passes near the Moon after 3.5 time units and wanders between the two primaries, with a Lyapunov exponent near 0.2. Starts of a larger constant are confined around the Earth, such as vy = 0.8 with the constant 3.52, which traces a regular precessing rosette. The system has the coordinates body.x and body.y and the momenta body.px and body.py.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A massive particle on a bound orbit around a static mass.

Its perihelion advances every turn.

The particle follows a timelike geodesic of the Schwarzschild spacetime SchwarzschildSpace, in units with G = c = 1 and with its proper time as the time of the system. It starts at the periapsis r₁ = a (1 - e) of an orbit whose apoapsis is r₂ = a (1 + e), with the energy E and the angular momentum L for which both are turning points of E² = (1 - 2M/r) (1 + L²/r²) + (dr/dτ)². Unlike a Kepler ellipse, the orbit does not close: the periapsis advances by 6 π M / (a (1 - e²)) per turn when the orbit is far from the horizon, or 6 π G M / (c² a (1 - e²)) in other units, which accounts for the anomalous 43 arcseconds per century of Mercury. The system has the position particle.x = (t, r, theta, phi) and the four-velocity particle.x_d1.

Parameters:

The semi-major axis a of the orbit.

100.0 eccentricity float

The eccentricity e of the orbit, in [0, 1).

0.5 mass float

The mass M of the central body.

1.0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A charged particle moving in the magnetic dipole field of a planet.

This is the Störmer problem.

The charge follows the Euler-Lagrange equations of |x'|² / 2 + alpha (x y' - y x') / r³, the kinetic energy and the coupling of the velocity to the vector potential of the dipole, whose Lorentz force gives x'' = 3 alpha z (y' z - z' y) / r⁵ - alpha y' / r³, y'' = -3 alpha z (x' z - z' x) / r⁵ + alpha x' / r³, and z'' = 3 alpha z (x' y - y' x) / r⁵, with alpha = q M / m for a dipole of moment M along the z axis. The magnetic force does no work, so the speed is conserved, and the symmetry about the axis conserves x y' - y x' + alpha (x² + y²) / r³. Bounded orbits near the planet trace the radiation belts, and many of them are chaotic. The system has the coordinates charge.x, charge.y, and charge.z, all of order 2.

1.0 y float

The initial first velocity.

0.0 vy float

The initial second velocity.

0.1 vz float

The initial third velocity.

0.1 alpha float

The product of the charge and the dipole moment, divided by the mass.

1.0 label str

>>> StormerProblemSystem(alpha=2.0).prepare().system_.elements[0].alpha

docs.title: BudykoSellersSystem(n_bands=30, T=15.0, *, Q=334.4, A=203.3, B=2.09, D=0.649, C=10.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Budyko-Sellers energy balance of one hemisphere.

The balance is resolved in the sine of latitude.

The temperature of a band at x = sin(latitude) follows C dT/dt = Q s(x) (1 - a(x, T)) - (A + B T) + D d/dx((1 - x^2) dT/dx), with the annual insolation s(x) = 1 - 0.482 P2(x), where P2(x) = (3x^2 - 1) / 2. The albedo is 0.319 + 0.202 P2(x) without ice and rises to 0.62 where the temperature falls below -10 °C. Bands are centred at x = (i + 1/2) / n_bands, with no heat flux across the equator or the pole. Present insolation keeps both a climate with polar ice caps and a snowball Earth. The system has the temperatures bands.T from the equator to the pole.

203.3 B float

Bases: DynamicalSystem

Rothman's excitable carbon cycle.

A large enough perturbation of the ocean sets off an excursion.

The carbonate ion concentration c and the dissolved inorganic carbon w, in μmol kg⁻¹, follow dc/dt = f(c) (mu (1 - b s(c, c_p) - theta (1 - s(c, c_x)) - nu) + w - w0) and dw/dt = mu (1 - b s(c, c_p) + theta (1 - s(c, c_x)) + nu) - w + w0, with the sigmoids s(c, c*) = c^gamma / (c^gamma + c*^gamma) of burial and respiration and the buffer f(c) = f0 c^beta / (c^beta + c_f^beta). The steady state near c = 83.6 and w = 2197 is stable, and from a dissolved carbon far enough below it the ocean returns only after a large excursion of c. The system has the concentrations ocean.c and ocean.w.

docs.title: EnergyReturnSystem(reserve=1000.0, capacity=0.1, *, initial_eroi=20.0, reinvestment=0.1, birth_rate=0.03, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The extraction of a finite energy reserve.

Its energy return on investment declines as it depletes.

The extraction capacity draws the gross energy from the reserve at a rate that falls with the remaining fraction, since the easy sources go first. Part of the gross energy pays for the extraction work, the gross energy divided by the energy return on investment (EROI), which falls from initial_eroi to one with the cube of the remaining fraction as the reserve empties. The rest is the net energy that society receives. Society reinvests a share of the net energy in extraction capacity, which depreciates, and the population grows exponentially with no feedback from the energy it receives. Energy is conserved, every unit leaving the reserve is either cost or net energy, so the gross energy rises exponentially and peaks, the net energy peaks before it, and the net energy per person peaks earlier still. The structure follows Mobus (2022, Section 9.6) and its figures of peak net energy, with illustrative parameters in energy units, persons, and years. The system has the reserve energy.reserve, the capacity energy.capacity, the population energy.population, and the flows energy.energy_cost, energy.net_energy, energy.births, and energy.deaths per year, over years. The observables of the system are energy.eroi, energy.gross_energy, energy.extraction_cost, and energy.net_per_capita.

Parameters:

The initial energy reserve, also its full size.

1000.0 capacity float

The initial extraction capacity, the gross energy per year from a full reserve.

0.1 initial_eroi float

The energy return on investment of a full reserve.

20.0 reinvestment float

The share of the net energy reinvested in extraction capacity.

0.1 birth_rate float

The relative birth rate of the population per year.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

Vegetation cover of a tropical forest.

Its growth rate falls on both sides of an optimal temperature.

The cover v runs from 0 for bare soil to 1 for full forest. Bare soil is warmer than forest by a, so the local temperature is T = Tv + a (1 - v), and the growth rate g = g0 (1 - ((T - Topt) / beta)²) peaks at Topt. A rate interaction gives the logistic growth g v (1 - v) and the disturbance gamma v, so the element holds the state and the parameters it reads.

docs.title: ForestDiebackSystem(v=0.8, *, Tv=30.0, g0=2.0, beta=10.0, Topt=28.0, a=5.0, gamma=0.2, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The forest dieback model of the Amazon.

The cover tips to bare soil when the ambient temperature rises.

The cover follows v' = g v (1 - v) - gamma v, with the growth rate g = g0 (1 - ((T - Topt) / beta)²) at the local temperature T = Tv + a (1 - v). Losing forest warms the soil, which lowers the growth and loses more forest, a positive feedback. Bare soil v = 0 is always a fixed point, and the forest survives at the root of (1 - v) g(v) = gamma. For the defaults the forest and bare soil are both stable for ambient temperatures between about 32.5 and 34.7 degrees, the bistable range of a hysteresis loop, and the forest dies beyond it. The system has the vegetation cover forest.v.

Bases: DynamicalSystem

Gissinger's geodynamo, whose dipole field reverses at irregular times.

The quadrupolar field Q, the dipolar field D, and the velocity V follow dQ/dt = mu Q - V D, dD/dt = -nu D + V Q, and dV/dt = Gamma - V + Q D. docs.title: LeadingFollowingCascadeSystem(follower='fold', *, coupling=0.4, rate=0.004, sigma=0.02, phi0=-1.0, phi1=1.0, c=0.0, mu=0.0, omega=1.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A cascade of two tipping elements.

A leading fold is driven by a ramp and a follower is forced by the leader.

The leading element follows dx = (-x³ + x + phi(t)) dt + sigma dW, whose control rises as phi = phi0 + rate t until phi1, and it tips from its lower to its upper branch when phi passes 2 / (3 √3). The following element is forced linearly by the state of the leader, Eq. 10 of Fang et al. after Dekker et al. A fold follower obeys dy = (-y³ + y + c + coupling x) dt + sigma dW, and it tips too, a domino cascade, when the tipped leader moves its control c + coupling x past 2 / (3 √3). A Hopf follower obeys dw = ((mu + coupling x + i omega) w - |w|² w) dt + sigma dW, and the tipped leader can carry it through its Hopf bifurcation onto an oscillation of radius sqrt(mu + coupling x). The follower can show rising variance and autocorrelation before the leader tips even when it stays far from its own tipping point. The system has the leader leader.x and the follower follower.y, and also follower.z for the Hopf follower.
