docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The pollution model of Bala, Arshad, and Noh.

A population degrades its environment.

The population generates pollution at pollution_normal per person per year, and the environment absorbs the pollution over a time that lengthens from 0.6 to 20 years as the pollution ratio, pollution over its standard, rises from 0 to 60. This makes the absorption saturate, so a growing population can drive the pollution up steeply. Pollution lowers births, food, and the quality of life, and raises deaths, through table multipliers, while food per capita over the subsistence food raises births and lowers deaths. The cropping intensity rises from 1.75 to 2.5 crops per year over 50 years. The model follows Section 4.11.9 of Bala et al. (2017), with its tables and parameters, and time in years. The system has the stocks region.population and region.pollution, and the observables region.food_per_capita and region.quality_of_life.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A stochastic fold whose control is ramped through a tipping point.

The tipping point is that of its lower branch.

The state follows dx = (a x^3 + b x + phi(t)) dt + sigma dW with phi = phi0 + rate t until it reaches phi1, Eq. 4 of Fang et al. with phi = -1 + 0.004 t. It starts on the lower branch, which vanishes at the static fold phi_c = sqrt(-4 b^3 / (27 a)), 2 / (3 sqrt(3)) for a = -1 and b = 1. Near the fold, recovery slows down, so the variance and the lag-1 autocorrelation of the state rise. A ramp faster than the relaxation carries the control past phi_c before the state tips, by a lag that grows with the rate. The system has the state system.x, starting on the lower branch at phi0.

Bases: BaseSystem

The glacial cycles of Saltzman and Maasch.

The cycles are a self-sustained oscillation of ice, carbon, and ocean.

Without forcing the default parameters give a limit cycle of about 100 kyr. The system has the anomalies climate.x, climate.y, and climate.z.

Bases: BaseSystem

The forest dieback model coupled with the replicator dynamics of mitigators.

The mitigators perceive the warming of the forest.

The forest grows as in ForestDiebackSystem, with its growth rate scaled by 0.2 + 0.4 x, so that mitigation by the share x of the population helps it. The share follows the replicator equation x' = x (1 - x) (-alpha + f(Tf) + delta (2 x - 1)), where the cost of warming f = fmax / (1 + exp(-w (Tf - Tc))) reads the warming Tf = tf / tp (T(t) - T(t - tp)) projected from the last tp years, a delay differential equation. Before the start the cover keeps its initial value. With no warming the shares 0 and 1 are stable and the share x* = 1 - (fmax / 2) / (1 + exp(w Tc)) between them is unstable, for the defaults of alpha, delta, and w. The population converges to all or no mitigators, and the forest to a positive cover or to bare soil, the green, brown, and barren outcomes, with long swings for some temperatures. The system has the vegetation cover forest.v and the share of mitigators people.x.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The Sutera-Fraedrich stochastic energy balance set up for tipping.

The tipping is bifurcation-, noise-, or rate-induced.

The temperature follows dT = c0 [-T^4 + c1 mu (b2 T^2 - a2)] dt + sqrt(nu) dW with the parameters of Table 1 of Fang et al. and starts at its warm stable equilibrium. In bifurcation-induced tipping, mu decreases at 4e-4 per year until the warm equilibrium meets the unstable one in a fold near mu = 0.76. In noise-induced tipping, the controls are fixed and noise of variance nu = 1 carries the state over the unstable equilibrium. In rate-induced tipping, b2 and a2 ramp logistically at the rate rho with the equilibria preserved, and the state fails to track the moving warm equilibrium when rho exceeds about 0.175. A tipped state leaves the warm branch and falls to the other stable root of the quartic. The system has the temperature earth.T, the control earth.mu, and the ramp progress earth.lam.

Bases: Element

Tipping element in the normal form of a fold.

Tipped neighbours push the element toward its upper state.

The state follows dx_i/dt = -x_i^3 + x_i + sqrt(4/27) c_i + d Σ_j A_ij (x_j + 1). Alone, the element has a lower and an upper stable state for |c| < 1 and only the upper one beyond the critical value c = 1. A neighbour in its lower state x_j ≈ -1 adds almost nothing, while a tipped neighbour at x_j ≈ 1 adds about 2 d. The element carries the fold, and the coupling of TippingCascadeNetworkSystem adds the pushes of the neighbours.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

Glacial cycles as a Van der Pol relaxation oscillator.

The oscillator is optionally paced by orbital forcing.

Time is in thousands of years. The slow variable x stands for ice volume and the fast variable y for the climate state, with tau x' = -(y + beta + gamma F(t)) and tau y' = -alpha (y^3/3 - y - x), where F(t) = cos(2 pi t/23) + cos(2 pi t/41) stands for precession and obliquity. For |beta| < 1 the unforced oscillator has a relaxation limit cycle of slow ice build-up and fast terminations, and gamma sets how strongly the orbit paces it. The system has the states climate.x and climate.y.

docs.title: early_warning(source, *, variables=None, window=None, detrend=True)
docs.text:
Return the rolling indicators of critical slowing down before a tipping point.

The indicators are computed for every series of a source.

The main indicator is the rolling lag-one autocorrelation of detrended windows, and the others of Dakos et al. (2012) follow: the rolling variance and skewness, and the reddening, the ratio of the mean power of the lowest eighth of frequencies to that of the highest half, which rises as fluctuations slow down. The trend of every indicator is Kendall's tau against time.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source Source

The trajectory, or an array with one row per time and one column per series.

required variables Sequence[str] | None

The variables of a trajectory to read, or None for every scalar series.

None window int | None

The number of values in every rolling window.

None detrend bool

Whether to remove a linear trend in every window first.

True

Returns:

Name Type Description result EarlyWarningResult

The rolling indicators of every series and their trends.

Raises:

Type Description AnalysisError

The window is missing or does not fit the series.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.climate import early_warning
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
>>> x = np.zeros(2000)
>>> for t in range(1, 2000):
...     x[t] = (0.2 + 0.79 * t / 2000) * x[t - 1] + rng.standard_normal()
>>> bool(early_warning(x, window=200).autocorrelation_trend[0] > 0.5)
True
Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/physics/climate/_early_warning.py 
def early_warning(
    source: Source,
    *,
    variables: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    window: int | None = None,
    detrend: bool = True,
) -> EarlyWarningResult:
    """Return the rolling indicators of critical slowing down before a tipping point.

    The indicators are computed for every series of a source.

    The main indicator is the rolling lag-one autocorrelation of detrended windows, and the others of Dakos et al.
    (2012) follow: the rolling variance and skewness, and the reddening, the ratio of the mean power of the lowest
    eighth of frequencies to that of the highest half, which rises as fluctuations slow down. The trend of every
    indicator is Kendall's tau against time.

    Args:
        source:
            The trajectory, or an array with one row per time and one column per series.

        variables:
            The variables of a trajectory to read, or `None` for every scalar series.

        window:
            The number of values in every rolling window.

        detrend:
            Whether to remove a linear trend in every window first.

    Returns:
        result:
            The rolling indicators of every series and their trends.

    Raises:
        AnalysisError:
            The window is missing or does not fit the series.

    Examples:
        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.climate import early_warning
        >>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
        >>> x = np.zeros(2000)
        >>> for t in range(1, 2000):
        ...     x[t] = (0.2 + 0.79 * t / 2000) * x[t - 1] + rng.standard_normal()
        >>> bool(early_warning(x, window=200).autocorrelation_trend[0] > 0.5)
        True
    """
    autocorrelation = rolling(source, kind='autocorrelation', variables=variables, window=window, detrend=detrend)
    variance = rolling(source, kind='variance', variables=variables, window=window, detrend=detrend)
    skewness = rolling(source, kind='skewness', variables=variables, window=window, detrend=detrend)
    size = int(window or 0)
    reddening = np.asarray([_reddening_of(column, size, detrend=detrend) for column in autocorrelation.values.T])
    return EarlyWarningResult(
        values=autocorrelation.values,
        labels=autocorrelation.labels,
        statistic=autocorrelation.statistic,
        trend=autocorrelation.trend,
        variance=variance.statistic,
        autocorrelation=autocorrelation.statistic,
        skewness=skewness.statistic,
        reddening=reddening,
        variance_trend=variance.trend,
        autocorrelation_trend=autocorrelation.trend,
        skewness_trend=skewness.trend,
        reddening_trend=np.asarray([_trend(row) for row in reddening]),
    )

docs.title: TopplingInteraction(label, *, target, state='x', threshold=1.0, share=0.0, mode='redistribute', drive=None, neighborhood=None, layer=None)
docs.text:
Bases: NeighborInteraction

Cascade of the members whose state reaches a threshold.

These members relax and pass shares to their neighbours. At every step the drive changes the state, and then every member whose state reaches threshold relaxes, all at once, until no member does. In the mode 'redistribute' a relaxing member loses threshold and each of its neighbours gains share. In the mode 'reset' a relaxing member falls to 0 and each of its neighbours gains share times the state it relaxed from. In the mode 'random' a relaxing member loses threshold in parcels of share, and every parcel goes to one of its neighbours drawn at random. Neighbours outside a fixed boundary take no share, so it leaves the system, and the mode 'random' treats every lattice as bounded. Every cascade is recorded as an event with its size, the number of relaxations, its duration, and its area.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec(elements=(ANY,), states=(state,))]

The path of the group on the nodes or sites.

required state str

The name of the state of the members.

'x' threshold float

The value of the state at which a member relaxes, fixed during a run.

1.0 share float

What a neighbour of a relaxing member gains, an amount, a fraction of the state in the mode 'reset', or the amount of one parcel in the mode 'random', fixed during a run.

0.0 mode str

'redistribute', 'reset', or 'random'.

'redistribute' drive Callable[..., Array] | None

A function f(values, *, random) of the array of the states and the random generator of the simulation that returns the states after the drive of a step, or None for no drive.

None neighborhood BaseNeighborhood | None

The neighbourhood of the member itself first and its neighbours, or None for the von Neumann neighbourhood of a square lattice with its centre. A network takes AdjacencyNeighborhood(center=True), and the mode 'random' takes a lattice neighbourhood.

None layer str | None

The layer of the network whose edges the interaction runs on, or None for the graph of the network.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The mode is unknown, the drive is not callable, the neighbourhood leaves out the member itself, or the mode 'random' has no lattice neighbourhood or a threshold that is not a whole number of parcels.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.avalanches import TopplingInteraction
>>> cascade = TopplingInteraction('cascade', target='sites', state='height', threshold=4, share=1)
>>> cascade.mode
'redistribute'

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field realizations shared by the physics packages.

The package holds advection by a drift, diffusion by a diffusivity, the one-particle density of kinetic theory, and the Monte Carlo sampling of lattice gauge fields.

docs.title: AdvectionInteraction(label, *, target, state='u', drift=None, source=None, limiter='minmod', riemann='rusanov', sources=())
docs.text:
Bases: ConservationInteraction

Advection du/dt + divergence(a u) = source(ns) of a state u of a field by a drift.

Physics names it advection, the transport of a state by a flow or by the streaming of a phase-space density. The drift field is a(ns). The flux of the conservation law is the drift times the state, written in conservative form, so the total of the state on a periodic field stays constant and, on a spectral field, the dealiasing of products applies to it. The drift is one expression for a field of one dimension, or one per dimension, of the states and parameters of the field, and may read other states than the one it carries, such as the flow of a fluid derived from a streamfunction, or the drift of a probability density in a Fokker-Planck equation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target str

The path of the field whose state is carried.

required state str

The name of the carried state of the field.

'u' drift Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object] | None

A function of the namespace that returns the drift, or one drift per dimension.

None source Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object] | None

A function of the namespace that returns the source, or None for none.

None limiter str | None

The slope limiter of the reconstruction of a finite-volume field, 'minmod', 'van-leer', or None.

'minmod' riemann str | None

The numerical flux of a finite-volume field, 'rusanov' or 'godunov', or None for the divergence of the flux on a field of another discretization.

'rusanov' sources Sequence[str]

The paths of other elements the drift and the source read, as the namespaces sources. A field over the position lattice of a target on a phase space is read broadcast along the class axes.

()

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The state is not a name, a function is not callable, or the limiter or the numerical flux is unknown.

Examples:

>>> from typing import Annotated
>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, FieldElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.fields import AdvectionInteraction
>>> class CellElement(Element):
...     def __init__(self, label, u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
...         super().__init__(label)
...         self.u = u
>>> space = LatticeSpace((50,), spacing=0.1, boundary='periodic')
>>> values = {'u': np.exp(-((np.arange(50) - 25) / 5.0) ** 2)}
>>> volumes = 'finite-volume'
>>> field = FieldElement('tracer', element=CellElement, space=space, values=values, discretization=volumes)
>>> drift = AdvectionInteraction('drift', target='tracer', state='u', drift=lambda s: 1.0)
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[field], interactions=[drift])
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=1.0, dt=0.01)
>>> total = trajectory.get_values('tracer.u')[-1].sum()
>>> round(float(total), 6) == round(float(values['u'].sum()), 6)
True

Bases: RateInteraction

Diffusion du/dt = D laplacian(u) of a state u of a field by a diffusivity D.

Physics names the coefficient a diffusivity, as the thermal diffusivity of heat conduction or the kinematic viscosity of the vorticity of a fluid. The diffusivity is uniform in space, a number or a function of the namespace that returns an expression of parameters and time. The rate is the Laplacian of the field, which its discretization evaluates, so the total of the state on a periodic field stays constant and a point mass spreads as the heat kernel.

docs.title: HolonomyScoreSpec(function, group, hits=1) dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSpec

Spec of an objective of a matrix group state on the edges of a cell complex.

The objective is a sum over the holonomies of faces. The objective is the sum over the faces of a class function of the holonomy of every face, the path-ordered product of the matrices of the edges around it. A class function, such as the real part of the trace, has the same value on every cyclic order of the product, so the local objective of an edge sums it over the holonomies of the faces around the edge that start at the edge.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default function Callable[..., object]

The function function(holonomies, **parameters) of an array of holonomies, matrices on the last two axes, and the parameters of the system that it names, which returns one number per holonomy.

required group MatrixGroupSpec

The matrix group of the state.

required hits int

The number of moves proposed per edge and sweep.

1

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The function is not callable, the group is invalid, or the number of hits is not positive.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.core.specs import MatrixGroupSpec
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.fields import HolonomyScoreSpec
>>> trace = lambda holonomies: -np.trace(holonomies, axis1=-2, axis2=-1).real
>>> HolonomyScoreSpec(trace, MatrixGroupSpec('SU', 2), hits=4).hits
4

docs.text:
Bases: SamplingInteraction

Monte Carlo sampling of link variables.

The sampling uses the local Wilson action of the plaquettes of a link.

For link angles the action is -beta sum_p cos(theta_p), where theta_p is the oriented sum of the link angles around the plaquette p. For the matrices of a group SU(N) it is -(beta / N) sum_p Re tr U_p, where U_p is the path-ordered product of the link matrices around p, and the move 'rotate' multiplies a link by a random matrix of the group near the identity of spread width.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the group on the edges of a cell complex.

required beta Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=closed_open(0, oo))]

The inverse coupling of the Wilson action.

2.0 state str

The name of the state that holds the link angles.

'theta' move str

'rotate' for U(1) or a matrix group, or 'random-value' for Z_N.

'rotate' values Sequence[float]

The angles a random-value move draws from.

() width float

The largest change of a rotation.

1.5 rule str

The acceptance, 'metropolis', 'glauber', or 'heat-bath'.

'metropolis' schedule str

'colored' or 'random-sequential'.

'colored' group MatrixGroupSpec | None

The matrix group of the links, or None for link angles.

None hits int

The number of moves proposed per link and sweep of matrix links.

1

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.fields import WilsonSamplingInteraction
>>> WilsonSamplingInteraction('wilson', target='links', beta=2.0).beta
2.0
>>> from skcomplex.core.specs import MatrixGroupSpec
>>> color = WilsonSamplingInteraction('wilson', target='links', state='U', group=MatrixGroupSpec('SU', 3))
>>> color.objective.group.degree
3

Bases: EulerLagrangeInteraction

Motion of a pendulum.

The motion is the Euler-Lagrange equation of L = m l² θ'² / 2 + m g l cos θ.

The equation is Newton's law m l² θ'' = -m g l sin θ for the angle θ of the target, whose mass m, length l, and gravity g are parameters of the target.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

docs.title: ReflectionInteraction(label, *, target, guard, positions=('x',), velocities=('x_d1',), direction=0, restitution=1.0, region=None)
docs.text:
Bases: CrossingInteraction

Reflection of a moving point off a wall g(x) = 0.

The reflection has a coefficient of restitution e.

When the guard g crosses zero, the velocity v of the point becomes v - (1 + e) (v . n) n / |n|**2, where n is the gradient of g with respect to the position. The normal velocity is reversed and scaled by e, and the tangential velocity is kept, so e = 1 is a specular, elastic reflection. The position and the velocity are given by the names of their states, scalar or vector, whose components pair up in order. A region restricts the wall to the part of the surface where it holds, and the point crosses the rest of the surface freely.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the element that reflects.

required guard Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object]

The function guard(namespace) of the wall, an expression of the position that is zero on the wall.

required positions Sequence[str]

The names of the states that hold the position.

('x',) velocities Sequence[str]

The names of the states that hold the velocity, the first derivatives of the position.

('x_d1',) direction int

1 for crossings from negative to positive, -1 for the opposite, and 0 for both.

0 restitution Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=closed(0, 1))]

The coefficient of restitution, the ratio of the normal speeds after and before the reflection.

1.0 region Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object] | None

The function region(namespace) of the condition that holds on the part of the surface that is a wall, or None for a wall on the whole surface.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The positions and the velocities have different numbers of names, or a function is not callable.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import PointElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.mechanics import ReflectionInteraction
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> wall = ReflectionInteraction('wall', target='ball', guard=lambda s: s.target.x[0] - 1, direction=1)
>>> ball = PointElement('ball', x=[0.0, 0.0], x_d1=[1.0, 1.0])
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[ball], interactions=[wall], space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2))
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=2.0, dt=0.5)
>>> trajectory.get_values('ball.x')[-1].tolist()
[0.0, 2.0]

docs.title: KuramotoCouplingInteraction(label, *, target, source=None, K=1.0, alpha=0.0, state='theta', reduce='sum', mode='edges', weights=None, include_self=False, delay=0.0, neighborhood=None, layer=None)
docs.text:
Bases: CouplingInteraction

Kuramoto coupling theta_i' += K sum_j sin(theta_j - theta_i - alpha).

The coupling acts on the phases of a group.

The sum, or the mean, runs over the members j that the mode selects: the neighbours along the edges of a lattice or network, or within a neighbourhood such as RadiusNeighborhood(r), every other member of the group, every member of a separate source group, or the next member. With include_self it also runs over j = i, whose term -K sin(alpha) slows every phase. Over the whole group without weights or delay, the coupling reads the group sums of sin theta and cos theta once, so it costs time linear in the size of the group.

The phase lag.

The name of the state of the edge group in the mode 'edges', a matrix in the mode 'group', or None.

docs.title: StuartLandauElement(label, visual=None, *, x=1.0, y=0.0, mu=1.0, omega=1.0, beta=0.0, kappa=1.0, tau=1.0)
docs.text:
Bases: Element

Stuart-Landau oscillator of z = x + i y.

The oscillator follows z' = tau ((mu + i omega) z - kappa (1 + i beta) |z|^2 z).

It is the normal form of a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. For mu > 0 the oscillator settles on the limit cycle of radius sqrt(mu / kappa), which it turns at the frequency tau (omega - beta mu), and for mu < 0 it decays to the fixed point 0. The twist beta makes the frequency depend on the amplitude, and the time scale tau speeds up or slows down the whole flow.

docs.text:
Return the complex mean field of a group's phases and its modulus.

The modulus is the order parameter.

The mean field Z = <exp(i theta)> averages the unit vectors of the phases theta of the group's members, and the order parameter r = |Z| is 0 for scattered phases and 1 for locked phases.

def order_parameter(label: str, group: str) -> list[ObservableSpec]:
    """Return the complex mean field of a group's phases and its modulus.

    The modulus is the order parameter.

    The mean field `Z = <exp(i theta)>` averages the unit vectors of the phases `theta` of the group's members, and the
    order parameter `r = |Z|` is 0 for scattered phases and 1 for locked phases.

    Args:
        label:
            The label of the order parameter. The mean field has the label `<label>_field`.

        group:
            The path of the group of oscillators, whose members have the phase `theta`.

    Returns:
        observables:
            The mean field and the order parameter.

    Examples:
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.oscillators import order_parameter
        >>> [observable.label for observable in order_parameter('order', 'oscillators')]
        ['order_field', 'order']
    """
    return [
        ObservableSpec(f'{label}_field', _phase_vector, group=group),
        ObservableSpec(label, partial(_modulus, f'{label}_field')),
    ]

docs.text:
Bases: RelaxationTimeInteraction

Langevin thermostat.

The thermostat adds a drag -gamma * v and a random force that hold particles at a temperature.

Every velocity component follows dv = -gamma * v / m * dt + sqrt(2 * gamma * temperature) / m * dW, with the temperature in energy units, a relaxation of the velocity towards rest over the time m / gamma with additive noise. The velocity is the first derivative of the position, a state of order 2, and the mass is the divisor. A system with a thermostat is stochastic, and its velocities relax to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at that temperature.

docs.text:
Bases: RateInteraction

Relaxation of a state towards a goal over a relaxation time.

Physics names it a relaxation-time approximation, as in Newton cooling, a Langevin bath, or the BGK collision term. The rate is (goal(ns) - x) / time(ns) of a state x of a target, with optional noise. With a constant goal and time and an additive noise of amplitude sigma, the state follows the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process dx = (goal - x) / time dt + sigma dW, whose stationary variance is sigma**2 time / 2. A goal or a time function takes the namespace of the interaction, as for RateInteraction, and a number stands for a constant. A goal that is a number applies to every component of a vector state.

docs.title: StokesianMobilityInteraction(label, *, target, position='x', orientation=None, tensor='rotne-prager-yamakawa', form='rate', force=None, torque=None, velocity=None, stresslet=None, dipole=None, potential=None, cutoff=None, root='cholesky', tolerance=1e-06, radius=1.0, viscosity=1.0, temperature=0.0, dt=0.01)
docs.text:
Bases: Interaction

Stokesian mobility of spheres in a Stokes fluid.

Physics names it the mobility of Stokesian dynamics. It is the linear map from forces and torques to velocities and spins. Every member of the group target of spheres of radius a in a fluid of viscosity eta moves at the velocity U_i and spins at the angular velocity Omega_i of

(U_i, Omega_i) = sum_j M_ij (F_j, T_j) + (V_i, 0) + sum_{j != i} (u_j(x_i), w_j(x_i) / 2)

where M is the grand mobility, F_j and T_j the force and torque on member j, V_i an intrinsic velocity, and u_j and w_j the flow and vorticity of the force-free sources of member j. The self mobilities are 1 / (6 pi eta a) and 1 / (8 pi eta a^3). Between members at the separation r = x_i - x_j the translational block is the Oseen tensor (I + r r / r^2) / (8 pi eta r), or with tensor='rotne-prager-yamakawa' the Rotne-Prager-Yamakawa tensor, which adds the finite size a^2 (I / 3 - r r / r^2) / (4 pi eta r^3) and turns to its regularized form when the spheres overlap. The rotlet couples a torque on j to the velocity T_j x r / (8 pi eta r^3) of i, a force on j to the angular velocity F_j x r / (8 pi eta r^3) of i, and a torque to the angular velocity (3 r r / r^2 - I) T_j / (16 pi eta r^3). With tensor='free-draining' no member moves another, the baseline without hydrodynamic interactions.

The sources are a stresslet S_j, a symmetric traceless tensor whose flow is -3 (r.S.r) r / (8 pi eta r^5), and a potential dipole D_j, whose flow is (3 r r / r^2 - I) D_j / r^3. Together with the intrinsic velocity they carry the active slip of a swimmer. These are point singularities, accurate at separations of a few radii. The forces of a pair potential(namespace, r) of the distance, a function of the distance and of the parameters of the interaction, act on every pair closer than cutoff, and add to the forces F_j. With an orientation, a unit vector state, the orientation turns as dp/dt = Omega x p.

In the form 'rate' the velocities are the rates of the position and the orientation in continuous time. In the form 'map', in discrete time, every step of length dt is the Ermak-McCammon step x + U dt + sqrt(2 kT dt) (B xi)_x at the temperature kT, where B B^T = M and xi is standard normal, and the orientation turns by Omega dt + sqrt(2 kT dt) (B xi)_p and is normalized. The divergence of both tensors vanishes in an unbounded fluid, so the step needs no drift correction. root='cholesky' factors the dense mobility, and root='lanczos' applies a Krylov approximation of its square root to xi with the matrix-free product, until the relative change of the sample falls below tolerance. In the map form the time of the namespace counts steps, so a force of the physical time reads s.t * s.dt.

Positions in the plane are the plane z = 0 of a three-dimensional fluid. A torque is then a number, the torque about z, and the stresslet is its block in the plane. The product costs O(N^2) per evaluation, Cholesky O(N^3), and every evaluation runs as one call over the group.

Its operators are annihilate, create, and number, and its basis state n holds n quanta.

Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/physics/common/quantum/_mode.py 
def mode_space(quanta: int = 4) -> HilbertSpec:
    """Return the Hilbert space of a bosonic mode truncated at a number of quanta.

    Its operators are `annihilate`, `create`, and `number`, and its basis state `n` holds `n` quanta.

    Args:
        quanta:
            The largest number of quanta, so the dimension is `quanta + 1`.

    Returns:
        space:
            The Hilbert space.

    Raises:
        ValidationError:
            The number of quanta is not a positive integer.

    Examples:
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.quantum import mode_space
        >>> mode_space(4).dimension
        5
    """
    if isinstance(quanta, bool) or not isinstance(quanta, int | np.integer) or quanta < 1:
        error_msg = f'A mode has quanta = {quanta!r}, which is not a positive integer.'
        raise ValidationError(error_msg)
    size = int(quanta) + 1
    operators = {
        'annihilate': (qutip.destroy(size).full(), False),
        'create': (qutip.create(size).full(), False),
        'number': (qutip.num(size).full(), True),
    }
    return HilbertSpec(size, operators, display='number')

docs.title: Relativity
docs.text:
Relativity shared by the physics packages.

Spacetimes derive their geometry from a metric with EinsteinPy, and free bodies follow their geodesics.

docs.title: GeodesicInteraction(label, *, target, state='x', space=None)
docs.text:
Bases: Interaction

Geodesic equation x''^mu = -Γ^mu_(alpha beta)(x) x'^alpha x'^beta of a point.

The point is a point of a pseudo-Riemannian space. The state is a vector of order 2 with one component per coordinate of the space, the position x^mu of a test particle, and its companion holds the tangent x'^mu. The time of the system is the affine parameter of the geodesic, the proper time of a timelike geodesic when the tangent starts with g_(mu nu) x'^mu x'^nu = -1. A tangent that starts null, with g_(mu nu) x'^mu x'^nu = 0, follows a light ray. Either norm is conserved along the geodesic, so it measures the error of a run. The Christoffel symbols are those the space derives from its metric.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec(elements=(ANY,), states=(state,))]

The path of the element or group whose state is the position.

required state str

The name of the vector state of order 2 that is the position.

'x' space SpacetimeSpace | None

The pseudo-Riemannian space whose geodesics the point follows, usually the space of the system too.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description space_

The prepared space, whose Christoffel symbols the rate reads.

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The state is not a name.

SpaceError

The space is not a pseudo-Riemannian space, raised by prepare.

Examples:

>>> from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import SR, matrix
>>> from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import PointElement
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.relativity import GeodesicInteraction
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.relativity import SpacetimeSpace
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> r, phi = SR.var('r phi')
>>> plane = SpacetimeSpace(matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, r**2]]), (r, phi))
>>> line = GeodesicInteraction('line', target='particle', space=plane)
>>> particle = PointElement('particle', x=[1.0, 0.0], x_d1=[0.0, 1.0])
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[particle], interactions=[line], space=plane)
>>> trajectory = simulate(system, until=1.0, dt=0.001)
>>> [round(float(value), 3) for value in trajectory.get_values('particle.x')[-1]]
[1.414, 0.785]

docs.title: SpacetimeSpace(metric=None, coordinates=(), *, curvature=True, label='space')
docs.text:
Bases: ContinuousSpace

Chart of coordinates with a symbolic metric g_(mu nu).

The connection and the curvature follow from the metric. The metric is a symmetric, nondegenerate Sage matrix whose entries are expressions of the coordinates, numbers, and symbolic functions of the coordinates. A function stands for an unknown of an ansatz, such as the scale factor a(t) of a homogeneous universe, which a field equation of the metric solves for. The space is an unbounded continuous space with one dimension per coordinate, so a point on it has one component per coordinate, as a test particle of GeodesicInteraction does.

prepare derives, through EinsteinPy, the Christoffel symbols Γ^mu_(alpha beta) = g^(mu lambda) (∂_alpha g_(lambda beta) + ∂_beta g_(lambda alpha) - ∂_lambda g_(alpha beta))/2 and, with curvature, the Riemann tensor R^rho_(sigma mu nu), its contraction the Ricci tensor R_(mu nu) = R^rho_(mu rho nu), the Ricci scalar R = g^(mu nu) R_(mu nu), and the Einstein tensor G_(mu nu) = R_(mu nu) - R g_(mu nu) / 2. The curvature of a metric with many entries, such as Kerr's, takes long to simplify, so it can be left out when only the connection is needed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default metric Matrix | Sequence[Sequence[object]] | None

The metric, a square matrix of expressions, or None for the metric a subclass derives.

None coordinates Sequence[Expression | str]

The coordinates, Sage variables or their names, in the order of the rows of the metric.

() curvature bool

Whether prepare derives the curvature tensors besides the Christoffel symbols.

True label str

The label of the space in its system.

'space'

Attributes:

Name Type Description coordinates_

The coordinates, as Sage variables.

metric_

The metric g_(mu nu).

inverse_metric_

The inverse metric g^(mu nu).

christoffel_

The Christoffel symbols, with christoffel_[mu][alpha][beta] the symbol Γ^mu_(alpha beta).

riemann_

The Riemann tensor, with riemann_[rho][sigma][mu][nu] the component R^rho_(sigma mu nu), or None without curvature.

ricci_

The Ricci tensor R_(mu nu), or None without curvature.

ricci_scalar_

The Ricci scalar, or None without curvature.

einstein_

The Einstein tensor G_(mu nu), or None without curvature.

derived_from_

The metric, the coordinates, and the curvature flag the tensors were derived from, which a later prepare compares by value to skip the derivation when they have not changed.

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The metric is not a symmetric square matrix of one row per coordinate, a coordinate is not a variable, two coordinates coincide, or the metric is degenerate.

Examples:

>>> from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import SR, matrix, sin
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.relativity import SpacetimeSpace
>>> theta, phi = SR.var('theta phi')
>>> sphere = SpacetimeSpace(matrix(SR, [[1, 0], [0, sin(theta) ** 2]]), (theta, phi)).prepare()
>>> sphere.christoffel_[0][1][1]
-cos(theta)*sin(theta)
>>> sphere.ricci_scalar_
2

docs.title: EinsteinFieldEquationsInteraction(label, *, target, states='x', space=None, components=(), source=None, coupling=8 * math.pi, cosmological_constant=0.0, time=0, axes=None)
docs.text:
Bases: Interaction

Einstein equations G^mu_nu + Λ δ^mu_nu = κ T^mu_nu of a metric ansatz.

The equations are reduced to rate laws of the unknowns of the ansatz. The metric of the space is an ansatz: a symmetric matrix whose unknowns are symbolic functions of the coordinates, each named after a state or a parameter of the target, such as the scale factor a(t) of a homogeneous universe or the areal radius R(t, r) of the shells of a spherical dust ball. The interaction takes the mixed Einstein tensor G^mu_nu = g^(mu lambda) G_(lambda nu) the space derives, keeps one component (mu, nu) per state, and solves these equations, linear in the second time derivatives, for them, which gives one rate law per state of order 2.

The time coordinate becomes the time of the system, a derivative of an unknown along it the time derivative of its state, and a derivative along a coordinate that axes maps to an axis of the lattice of a field the derivative partial of the field along that axis, so a spherical ansatz reduces to a field in 1 + 1 dimensions. An equation that keeps another coordinate, a mixed derivative in time and space, or a derivative above the second does not reduce to such laws and raises an error, as does a set of components that does not fix the second derivatives: the remaining components are constraints, such as the Friedmann equation, which the initial values satisfy and the laws keep.

The source function takes the namespace of the interaction, with the namespace target, and returns the mixed energy-momentum tensor T^mu_nu, such as diag(-rho, p, p, p) of a perfect fluid at rest, in terms of the states and parameters of the target.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec(elements=(ANY,), states=(states,))]

The path of the element or field whose states and parameters are the unknowns of the ansatz.

required states str | Sequence[str]

The name of the state of order 2 that an equation determines, or the names of several states.

'x' space SpacetimeSpace | None

The pseudo-Riemannian space of the ansatz, with the curvature.

None components Sequence[tuple[int, int]]

The index pair (mu, nu) of the mixed equation of every state, in the order of the states.

() source Callable[[SimpleNamespace], object] | None

A function of the namespace that returns the mixed energy-momentum tensor, or None for vacuum.

None coupling float

The coupling κ = 8 π G / c⁴ of the source.

8 * pi cosmological_constant float

The cosmological constant Λ.

0.0 time int

The index of the time coordinate.

0 axes Mapping[int, int] | None

The axis of the lattice of the target along every spatial coordinate the unknowns depend on, by the index of the coordinate.

None

Attributes:

Name Type Description space_

The prepared space.

equations_

The mixed Einstein tensor G^mu_nu of the space, whose kept components the laws simplify.

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

A state is not a name, the components do not give one index pair per state, the source is not callable, or an equation does not reduce to rate laws of the states.

SpaceError

The space is not a pseudo-Riemannian space with curvature, raised by prepare.

Examples:

>>> from typing import Annotated
>>> from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import SR, diagonal_matrix, function, sin
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.cosmology import EinsteinFieldEquationsInteraction
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.common.relativity import SpacetimeSpace
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> class UniverseElement(Element):
...     def __init__(self, label, a: Annotated[float, StateSpec(order=2)] = 1.0, a_d1: float = 0.0):
...         super().__init__(label)
...         self.a = a
...         self.a_d1 = a_d1
>>> t, r, theta, phi = SR.var('t r theta phi')
>>> a = function('a')(t)
>>> metric = diagonal_matrix(SR, [-1, a**2, a**2 * r**2, a**2 * r**2 * sin(theta) ** 2])
>>> flat = SpacetimeSpace(metric, (t, r, theta, phi))
>>> vacuum = EinsteinFieldEquationsInteraction(
...     'vacuum', target='universe', states='a', space=flat, components=[(1, 1)], cosmological_constant=3.0

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A homogeneous universe whose expansion follows from the Einstein equations.

The equations are those of the Robertson-Walker metric.

The metric of RobertsonWalkerSpace gives, through its Einstein tensor, the two Friedmann equations of a perfect fluid of density rho and pressure p. The space-space component G^r_r = -(2 a a'' + a'² + k) / a² = κ p is the law of the scale factor, and the time-time component G^t_t = -3 (a'² + k) / a² = -κ rho is the constraint (a'/a)² = κ rho / 3 - k / a², which sets the initial rate and which the evolution keeps. The fluid holds matter of pressure 0, radiation of pressure rho / 3, and the vacuum energy of a cosmological constant of pressure -rho, with the density parameters today, at a = 1, and the curvature k = -Ω_k H0² of the remainder Ω_k = 1 - Ω_m - Ω_r - Ω_Λ. Units have G = c = 1. The system has the scale factor universe.a of order 2 and its rate universe.a_d1.

The density parameter of matter.

Bases: BaseSystem

The scale factor of a homogeneous universe of matter and dark energy.

The system follows Friedmann and Lemaître.

The acceleration equation a² a'' = -4 pi G M / 3 + Lambda a³ / 3 is written with the density parameters of matter Ω_m = 8 pi G M / (3 H0²) and of the cosmological constant Ω_Λ = Lambda / (3 H0²) in units of the Hubble constant H0 at a = 1, so a² a'' = -Ω_m H0² / 2 + Ω_Λ H0² a³. docs.title: OppenheimerSnyderCollapseSystem(n_shells=32, *, radius=10.0, mass=1.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A ball of dust at rest that collapses under its own gravity into a black hole.

The collapse follows Oppenheimer and Snyder.

The ball is a field of comoving shells on a radial lattice, the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi ansatz of LemaitreTolmanBondiSpace in units with G = c = 1. Dust has no pressure, so the radial component of the Einstein equations, G^r_r = -(R'² + 2 R R'' - 2 E) / R² = 0 with ' the derivative by proper time, is the law of the areal radius R of every shell, and its first integral R'² = 2 M(r) / R + 2 E(r), from G^t_t, holds the mass M(r) inside the shell. A uniform ball of mass M and radius R₀ at rest has M(r) = M (r / R₀)³ and E(r) = -M(r) / r, so every shell follows the same cycloid R = r (1 + cos η) / 2 with t = (η + sin η) / (2 √k) and k = 2 M / R₀³, as the interior of Oppenheimer and Snyder. The surface crosses its Schwarzschild radius 2 M and the ball reaches zero size at the proper time π / (2 √k). The system has the areal radius ball.R of every shell and its rate ball.R_d1.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_shells int

The number of shells, which split the comoving radius R₀ evenly, the outermost at the surface.

The initial radius R₀ of the ball.

The mass M of the ball.

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

>>> round(float(OppenheimerSnyderCollapseSystem(4).prepare().system_.elements[0].values['energy'][-1]), 3)

Bases: TopplingInteraction

Slowly driven sandpile.

Every step drops one grain on a random site, and the full sites topple in avalanches.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Langevin field theory of an absorbing-state transition.

An active density is fed by an energy field.

The active density rho grows at the local rate a + b nu, saturates through -c rho^2, spreads with the diffusivity d, and fluctuates with the multiplicative noise e sqrt(rho), which vanishes in the absorbing state rho = 0. The energy field nu diffuses, gains the drive f, and loses the dissipation g rho, so rho_t = (a + b nu) rho - c rho^2 + d laplacian(rho) + e sqrt(rho) xi and nu_t = laplacian(nu) + f - g rho (Tian et al., Eqs. 3-4). Both fields stay nonnegative. Without drive and dissipation the energy is a fixed control parameter: below the threshold nu_c = -a / b activity dies out, and above it the density settles near (a + b nu) / c. The system has the activity neurons.rho and the energy neurons.nu.

docs.title: EvolutionarySKGameSystem(n_agents=256, *, memory=0.75, temperature=None, max_temperature=2.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The evolutionary Sherrington-Kirkpatrick game.

The game self-organises to the edge of ergodicity breaking.

After Lesmana et al. (2026, arXiv 2604.15669), N agents play ±1 on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick landscape with symmetric Gaussian couplings of variance 1 / N. Each learns the incentive of its actions with memory alpha and plays by a softmax policy at its own temperature, and the least fit agent is replaced, as in the Bak-Sneppen system, by a newcomer whose temperature is drawn uniformly on [0, max_temperature]. The temperatures evolve to the edge between ergodic and frozen learning, the replacement cascades have sizes distributed as S^(-3/2), and the mean reward exceeds that of the game at any fixed temperature. With a fixed temperature, no agent is replaced and the system is the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick game of Galla and Farmer. The system has the group agents of states incentive, spin, temperature, fitness, and reward, and the observables mean_reward, mean_temperature, and least_fitness.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_agents int

The number of agents N.

256 memory float

The weight alpha of the latest field in the incentive.

0.75 temperature ArrayLike | None

The temperature of every agent, or one per agent, of the game without replacement, or None for the evolving game.

None max_temperature float

The largest temperature of a newcomer, and of the initial temperatures drawn uniformly.

2.0 random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the couplings, the initial actions, and the initial temperatures.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.criticality import EvolutionarySKGameSystem

Bases: BaseSystem

The fixed-energy sandpile.

It is a Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld pile with no drive and no loss on a periodic lattice.

Every step, every site with at least four grains gives one grain to each of its four neighbours, all at once. The lattice is periodic, so the density of grains density is conserved, and it controls an absorbing phase transition. Below the critical density, about 2.125 on the square lattice, the topplings stop in an absorbing configuration, and above it the pile stays active forever. The density of active sites, the observable activity, is the order parameter. The grains start scattered uniformly at random over the sites. The system has the heights pile.height and the observable activity, the density of active sites.

Bases: Element

Agent of the evolutionary Sherrington-Kirkpatrick game.

The agent learns a binary action and may be replaced.

The agent keeps an incentive Q, the value of action +1, and plays the action s = ±1 by the softmax policy at its temperature T. Every step the incentive becomes (1 - alpha) Q + alpha h for the local field h = Σ_j J_ij s_j, and the fitness is s Q. When the agent evolves and its fitness is the least of the group, it is replaced by a newcomer with no incentive and a temperature drawn uniformly up to max_temperature, who learns from the field at once. The reward s h of the last actions is kept.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The SK game of reinforcement learners.

The rewards come from quenched Sherrington-Kirkpatrick couplings.

Every agent plays sigma_i = ±1 and earns sigma_i sum_j J_ij sigma_j, with symmetric Gaussian couplings of mean 0, variance 1 / N, and zero diagonal. It discounts its rewards with the memory alpha into the incentive Q_i and plays from a softmax policy at the temperature T (Lesmana et al., Eqs. 1-3). All agents start with zero incentives, so their first actions are random, and update in parallel. At low temperature the agents freeze into one of many ordered states with a high collective reward, and at high temperature they explore noisily with a low one. The system has the actions agents.sigma, the incentives agents.Q, and the coupling matrix in the values of the group. Its standard observable reward is the mean reward per agent.

docs.title: SelfOrganizedBranchingSystem(p=0.3, *, generations=10, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The self-organized branching process of Zapperi, Lauritsen, and Stanley.

It is a mean-field sandpile.

An avalanche starts from one active site at the top of a binary tree of generations generations. Every active site relaxes with the probability p into two active sites of the next generation, and stays still otherwise, so every generation has 2 Binomial(z, p) active sites. The sigma active sites that reach the last generation leave the system as dissipation. After every avalanche one unit of energy has entered and sigma have left, so the probability changes by (1 - sigma) / N with N = 2^(generations + 1) - 1 sites. A supercritical p makes large dissipating avalanches that lower it, and a subcritical one lets energy accumulate, so p organizes itself to the critical value p_c = 1 / 2, where the branching ratio 2 p is 1. The process advances one generation per step, so a step is a time of the avalanche and avalanches follow each other without pause. The system has the probability tree.p, the active sites tree.z, and the generation tree.g.

Bases: BaseSystem

The Zhang sandpile.

It is a continuous sandpile whose unstable sites give away all their energy.

Every step loads a site chosen at random with a packet of energy of uniform size in [0, threshold]. A site whose energy reaches the threshold relaxes: its energy falls to 0 and each of its four neighbours gains a quarter of it, all at once, until no site is unstable. Energy that would go beyond the open edges is lost. The pile organizes itself into a critical state with avalanches of every size, recorded as avalanche events with their sizes, durations, and areas, and the energies of the sites cluster near a few values. The energies start uniformly at random below the threshold. The system has the energies pile.energy.

Return the crackling-noise scaling of avalanches.

The avalanches are those of an activity series or the relaxations of a lattice.

It finds the avalanches as the events of kind 'excursions', then fits the exponent gamma of the mean size against the duration, <S>(T) ~ T^gamma, predicts it as (tau_T - 1) / (tau_S - 1) from the exponents of the size and duration laws, such as those fit_law(..., law='power') fits, and collapses the mean shapes of the chosen durations, which agree after scaling at a critical point.

>>> activity = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 2, 0]
>>> round(crackling_noise(activity, min_count=1).exponent, 2)
1.55
Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/physics/criticality/_crackling_noise.py 
def crackling_noise(
    source: Source,
    *,
    variables: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    threshold: float = 0.0,
    durations: Sequence[int] = (),
    min_count: int = 10,
    min_duration: int = 1,
    size_exponent: float | None = None,
    duration_exponent: float | None = None,
) -> CracklingNoiseResult:
    """Return the crackling-noise scaling of avalanches.

    The avalanches are those of an activity series or the relaxations of a lattice.

    It finds the avalanches as the events of kind `'excursions'`, then fits the exponent `gamma` of the mean size
    against the duration, `<S>(T) ~ T^gamma`, predicts it as `(tau_T - 1) / (tau_S - 1)` from the exponents of the
    size and duration laws, such as those `fit_law(..., law='power')` fits, and collapses the mean shapes of the chosen
    `durations`, which agree after scaling at a critical point.

    Args:
        source:
            The trajectory, an array that holds the activity series, or records of avalanches.

        variables:
            The one variable of a trajectory to read, or `None` for the only scalar series.

        threshold:
            The activity an avalanche exceeds at every step, subtracted from its profile.

        durations:
            The durations whose mean shapes are compared.

        min_count:
            The fewest avalanches of a duration used in the fit of the mean size.

        min_duration:
            The shortest duration used in the fit of the mean size.

        size_exponent:
            The exponent `tau_S` of the power law of the sizes, or `None` to leave out the prediction.

        duration_exponent:
            The exponent `tau_T` of the power law of the durations, or `None` to leave out the prediction.

    Returns:
        result:
            The avalanches, the exponent of the mean size and its prediction, and the mean shapes.

    Raises:
        AnalysisError:
            The fewest avalanches of a duration is not positive, or fewer than 2 durations have that many avalanches.

    Examples:
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.criticality import crackling_noise
        >>> activity = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 2, 0]
        >>> round(crackling_noise(activity, min_count=1).exponent, 2)
        1.55
    """
    if min_count < 1:
        error_msg = f'crackling_noise has min_count={min_count!r}. Use a positive value.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    found = events(source, kind='excursions', variables=variables, threshold=threshold)
    sizes = np.asarray(found.sizes, dtype=float)
    lasting = np.asarray(found.durations, dtype=float)
    shapes = list(found.shapes or [])
    distinct, counts = np.unique(lasting, return_counts=True)
    kept = distinct[(counts >= min_count) & (distinct >= max(min_duration, 1))]
    if kept.size < MIN_POINTS:
        error_msg = (
            f'Fewer than {MIN_POINTS} durations have {min_count} avalanches. Give more avalanches or lower '
            '`min_count`.'
        )
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    means = np.asarray([sizes[lasting == duration].mean() for duration in kept])
    predicted = float('nan')
    if size_exponent is not None and duration_exponent is not None:
        predicted = float((duration_exponent - 1) / (size_exponent - 1))
    mean_shapes = {
        int(duration): _mean_shape([shape for shape in shapes if shape.size == duration])
        for duration in durations
        if any(shape.size == duration for shape in shapes)
    }
    shape_spread = float('nan')
    if len(mean_shapes) >= MIN_POINTS:
        stacked = np.asarray(list(mean_shapes.values()))
        inner = slice(SHAPE_GRID // 10, SHAPE_GRID - SHAPE_GRID // 10)
        spread = (stacked.max(axis=0) - stacked.min(axis=0))[inner] / stacked.mean(axis=0)[inner]
        shape_spread = float(np.mean(spread))
    return CracklingNoiseResult(
        found.times,
        found.values,
        found.labels,
        sizes,
        lasting,
        shapes,
        float(np.polyfit(np.log(kept), np.log(means), 1)[0]),
        predicted,
        mean_shapes,
        shape_spread,
    )

docs.title: BenardMarangoniSystem(shape=(64, 64), *, length=16 * math.pi, r=0.1, g=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The order-parameter equation of Bénard-Marangoni convection.

The convection forms hexagonal cells.

The field u is the vertical velocity at mid-depth of a heated layer whose open surface has a surface tension that falls with temperature. It follows u_t = r u - (1 + laplacian)^2 u + g u^2 - u^3, the Swift-Hohenberg equation of convection with the quadratic term that the thermocapillary surface adds by breaking the symmetry between rising and sinking fluid. With g > 0 and small r > 0, the cells are hexagons of rising fluid with a wavenumber near 1, and with g = 0, the layer of a fixed surface, they are rolls. The system has the field layer.u.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

Vorticity and temperature of Boussinesq convection.

The units are those of the thermal diffusion time.

The temperature theta is the departure from the linear profile between a hot bottom and a cold top, so dtheta/dt + u . grad(theta) = w + laplacian(theta) and domega/dt + u . grad(omega) = Pr laplacian(omega) + Ra Pr dtheta/dx. The densities f_plus and f_minus move at the speeds c and -c.

The HPP lattice gas on a periodic square lattice.

Its particles move along four directions and collide.

Every site holds up to four particles, one per direction. Every step the particles first collide, where a site with exactly two particles of opposite directions turns them by a quarter turn and every other site keeps its particles, and then every particle moves one site along its direction. The rules are deterministic and reversible, and they conserve the number of particles and the momentum, and also the momentum along every row and every column, a spurious invariant that keeps the HPP gas from isotropic hydrodynamics. Every channel is occupied at random with probability density, or bump inside a disc at the centre. With full, as in Problem 4.3 of Lindgren, the particles start only in full cells, which hold all four directions, placed at random with probability density. The system has the channels gas.n0 to gas.n3 and the particle numbers gas.density.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation u_t = -u u_x - u_xx - u_xxxx.

The equation is spatiotemporally chaotic.

The field is spectral on a periodic line, started from cos(x / 16) (1 + sin(x / 16)) as in Kassam and Trefethen, and the stiff fourth derivative suits exponential time differencing.

The derivative of the nonlinear term u²/2 is dealiased by the two-thirds rule: it keeps only the wavenumbers below a third of 2 π modes / length, 2.67 for the defaults, so the spectrum drops to round-off from q = 2.69 on. The cut costs little, since the modes there decay at the rate q⁴ - q² above 45, and with the defaults the power at the last kept mode is five decades below the peak near q = 0.6. More modes on the same length move the cut up in proportion. The system has the field line.u.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Rayleigh-Bénard convection between free-slip walls.

The convection starts from a small perturbation of the critical mode.

The layer has height 1 and width 2 sqrt(2), the wavelength of the critical mode, and convection sets in above Ra = 27 pi^4 / 4, about 657.5. The lattice holds twice the layer's height with odd states, which gives the free-slip walls. The registered step ETDRK4Solver(dt=0.005) is stable up to about Ra = 4000, and faster convection needs a smaller step, such as ETDRK4Solver(dt=0.0025) at Ra = 5000. The system has the vorticity flow.omega and the temperature departure flow.theta.

def incompressible_flow(
    shape: Sequence[int] = (64, 64),
    size: Sequence[float] = (2 * math.pi, 2 * math.pi),
    *,
    nu: float = 1e-3,
    forcing: npt.ArrayLike | None = None,
    buoyancy: Mapping[str, float] | None = None,
    walls: bool = False,
    vorticity: npt.ArrayLike | None = None,
    temperature: npt.ArrayLike | None = None,
    label: str = 'system',
) -> CompositeSystem:
    """Return incompressible two-dimensional flow in vorticity-streamfunction form.

    The flow is on a periodic spectral lattice.

    Args:
        shape:
            The number of sites along both axes.

        size:
            The lengths of the domain along both axes.

        nu:
            The kinematic viscosity, unused with buoyancy, whose viscosity is the Prandtl number.

        forcing:
            The forcing of the vorticity at every site, or `None`.

        buoyancy:
            The Rayleigh number `Ra` and the Prandtl number `Pr` of Boussinesq convection with a temperature field,
            or `None` for a flow without temperature.

        walls:
            Whether the second axis is twice the height of a layer between free-slip walls in its middle and at its
            ends, the vorticity and temperature being odd about them.

        vorticity:
            The initial vorticity, or `None` for rest.

        temperature:
            The initial temperature departure of convection, or `None` for zero.

        label:
            The label of the system.

    Returns:
        system:
            The flow, with the vorticity `flow.omega` and, with buoyancy, the temperature `flow.theta`.

    Examples:
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.fluids import incompressible_flow
        >>> incompressible_flow((16, 16), buoyancy={'Ra': 800.0, 'Pr': 1.0}).elements[0].element.__name__
        'BoussinesqElement'
    """
    shape = tuple(int(item) for item in shape)
    space = LatticeSpace(shape, spacing=tuple(length / count for length, count in zip(size, shape, strict=True)))
    values: dict[str, object] = {}
    if vorticity is not None:
        values['omega'] = np.asarray(vorticity, dtype=float)
    if buoyancy is None:
        element: type[Element] = VorticityElement
        values['nu'] = nu
        if forcing is not None:
            values['f'] = np.asarray(forcing, dtype=float)
    else:
        element = BoussinesqElement
        values.update({key: float(value) for key, value in buoyancy.items()})
        if temperature is not None:
            values['theta'] = np.asarray(temperature, dtype=float)
    states = ['omega'] if buoyancy is None else ['omega', 'theta']
    symmetry = dict.fromkeys(states, (None, 'odd')) if walls else None
    field = FieldElement(
        'flow',
        element=element,
        space=space,
        values=values,
        discretization='spectral',
        symmetry=symmetry,
    )
    return CompositeSystem(label, elements=[field], interactions=_get_flow_interactions(buoyancy is not None))

def harmonic(x: Array, y: Array) -> Array:
    """Return the harmonic function `exp(x) sin(y)`.

    It is a steady temperature known in closed form.

    Args:
        x:
            The first coordinates.

        y:
            The second coordinates.

    Returns:

docs.title: BeamBeamMapSystem(x=0.5, y=0.0, *, nu=0.3, c=0.05, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The beam-beam map of a particle of an accelerator beam.

The particle meets the opposite beam once every turn.

Every turn the transverse position and momentum rotate by the angle pi nu of the tune, u = a x + b y with a = cos(pi nu) and b = sin(pi nu), and the round Gaussian charge of the opposite beam kicks the momentum: x' = u, y' = -b x + a y - 8 pi c (1 - exp(-u² / 2)) / u. The map preserves area, as the composition of a rotation and a kick. The origin is a fixed point, whose linearisation has the trace 2 a - 4 pi c b and is elliptic when the trace lies in (-2, 2), and the phase space mixes invariant curves, island chains, and chaotic layers. The system has the states particle.x and particle.y.

Parameters:

The initial transverse position.

0.5 y float

The initial transverse momentum.

Bases: EulerLagrangeInteraction

Motion of a pendulum clock on a moving support.

The motion is the Euler-Lagrange equations with the escapement.

The Lagrangian is (M + m) x'² / 2 + m l x' θ' cos θ + m l² θ'² / 2 + m g l cos θ. The Rayleigh dissipation λ l sgn(|θ| - θ_c) θ'² + rho x'² damps the support and gives the escapement 2 λ l sgn(|θ| - θ_c) θ', which pumps energy into the pendulum below the angle θ_c and takes it out beyond.

The spring stretches with the horizontal distance l2 sin θ2 - l1 sin θ1 of the bobs and adds the torque k l1 (l2 sin θ2 - l1 sin θ1) cos θ1 to the first pendulum and the opposite one to the second. Identical pendulums have the normal modes sqrt(g / l) in phase and sqrt(g / l + 2 k / m) in antiphase. The system has the pendulums left and right and their angles left.theta and right.theta.

docs.title: FrictionOscillatorSystem(x=1.03, v=0.0, *, m=1.0, k=1.0, c=0.0, mu_s=0.06, mu_k=0.05, g=1.0, v_stick=0.01, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

A mass on a linear spring with static, Coulomb, and viscous friction.

The mass follows m x'' + c x' + k x + f = 0.

While the mass slides, the friction f = mu_k m g sign(x') opposes its motion, so in each half of the phase plane the motion is linear, around the shifted centres x = ∓ mu_k m g / k. At rest the static friction holds the mass while |k x| <= mu_s m g, so the system has a whole segment of equilibria rather than isolated ones. Without viscous friction, every half swing ends 2 mu_k m g / k closer to the origin, and the mass sticks at the first turning point inside the segment, after finitely many swings. The friction is discontinuous, so the mass counts as at rest below the speed v_stick. The system has the position mass.x and the velocity mass.v.

Bases: BaseSystem

A gyroscope in a gimbal.

A rotor in an inner ring turns in an outer ring about a fixed axis.

The outer ring turns by alpha about the fixed axis, the inner ring by beta in the outer ring, and the rotor spins by gamma in the inner ring. The equations are the Lagrange equations of the kinetic energy [A2 + (A + A1) cos² beta + (C + C1) sin² beta] alpha'² / 2 + (A + B1) beta'² / 2 + C alpha' gamma' sin beta + C gamma'² / 2, with a torque on the axis of the inner ring, which makes the fast rotor precess about the fixed axis. The momenta conjugate to alpha and gamma are conserved. The system has the angles gyroscope.alpha, gyroscope.beta, and gyroscope.gamma, all of order 2.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Pendulum clocks on supports joined by springs.

The clocks synchronize through the motion of the supports.

Every pendulum hangs from a support of mass M that moves horizontally with damping rho, and neighbouring supports are joined by springs of stiffness k. A pendulum follows m l θ'' + f(θ) θ' + m g sin θ = -m x'' cos θ and its support (M + m) x'' + 2 rho x' + m l θ'' cos θ = m l θ'² sin θ + spring forces. The escapement f(θ) = 2 λ sgn(|θ| - θ_c) is -2 λ for |θ| < θ_c, pumping energy in, and 2 λ beyond, so every clock has a limit cycle. With λ = 0 the clocks are plain pendulums. Two identical clocks synchronize in antiphase. The first clock starts at theta, away from the switch of the escapement at θ_c, and the others at rest. The system has the angles clock_<i>.theta and the support positions clock_<i>.x, all of order 2.

docs.title: ParametricPendulumInteraction(label, *, target, direction='vertical')
docs.text:
Bases: EulerLagrangeInteraction

Motion of a pendulum whose suspension point oscillates.

The point oscillates vertically or horizontally, and the motion is an Euler-Lagrange equation.

The suspension point accelerates by ε g cos Ω t. Vertically, the Lagrangian per moment of inertia is θ'² / 2 + (g / l)(1 + ε cos Ω t) cos θ, and the acceleration modulates gravity, a parametric forcing. Horizontally, it is θ'² / 2 + (g / l)(cos θ - ε cos Ω t sin θ), and the acceleration pushes the bob sideways, an external forcing. The Rayleigh dissipation c θ'² / 2 adds the friction, so the angle follows θ'' + c θ' + (g / l)(1 + ε cos Ω t) sin θ = 0 or θ'' + c θ' + (g / l)(sin θ + ε cos Ω t cos θ) = 0, with the parameters of the target.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the pendulum.

required direction str

The direction in which the suspension point oscillates, 'vertical' or 'horizontal'.

'vertical'

Raises:

Type Description ValidationError

The direction is unknown.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.mechanics import ParametricPendulumInteraction
>>> ParametricPendulumInteraction('swing', target='pendulum').states
'theta'

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A pendulum whose suspension point oscillates vertically or horizontally.

The suspension point has the acceleration ε g cos Ω t.

Vertically, the acceleration of the suspension point modulates gravity, θ'' + c θ' + (g / l)(1 + ε cos Ω t) sin θ = 0. Small oscillations grow when Ω is close to twice the natural frequency sqrt(g / l), the parametric resonance of a swing, while a pendulum at rest stays at rest. Horizontally, the acceleration pushes the bob sideways, θ'' + c θ' + (g / l)(sin θ + ε cos Ω t cos θ) = 0, which for small angles is a harmonic oscillator under an external force. Its amplitude grows linearly in time, as ε Ω t / 2, when Ω equals the natural frequency, the linear resonance, and the pendulum starts to swing even from rest. The system has the angle swing.theta of order 2.

Bases: BaseSystem

Two balls on rods that turn about a vertical axis.

The balls conserve their angular momentum.

docs.text:
Bases: EulerLagrangeInteraction

Motion of a rotating swing.

The motion is the Euler-Lagrange equations with a torque and friction on the stand.

The Lagrangian is [J + n m (a + l sin θ)²] φ'² / 2 + n m l² θ'² / 2 + n m g l cos θ, the torque drives the angle φ of the stand, and the Rayleigh dissipation c φ'² / 2 adds the friction of its axis.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the swing.

required

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.mechanics import RotatingSwingInteraction

Chairs on chains hang from the rods of a stand that turns about a vertical axis.

docs.title: BilliardsSystem(shape='sinai', x=0.1, y=0.6, vx=0.6, vy=0.8, *, size=1.0, disc_radius=0.4, cap_radius=1.0, width=0.4, height=1.0, spacing=2.4, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A particle moving freely on a billiard table.

The particle reflects specularly off the walls of the table.

The Sinai table is the square [-size, size]² with a disc of radius disc_radius at its center, and its motion is chaotic. The mushroom table is the upper half of a disc of radius cap_radius on a stem of half width width and height height, and its phase space mixes regular orbits that stay in the cap with chaotic orbits that enter the stem. The three-disk table is open: three discs of radius disc_radius sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side spacing centered at the origin, with one disc below the origin. A particle that comes from far away is scattered chaotically between the discs and leaves again, and the number of its collisions and its outgoing angle depend on its incoming direction through a fractal scattering function. Every bounce is an event, and the speed is conserved. The system has the position particle.x, particle.y and the velocity particle.vx, particle.vy.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The forced Toda oscillator x'' + d x' + e^x - 1 = a sin(omega t).

It is a passive asymmetric oscillator.

The exponential spring is stiff for x > 0 and soft for x < 0, unlike the symmetric spring of the Duffing oscillator. Its free frequency falls from 1 as the amplitude grows, so the resonance curve bends to low driving frequencies and the response swings far to the soft side. Stronger driving gives coexisting responses and period doubling cascades to chaos as the driving period 2π / ω changes. The system has the displacement toda.x of order 2 and its velocity toda.x_d1.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

An oscillator kicked by a periodic train of impulses of alternating sign.

The stiff spring gives x'' + tan(x) / cos²(x) = 2 H Σ_k (-1)^k δ(t - (2 k - 1) a), a strongly nonlinear oscillator whose free motion sin x = sin A sin(t / cos A) of amplitude A < π / 2 is known exactly. Between the impulses the oscillator rings freely, and every impulse is an event that kicks its velocity, by -2 H at the times (4 k + 1) a and by 2 H at the times (4 k + 3) a. A motion of amplitude A is periodic with the period 4 a of the impulses when an impulse reverses its velocity, which gives a = q arccos(H q² / sqrt((1 - q²) (1 - q² H²))) with q = cos A, for arctan H < A < π / 2. The defaults start the orbit of amplitude A = 1.2 for H = 2, from x = 0 with the speed tan A.

The temporal dipole shift gamma in (-1, 1) replaces the rectangular wave whose derivative gives the impulses with the derivative of an asymmetric saw-tooth wave: the negative impulses move to (4 k + 1 - gamma) a, the positive ones to (4 k + 3 + gamma) a, and both grow to 2 H / (1 - gamma²). The linear spring gives the harmonic oscillator x'' + omega0² x under the same impulses. The system has the displacement oscillator.x of order 2 and its velocity oscillator.x_d1, kicked by the impulses pull and push.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The quadrupole vibrations of a nuclear surface.

The vibrations are a Hamiltonian system of two degrees of freedom.

The deformation coordinates q = (q1, q2) and their momenta p move under the Hamiltonian H = (q² + p²) / 2 + B q1 (3 q2² - q1²) / √2 + q⁴ / 8, which is conserved. The cubic term has the threefold symmetry of the Hénon-Heiles potential, and the quartic term keeps every orbit bounded, so the motion is regular at low and high energies and largely chaotic in between. The system has the coordinates nucleus.q1 and nucleus.q2, their momenta nucleus.p1 and nucleus.p2, and the observable nucleus.energy.

Bases: BaseSystem

The Stuart-Landau oscillator z' = (μ + i ω) z - (1 + i β) |z|² z.

It is the normal form of a Hopf bifurcation.

Oceanography systems.

The package covers the thermohaline circulation and the wind-driven gyres.

docs.title: DoubleGyreSystem(n_sites=64, *, length=1.0, beta=1.0, Rd=1.0, nu=0.000125, tau0=1e-05, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The quasi-geostrophic double gyre.

It is the wind-driven circulation of a closed ocean basin.

The potential vorticity q = laplacian(psi) - psi / Rd**2 + beta y of a square basin of side length is carried by the geostrophic velocity (-psi_y, psi_x) of the streamfunction psi, driven by the curl of the wind stress -tau0 cos(2 pi y / length), and damped by the viscosity nu. The state is the relative potential vorticity zeta = q - beta y, held at zero on the walls for free slip, so that

zeta_t + divergence(u zeta) = -beta psi_x - tau0 (2 pi / length) sin(2 pi y / length) + nu laplacian(zeta),

with psi = inverse_helmholtz(zeta, 1 / Rd, ('fixed', 0)). In the viscous steady regime the interior follows the Sverdrup balance beta psi_x = curl(tau), and the return flow closes in Munk western boundary layers of width (nu / beta) ** (1 / 3), so the streamfunction forms a subtropical and a subpolar gyre of opposite sign whose extrema lie close to the western wall. The defaults keep the wind weak, so the boundary layers stay viscous rather than inertial, and the circulation is steady after a few hundred units of time. The catalog entry streams the streamfunction as the observable psi. The system has the relative potential vorticity basin.zeta.

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

Stommel's two-box thermohaline circulation.

The circulation is bistable between a thermal and a haline mode.

The dimensionless differences of temperature T and salinity S between an equatorial and a polar box relax to their forcing and are mixed by a flow proportional to the density difference |T - S|: dT/dt = eta1 - T (1 + |T - S|) and dS/dt = eta2 - S (eta3 + |T - S|). For the default parameters a strong circulation driven by temperature and a weak one driven by salinity are both stable. The system has the differences ocean.T and ocean.S.

docs.title: AllenCahnSystem(shape=(128, 128), *, length=128.0, mean=0.0, kappa=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Allen-Cahn equation, System A.

It is the non-conserved relaxation of an order parameter in a double well.

The order parameter follows phi_t = phi - phi^3 + kappa laplacian(phi), the gradient descent of the free energy density -phi^2 / 2 + phi^4 / 4 + kappa |grad(phi)|^2 / 2. From small noise, domains of phi = 1 and phi = -1 form and coarsen as their walls move by curvature, so their size grows as t^(1/2). The mean of phi is not conserved, and a domain shrinks away instead of exchanging material with its neighbours. The system has the field mixture.phi.

1.0 random_state int | Generator | None

0 label str

'system'

Examples:

>>> AllenCahnSystem((8, 8), kappa=2.0).prepare().system_.interactions[0].kappa

docs.title: CahnHilliardSystem(shape=(64, 64), *, length=64.0, mean=0.0, kappa=1.0, temperature=0.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Cahn-Hilliard equation, System B.

It is the conserved relaxation of an order parameter in a double well.

The order parameter follows phi_t = laplacian(-phi + phi^3 - kappa laplacian(phi)), a diffusion down the gradient of the chemical potential of the same free energy as the Allen-Cahn equation. Inside the spinodal, |mean| < 1 / sqrt(3), small noise decomposes into domains of phi near 1 and -1, which coarsen by diffusion through the bulk so that their size grows as t^(1/3), while the mean of phi stays fixed.

A positive temperature adds the thermal noise of System B, div(sqrt(2 temperature) eta), which conserves the mean of phi as well. The field then uses finite differences, and an SDE solver such as EulerMaruyamaSolver integrates it, with a step below spacing^4 / (32 kappa). The system has the field mixture.phi.

The number of sites along every axis of the periodic lattice.

(64, 64) length float

0.0 kappa float

The stiffness of the interfaces.

1.0 temperature float

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The nonreciprocal Cahn-Hilliard equations.

A demixing field is coupled to a diffusing one.

The conserved field phi phase separates and the conserved field psi diffuses, and they are coupled through cross-diffusion, phi_t = laplacian(-phi + phi^3 - kappa laplacian(phi) + (chi + alpha) psi) and psi_t = laplacian(D psi + (chi - alpha) phi), the minimal system of Brauns and Marchetti. The coupling chi is reciprocal and alpha is not. When alpha^2 - chi^2 exceeds D^2, the unstable band of the dispersion relation of the mixed state reaches the propagating modes, and the demixed domains travel instead of coarsening. The system has the demixing field mixture.phi and the diffusing field mixture.psi.
