docs.title: Seismology
docs.text:
Seismology systems.

The package covers earthquakes on loaded faults.

docs.title: BurridgeKnopoffSystem(n_blocks=20, *, k_c=2.5, k_p=1.0, velocity=0.01, F0=1.0, v_c=0.5, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Burridge-Knopoff fault.

A chain of blocks pulled by a moving plate sticks and slips.

Every block is coupled to its neighbours by springs of stiffness k_c and to a plate moving at velocity by a leaf spring of stiffness k_p. A block at rest stays stuck until its spring force exceeds the static friction F0, and a sliding block feels the friction F0 / (1 + v / v_c), which weakens with its speed, so slips spread as earthquakes of many sizes. The ends of the chain are free, and the blocks start at small random offsets.

The drift switches whenever a block sticks or starts to slide, and these switches of single blocks give no events, so the adaptive default solver stalls on them: LSODA gives way to RK45 after its stall guard fires, and 2000 time units take about 24 s. The registered solver is RK4Solver(dt=0.05), well inside the stability limit set by the highest frequency sqrt(k_p + 4 k_c), which runs the same span in about 3.5 s with the same statistics of slips. The system has the positions fault.x and velocities fault.v of the blocks.

The number of blocks.

The stiffness of the springs between neighbouring blocks.

Springs and a moving plate pull the block against a friction that weakens.

docs.title: Soft matter
docs.text:
Soft matter systems.

The package covers Brownian particles, optical and hydrodynamically coupled traps, anomalous diffusion, and transitions.

docs.title: AnisotropicBrownianParticlesSystem(n_particles=200, *, D_par=1.0, D_perp=1.0, D_r=0.75, D_spin=0.75, D_c=0.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Overdamped axisymmetric Brownian particles in three dimensions.

The particles translate and rotate.

Every particle diffuses with D_par along its axis u and with D_perp across it, its axis diffuses on the unit sphere with D_r, so that <u(t) . u(0)> = exp(-2 D_r t), and it spins about its axis with D_spin. The defaults are a Janus sphere of unit radius, D_par = D_perp = D_t and D_r = 3 D_t / 4, whose orientation is visible although its diffusion is isotropic. A prolate ellipsoid has D_par > D_perp from Perrin's factors, so its displacement over times shorter than 1 / D_r is elongated along its axis. A chiral body, such as a spiral, has a coupling D_c of the translation along its axis and the rotation about it, <dr_par dpsi> = 2 D_c dt. These are Challenges 5.1 to 5.3 of Argun et al. The axis is held as a unit vector and rescaled to unit length after every step, and the particles start at the origin with axes drawn uniformly on the sphere. The system has the positions particles.x, particles.y, particles.z, the axes particles.ux, particles.uy, particles.uz, and the spins particles.psi.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

Axisymmetric Brownian particle in three dimensions.

Its diffusion tensor turns with its axis.

The position r = (x, y, z) diffuses with D_par along the unit axis u = (ux, uy, uz) and with D_perp across it, dr = (sqrt(2 D_par) u u + sqrt(2 D_perp) (I - u u)) dW. The axis diffuses on the unit sphere, du = -2 D_r u dt + sqrt(2 D_r) (I - u u) dW_r in the Itô form, and a boundary rescales it to unit length after every step against the drift of the discrete steps. The spin psi about the axis diffuses with D_spin, and its noise is correlated with the displacement along the axis through the coupling D_c of a chiral body, so that <dr_par dpsi> = 2 D_c dt, which needs D_c² <= D_par D_spin.

The diffusion coefficient of Brownian walkers changes at random times.

docs.title: BiasedTrapWalkSystem(n_walkers=100, *, n_sites=300, alpha=0.5, tau0=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Walkers that hop always to the right through quenched traps.

The trapping times are broadly distributed.

Every walker moves along its own line of sites and stays tau_i steps on site i before it hops to site i + 1. The trapping times are drawn once, as ceil(tau0 u^(-1 / alpha)) for uniform numbers u, so their distribution decays as tau0^alpha / tau^(1 + alpha). For alpha < 1 their mean diverges, the time to cross N sites grows as N^(1 / alpha), and the displacement grows subdiffusively as x ~ (t / tau0)^alpha, with the mean <x> = (t / tau0)^alpha sin(pi alpha) / (pi alpha) at long times. The walkers start on the first site. The system has the lattice traps of shape (n_walkers, n_sites) and the mean displacement position.

Parameters:

docs.text:
Bases: StokesianMobilityInteraction

Blinking optical traps on spheres that move through a shared fluid.

The spheres move in steps of Brownian dynamics.

Every sphere feels the harmonic force -k (x - center) of its own trap while the traps are on, for on_time of every period on_time + off_time, and no force while they are off. The mobility turns the forces on all spheres into their velocities, and the thermal energy temperature adds Brownian displacements whose correlations between spheres follow the same mobility, so spheres released from their traps diffuse together (Batchelor 1976). Every step lasts dt, and the time of the system counts steps.

A Brownian particle that settles on a wall.

Its diffusion slows near the wall, D(z) = D0 z² / (z² + a²).

The diffusion is a smooth form of the hydrodynamic hindrance that vanishes at the wall, and the drift is the settling velocity scaled by the same mobility. The laws are symmetric about the wall at z = 0, which reflects the particle at every frame. The system has the distance particle.z.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Particles whose velocity is driven by Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise xi.

The velocity follows dv/dt = -gamma v + xi.

The noise follows tau dxi = -xi dt + sqrt(2 D) dW, so its correlation is <xi(t) xi(t')> = D / tau exp(-|t - t'| / tau), and it tends to the white noise of intensity 2 D as tau goes to 0. The stationary velocity variance is <v^2> = D / (gamma (1 + gamma tau)), which is D / gamma in the white noise limit. The velocities start at 0 and the noise starts in its stationary state. Solver steps must be short against tau. The system has the velocities particles.v and the noise particles.xi.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Brownian particles in a random speckle field.

The particles are trapped at hotspots for longer as the field grows stronger.

The hotspots sit at random places in a square, with intensities r^(-1/2) and decay lengths length r^(-1/2) for independent uniform numbers r. The particles start at random places in the middle half of the square.

The default strength 30 draws the particles into the hotspots over the first ten time units and lets them escape now and then, so from time 10 to 60 their mean squared displacement grows as t^0.36, a tenth of free diffusion. A strength of 100 or more traps every particle within the first frames and leaves only the rattling inside one hotspot, with a flat mean squared displacement. The system has the positions beads.x.

Bases: Element

Two Brownian or active spheres joined by a rigid rod.

The dimer is described by the centre and the angle of the rod.

Each sphere diffuses with D_t and swims at the speed v0 along its own orientation, theta1 or theta2, which diffuse with D_r, and the rod keeps them at the distance L. Moving both spheres freely and then restoring their distance moves the centre c by the mean of their displacements and turns the rod by the part of their relative displacement across it, so in the limit of small steps dc = v0 (n1 + n2) / 2 dt + sqrt(D_t) dW and dphi = v0 (n1 - n2) . e / L dt + 2 sqrt(D_t) / L dW, with e = (-sin phi, cos phi) across the rod.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The on-off flashing ratchet.

Brownian particles move in a sawtooth potential switched on and off at random.

The potential switches at the rate rate, so on and off phases last 1 / rate on average. While it is off the particles diffuse freely, and while it is on they slide to the minima of the sawtooth. A potential that rises over a short fraction asymmetry of its period sends more particles over its near maximum than over its far one, so the particles drift with a mean velocity of the sign of 0.5 - asymmetry, and a symmetric potential gives no current. The switching times are drawn once, as a Poisson process over duration shared by every particle. The particles start at the minimum at the origin. The system has the positions particles.x.

Bases: RateInteraction

Sawtooth potential on overdamped particles on a line.

The potential is turned on and off at given times.

Its force is the rate of the position, divided by the friction gamma of the target.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Two Brownian spheres in blinking optical traps.

The free motion of the spheres is correlated through the fluid.

The traps hold the spheres at a distance separation along x, and switch off for off_time after every on_time. While they are off the spheres diffuse freely, and the force on one moves the other through the mobility, so their displacements correlate as M_12 / M_11. That is about 3 a / (2 r) along the line of centres and 3 a / (4 r) across it. The units are micrometres, seconds, and piconewtons, so the defaults are spheres of radius 1 um in water at room temperature, and each step of the system lasts step seconds. The system has the positions spheres.x.

docs.title: RigidDimersSystem(n_dimers=100, *, L=1.0, v0=0.0, D_t=0.1, D_r=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Colloidal molecules.

Pairs of Brownian or active spheres are joined by rigid rods, free in the plane.

Each sphere diffuses with D_t, and an active sphere also swims at the speed v0 along its own orientation, which diffuses with D_r. The rod keeps the spheres at the distance L. Diffusing both spheres freely and then restoring their distance, the scheme of Problem 5.1 of Argun et al., gives in the limit of small steps a centre that diffuses with D_t / 2 and a rod angle that diffuses with 2 D_t / L², so the rotational diffusion of the molecule falls as L^-2 in this free-draining model. Active spheres, Problem 9.3, swim together along the mean of their orientations and turn the rod with the part of their difference across it, which raises the long-time diffusion of the centre to D_t / 2 + v0² / (4 D_r). The dimers start at the origin with random rod angles and orientations. The system has the centres dimers.c, the rod angles dimers.phi, and the orientations dimers.theta1 and dimers.theta2. The spheres sit at c ± (L / 2) (cos phi, sin phi).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_dimers int

The number of dimers.

100 L float

The length of the rod.

1.0 v0 float

The swimming speed of each sphere, 0 for Brownian spheres.

0.0 D_t float

The translational diffusion coefficient of each sphere.

0.1 D_r float

The rotational diffusion coefficient of the orientation of each sphere.

1.0 random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the initial angles and orientations.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.soft_matter import RigidDimersSystem
>>> RigidDimersSystem(5, L=2.0).prepare().system_.elements[0].values['L']

docs.title: ShakenSpringBlockSystem(n_blocks=50, *, k=1.0, anchor=0.0, mu_s=1.0, mu_d=0.8, amplitude=2.0, shake_time=2.0, relax_time=8.0, v_stick=0.02, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A chain of blocks joined by springs on a frictional substrate.

The chain is shaken and relaxed in turn.

Every block of unit weight feels the springs to its neighbours, k (x_{i+1} + x_{i-1} - 2 x_i), an optional spring of stiffness anchor to its rest position, and Coulomb friction. A sliding block feels the dynamic friction -mu_d sign(v), and a block at rest stays at rest while the spring force on it is below the static friction mu_s. In every cycle a random force of intensity amplitude^2 shakes the blocks for shake_time, and then the chain relaxes for relax_time to a blocked configuration, where the elongations xi_i = x_{i+1} - x_i satisfy k |xi_{i+1} - xi_i| < mu_s. Repeated cycles sample blocked configurations, whose energy per spring grows with the shaking, and whose elongations are correlated over a length that grows with that energy. Without springs between blocks and with an anchor, the blocks are independent, and their blocked positions satisfy |x_i| < mu_s / anchor. A block counts as at rest below the speed v_stick, which must exceed the change of speed (mu_s + mu_d) h of a solver step h. The ends of the chain are free, and the blocks start at rest. The system has the positions chain.x and velocities chain.v of the blocks.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_blocks int

The number of blocks.

50 k float

The stiffness of the springs between neighbouring blocks.

1.0 anchor float

The stiffness of the springs that hold every block to its rest position.

0.0 mu_s float

The static friction coefficient.

1.0 mu_d float

The dynamic friction coefficient.

0.8 amplitude float

The amplitude of the random shaking force.

2.0 shake_time float

The duration of the shaking in every cycle.

2.0 relax_time float

The duration of the relaxation in every cycle.

8.0 v_stick float

The speed below which a block counts as at rest.

0.02 label str

Examples:

>>> ShakenSpringBlockSystem(5).prepare().system_.elements[0].prepare().size_

docs.title: TiltedPeriodicPotentialSystem(n_particles=500, *, f=1.0, U0=0.5, L=1.0, gamma=1.0, kT=0.5, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Overdamped particles in a tilted periodic potential.

The potential is V(x) = U0 cos(2 pi x / L) - f x.

The force f breaks the left and right symmetry, so the particles reach a nonequilibrium steady state with a uniform probability current J. The particles start at the origin. The system has the positions particles.x.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

Site of a line of traps.

The site holds a walker for its trapping time tau before the walker hops to the right.

The walker on a site counts the steps it has spent there with clock and hops to the next site after tau steps, and every site keeps a record of whether a walker has visited it. docs.title: ASEPSystem(n_sites=100, *, alpha=0.3, gamma=0.7, p=1.0, q=0.0, density=0.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The asymmetric simple exclusion process on an open line, in continuous time.

A particle hops to the empty right neighbour at rate p and to the empty left neighbour at rate q, enters the empty first site at rate alpha, and leaves the last site at rate gamma, the exit rate that Bertin writes gamma and others write beta. For p = 1 and q = 0 the current is alpha (1 - alpha) in the low-density phase alpha < 1/2, gamma > alpha, gamma (1 - gamma) in the high-density phase gamma < 1/2, gamma < alpha, and 1/4 in the maximal-current phase alpha, gamma > 1/2. The system has the occupations lane.n.

docs.title: AbsorbingBirthDeathSystem(*, kappa=2.0, nu=1.0, lam=1.0, volume=100.0, density=1.0, epsilon=0.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The fully connected branching and annihilation process.

The process is active above kappa = nu until it dies out.

The deterministic density obeys d rho / dt = (kappa - nu) rho - lambda rho^2, with the active fixed point rho_0 = (kappa - nu) / lambda. With fluctuations the empty state absorbs every run, but above the transition the active state is metastable, with relative fluctuations sigma / rho_0 = (lambda / (kappa - nu)) sqrt(kappa / (lambda V)) and a lifetime that grows like exp(V phi(0)) / nu. Below the transition the particles die out in a time of order 1 / (nu - kappa). A small epsilon makes the empty state leave, as in exercise 3.3 of Bertin. The system has the number of particles particles.n.

The branching rate.

The decay rate.

docs.title: BoltzmannSumInteraction(label, *, target, levels, temperature=1.0, n_spins=1.0)
docs.text:
Bases: Interaction

Boltzmann sums over a group of levels.

The sums give the log partition function, mean energy, and entropy per spin.

The log partition function is ln Z = log sum_j exp(-E_j / T), the mean energy is U = sum_j E_j exp(-E_j / T - ln Z), and the entropy per spin is (ln Z + U / T) / N. The sums reduce in log space, so they do not overflow at any temperature.

docs.title: DissipativeZeroRangeSystem(n_levels=5, *, branches=2, nu=1.0, alpha=0.5, beta_ext=1.0, epsilon0=1.0, dissipation=1.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The dissipative zero-range process on a tree.

Energy is injected at the root and lost at the leaves.

Level j of the tree has m^(j - 1) nodes, each with m branches to the next level. A quantum epsilon0 of energy crosses a branch between levels j and j + 1 at rate nu_j = nu k_j^alpha, k_j = m^(j - 1), in either direction from an occupied node. A reservoir at the inverse temperature beta_ext exchanges quanta with the root, adding one at rate nu exp(-beta_ext epsilon0) and removing one at rate nu, and every leaf loses a quantum at the rate dissipation. The stationary distribution is a product of geometric laws z_j^n, with z_j the solution of the linear balance of the currents nu_j (z_j - z_(j + 1)) at every level, and the injected flux is nu (exp(-beta_ext epsilon0) - z_1). The system has the quanta nodes.n of the nodes in breadth-first order, from the root to the leaves.

Parameters:

The number of levels M.

5 branches int

The number m of branches of every node above the leaves.

1.0 alpha float

The exponent of the growth of the transfer rate with the pseudo wave number k_j.

0.5 beta_ext float

The inverse temperature of the reservoir.

1.0 epsilon0 float

The quantum of energy.

1.0 dissipation float

The rate at which every leaf loses a quantum.

>>> system.elements[0].size, len(system.interactions)

docs.text:
Bases: DynamicalSystem

The Ehrenfest urn system.

Balls move one at a time between two boxes, and the system relaxes to equal counts.

At every step one of the N numbered balls is drawn at random and moved to the other box, so the count n of the first box falls by one with probability n / N and rises by one otherwise. Started with all balls in the first box, the count relaxes to N / 2 with the exponential mean N / 2 + (n_0 - N / 2) (1 - 2 / N)^t, and then fluctuates around it: the chain is reversible, yet the relaxation looks irreversible. Its stationary distribution is the binomial distribution of N balls with probability one half. The system has the count urn.n of balls in the first box.

docs.text:
Bases: Element

State of a discrete master equation on a ring.

The state has a probability P and a potential U.

Every step the probability moves to each neighbouring state B from a state A with the Glauber probability w / (1 + exp(beta (U_B - U_A))), so P_A(t + 1) = P_A + sum_B T_AB P_B - sum_B T_BA P_A, and the stationary distribution is exp(-beta U) / Z.

docs.title: QuantumHeisenbergSystem(n_sites=12, *, J=1.0, delta=1.0, h=0.0, gamma=0.0, boundary='periodic', initial='flip', label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A chain of spins one half with the XXZ Hamiltonian.

The chain has a field and optional dephasing.

The Hamiltonian is J Σ (S^x_i S^x_j + S^y_i S^y_j + Δ S^z_i S^z_j) - h Σ S^z_i over neighbouring pairs, with ħ = 1. A dephasing rate gamma > 0 adds the dissipator S^z_i on every site, so the state is a density matrix that loses its coherence. One flipped spin in a ferromagnetic background spreads as a magnon, whose probability at distance d is J_d(J t)² in the XX chain, a light cone in the space-time image of S^z. The total magnetisation is conserved. The system has the observables sz of every site, magnetization, and the energy.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The random energy system.

It has 2^N quenched Gaussian energies of variance N / 2 at a temperature.

The entropy per spin follows ln 2 - 1 / (4 T^2) above the glass temperature T_g = 1 / (2 sqrt(ln 2)) and freezes below it, where the Boltzmann weight falls on the few lowest levels (Bertin 2021 §1.5.3). The energies are drawn from random_state, so a disorder average sweeps it with sweep. The system has the states ensemble.log_partition, ensemble.energy, and ensemble.entropy.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import RandomEnergySystem
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass with Glauber dynamics.

The glass freezes below the temperature T_c = J.

The energy is -sum_{i<j} J_ij s_i s_j - h sum_i s_i with quenched Gaussian couplings J_ij of mean 0 and variance J^2 / N, drawn once. Above T_c the energy per spin is -J^2 / (2 T), and below it the spins freeze in random directions, with no magnetization. The spins are drawn in a row, which orders the drawing only. The system has the spins spins.spin, the coupling matrix of unit scale in the values of the group, and the observable magnetization.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The totally asymmetric simple exclusion process with parallel update.

The process runs on an open line or a ring.

Every step all particles whose right neighbour is empty hop to it with probability p at once, a transfer along every edge of the lane with one draw per edge. On an open line particles enter the first site with probability alpha and leave the last site with probability beta. On a ring at density rho the current is (1 - sqrt(1 - 4 p rho (1 - rho))) / 2. On an open line the entry and exit probabilities select the low-density, high-density, or maximal-current phase. The system has the occupations lane.occupied and the hops lane.hops, and on an open line the entries entry.flow_0 and the exits exit.flow_0.

Bases: BaseSystem

The Bouchaud trap system.

Walkers escape from traps of exponentially distributed depths.

The escape times tau0 exp(E / T) of depths with the density exp(-E) have the tail tau^(-1 - T). Stick next to the aggregate, or step to a random neighbouring cell.

def walk(self, agent: WalkerView, system: SystemView) -> None:
    """Stick next to the aggregate, or step to a random neighbouring cell.

    Args:
        agent:
            The walker.

        system:
            The system.
    """
    if agent.stuck:
        return
    if any(isinstance(other, WalkerView) and other.stuck for other in agent.get_neighbors()):
        agent.stuck = 1.0
        return
    cells = agent.get_neighbor_cells()
    agent.move_to(cells[int(system.rng.integers(len(cells)))])

    """Return the kinetic temperature `m <|v|²> / d` of the agents of every frame.

    The agents move in `d` dimensions, with `k_B = 1`.

    It is the second moment of the speeds of the agents scaled by the mass over the dimension, as equipartition gives
    `k_B T / 2` per degree of freedom. It reads the velocities of the agents or particles of a trajectory, as the
    alignment of the agents reads them, or an array of velocities of one snapshot, one row per agent, or of one
    snapshot per frame along its first axis.

docs.text:
Return the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the speeds of every frame.

The test compares the speeds with the Maxwell-Boltzmann law.

It is the test of the named law 'maxwell' of fit_law, generalized to d dimensions: the speeds of an ideal gas at temperature T follow a chi law of d degrees of freedom and scale sqrt(T / m), the Maxwell law in three dimensions and the Rayleigh law in two. The temperature is the kinetic temperature of every frame unless it is given. It reads the velocities of the agents or particles of a trajectory, or an array of velocities of one snapshot, one row per agent, or of one snapshot per frame along its first axis.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source Source

The trajectory, or an array of velocities.

required group str | None

The path of the agent or particle group of a trajectory, or None for the first one.

None mass float

The mass of every agent.

1.0 temperature float | None

The temperature of the law, or None for the kinetic temperature of every frame.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description result MaxwellBoltzmannResult

The velocities, the temperature of the law, and the test of every frame.

Raises:

Type Description AnalysisError

The mass or the temperature is not positive, the source is neither a trajectory nor an array, or the agents have no velocities.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import maxwell_boltzmann
>>> velocities = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((2000, 3))
>>> bool(maxwell_boltzmann(velocities).p_value[0] > 0.05)
True
Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/physics/statistical_mechanics/_maxwell_boltzmann.py 
def maxwell_boltzmann(
    source: Source,
    *,
    group: str | None = None,
    mass: float = 1.0,
    temperature: float | None = None,
) -> MaxwellBoltzmannResult:
    """Return the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the speeds of every frame.

    The test compares the speeds with the Maxwell-Boltzmann law.

    It is the test of the named law `'maxwell'` of `fit_law`, generalized to `d` dimensions: the speeds of an ideal gas
    at temperature `T` follow a chi law of `d` degrees of freedom and scale `sqrt(T / m)`, the Maxwell law in three
    dimensions and the Rayleigh law in two. The temperature is the kinetic temperature of every frame unless it is
    given. It reads the velocities of the agents or particles of a trajectory, or an array of velocities of one
    snapshot, one row per agent, or of one snapshot per frame along its first axis.

    Args:
        source:
            The trajectory, or an array of velocities.

        group:
            The path of the agent or particle group of a trajectory, or `None` for the first one.

        mass:
            The mass of every agent.

        temperature:
            The temperature of the law, or `None` for the kinetic temperature of every frame.

    Returns:
        result:
            The velocities, the temperature of the law, and the test of every frame.

    Raises:
        AnalysisError:
            The mass or the temperature is not positive, the source is neither a trajectory nor an array, or the agents
            have no velocities.

    Examples:
        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import maxwell_boltzmann
        >>> velocities = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((2000, 3))
        >>> bool(maxwell_boltzmann(velocities).p_value[0] > 0.05)
        True
    """
    if mass <= 0 or (temperature is not None and temperature <= 0):
        error_msg = f'maxwell_boltzmann has mass={mass!r} and temperature={temperature!r}. Use positive values.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    velocities = _read_velocities(source, group, 'maxwell_boltzmann')
    tests = [_maxwell_boltzmann(frame, mass, temperature) for frame in velocities]
    temperatures, statistics, p_values = np.asarray(tests).T
    return MaxwellBoltzmannResult(velocities, temperatures, statistics, p_values)

The samples are those of an order parameter.

It is the distribution of kind 'moments' of the absolute samples, whose variance it scales by the system size N and divides by the temperature when temperatures are given. Over a sweep of a control parameter, one series per control value, the susceptibility peaks near the transition, and the peak is refined by a parabola through its neighbours.

None parameters Sequence[float] | None

The control parameter value of every series, or None without a peak.

>>> susceptibility([0.5, -1.0, 0.5, -1.0], size=4).susceptibility.tolist()

Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/physics/statistical_mechanics/_susceptibility.py 
def susceptibility(
    source: Source,
    *,
    variables: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    group: str | None = None,
    size: float = 1.0,
    temperatures: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    parameters: Sequence[float] | None = None,
) -> SusceptibilityResult:
    """Return the susceptibility `N (<m²> - <|m|>²)` of every series of samples.

    The samples are those of an order parameter.

    It is the distribution of kind `'moments'` of the absolute samples, whose variance it scales by the system size `N`
    and divides by the temperature when `temperatures` are given. Over a sweep of a control parameter, one series per
    control value, the susceptibility peaks near the transition, and the peak is refined by a parabola through its
    neighbours.

    Args:
        source:
            The trajectory, or an array with one column per series of samples.

        variables:
            The variables of a trajectory to read, or `None` for every scalar series.

        group:
            The path of the agent or particle group whose speeds are read, or `None` for the series of a trajectory.

        size:
            The system size `N` that scales the variance.

        temperatures:
            The temperature of every series that divides the susceptibility, or `None` to leave it undivided.

        parameters:
            The control parameter value of every series, or `None` without a peak.

    Returns:
        result:
            The moments of the absolute samples, the susceptibility, and its peak.

    Raises:
        AnalysisError:
            The system size is not positive.

    Examples:
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import susceptibility
        >>> susceptibility([0.5, -1.0, 0.5, -1.0], size=4).susceptibility.tolist()
        [0.25]
    """
    if size <= 0:
        error_msg = f'susceptibility has size={size!r}. Use a positive size.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    moments = distribution(source, kind='moments', variables=variables, group=group, absolute=True)
    if moments.mean is None or moments.variance is None or moments.skewness is None or moments.kurtosis is None:
        error_msg = 'The distribution of kind moments returned no moments.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    values = size * moments.variance
    if temperatures is not None:
        values = values / np.asarray(temperatures, dtype=float)
    peak = None if parameters is None else _refined_peak(np.asarray(parameters, dtype=float), values)
    return SusceptibilityResult(
        moments.values,
        moments.labels,
        moments.mean,
        moments.variance,
        moments.skewness,
        moments.kurtosis,
        values,
        peak,
    )

The weights relax towards a phase-lagged sine of the phase difference.

docs.title: AdaptiveKuramotoSystem(n_oscillators=50, *, alpha=0.3 * math.pi, beta=0.23 * math.pi, epsilon=0.01, omega=0.0, seed=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Globally coupled phase oscillators with adaptive coupling weights.

The weights adapt to the phase differences.

The oscillators follow the Kuramoto-Sakaguchi model theta_i' = omega - (1 / N) Σ_j kappa_ij sin(theta_i - theta_j + alpha), and every weight of the directed link from j to i adapts as kappa_ij' = -epsilon (kappa_ij + sin(theta_i - theta_j + beta)), Eqs. 28-29 of Berner et al. The weights are states of a group on the edges of the complete directed graph. Even identical oscillators split into frequency clusters: groups whose members share one mean frequency, strongly coupled within and weakly coupled across, with the weights inside a cluster near -sin(theta_i - theta_j + beta). The phases and the weights start uniformly at random in [0, 2 pi) and [-1, 1]. The system has the phases nodes.theta and the weights links.kappa, one per directed link.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Two chaotic maps coupled by aggregate averaging.

The maps synchronize their chaos for strong coupling.

Each map iterates on the aggregate of its own value and the other's, x_i(t + 1) = f(a_i) with a_1 = (1 - kappa) x_1(t) + kappa x_2(t - T) and a_2 = (1 - kappa) x_2(t) + kappa x_1(t - T), for the delay T. The logistic map is f(a) = r a (1 - a). Without delay, its synchronized orbit is stable for kappa > (r - 1) / (2 r), which is 3 / 8 for r = 4, and the maps agree in one step for kappa = 1 / 2. The Bernoulli shift f(a) = r a mod 1 has the constant slope r, so a difference d of the maps follows d(t + 1) = r ((1 - kappa) d(t) - kappa d(t - T)) exactly, and the maps synchronize when every root of z^(T + 1) - r (1 - kappa) z^T + r kappa lies in the unit disk, which for T = 0 is |r (1 - 2 kappa)| < 1. The delay shrinks the window of synchronizing couplings: for r = 1.5 it is 0.17 < kappa < 0.83 without delay, 0.17 < kappa < 0.66 for T = 1, and 0.17 < kappa < 0.44 for T = 2, and it closes for T >= 5. Before the start, the delayed values equal the initial values. An integer slope such as 2 loses one binary digit of the value per step in floating point and falls onto 0, so a slope that is not an integer, such as 1.5, keeps the chaos. The system has the values first.x and second.x, and their lags first.x_lag<j> and second.x_lag<j> for a delay.

Bases: BaseSystem

Chaotic logistic maps on the nodes of a network.

Each map is pulled towards the mean of its neighbours.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Chaotic Rössler oscillators on a ring.

The oscillators are diffusively coupled through their second variable.

Oscillator i follows x1' = -ω_i x2 - x3, x2' = ω_i x1 + a x2 + k sum_j (x2_j - x2_i), and x3' = b + x3 (x1 - c), summed over its neighbours on the ring. Identical oscillators, with no mismatch, synchronize completely when every nonzero eigenvalue of the ring's Laplacian times k falls where the master stability function is negative. The system has the states oscillator_<i>.x1, oscillator_<i>.x2, and oscillator_<i>.x3.

docs.title: HeterogeneousGlobalCouplingSystem(n_systems=100, *, k=2.0, beta=0.1, gamma=2.0, heterogeneity=0.8, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Globally coupled oscillators with heterogeneous time scales.

The coupling restabilizes their fixed point.

System j follows x_j' = τ_j g(x_j, y_j) + k (X - x_j) and y_j' = τ_j h(x_j, y_j) + k (Y - y_j), where X and Y are the population means and g + ih = (beta + i gamma) z - |z|² z is the Hopf normal form of z = x + iy. Its fixed point 0 is an unstable focus with eigenvalues beta ± i gamma. The time scales τ_j are spread evenly over [1 - heterogeneity, 1 + heterogeneity], with mean 1 and variance sigma². The order parameters X, Y, V = <δτ δx>, and W = <δτ δy> close on four equations. The global fixed point is stable when their eigenvalues nu - k / 2 ± √(k² / 4 + sigma² nu²), for nu = beta ± i gamma, have negative real parts, which holds roughly for 2 beta (1 + sigma) < k < (gamma² - beta²) sigma² / beta. The system has the states systems.x and systems.y and the observables amplitude, the mean amplitude, and the order parameters X, Y, V, and W.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Kuramoto oscillators coupled in pairs and by three-body interactions.

The three-body interactions act on the triangles of a hypergraph.

Oscillator i follows theta_i' = omega_i + (K1 / <k1>) sum_j sin(theta_j - theta_i) + (K2 / <k2>) sum_jk sin(theta_j + theta_k - 2 theta_i) over the links ij and the triangles ijk of a random hypergraph, where <k1> and <k2> are the mean numbers of links and of triangles of a node. All-to-all, the triangle term is the three-body coupling of Skardal and Arenas, and the Ott-Antonsen reduction of Lorentzian frequencies of half width width gives r' = -width r + K1 (r - r^3) / 2 + K2 (r^3 - r^5) / 2. Without links, the incoherent state stays stable for every K2, and for K2 > 8 width a synchronized state of r^2 = (1 + sqrt(1 - 8 width / K2)) / 2 coexists with it, so the order parameter depends on the initial phases and sweeps of the coupling show hysteresis. The system has the phases oscillators.theta and the order parameter order.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Kuramoto oscillators coupled along the edges of a network.

The oscillators follow theta_i' = omega_i + K sum_j A_ij sin(...).

Oscillator i follows theta_i' = omega_i + (K / <k>) sum_j w_ij sin(theta_j - theta_i) over its neighbours j, where the weights w_ij = 1 live on a group on the edges and <k> is the mean degree. The coupling runs once per edge. The natural frequencies are drawn from a normal distribution of width sigma, and the phases uniformly from the circle. Above a critical coupling of the order of the all-to-all value 2 sigma sqrt(2 / pi), the order parameter r = |<exp(i theta)>| grows from about 1 / sqrt(N) towards 1, and small-world shortcuts lower it. The system has the phases oscillators.theta, the weights links.w, and the order parameter order.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_oscillators int

The number of oscillators, the nodes of the network.

200 network str

The generator, 'watts_strogatz', 'erdos_renyi', or 'barabasi_albert'.

'watts_strogatz' degree int

The mean degree of the network, even for the Watts-Strogatz ring.

6 rewiring float

The probability of rewiring every edge of the Watts-Strogatz ring.

0.1 K float

The coupling strength, divided by the mean degree.

1.0 sigma float

The standard deviation of the natural frequencies.

0.5 seed int

The seed of the network, the frequencies, and the phases.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

The network is unknown.

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.synchronization import KuramotoOnNetworksSystem
>>> system = KuramotoOnNetworksSystem(20, degree=4).prepare().system_
>>> system.elements[1].prepare().size_
40

docs.title: KuramotoSakaguchiChimeraSystem(n_oscillators=32, *, A=0.2, beta=0.1, spread=0.1, seed=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Two populations of identical phase oscillators with phase lag.

One population synchronizes and one drifts.

Oscillator i of population p follows theta_i' = sum_q (K_pq / N) sum_j sin(theta_j - theta_i - alpha), with the stronger coupling mu = (1 + A) / 2 inside a population, the weaker nu = (1 - A) / 2 between them, and the lag alpha = pi / 2 - beta. Every population reads the means of cos theta and sin theta of both populations. The first population starts nearly synchronized and the second spread over the circle. The populations settle in a chimera, where one is fully synchronized and the other keeps drifting with a partial order parameter, which breathes for A = 0.2. Which population ends up coherent depends on the initial phases. The system has the phases first.theta and second.theta and the order parameters first_order and second_order.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_oscillators int

The number of oscillators of every population.

32 A float

The disparity of the couplings inside and between the populations.

0.2 beta float

The distance of the phase lag from pi / 2.

0.1 spread float

The width of the initial phases of the first population.

0.1 seed int

The seed of the initial phases.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.synchronization import KuramotoSakaguchiChimeraSystem
>>> len(KuramotoSakaguchiChimeraSystem(4).prepare().system_.interactions)
4

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Kuramoto oscillators coupled all to all.

The oscillators follow theta_i' = omega_i + (K / N) sum_j sin(theta_j - theta_i).

Every oscillator reads the group means of cos theta and sin theta, so the coupling costs time linear in the number of oscillators. The natural frequencies are drawn from a normal distribution of width sigma, and the phases uniformly from the circle. Above the critical coupling K_c = 2 sigma sqrt(2 / pi) a synchronized cluster forms, and the order parameter r, the modulus of the mean of exp(i theta), grows from about 1 / sqrt(N) towards 1. The system has the phases oscillators.theta and the order parameter order.

docs.title: LogisticCouplingInteraction(label, *, target, state='x')
docs.text:
Bases: CouplingInteraction

Coupled logistic maps.

The maps follow x_i(t + 1) = (1 - epsilon) f(x_i) + epsilon mean_j f(x_j) with f(x) = r x (1 - x).

The map of every node mixes with the mean of the maps of its neighbours j on its lattice or network, with the parameters r and epsilon of the node. A node with no neighbours keeps (1 - epsilon) f(x_i). It is the map form of coupling, with the mean of the maps of the neighbours combined with the map of the node.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default label str

The label of the interaction, unique among the parts of its system.

required target Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]

The path of the group of maps, on the nodes of a lattice or network.

required state str

The name of the state that the maps iterate.

'x'

Examples:

>>> import networkx as nx
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.elements import GroupElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime, NetworkSpace
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.synchronization import LogisticCouplingInteraction, LogisticNodeElement
>>> from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
>>> maps = GroupElement(
...     'maps',
...     element=LogisticNodeElement,
...     space=NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(2)),
...     values={'x': [0.25, 0.5], 'epsilon': 0.5},
...     on='sites',
... )
>>> coupling = LogisticCouplingInteraction('coupling', target='maps')
>>> system = CompositeSystem(elements=[maps], interactions=[coupling], time=DiscreteTime())
>>> simulate(system, until=1).get_values('maps.x')[-1].tolist()
[0.875, 0.875]

docs.title: MirolloStrogatzSystem(n_oscillators=5, *, S=2.0, gamma=1.0, epsilon=0.1, seed=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Integrate-and-fire oscillators coupled by pulses.

The oscillators end up firing in unison.

Every oscillator of the group charges as x' = S - gamma x, a concave rise, and fires when it reaches 1. Firing is an event whose guard is the group maximum of the charges, and it resets the most charged oscillators to 0 and lifts every other one by epsilon. An oscillator lifted to 1 fires at the same instant and is absorbed into the group that fired, so the groups merge until all oscillators fire together. The system has the charges oscillators.x of the group members and the firings as fire events.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_oscillators int

The number of oscillators.

5 S float

The charging input.

2.0 gamma float

The leak rate, below S so that the oscillators fire.

1.0 epsilon float

The strength of a pulse.

0.1 seed int

The seed of the initial charges.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Examples:

>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.synchronization import MirolloStrogatzSystem
>>> MirolloStrogatzSystem(3).prepare().system_.elements[0].prepare().size_
3

docs.title: OscillatorDeathSystem(n_oscillators=100, *, K=3.0, width=1.5, distribution='lorentzian', random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Globally coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators.

Their oscillations all die for strong coupling and spread.

Oscillator j follows z_j' = (1 + iω_j) z_j - |z_j|² z_j + (K / N) Σ_k (z_k - z_j) for z_j = x_j + i y_j. Alone it settles on the unit circle. The frequencies are the midpoint quantiles of a density of width ω0, the Lorentzian ω0 / (π (ω² + ω0²)) or the quartic g0 / (ω⁴ + ω0⁴). For many oscillators, the common fixed point z = 0 is stable for K > 1 and ω0 above a critical width, 1 for the Lorentzian and (1 + √(2K - 1)) / √2 for the quartic density, and every amplitude then decays to zero. For the Lorentzian, the slowest perturbation decays at the rate ω0 - 1. The system has the states oscillators.x and oscillators.y and the observables amplitude, the mean amplitude, X and Y, the mean field, and order, its modulus.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n_oscillators int

The number of oscillators.

100 K float

The coupling strength.

3.0 width float

The width ω0 of the density of frequencies.

1.5 distribution str

The density of frequencies, 'lorentzian' or 'quartic'.

'lorentzian' random_state int | Generator | None

The seed or generator of the initial phases.

0 label str

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

'system'

Raises:

The distribution is neither 'lorentzian' nor 'quartic'.

Examples:

>>> OscillatorDeathSystem(4, distribution='quartic').prepare().system_.elements[0].prepare().size_

docs.title: OttAntonsenSystem(r=0.1, *, K=2.0, Delta=0.5, omega=0.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Ott-Antonsen equation for the order parameter of Kuramoto oscillators.

The oscillators are infinitely many.

For natural frequencies with a Lorentzian distribution of center omega and half width Delta, the complex order parameter z = x + i y follows exactly z' = (i omega - Delta) z + (K / 2)(1 - |z|²) z, a Stuart-Landau oscillator with the growth rate K / 2 - Delta and the saturation K / 2. Its modulus settles at sqrt(1 - 2 Delta / K) above the critical coupling K_c = 2 Delta, and at 0 below it. The system has the real part field.x and the imaginary part field.y of the order parameter.

Parameters:

The coupling strength.

0.5 omega float

The center of the distribution of natural frequencies.

The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

Examples:

docs.title: RosslerDrivenLorenzSystem(k=8.0, *, auxiliary=True, p=1 / 6, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A chaotic Rössler system that drives a Lorenz-63 system.

The drive acts through the second variable.

The drive follows p x1' = -x2 - x3, p x2' = x1 + 0.2 x2, p x3' = 0.2 + x3 (x1 - 5.7), with the time scale p = 1 / 6 that brings it close to the Lorenz system, and the response follows y1' = 10 (y2 - y1), y2' = 28 y1 - y2 - y1 y3 + k x2, y3' = y1 y2 - 2.666 y3. The two systems have nothing in common, yet for a coupling above k ≈ 6.66 the response forgets its initial state and becomes a function of the state of the drive, generalized synchronization. With auxiliary, a second copy of the response from another initial state receives the same drive, and the two copies converge to each other exactly when generalized synchronization holds, the auxiliary system method. The system has the drive drive.x1, drive.x2, drive.x3, the response response.x, response.y, response.z, and with auxiliary the copy auxiliary.x, auxiliary.y, auxiliary.z.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default k float

The strength of the coupling.

8.0 auxiliary bool

Whether a second copy of the response, auxiliary, receives the drive too.

True p float

The time scale of the drive.

1 / 6 label str

Examples:

docs.title: SwarmalatorCouplingInteraction(label, first, second, cutoff=1000000.0, position='x', *, A=1.0, B=1.0, J=1.0, K=0.0, period=None, n_units=1)
docs.text:
Bases: PairInteraction

Coupling of two swarmalators.

The coupling acts through their separation r and their phase difference dtheta.

Each swarmalator moves toward the other at the speed (A + J cos(dtheta)) / N, away from it at B / (N |r|), and turns its phase toward the other's at the rate K sin(dtheta) / (N |r|), as in O'Keeffe, Ceron, and Petersen. It is a pair coupling of the positions and the phases jointly.

docs.title: SwarmalatorsSystem(n_units=100, *, J=1.0, K=0.0, A=1.0, B=1.0, random_state=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Swarmalators.

The phases of identical oscillators set their attraction and their positions their coupling.

Every swarmalator i moves by (1 / N) sum_j [(x_j - x_i) / |x_j - x_i| (A + J cos(theta_j - theta_i)) - B (x_j - x_i) / |x_j - x_i|^2] and turns by (K / N) sum_j sin(theta_j - theta_i) / |x_j - x_i|. With J > 0 like phases attract. With K = 0 and J = 1 the swarm settles into a static phase wave, a disk whose phase winds once around its center, so one of the order parameters S± = |mean(exp(i (phi ± theta)))| of the spatial angle phi and the phase approaches 1. With K > 0 the phases synchronize into a uniform disk, and with K < 0 and small J they stay asynchronous. The system has the positions units.x and the phases units.theta.

docs.title: TopologicalKuramotoSystem(n_nodes=30, *, density=0.4, coupling=2.0, width=1.0, seed=0, model='NL', label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Phases on the nodes and links of a clique complex.

The phases are coupled through its incidence by order parameters.

Node phases follow theta' = omega + K R_links codifferential(sin(d theta)). Link phases follow phi' = omega + K R_nodes d(sin(codifferential(phi))) - K codifferential(sin(d phi)). With the signs of codifferential, these are the Nodes-Links system of Ghorbanchian et al. (2021), Eq. 6 of the review of Majhi, Perc, and Ghosh (2022, arXiv 2203.06601 §III), which is the source at hand. Here R_nodes is the order parameter of the node phases and R_links that of the projection of the link phases on the nodes. The review takes frequencies of mean Omega and standard deviation 1 / tau, with Omega = 2 and tau = 1 for its Fig. 2, on complexes of 500 nodes. The mean 0, the size, and the random graph are choices of this system.

The Nodes-Links-Triangles system, model='NLT', Eq. 8 of the review, scales the coupling of the link phases through the nodes by R_nodes R_up and through the triangles by R_links, where R_up is the order parameter of the projection of the link phases on the triangles. Every projection then couples to another, so all three order parameters jump together at one explosive transition, while in the Nodes-Links system R_up moves on its own. The system has a group triangles of unit weights on the faces for the Nodes-Links-Triangles system, which only gives the order parameter of the projection on the triangles.

The coupling K.

The standard deviation of the natural frequencies of the nodes and the links.

1.0 seed int

The seed of the graph, the frequencies, and the initial phases.

docs.title: WinfreeSystem(n_oscillators=50, *, K=0.5, spread=0.1, seed=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The Winfree system.

The system follows theta_i' = omega_i + (K / N) sum_j P(theta_j) R(theta_i), with the sum over all j.

The influence P(theta) = 1 + cos(theta) and the sensitivity R(theta) = -sin(theta) make every oscillator respond to the mean influence of the population, which every oscillator reads as a group mean. The natural frequencies are spread evenly over [1 - spread, 1 + spread]. Weak coupling leaves the oscillators incoherent, moderate coupling locks them to one frequency, and strong coupling stops them, which is oscillator death. The system has the phases oscillators.theta and the order parameter order.

docs.title: ChargedSchrodingerSystem(n_sites=256, *, length=80.0, D=0.5, q=1.0, momentum=0.0, width=2.0, A_x=0.0, A_t=0.0, E=1.0, duration=2.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A Gaussian wave packet of a charge in a prescribed electromagnetic potential.

The system follows Schwichtenberg 4.3.

The wave function follows the Schrödinger equation with the covariant derivatives d - i q A, (d_t - i q A_t) psi = i D (d_x - i q A_x)^2 psi, on a periodic line with spectral derivatives. A mode of wave number k turns at the frequency D (k - q A_x)^2 - q A_t, so the packet moves at the group velocity 2 D (k - q A_x). A constant A_x is a pure gauge that only shifts the canonical momentum, while the electric field E switched on for duration changes A_x and accelerates the packet at the rate 2 D q E. The system has the real part packet.u and the imaginary part packet.w of the wave function.

The variables are sampled or evolved in real time.

With Monte Carlo dynamics, link angles sample the Wilson action -beta sum_p cos(theta_p) under discrete time, as U(1) angles or as the angles 2 pi k / n of Z_n. docs.title: LatticeYangMillsSystem(size=6, *, dimension=4, extent=None, colors=2, beta=2.3, width=0.5, hits=4, links=None, seed=0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

SU(2) or SU(3) matrices on the links of a periodic lattice.

The matrices are sampled by the Wilson action.

The link matrices sample the Wilson action -(beta / N) sum_p Re tr U_p under discrete time, where U_p is the ordered product of the link matrices around the plaquette p, with the inverse of a link traversed against its orientation. Every sweep proposes hits Metropolis moves per link, each a product with a random matrix of the group near the identity, and projects the links back onto the group. SU(2) is the isospin connection of the weak force, and SU(3) the color connection of the strong force, so that SU(3) is pure lattice QCD. The last axis has extent sites, the inverse temperature of the lattice, along which the Polyakov loop winds. In two dimensions the plaquettes are independent, and the SU(2) mean plaquette at large size is I_2(beta) / I_1(beta).

docs.title: SchrodingerSystem(n_sites=256, *, length=40.0, D=0.5, momentum=2.0, width=1.0, omega=0.0, formulation='fields', gamma=0.0, label='system')
docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

A Gaussian wave packet that follows the Schrödinger equation.

The packet is written as its real and imaginary parts.

The wave function psi = u + i w follows psi_t = i D laplacian(psi) - i V psi, written as u_t = -D laplacian(w) + V w and w_t = D laplacian(u) - V u, on a periodic lattice with spectral derivatives. In units with ħ = 1, D = 1 / (2 m). The potential is the harmonic well V = omega² x² / (4 D), or zero for a free packet. A free packet of momentum k moves at the group velocity 2 D k and spreads, and its norm sum(u² + w²) is conserved.

The operator formulation builds the same particle as one quantum subsystem whose basis states are the sites, with the Hamiltonian -D laplacian + V of the same spectral Laplacian, normalised so that |psi|² is the probability of every site. It runs with the quantum solvers, and it accepts position dephasing at the rate gamma, which turns the state into a density matrix. The system has the real part packet.u and the imaginary part packet.w of the wave function, or the quantum state <label>.state of the operator formulation.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Masses joined in a row by springs of zero rest length between two anchors.

The chain is a discrete string.

The masses start evenly spaced between the anchors at 0 and length, stretched, so the chain carries tension. With pluck, the masses start on a triangle of that height peaking at the fraction pluck_at of the length, the pluck of a guitar string. With amplitude, the left anchor moves transversally as amplitude sin(omega t) and sends a transverse wave along the chain. Springs of zero rest length are linear, so the transverse modes are independent, with frequencies 2 sqrt(k / m) sin(n pi / (2 (N + 1))). The system has the masses mass_<i> and their positions mass_<i>.x in two dimensions.

docs.title: gauge_observables(source, *, kind, space, variables=None, extents=(1, 1), charges=None, group=None)
docs.text:
Return a gauge observable of a link state on a periodic lattice's cell complex.

There is one value per frame.

The kind 'wilson' is the mean cosine of the oriented sum of the link angles around the rectangles of given extents in every plane. The kind 'polyakov' is the mean cosine of the sum of the link angles along the last axis. The kind 'charge' is the sum over the plaquettes of a two-dimensional lattice of the oriented sums wrapped into one period around 0, over 2 pi. The kind 'gauss' is the largest absolute value of the codifferential of an electric link state minus a site charge.

An array of one dimension holds one snapshot, and an array of two dimensions one frame per row.

With a matrix group, the link states are the real components of the link matrices, and a loop is the path-ordered product of the link matrices around it. The kind 'wilson' is then the mean of Re tr W / N over the rectangles of every plane, and the kind 'polyakov' the modulus of the mean of tr P / N over the loops P that wind once along the last axis, the order parameter of deconfinement. An array of two dimensions then holds one snapshot, with the components of every link on the last axis, and an array of three dimensions one frame per row.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source object

A trajectory, or an array of link states.

required kind str

'wilson', 'polyakov', 'charge', or 'gauss'.

required space CellComplexSpace

The cell complex of the links.

required variables str | None

The dotted name of the state of a trajectory, or None for a source that is an array.

None extents tuple[int, int]

The sides of the rectangles of the kind 'wilson'.

(1, 1) charges Sequence[float] | None

The charge of every site for the kind 'gauss', or None for none.

None group MatrixGroupSpec | None

The matrix group of the links, or None for link angles.

None

The link states and the observable of every frame.

The kind is unknown, the space is not the cell complex of a periodic lattice, the charge is asked of a lattice that does not have two dimensions, or a kind other than a loop is asked of matrix links.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import CellComplexSpace, LatticeSpace
>>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.waves import gauge_observables
>>> space = CellComplexSpace(LatticeSpace((4, 4))).prepare()
>>> gauge_observables(np.zeros(32), kind='wilson', space=space).value.tolist()

        variables:
            The dotted name of the state of a trajectory, or `None` for a source that is an array.

        extents:
            The sides of the rectangles of the kind `'wilson'`.

        charges:
            The charge of every site for the kind `'gauss'`, or `None` for none.

        group:
            The matrix group of the links, or `None` for link angles.

    Returns:
        result:
            The link states and the observable of every frame.

    Raises:
        AnalysisError:
            The kind is unknown, the space is not the cell complex of a periodic lattice, the charge is asked of a
            lattice that does not have two dimensions, or a kind other than a loop is asked of matrix links.

    Examples:
        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import CellComplexSpace, LatticeSpace
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.physics.waves import gauge_observables
        >>> space = CellComplexSpace(LatticeSpace((4, 4))).prepare()
        >>> gauge_observables(np.zeros(32), kind='wilson', space=space).value.tolist()
        [1.0]
        >>> from skcomplex.core.specs import MatrixGroupSpec
        >>> group = MatrixGroupSpec('SU', 2)
        >>> identity = np.tile(group.identity, (32, 1))
        >>> gauge_observables(identity, kind='polyakov', space=space, group=group).value.tolist()
        [1.0]
    """
    if kind not in KINDS:
        error_msg = f'gauge_observables has kind={kind!r}. Use one of {", ".join(KINDS)}.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    place = getattr(space, 'space', None)
    if not isinstance(place, LatticeSpace) or place.boundary != 'periodic':
        error_msg = f'gauge_observables reads the cell complex of a periodic lattice, not {space!r}.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    if group is not None and kind not in MATRIX_KINDS:
        error_msg = f'The kind {kind!r} reads link angles. Matrix links take the kind wilson or polyakov.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    if kind == 'charge' and len(np.ravel(place.shape)) != CHARGE_DIMENSIONS:
        error_msg = f'The topological charge is defined on a two-dimensional lattice, not on {place!r}.'
        raise AnalysisError(error_msg)
    space.prepare()
    if isinstance(source, Trajectory):
        values = np.asarray(source.get_values(str(variables)), dtype=float)
    else:
        values = np.asarray(source, dtype=float)
        frame = 1 if group is None else 2
        values = values[None] if values.ndim == frame else values
    if group is not None:
        if kind == 'wilson':
            return GaugeObservablesResult(values, _matrix_wilson(space, values, group, extents))
        return GaugeObservablesResult(values, _matrix_polyakov(space, values, group))
    return GaugeObservablesResult(values, _angle_observable(space, values, kind, extents, charges))

docs.title: GameTransitionsInteraction(label, *, target, first_benefit=3.5, second_benefit=2.6, cost=1.0, selection=0.1, after_cooperation=0.0, after_defection=1.0, transitions=True, update='death-birth')
docs.text:
Bases: Interaction

Evolutionary dynamics with game transitions.

The game on every edge follows the actions played on it. Every edge of the graph carries game 1 or game 2, donation games where a cooperator pays c to give its partner b1 or b2, and every edge starts with game 1. In every time step every player plays the game of every edge with its neighbour and accumulates the payoff pi, of fitness 1 - delta + delta pi. Under death-birth updating a uniformly drawn player dies and its neighbours compete for the site in proportion to their fitness, and under pairwise comparison a uniformly drawn player copies a random neighbour with the probability 1 / (1 + exp(-delta (pi_j - pi_i))). The games then change: an edge goes to game 2 with the probability after_cooperation after mutual cooperation, with after_defection after one defection, and surely after mutual defection, and to game 1 otherwise. The newcomer of a site plays the games of its prior occupant. Every step of the system has one time step per player, and the share of edges with game 1 is reported as game_one.

Run one time step per player.

The step plays the games, replaces one player, and changes the games.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default system SystemView

The system.

required Source code in src/skcomplex/systems/social/cooperation/_game_transitions.py 
def evolve(self, system: SystemView) -> None:
    """Run one time step per player.

    The step plays the games, replaces one player, and changes the games.

    Args:
        system:
            The system.
    """
    players = system.get_agents(self.target, DonorView)
    storage = system.storage
    if 'first' not in storage:
        sources, targets = self._get_edges(players)
        storage['first'], storage['second'] = sources, targets
        storage['games'] = np.ones(sources.size)
        storage['neighbors'] = [
            np.concatenate([targets[sources == node], sources[targets == node]]) for node in range(len(players))
        ]
    first, second, games = storage['first'], storage['second'], storage['games']
    neighbors = storage['neighbors']
    if not isinstance(first, np.ndarray) or not isinstance(second, np.ndarray) or not isinstance(games, np.ndarray):
        return
    if not isinstance(neighbors, list):
        return
    rng = system.rng
    strategies = np.array([player.strategy for player in players])
    payoffs = np.zeros(len(players))
    for _ in range(len(players)):
        payoffs = self._get_payoffs(strategies, games, first, second)
        actions = strategies[first] + strategies[second]
        self._replace(strategies, payoffs, neighbors, rng)
        if self.transitions:
            second_game = np.where(actions == MUTUAL_COOPERATION, self.after_cooperation, self.after_defection)
            second_game = np.where(actions == 0, 1.0, second_game)
            games[:] = np.where(rng.random(games.size) < second_game, 2.0, 1.0)
    for player, strategy, payoff in zip(players, strategies.tolist(), payoffs.tolist(), strict=True):
        player.strategy = strategy
        player.payoff = payoff
    system.report('game_one', float(np.mean(games == 1)) if games.size else 1.0)

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Evolutionary dynamics with game transitions on a random regular graph.

It follows Su, McAvoy, Wang, and Nowak. Every edge carries a donation game, game 1 of benefit b1 or game 2 of benefit b2 < b1, at the same cost c. Players accumulate the payoffs of the games with all their neighbours, one player is replaced every time step by death-birth updating or pairwise comparison, and the game of every edge changes with the actions played on it: with the default transitions mutual cooperation leads to game 1 and every other outcome to game 2 (arXiv 1905.10269 section 2 and section 3.1). Under weak selection and death-birth updating on a k-regular graph, cooperation is favoured if b1 / c > k - xi (b1 - b2) / c with xi = (k - 1) / 2, lowered from the rule b1 / c > k of a single game, and with the probabilities p and q of game 2 after mutual cooperation and after one defection, xi = (k - 1) q / 2 - (k + 1) p / 2 (Eq. 1 and Eq. 3). Under pairwise comparison cooperation is favoured if (b1 - b2) / (2 c) > 1 (Eq. 2), whatever b1, and never with a single game. The defaults b1 = 3.5, b2 = b1 - 0.9, and k = 4 lie in the range of Fig. 2 where transitions favour cooperation, since 3.5 > 4 - 1.5 * 0.9, and game 1 alone does not, since 3.5 < 4.

The system has the group players on the nodes of the graph, and the reporter evolution.game_one.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The public goods game on a hypergraph, played in every hyperedge.

The imitation follows the Fermi rule. Every hyperedge is a group that plays the public goods game: a cooperator pays 1, and the pot multiplied by synergy is shared by the members. Every step has two phases. In the phase play every player takes the sum of its shares minus its contributions over the hyperedges around it, and in the phase imitate every player copies a random neighbour, a member of one of its hyperedges, with the Fermi probability 1 / (1 + exp((P_own - P_other) / K)) of the payoffs of the same step, at the noise K. In a well-mixed population defection wins in a group of m for synergy < m, so cooperation needs a synergy near the sizes of the hyperedges.

The system has the strategies players.strategy and the payoffs players.payoff.

docs.text:
Bases: LocalRuleInteraction

Play of the iterated prisoner's dilemma between neighbours.

The play is followed by revision to the best strategy, and mutation. It is a stochastic LocalRuleInteraction of the strategies over the cells within two von Neumann steps of a player. Every step each player plays the N-round prisoner's dilemma with its four von Neumann neighbours and sums its years in prison. A player of strategy n against one of strategy m < n gets m R + S + (N - m - 1) P, the other m R + T + (N - m - 1) P, and two players of strategy n get n R + (N - n) P. Every player then adopts the strategy of the lowest score among itself and its four neighbours, a random one of them on ties, and finally mutates to a uniformly drawn strategy with the probability mu.

            The punishment `S` of a betrayed cooperator.

        temptation:
            The punishment `T` of a defector who betrays.

        punishment:
            The punishment `P` of mutual defection.

    Returns:
        years:
            The years in prison of every player.

    Examples:
        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> from skcomplex.systems.social.cooperation import IteratedDilemmaInteraction
        >>> years = IteratedDilemmaInteraction.get_years(
        ...     np.arange(11.0), np.full(11, 6.0), rounds=10, reward=0.5, sucker=1.5, temptation=0.0, punishment=1.0
        ... )
        >>> int(np.argmin(years))
        5
    """
    first = np.minimum(own, other)
    betrayal = np.where(own < other, temptation, sucker)
    mixed = first * reward + betrayal + (rounds - first - 1) * punishment
    return np.where(own == other, own * reward + (rounds - own) * punishment, mixed)

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

Argun's evolutionary iterated prisoner's dilemma on a lattice.

Its strategies are of n cooperation rounds. The payoffs are years in prison, T < R < P < S, so lower is better. A strategy n cooperates until round n or until the opponent defects, and defects afterwards, so n = 0 always defects and n = N always cooperates. Against a strategy m the best reply is n = m - 1. Every step each player plays the N-round game with its four von Neumann neighbours, adopts the strategy of the lowest total among itself and its neighbours, random on ties, and mutates to a random strategy with the probability mu (Argun et al. 2021 sections 13.2 and 13.3). With every strategy allowed and S = 1.5, cooperative strategies prevail for R below about 0.5, all strategies coexist and cycle between about 0.5 and 0.75, and defecting strategies dominate above, so the default R = 0.6 lies in the middle of the cycling regime, where a finite lattice is not absorbed by defection. With only the two extreme strategies, extremes=True, cooperation dominates at R = 0.82, coexists with defection at R = 0.84, and vanishes at R = 0.86 (Exercise 13.3).

The system has the strategies players.strategy.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The density of groups of defectors and altruistic punishers.

The groups are under pairwise group conflict. The density f(z) of groups with a fraction z of punishers is advected by the replicator dynamics within groups, z (1 - z) (pi_P - pi_D), and groups win pairwise conflicts, copying themselves over the loser, at the rate group_strength f(z) int (rho(z, u) - rho(u, z)) f(u) du. The victory probability rho is not additively separable: the group Fermi rule (1 + tanh(s (G(z) - G(u)))) / 2 ('fermi'), the local rule normalized by the payoffs of both groups ('local'), or the Tullock contest function of the payoffs above their minimum with the exponent 1 / a ('tullock'), where G(z) is the average payoff of a group (Cooney 2024, arXiv 2405.18419 §3.1 and §6). The density starts uniform, and the integral against the two-point kernel rho(z, u) - rho(u, z) keeps its total at one.

The system has the density groups.x.

Bases: LocalRuleInteraction

Play of the weak prisoner's dilemma between neighbours.

The play is followed by imitation of more successful neighbours. It is a stochastic LocalRuleInteraction of the strategies over the 5 by 5 square around a player, a cooperator at 1 and a defector at 0. Every step each player plays the weak dilemma, with reward 1, temptation temptation, and 0 otherwise, against itself and its eight neighbours. It then copies the best player among them, or a random neighbour with the Fermi probability 1 / (1 + exp((P_own - P_other) / noise)). The temptation and the noise are parameters of the players.

The groups hold a player and its four neighbours, and the play sets the payoffs. docs.text:
Bases: ConservationInteraction

Selection drift du/dt + divergence(a u) = source(ns) of a density u over a trait.

Evolutionary game theory names it the selection within groups, the drift of a density of traits by selection. The drift field is a(ns). The flux of the conservation law is the drift times the state, written in conservative form, so the total of the state on a periodic field stays constant and, on a spectral field, the dealiasing of products applies to it. The drift is one expression for a field of one dimension, or one per dimension, of the states and parameters of the field, and may read other states than the one it carries, such as the flow of a fluid derived from a streamfunction, or the drift of a probability density in a Fokker-Planck equation.

Bases: CouplingInteraction

Play of two-player games along the links of the triangles of a complex.

The complex is simplicial. The play sets the payoffs. It is a CouplingInteraction over the hyperedges of a network in the map form, a cooperator at 1 and a defector at 0. Every game pays 1 for mutual cooperation, 0 for mutual defection, and the sucker's payoff S and the temptation T when the strategies differ. A triangle of three links is three hyperedges of two members, along which the players play game 1 of S1 and T1. A triangle filled as a 2-simplex is one hyperedge of three members, where a player plays each other member while the third looks on: game 2 of S2 and T2 when the third member shares the player's strategy, and game 3 of S3 and T3 otherwise. The payoff of a player is the sum over the two links of every triangle around it divided by twice its number of triangles, a parameter of the players.

docs.text:
Bases: BaseSystem

The social dilemmas of Guo et al. on a simplicial complex.

They are played on the links and the 2-simplices of the complex. The network grows from a complete graph on five nodes, every new node joining both ends of a random link, which forms one new triangle. A share simplices of the triangles, drawn at random, are 2-simplices, and the others are three links. Players play game 1 along the links of a plain triangle, and in a 2-simplex game 2 against a member when the third member shares their strategy and game 3 otherwise, every game paying 1 for mutual cooperation, 0 for mutual defection, and S and T to a cooperator and a defector that meet. The payoff of a player is the mean over the two links of every triangle around it. Every step has two phases: in play every player takes its payoff, and in imitate every player copies a random neighbour with the Fermi probability 1 / (1 + exp((P_own - P_other) / K)) at the noise K.

The review of Majhi et al. writes the payoff as a mean over the links of a player of the mean over the triangles of each link, and picks game 2 when s_ki = s_kj. This system takes the mean over the links of the triangles, which counts a link once per triangle, and reads the condition as the third member sharing the strategy of the player. The system has the strategies players.strategy and the payoffs players.payoff.

def act_on(self, members: list[AgentViewProtocol], system: SystemViewProtocol) -> None:
    """Set the fitness of the first member to its mean score per round.

    The score is against the two others.

    Args:
        members:
            The agent, followed by its two neighbours in the ring.

        system:
            The system view of the rule.
    """
    agent, *opponents = [member for member in members if isinstance(member, StrategistView)]
    total = sum(play(agent.genome, opponent.genome, self.rounds)[0] for opponent in opponents)
    agent.fitness = total / (PAIR * self.rounds)

Bases: BaseSystem

The density of groups of cooperators, defectors, and altruistic punishers.

It lives on the 2-simplex. The density f(x, y) of groups with fractions x of cooperators, y of defectors, and 1 - x - y of punishers lives on the 2-simplex. The replicator dynamics within groups advect it, and groups win pairwise conflicts at the rate group_strength f(x, y) int (rho(x, y; u, v) - rho(u, v; x, y)) f(u, v) du dv over the simplex. The density starts uniform at two, so its integral is one, the cells along the slanted face are half cells, and no flux leaves the simplex.

The system has the density groups.x.

Two-level birth-death process of Luo and coauthors.

Groups have pairwise conflicts between them. Within a group of n members with i punishers, a punisher reproduces at the rate 1 + w pi_P(i / n) and a defector at 1 + w pi_D(i / n), and the offspring replaces a random member of the group, the parent included. def compete(self, system: SystemView) -> None:
    """Draw the births, deaths, and conflicts of one unit of time.

    Args:
        system:
            The system.
    """
    groups = system.get_agents(self.target, PunisherGroupView)
    size = len(groups)
    if size < PAIR:
        return
    rng = system.rng
    members = float(self.members)
    punishers = np.array([group.punishers for group in groups])
    time = 0.0
    while True:
        punisher_births, defector_births = self._get_birth_rates(punishers)
        rates = np.concatenate([punisher_births, defector_births, np.full(size, float(self.conflict_rate))])
        total = rates.sum()
        time += rng.exponential(1 / total)
        if time > 1.0:
            break
        event = int(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(rates), rng.random() * total, side='right'))
        group, kind = event % size, event // size
        if kind == 0:
            punishers[group] += rng.random() >= punishers[group] / members
        elif kind == 1:
            punishers[group] -= rng.random() < punishers[group] / members
        else:
            other = int(rng.integers(size - 1))
            other += other >= group
            victory = 0.5 + (punishers[group] - punishers[other]) / (2 * members)
            winner, loser = (group, other) if rng.random() < victory else (other, group)
            punishers[loser] = punishers[winner]
    for group_view, value in zip(groups, punishers.tolist(), strict=True):
        group_view.punishers = value

Bases: BaseSystem

The finite two-level birth-death process of defectors and altruistic punishers.

The punishers and defectors live in competing groups. The population has m groups of n members. Within groups, punishers and defectors reproduce at the rates 1 + w pi_P(z) and 1 + w pi_D(z) of the fraction z of punishers, with pi_P = (b + k) z - (c + q + k) and pi_D = (b - p) z, and the offspring replaces a random member of the group. Every group fights a random other group at the rate Lambda and wins with the probability 1/2 + (z - u) / 2, and the winner's copy replaces the loser (Cooney 2024, arXiv 2405.18419 section 3.1 and appendix A.1). With many large groups, the density of the fractions of punishers follows TwoLevelReplicatorSystem with lambda = Lambda / w, so between-group conflict sustains the punishers above lambda* = c + q - p and the defectors take over without it. The groups start with uniformly drawn numbers of punishers.

The system has the group groups.

Bases: BaseSystem

The two-level replicator equation of defectors and altruistic punishers.

The group conflict is additive and pairwise. The density f(z) of groups with a fraction z of punishers is advected by the replicator dynamics within groups, z (1 - z) (pi_P - pi_D), and groups replicate at the rate group_strength f(z) (G(z) - int G(u) f(u) du) (Cooney 2024, arXiv 2405.18419 Eq. 3.3). Pairwise group conflict with an additively separable victory probability rho(z, u) = 1/2 + (G(z) - G(u)) / 2 reduces to this equation (Eq. 3.11): G(z) = z for the probability of Boyd and coauthors based on the fraction of punishers ('punishers', Eq. 3.6 and section 5.1), or the average payoff of a group normalized by its range, G(z) / (G* - G_*) ('payoff', Eq. 3.8 and section 5.2). From a uniform density with G(z) = z and p < c + q, the groups concentrate at the all-defector state below the threshold lambda* = c + q - p, and above it the mean fraction of punishers tends to 1 - (c + q - p) / lambda (Eq. 5.4).

The system has the density groups.x.
