prepare builds the parts of the system from its model parameters and checks them. A system class, a BaseSystem, keeps them in its attribute system_, a CompositeSystem. Here it holds the populations prey and predators, and the interactions growth, predation, and death, the three terms of the equations of Lotka and Volterra.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Every part says what it is through its tags, which come from its declarations and its arguments alone. get_tags() of an element returns the domains of its states, the set of values a state may take, such as real. get_tags() of an interaction returns the kinds of the laws it emits and the time they run in. get_tags() of a system joins those of its parts.

tags = system.get_tags()
sorted(tags.time), sorted(tags.laws), sorted(tags.domains), tags.randomness

(['continuous'], ['rate'], ['real'], 'deterministic')

The system runs in continuous time, its laws are rates, its states are real numbers, and it draws no random numbers. So it is an ordinary differential equation. The tags of one part show where each tag comes from.

prey, predators = system.system_.elements
growth, predation, death = system.system_.interactions
sorted(prey.get_tags().domains), sorted(predation.get_tags().laws), sorted(predation.get_tags().time)

(['real'], ['rate'], ['continuous'])

The population prey gives the domain real, and predation gives the law kind rate and the time continuous. The parts pages list the tags of every element, interaction, law, solver, and backend of the core, each with a compatible and an incompatible example. Start there to find candidates, and check a candidate in code as the sections below do.

docs.title: What an element carries
docs.text:
An element carries the states it declares, and get_states() returns them with their specs. The spec of a state holds its domain, here the numbers from zero up, since a population cannot be negative.

{name: str(spec.domain) for name, spec in prey.get_states().items()}

{'x': '[0, +oo)'}

The population carries one state x with the domain [0, +oo). Every element is also of one kind, and the kind is what a role accepts or rejects.

  • An Element or a DeclaredElement is of the kind element, one member with its states.
  • A GroupElement is of the kind group, many identical members. With variable=True it is a variable-group, whose members appear and disappear.
  • A group on a space is a site-group, an edge-group, or a hyperedge-group, by what its members sit on. A GroupElement on 'sites' and a FieldElement are site groups.

docs.title: What an interaction needs
docs.text:
An interaction binds elements to its roles, the named slots it reads and changes, such as predator and prey. get_requirements() returns what it needs for the arguments it was given: the time and the space its laws run in, the law classes it may emit, and, for every role, the kinds of element it accepts, the states it reads, and their domains. An empty tuple means no restriction.

needs = predation.get_requirements()
[time.__name__ for time in needs.time], needs.space, list(needs.roles)

(['ContinuousTime'], (), ['predator', 'prey'])

predation needs ContinuousTime, accepts any space, and has the roles predator and prey. A RateInteraction of the build tutorial states more about its role, because it knows the state it changes.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction

births = RateInteraction('births', target='hares', state='x', rate=lambda s: 0.55 * s.target.x)
target = births.get_requirements().roles['target']
target.elements, target.states, target.domains

((<ElementKind.ANY: 'any'>,), ('x',), ('real', 'integer', 'complex', 'vector'))

The role target accepts an element of any kind, reads its state x, and accepts the domains real, integer, complex, and vector. A rate needs a number it can differentiate, so a boolean state does not fit. The method accepts of the role compares it with the kind of an element.

from skcomplex.core.types import ElementKind

target.accepts(ElementKind.ELEMENT), target.accepts(ElementKind.GROUP)

(True, True)

Both are True, because the kind any accepts every kind of element.

docs.title: Time and space
docs.text:
The time decides whether a system flows or steps. A RateInteraction returns rates, so it needs continuous time. A MapInteraction returns the next value of a state, so it needs DiscreteTime.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import MapInteraction

step = MapInteraction('step', target='hares', state='x', function=lambda s: 1.55 * s.target.x)
[time.__name__ for time in births.get_requirements().time], [time.__name__ for time in step.get_requirements().time]

(['ContinuousTime'], ['DiscreteTime'])

The rate needs ContinuousTime and the map needs DiscreteTime. The tags say the same: sorted(step.get_tags().time) is ['discrete'].

docs.title: Roles that accept some kinds
docs.text:
A role may accept some kinds of element and reject the others. A census that counts the members of a group declares in its RoleSpec that its target accepts a group and not a single element.

from typing import Annotated, ClassVar

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import Interaction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RuleLaw
from skcomplex.core.specs import RoleSpec


class CensusInteraction(Interaction):
    law_classes: ClassVar[tuple[type, ...]] = (RuleLaw,)

    def __init__(self, label, *, target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec(elements=(ElementKind.GROUP,))]):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.target = target

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RuleLaw(lambda agent, system: None)]


census = CensusInteraction('census', target='hares').get_requirements().roles['target']
census.elements, census.accepts(ElementKind.GROUP), census.accepts(ElementKind.ELEMENT)

((<ElementKind.GROUP: 'group'>,), True, False)

The role accepts the kind group alone, so it rejects the single population of hares. The section on errors below shows what a run says when the two meet.

docs.title: Validation errors
docs.text:
A part that does not fit raises an error before anything compiles. prepare checks the arguments of each part and the domains of the states that each role binds. simulate then checks the whole system and raises one error that lists every problem, each with its path, its message, a fix, and its code in brackets. The variants below rebuild the model from the parts of the build tutorial and break one thing at a time.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import DeclaredElement
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import DeclaredVariableSpec, StateSpec

hares = DeclaredElement('hares', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(30.0, StateSpec())})
lynx = DeclaredElement('lynx', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(4.0, StateSpec())})
hunting = RateInteraction(
    'hunting', target='hares', state='x', sources=['lynx'], rate=lambda s: -0.028 * s.target.x * s.sources[0].x
)
pair = CompositeSystem(elements=[hares, lynx], interactions=[births, hunting])
round(float(simulate(pair, until=1).get_values('hares.x')[-1]), 1)

46.5

The two populations with births and hunting run without an error. The lynx keep 4.0 thousand without terms of their own, so the hares grow at the net rate 0.55 - 0.028 * 4.0, from 30.0 to 46.5 thousand in a year.

docs.title: A state the element does not carry
docs.text:
The most frequent error binds a role to an element that lacks the state the interaction reads. Here births change the state n of the hares, which carry x.

from skcomplex.core.errors import RoleElementError

wrong_state = RateInteraction('births', target='hares', state='n', rate=lambda s: 0.55)
try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[hares], interactions=[wrong_state]), until=1)
except RoleElementError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The system is not valid, with 1 error(s):
- births: The role 'target' of births reads the state 'n', but the element hares bound to it carries x. Bind the role to an element that carries the state, declare the state on the element, or read another state. `get_requirements()` of an interaction and `get_states()` of an element show what they need and carry. [role-element]

The error has the code role-element. Its message says that the role target of births reads the state n, but the element hares bound to it carries x. The fix is state='x', or a state n declared on the element. The check covers more than declared reads.

  • A RoleSpec(states=('n',)) states the read in advance, so get_requirements() shows it.
  • An interaction that declares nothing is still checked, when simulate builds its laws and a law reads a state that the element does not have.
  • A function passed to an interaction, such as the rate of births, is covered in the same way.
  • An error of another kind inside a law reaches the caller unchanged.

docs.title: A role bound to a missing element
docs.text:
A role names an element by its label, so a typing error or a forgotten element leaves it bound to nothing. Here the lynx are left out of the system.

from skcomplex.core.errors import RoleError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[hares], interactions=[hunting]), until=1)
except RoleError as error:
    message = str(error)
message.splitlines()[-1]

- hunting: Interaction hunting binds the role 'sources' to 'lynx', which is not an element or group path relative to the root system. Bind every role to the path of an element, group, or member of the system. [role]

The code is role. The message says that hunting binds the role sources to lynx, which is not an element or group path relative to the root system. The fix adds the element lynx to the system, or binds the role to the label of an element it holds. A nested system is reached by a path such as village/farmers.

docs.title: Two parts with one label
docs.text:
Every child of a system needs a label of its own, because roles, states, and parameters are named by it.

from skcomplex.core.errors import LabelError

twins = DeclaredElement('hares', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(4.0, StateSpec())})
try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[hares, twins], interactions=[births]), until=1)
except LabelError as error:
    message = str(error)
message.splitlines()[-1]

- system: Label 'hares' is used by more than one child of the root system. Give every child of a system a unique label of letters, digits, and underscores. [label]

The code is label, and the message asks for a unique label of letters, digits, and underscores. Renaming the second element to lynx fixes it.

docs.title: A role that rejects the kind of its element
docs.text:
The census above accepts groups, and the population of hares is a single element.

counted = CompositeSystem(elements=[hares], interactions=[CensusInteraction('census', target='hares')])
try:
    simulate(counted, until=1)
except RoleElementError as error:
    message = str(error)
message.splitlines()[-1]

- census: The role 'target' of census accepts group, but hares is of kind element. Bind the role 'target' to an element of kind group. [role-element]

The code is again role-element. The message says that the role target of census accepts group, but hares is of the kind element. The fix binds the role to a GroupElement, such as a group of individual hares.

docs.title: A state of a domain the role rejects
docs.text:
A rate cannot change a state whose values are only 0 and 1. prepare catches it, so the error appears before a run.

from sage.sets.finite_enumerated_set import FiniteEnumeratedSet

present = DeclaredElement(
    'hares', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(1, StateSpec(domain=FiniteEnumeratedSet([0, 1])))}
)
try:
    CompositeSystem(elements=[present], interactions=[births]).prepare()
except RoleElementError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The role 'target' of 'births' accepts the domains real, integer, complex, vector, but the element 'hares' bound to it has the state 'x' of the domain 'boolean'.

The message says that the role target of births accepts the domains real, integer, complex, and vector, but the element hares has the state x of the domain boolean. The fix is a real state, or an interaction for booleans, such as a MapInteraction that flips the state under discrete time.

docs.title: A law in the wrong time
docs.text:
A system that declares one time and holds laws of the other cannot run.

from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime
from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[hares], interactions=[births], time=DiscreteTime()), until=1)
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message.splitlines()[-1]

- births: The RateLaw of births needs ContinuousTime, but its system declares DiscreteTime. Declare `ContinuousTime()` for its system, or use laws that run in DiscreteTime. [law-time]

The code is law-time. The message says that the RateLaw of births needs ContinuousTime while the system declares DiscreteTime, and suggests either ContinuousTime() or laws that run in discrete time. Leaving the time out lets the system take it from its laws.

docs.title: A name that does not exist
docs.text:
Model parameters, states, and run parameters are named, and a wrong name fails at once. The catalog class names the birth rate of the prey r, not alpha as in the build tutorial, and its states prey.x and predators.x.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ParameterError

messages = []
try:
    system.set_params(alpha=0.6)
except ValueError as error:
    messages.append(str(error).split('. ')[-1])
try:
    simulate(system, until=20, initial_state={'hares.x': 10.0})
except ValidationError as error:
    messages.append(str(error))
try:
    simulate(system, until=20, schedule={'predation.alpha': lambda t: 0.0})
except ParameterError as error:
    messages.append(str(error))
messages

["Valid parameters are: ['K', 'a', 'b', 'd', 'label', 'predators', 'prey', 'r'].",
 'The initial state names hares.x, which are not states of the system. Use the dotted names of states, such as '
 'prey.x, predators.x.',
 "No parameter named 'predation.alpha' to schedule. Available names are: growth.r, predation.a, predation.b, "
 'death.d.']
  • set_params raises a ValueError, as scikit-learn does, and lists the valid parameters: K, a, b, d, label, predators, prey, and r.
  • An initial_state with a wrong name raises a ValidationError that suggests prey.x and predators.x.
  • A schedule names the parameters of the built parts by their path, and a wrong one raises a ParameterError that lists growth.r, predation.a, predation.b, and death.d.

docs.title: The solver
docs.text:
The solver advances the compiled system. It can be left out, because the tags of a system decide its default solver. Every solver class lists the tags it supports in get_supported_tags(), and simulate rejects a solver that lacks a tag of the system with a TagError that names it, before it compiles anything.

from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import IterationSolver, RK4Solver
from skcomplex.core.errors import TagError

fits = tags.laws <= RK4Solver.get_supported_tags().laws
try:
    simulate(system, until=20, solver=IterationSolver())
except TagError as error:
    message = str(error)
fits, message, simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0, solver=RK4Solver()).get_values('prey.x').round(1)[:6].tolist()

(True,
 'The solver IterationSolver does not support the time continuous of the system. Pass a solver that supports them, '
 'or none for the default.',
 [30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2, 48.8, 18.6])

RK4Solver, the classical Runge-Kutta method of order four, integrates the rates of the model, and its run matches the default solver of the build tutorial: 30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2, 48.8, 18.6 thousand hares from 1900 to 1905. IterationSolver, which iterates maps, does not support the time continuous, and the message says so. The solvers page lists what every solver supports, and the backends page what every backend supports. The tutorial Simulate runs the checked system.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text: This tutorial checks how well the predator and prey model fits the hare and lynx pelt records. It compares a run with the records, reads the goodness of fit of a calibration, checks a posterior against the data and against simulated truths, and asks whether the data determine the rates at all. The page Calibrate shows the fits themselves.

docs.title: The data and the model
docs.text:
The records and the model are those of the build tutorial. The counts are the pelts of 1900 to 1920, in thousands, as distributed with the case study of Carpenter (2018, Predator-Prey Population Dynamics: the Lotka-Volterra model in Stan) in the file knitr/lotka-volterra/hudson-bay-lynx-hare.csv of the Stan example models. That file cites the lecture notes of Howard (2009) at Texas A&M University, which trace the numbers through the notes of Mahaffy (Math 636, San Diego State University) to Purves, Sadava, Orians, and Heller, Life: The Science of Biology.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

years = np.arange(1900, 1921)
hares = np.array(
    [30.0, 47.2, 70.2, 77.4, 36.3, 20.6, 18.1, 21.4, 22.0, 25.4, 27.1]
    + [40.3, 57.0, 76.6, 52.3, 19.5, 11.2, 7.6, 14.6, 16.2, 24.7]
)
lynx = np.array(
    [4.0, 6.1, 9.8, 35.2, 59.4, 41.7, 19.0, 13.0, 8.3, 9.1, 7.4]
    + [8.0, 12.3, 19.5, 45.7, 51.1, 29.7, 15.8, 9.7, 10.1, 8.6]
)
system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
times = years - 1900.0
data = {'prey.x': (times, hares), 'predators.x': (times, lynx)}
bounds = {'r': (0.3, 0.9), 'a': (0.01, 0.05), 'b': (0.01, 0.05), 'd': (0.5, 1.2)}
system.r, system.d

(0.55, 0.8)

The system holds the rates that Carpenter estimated: r, the growth rate of the hares, a, the rate at which hunting removes hares, b, the rate at which it feeds the lynx, and d, the death rate of the lynx. Every run starts from the records of 1900.

docs.title: A run against the records
docs.text:
A run of the model gives the populations at the years of the records. Their differences are the residuals, and the root mean square of the residuals of each series measures how far the run lies from it.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

run = simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0)
residuals = {'hares': run.get_values('prey.x') - hares, 'lynx': run.get_values('predators.x') - lynx}
errors = {name: round(float(np.sqrt(np.mean(values**2))), 1) for name, values in residuals.items()}
worst = {name: int(years[np.abs(values).argmax()]) for name, values in residuals.items()}
errors, worst

({'hares': 7.8, 'lynx': 6.7}, {'hares': 1914, 'lynx': 1903})

The run lies 7.8 thousand pelts from the hares on average and 6.7 thousand from the lynx. The largest residuals show where the model departs from the records. The run misses the hares most in 1914, in the second cycle, and the lynx in 1903, the year their counts jump from 9.8 to 35.2 thousand. The rates of Carpenter came from a fit that also estimated the initial populations, so a run that starts from the counts of 1900 drifts out of phase over two cycles.

docs.title: The goodness of fit of a calibration
docs.text:
A calibration returns its own measures of fit, computed over all data points at the fitted rates. The local fit of calibrate below estimates the four rates by least squares. fit.simulated holds the fitted values at the data times, so the residuals of the fit come without a new run.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import calibrate

fit = calibrate(system, data, bounds)
fitted = fit.simulated['prey.x'] - hares
measures = round(fit.r2, 3), round(fit.rmse, 1), round(fit.mae, 1), round(fit.mape, 1)
measures, round(float(np.sqrt(np.mean(fitted**2))), 1)

((0.955, 4.2, 3.1, 17.0), 4.7)

The CalibrationResult holds four measures.

  • r2, the coefficient of determination, is the share of the variance of the counts that the fit explains, here 0.955.
  • rmse, the root mean squared error, is 4.2 thousand pelts.
  • mae, the mean absolute error, is 3.1 thousand pelts. It weighs large misses less than the RMSE does.
  • mape, the mean absolute percentage error, is 17.0%. It weighs the small counts of the troughs most.

The fit lies 4.7 thousand pelts from the hares, against 7.8 thousand for the first run.

docs.title: Posterior predictive checks
docs.text:
A posterior predictive check asks whether data simulated from the posterior look like the observed data. Each posterior method of calibrate runs it on at most 200 posterior draws. With the Gaussian likelihood every draw also adds the observation noise that its residuals imply. The result holds the 5%, 50%, and 95% quantiles of the simulated values at every data time, and the share of observed points inside the band from 5% to 95%.

posterior = calibrate(
    system, data, bounds, method='mcmc', loss='likelihood', n_samples=100, chains=1, random_state=0
)
band = posterior.predictive
low, high = band['q05']['prey.x'], band['q95']['prey.x']
bool(band['coverage'] > 0.75), low.shape, bool(np.all(low <= high))

(True, (21,), True)

The posterior of a short chain of Markov chain Monte Carlo covers more than three quarters of the 42 records with its 90% band. A band of 90% should hold about 90% of the points. A much lower share shows a model that misses the data, and a share near 100% a band wider than the noise. q05, q50, and q95 map each path to 21 values, one per year.

docs.title: Posterior coverage
docs.text:
A credible interval of level 90% should hold the true rate in 90% of studies. posterior_coverage checks this with simulated truths. It draws true rates from the prior, simulates data at each with Gaussian noise, calibrates every data set with a posterior method, and counts how often the central interval of each level holds the truth. It also gives the rank of every truth among its samples, the check of simulation-based calibration (Talts et al. 2018). Every calibration costs a full run of the sampler, so this example checks only the growth rate r, with the other rates fixed, on three data sets. It needs the times of the data but not the records, so its block starts afresh.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import posterior_coverage
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

check = posterior_coverage(
    LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80),
    {'r': (0.4, 0.7)},
    np.arange(21.0),
    method='mcmc',
    n=3,
    levels=(0.5, 0.9),
    noise=3.0,
    n_samples=50,
    chains=1,
    random_state=0,
)
check.levels, check.ranks['r'].shape, len(check.results)

((0.5, 0.9), (3,), 3)

coverage maps each level to the share of data sets whose interval holds the truth, by parameter. ranks holds the weighted share of samples below the truth, one per data set, and truths the true rates. results holds the CalibrationResult of every data set. A calibrated method covers the truth at about the rate of each level, and its ranks spread evenly between 0 and 1. Three data sets cannot show that. A real check uses 40 data sets, the default, or more, and a histogram of the ranks.

docs.title: Practical identifiability
docs.text:
A calibration returns estimates even when the data cannot pin them down. Practical identifiability asks whether the data at hand fix each rate within its bounds. identifiability answers it in two ways. The method 'refits' of Liyanage et al. (2025) adds Gaussian noise relative to the fitted values, fits n noisy copies again, and reports the average relative error of every rate at every level of noise. The block repeats the records, so this section runs on its own.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import identifiability
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

hares = np.array(
    [30.0, 47.2, 70.2, 77.4, 36.3, 20.6, 18.1, 21.4, 22.0, 25.4, 27.1]
    + [40.3, 57.0, 76.6, 52.3, 19.5, 11.2, 7.6, 14.6, 16.2, 24.7]
)
lynx = np.array(
    [4.0, 6.1, 9.8, 35.2, 59.4, 41.7, 19.0, 13.0, 8.3, 9.1, 7.4]
    + [8.0, 12.3, 19.5, 45.7, 51.1, 29.7, 15.8, 9.7, 10.1, 8.6]
)
system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
times = np.arange(21.0)
data = {'prey.x': (times, hares), 'predators.x': (times, lynx)}
bounds = {'r': (0.3, 0.9), 'a': (0.01, 0.05), 'b': (0.01, 0.05), 'd': (0.5, 1.2)}
refits = identifiability(system, data, bounds, method='refits', n=5, noise=(0.05,), random_state=0)
refits.verdicts, {name: bool(errors[0.05] < 0.05) for name, errors in refits.errors.items()}

({'r': 'strong', 'a': 'strong', 'b': 'strong', 'd': 'strong'}, {'r': True, 'a': True, 'b': True, 'd': True})

With all 21 years of both series, every rate has the verdict 'strong', because its average relative error under noise of 5% stays below 5%. The verdict is 'weak' for an error up to ten times the noise and 'none' above. Five copies are a demonstration. A study uses the default of 100 copies and several levels of noise, such as (0.01, 0.05, 0.1).

The default method, 'profile', computes the profile likelihood with pyPESTO. The profile of a rate fixes it at values on both sides of the best fit, fits the other rates again, and keeps the values whose likelihood ratio stays above the threshold of a chi-square test at level 0.95. A rate is identifiable when both ends of this interval lie inside its bounds. A profile costs many fits, so this example profiles two rates. The first three hare counts, from 1900 to 1902, come before the lynx rise.

early = {'prey.x': (times[:3], hares[:3])}
profile = identifiability(system, early, {'b': (0.01, 0.05), 'd': (0.5, 1.2)}, n_starts=1, random_state=0)
profile.verdicts, {name: np.round(ends, 3).tolist() for name, ends in profile.intervals.items()}

({'b': 'identifiable', 'd': 'not identifiable'}, {'b': [0.014, 0.032], 'd': [nan, nan]})

The early counts fix b, the feeding rate of the lynx, between 0.014 and 0.032. They do not fix d, the death rate of the lynx, whose interval is open at both bounds and so reads nan on both sides. A death rate anywhere between 0.5 and 1.2 fits three years of hares equally well. Widening the bounds and running again shows whether an open side closes. profiles holds the values and the likelihood ratios along every profile, ready to plot. A study profiles every rate with the default of five starts.

docs.title: Extend the library
docs.text: This page adds elements, interactions, laws, and other parts of your own without changing the library, and shows where every class lives. A part of your own is a subclass of a class of the core, so the checks and the laws of its parent keep working.

docs.title: Extending the general classes
docs.text: This section gives a general class of the library the words of your field. A general class names a mathematical operation, and a subclass names what it means in a field. The subclass overrides hooks, the private methods that a class reads to let a subclass change one step, and the checks and the laws of its parent keep working.

docs.title: Roles and parameters
docs.text:
This section renames a role or a parameter of a general interaction, or fixes a parameter to a value. A role is the name under which an interaction reads and changes an element. The example renames the role target of RateInteraction to stock, for an inflow that fills a tank at a fixed rate.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction, SamplingInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import neighbors
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime, LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, RoleSpec, StateSpec


class StockElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, level: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.level = level


class InflowInteraction(RateInteraction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, stock: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]):
        super().__init__(label, target=stock, state='level', rate=lambda s: 1.0)
        self.stock = stock

    def _get_role(self, role):
        return {'target': 'stock'}.get(role, role)


inflow = CompositeSystem(elements=[StockElement('tank')], interactions=[InflowInteraction('fill', stock='tank')])
round(float(simulate(inflow, until=1, dt=0.1).get_values('tank.level')[-1]), 3)

2.0

The level rises from 1.0 to 2.0 in one unit of time. _get_role renames a role, here target to stock, in the symbolic form and the agent form alike. _get_parameter renames a parameter in the same way. An argument that the class does not declare as a parameter is a plain value, so a subclass fixes a parameter by setting it, as InflowInteraction fixes the rate to 1.

The second example renames the intensity of SamplingInteraction, which samples the states of the members of a group by Monte Carlo moves, to the inverse temperature beta of a magnet. The spins sit on the sites of an 8 by 8 LatticeSpace, each one a member of a GroupElement, and the system steps in DiscreteTime.

class SpinElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, s: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.s = s


class ThermalSamplingInteraction(SamplingInteraction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], beta: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        energy = lambda s: -s.target.s * neighbors(s.target.other.s)
        super().__init__(label, target=target, state='s', objective=energy)
        self.beta = beta

    def _get_parameter(self, name):
        return {'intensity': 'beta'}.get(name, name)


spins = GroupElement('spins', element=SpinElement, space=LatticeSpace((8, 8)), on='sites')
magnet = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[spins],
    interactions=[ThermalSamplingInteraction('thermal', target='spins')],
    time=DiscreteTime(),
)
abs(simulate(magnet, until=20, random_state=0).states[-1].mean()) > 0.9

True

The check returns True. At beta = 1, a low temperature, the spins stay aligned, and the mean magnetization after twenty sweeps stays above 0.9.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
This section chooses the variant of a general interaction. A variant is given as a named value, a spec, or a function, and each argument takes some of these.

  • The pairing of a transfer or a grouping takes a PartnerSpec or a function.
  • The groups of a grouping, the action of a topology, and the mode of a coupling or a map take their named values or a spec of a subclass.
  • The move of a sampling takes its named values or a function. It takes no spec, because a function already says what a spec would. A spec given to it raises an error that lists what the argument takes.

Every other value raises the same error, so the checks of the parent keep working.

docs.title: Partners and settlement
docs.text:
This section says whom an agent pairs with in a transfer, and how both partners settle the amount. TransferInteraction moves an amount from a source to a target. In the example, three eaters buy a meal of 2 units from one of two providers, each agent a member of a group in a ContinuousSpace of 10 by 10.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import TransferInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RuleLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace, DiscreteTime
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import PartnerSpec, StateSpec


class EaterElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        level: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        sold: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.level = level
        self.sold = sold

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RuleLaw(lambda agent, system: None)]


def settle(source, target, amounts, system):
    source.level += sum(amounts)
    target.sold += 1.0


space = ContinuousSpace(extent=(10.0, 10.0))
eaters = GroupElement('eaters', element=EaterElement, size=3, space=space)
providers = GroupElement('providers', element=EaterElement, size=2, space=space)
meal = TransferInteraction(
    'meal',
    source='eaters',
    target='providers',
    state='level',
    into='sold',
    amount=lambda source, target, system: 2.0,
    pairing=PartnerSpec(1.0, fallback='nearest'),
    form='agent',
    settlement=settle,
)
system = CompositeSystem(elements=[eaters, providers], interactions=[meal], time=DiscreteTime())
trajectory = simulate(system, until=1, random_state=0)
trajectory.get_agents('eaters', 1).values['level'].tolist()

[2.0, 2.0, 2.0]

Each of the three eaters holds 2.0 after one step. PartnerSpec(candidates, choice, fallback, capacity, score) says whom an agent pairs with.

  • The candidates are 'all', 'neighbors', 'cell', 'local' for both of these, a distance, or the name of a state that holds a distance per agent. So it works in continuous space too.
  • The choice is 'uniform', 'score', 'nearest', or 'all'.
  • The fallback 'nearest' takes the nearest partner when no one is within reach.

Here the candidates lie within a distance of 1.0, and the fallback pairs an eater with its nearest provider when none does. A settlement(source, target, amounts, system) of a transfer receives both partners and the drawn amounts, so both ends credit one draw.

docs.title: Agent states that hold objects
docs.text:
This section gives an agent a state that holds any value, such as a tuple of orders, and tells analyses what a state means. Each queue below keeps its last two orders, and a RuleLaw appends the current time to them at each step.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RuleLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec


class QueueElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, orders: Annotated[object, StateSpec(domain=None)] = ()):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.orders = orders

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RuleLaw(self._step)]

    def _step(self, agent, system):
        agent.orders = (*agent.orders, int(system.time))[-2:]


group = GroupElement('queues', element=QueueElement, size=2, values={'orders': [(), (7,)]})
queues = CompositeSystem(elements=[group], time=DiscreteTime())
trajectory = simulate(queues, until=1, random_state=0)
trajectory.get_agents('queues', 1).values['orders'].tolist()

[(1,), (7, 1)]

After one step the first queue holds (1,) and the second (7, 1). A state of an agent with StateSpec(domain=None) or StateSpec(domain=object) holds any hashable value, such as a tuple, a string, or a frozen set. The library records such a state as follows.

  • A snapshot keeps one object per agent in a one-dimensional array.
  • A composition counts the agents by value.
  • A history keeps any value.
  • An analysis that needs numbers names the state and refuses it.

Symbolic systems hold numbers only, in the vectors of their solvers.

StateSpec(role='position'), StateSpec(role='direction'), StateSpec(role='phase'), and StateSpec(role='velocity') tell analyses what a state means. Analyses read positions, directions, phases, and velocities from these roles, not from the names of the states. So a state named phase is no phase unless it says so.

  • A group is a particle group when a state has the role 'position', and the first derivative of that state is its velocity.
  • The scalar states of any other group count as series, one per member. A displacement refuses them, since they are no positions.
  • A variable group has no fixed members, so its states are series only when named, with NaN in the rows that hold no member.
  • In a continuous space, a vector state with the role 'position' is the place of its element. The boundary acts on it, and neighbourhoods measure distances from it.
  • StateSpec(role='site') does the same for a place that does not make a member a particle, such as the fixed sites of oscillators on a ring.

docs.title: Checking arguments
docs.text:
This section checks the arguments of a new part. The constructor only stores its arguments, so a part with a bad argument is built without error. Preparing it, alone or within its system, raises the error. The check goes at the start of the hook _prepare, which begins with super()._prepare(context). The base of the parts checks the label and the declared specs first, and then the part checks its own arguments before it sets any attribute that ends in _.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError
from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec


class TankElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, level: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0, capacity=10.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.level = level
        self.capacity = capacity

    def _prepare(self, context=None):
        super()._prepare(context)
        if self.capacity <= 0:
            error_msg = f'The capacity of {self.label!r} is {self.capacity}. Give a positive capacity.'
            raise ValidationError(error_msg)
        self.free_ = self.capacity - self.level


tank = TankElement('tank', capacity=-1.0)
try:
    tank.prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message, hasattr(tank, 'free_'), TankElement('tank').prepare().free_

("The capacity of 'tank' is -1.0. Give a positive capacity.", False, 9.0)

The message reads "The capacity of 'tank' is -1.0. Give a positive capacity." The failed tank sets no free_, and a tank with the default capacity of 10 and level of 1 has 9.0 free. The fix is a positive capacity.

A spec, such as StateSpec, is a frozen value, not an estimator, so it has neither prepare nor run. The part that holds a spec checks it through the private hook _check of the spec when it reads it, as the base of the parts does for the specs of the annotated arguments.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
This section shows where every class lives, so you know what to import and where a part of your own belongs. The package has two parts.

  • skcomplex.core is the general library: what a system is, how it runs, and how you analyse it and experiment with it.
  • skcomplex.systems is the catalog of ready-made systems, built from the core.
from skcomplex.core.base import BaseConfig
from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import BaseSystem, CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

[issubclass(cls, BaseConfig) for cls in (Element, CompositeSystem, LotkaVolterraSystem)]

[True, True, True]

All three checks return True. Every estimator, an element, an interaction, a law, a system, and the engine that runs them, derives from one root class, BaseConfig. simulate, the analyses, and the experiments, calibration among them, are functions of these estimators. Every ready-made system belongs to a field and a subfield of the catalog.

issubclass(LotkaVolterraSystem, BaseSystem), LotkaVolterraSystem.field

(True, 'biology/ecology')

LotkaVolterraSystem is a BaseSystem of the field path 'biology/ecology'. The parts of the core are layered, so that each imports only the parts below it. From top to bottom:

  1. skcomplex.core.experiments runs many simulations.
  2. skcomplex.core.analysis measures systems, trajectories, and data.
  3. skcomplex.core.engine runs systems.
  4. skcomplex.core.components defines what a system is.
  5. skcomplex.core.specs holds the specs.
  6. skcomplex.core.base holds BaseConfig.
  7. skcomplex.core.types and skcomplex.core.errors hold the types and the errors.

No part of the core imports skcomplex.systems, and the systems import only the public modules of the core. Tests of the import contracts enforce the layering.

docs.title: Where a new part goes
docs.text:
This section decides where a part of your own belongs. One ordered test, the placement rule, decides where any part goes, and tests/test_sources.py checks it mechanically. The page General realizations quotes the rule word for word.

  1. A structural base, such as a Base class, the composite system, or a base where laws run per member, edge, hyperedge, or pair, goes to the core.
  2. A part that the engine handles by type, through a compile pass, a kernel, a solver, a backend lowering, or an analysis that checks the class or its spec, goes to the core, and so does an operator generated from one function. It is named by its mathematics and must be cross-domain in principle.
  3. Every other part is a recipe, expressible with core parts. Its users place it. Several fields: skcomplex.systems.general.<concept>. One field with several systems: systems/<field>/common/<family>. One system: that system's module. A field with its own term names it, and general uses neutral names.
  4. A recipe that needs something the core cannot express reveals a missing core primitive, which enters by step 2. Engine support never lives inside a recipe.
  5. The core never imports skcomplex.systems.

One example for each step follows.

  1. HyperedgeInteraction runs its laws once per hyperedge, and CompositeSystem holds the parts of a system, so both are structural bases of the core.
  2. GroupingInteraction stays in the core, since a compile pass lowers its symbolic form by type to kernels over random groups redrawn every step. Its name is the mathematics it does, and economics and social science both form groups.
  3. MovementInteraction returns agent rules, which the core already runs, and systems of biology, economics, engineering, mathematics, and social science use it, so it lives in skcomplex.systems.general.agents. The toppling of a sandpile serves several systems of physics only, so it lives in a family of the physics common package under the physics name TopplingInteraction. The satisfiability of logical constraints serves one system, so SatisfiabilityInteraction lives in the module of PerceptronSatisfiabilitySystem.
  4. The satisfiability once had a check of its own in the compiler, which is engine support inside a recipe. The check that a role accepts only Boolean states is a primitive of the core, RoleSpec(domains=...), so the recipe declares its role with it and the compiler keeps no code for the class.
  5. sparse_identification of the core returns a CompositeSystem of core parts, never a class of skcomplex.systems, so the core runs without the catalog.

docs.title: The root modules
docs.text:
This section lists the modules that every package of the core shares.

  • skcomplex.core.base holds BaseConfig, the root of every configurable class. It stores the settings of a class under their own names, as scikit-learn does, so get_params, set_params, and clone work on every class. It gives every class the main public methods prepare and run, and get_tags returns the capability tags of every part.
  • skcomplex.core.errors holds the errors and warnings, such as ValidationError, RoleError, SolverError, and RewritingError.
  • skcomplex.core.types holds the types that every layer reads, such as arrays, functions, keys, and kinds.
  • skcomplex.core.specs holds the specs, frozen values that declare, record, or hold what the classes read. These include the specs that annotate states, parameters, and roles, such as StateSpec, ParameterSpec, and RoleSpec, the specs of runs and structures, such as ObservableSpec and WienerProcessSpec, and the specs of rules, domains, and geometries, such as TableSpec, LinearRuleSpec, SubshiftSpec, and GeometrySpec.

docs.title: The core
docs.text:
This section lists the modules of skcomplex.core.components, which defines what a system is and nothing about how it runs. They are listed in their import order, so a module imports only the modules above it.

  • types: the types of the components, such as the targets of laws and the pairings of transfers.
  • base: BasePart, the base of every part of a system, built on BaseConfig.
  • spaces: the continuous, lattice, network, mesh, and Cayley spaces, their neighbourhoods, and the kinds of time.
  • laws: the BaseLaw base and every law. laws.utils holds what laws are written with besides Sage, such as where, reductions, draws, delays, and calls. The helpers that only the compiler reads, such as reductions_in, stay in its private modules, and the engine imports them from there.
  • elements and interactions: Element, GroupElement, FieldElement, and the other elements, and the binding bases Interaction, NeighborInteraction, PairInteraction, and HyperedgeInteraction, with the general interactions built on them.
  • systems: BaseSystem and its RunSettings, and the composite CompositeSystem.
  • specs: the specs that name classes of the components, as a compilation reads them, such as ScenarioSpec.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
This section lists the packages of skcomplex.core.engine, which runs systems. They are listed in their import order too.

  • types: the types that only the engine reads.
  • problems: the compiled problems, their layouts of states and parameters, and their numeric functions.
  • backends: the NumPy, Numba, and JAX backends, which lower expressions to numeric functions.
  • compile: the compilers and the passes that turn a system into a problem. They are private, except BaseCompiler, BasePass, and BaseLowering, through which a system package brings a form of its own with the compiler run setting.
  • solvers: the solver contract, step_count, and every solver.
  • runtime: simulate, clocks, observers, and trajectories.
  • viz: the visuals and the Rerun observer.
  • translators: the translators of system files of other tools, such as SystemDynamicsTranslator.

docs.title: Analysis and experiments
docs.text: This section names the two packages that study runs. skcomplex.core.analysis holds the analysis functions of systems, trajectories, and data, their frozen results, and bind_analysis, with the types that only they read in skcomplex.core.analysis.types. skcomplex.core.experiments holds the experiment functions over designs of parameters, scenarios, and replicates, sensitivity, basin stability, orbit diagrams, and calibration. Its types and specs hold the rows of a design and the runs of an experiment.

docs.title: The systems
docs.text:
This section describes the layout of the catalog. all_systems lists its classes, and each class is importable from its subfield package. The systems are organised by field, biology, chemistry, computer_science, economics, engineering, mathematics, physics, and social, and by subfield inside each field, such as physics.mechanics or biology.ecology.

  • A subfield package is self-contained, and imports no other subfield.
  • A realization that several subfields of one field share lives in a family of the common package of that field, such as physics.common.avalanches.
  • A realization that several fields share lives in a concept subpackage of skcomplex.systems.general, such as its agents or reactions, described in General realizations.
  • Every system is written with the same public classes of the core as a custom system, so its source also serves as a pattern.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: This page defines the mathematical and library terms that the user guide uses, in alphabetical order. Each entry ends with a link to the page or section where the term is at work.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text: An agent is an element whose laws are rules that read and change its own states, its neighbours, or the system, one member at a time. Agents move, choose, trade, and die, which equations of averages cannot express. The tutorial Agent-based systems builds them.

docs.title: Algebraic state
docs.text: An algebraic state has no derivative of its own, because the equations of its system fix its value at every time. It takes an equation or a linear program, never a rate. See EquationLaw.

docs.title: Approximate Bayesian computation
docs.text: Approximate Bayesian computation estimates a posterior without a likelihood. It draws parameters from the prior, runs the system, and keeps the draws whose summaries lie close to the data. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Attractor
docs.text: An attractor is the set of states that the runs of a dissipative system settle on, such as a fixed point, a cycle, or the strange set of a chaotic flow. Its dimension and its Lyapunov exponents describe it. See Analyse.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text: A backend turns the laws of a compiled problem into numeric functions. NumPy is the default, Numba compiles large systems, and JAX writes functions that can be differentiated. See Simulate.

docs.title: Basin stability
docs.text: Basin stability is the share of random initial states whose runs reach a given behaviour. It measures how stable the behaviour is against large disturbances. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Calibration estimates the parameters of a system from data. A point fit returns one value per parameter, and a posterior method returns samples of the posterior. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Chaos
docs.text: A chaotic system is deterministic, yet two runs that start close apart separate exponentially fast, so its long-term path cannot be predicted. A positive Lyapunov exponent is its signature. See Analyse.

docs.title: Co-simulation
docs.text: Co-simulation runs the partitions of one system, each with its own solver, and exchanges their values at synchronisation points. It joins parts that no single solver runs, such as agents beside a differential equation. See Simulate.

docs.title: Compiler
docs.text: The compiler reads the laws of a prepared system and builds one problem of a mathematical form, such as a system of ordinary differential equations. A solver then advances that problem. See How the parts fit.

docs.title: Credible interval
docs.text: A credible interval of level 90% holds the parameter with probability 0.9 under the posterior. A calibrated method covers the true value at about that rate over many studies. See Evaluate.

docs.title: Deterministic
docs.text: A deterministic system draws no random numbers, so one initial state gives one run. Its tag randomness is deterministic, the opposite of stochastic. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: The domain of a state is the set of values it may take, such as the real numbers, the integers, or the numbers from zero up. A role names the domains it accepts, and a state of another domain does not fit it. See Check a system.

docs.title: Dotted name
docs.text: A dotted name joins the label of a part and the name of one of its values, such as prey.x or predation.a. A trajectory, a schedule, and an experiment name states and parameters this way. See Simulate.

docs.title: Element
docs.text: An element holds states, the numbers that change as a system runs, such as the size of a population or the balance of an account. It may also hold parameters and laws of its own. See Elements.

docs.title: Ensemble
docs.text: An ensemble repeats the runs of a stochastic system with independent random streams. The spread of its outcomes shows what chance alone can do. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Field realization
docs.text: A field realization is a subclass of a core part that names it in the words of one field and fixes its arguments, such as a compartment of an epidemic written as a DeclaredElement. The catalog writes its systems this way. See System classes.

docs.title: Fixed point
docs.text: A fixed point is a state where every rate is zero, so a run that starts there stays there. Its stability says whether nearby states move toward it, away from it, or around it. See Analyse.

docs.title: Frame
docs.text: A frame is one recorded instant of a run, with the time, the states, and the parameters. The time between frames is dt, while the solver may take smaller steps inside it. See Simulate.

docs.title: Gillespie algorithm
docs.text: The Gillespie algorithm runs random events exactly in continuous time. It draws the time of the next event from the total rate and picks the event in proportion to its rate. See Simulate.

docs.title: Group
docs.text: A group holds many members of one element class, one per site of a lattice, node of a network, or point in space. A variable group lets members appear and disappear. See GroupElement.

docs.title: Identifiability
docs.text: A parameter is identifiable when the data fix its value. Practical identifiability asks this of the data at hand, by refitting noisy copies or by profiling the likelihood. See Evaluate.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text: An interaction reads states through its roles and returns laws that change them, such as hunting that lowers the prey and feeds the predators. See Interactions.

docs.title: Invariant
docs.text: An invariant is a quantity that must stay constant along a run, such as the energy of a frictionless oscillator. A run given an invariant checks it at every frame and raises an error when it drifts beyond its tolerance. See Simulate.

docs.title: Jacobian
docs.text: The Jacobian of a system is the matrix of the derivatives of its rates with respect to its states. Its eigenvalues at a fixed point decide the stability of that point. See Analyse.

docs.title: Jump
docs.text: A jump is a random event that changes states by a fixed amount at a random time, such as one birth or one reaction. Jump laws run under the Gillespie algorithm. See Simulate.

docs.title: Kind of data
docs.text: A kind of data is what an analysis consumes, such as a series, a jump path, a field, agent snapshots, a network, or an ensemble of runs. An analysis reads its kind from a trajectory or from measured arrays alike. See Analyse.

docs.title: Kind of element
docs.text: The kind of an element says how many members it holds and where they sit, such as element, group, or site-group. A role accepts some kinds and rejects the others. See Check a system.

docs.title: Label
docs.text: A label is the name of a part, unique among the parts of its system. Roles bind elements by label, and dotted names start with it. See Check a system.

docs.title: Law
docs.text: A law is one equation or rule for one state, such as a rate, the next value at a step, or a random jump. Elements and interactions return laws, and the compiler joins them into a problem. See Laws.

docs.title: Law kind
docs.text: The law kind of a part is the kind of law it returns, such as rate, update, or jump. The law kinds of a system decide its mathematical form and its default solver. See Check a system.

docs.title: Likelihood
docs.text: The likelihood of parameters is the probability of the observed data under them. Calibration maximises it or samples the posterior it implies. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Loss
docs.text: A loss scores how far a candidate set of parameters lies from the data, such as the sum of squared residuals. A calibration method minimises it or reads it as a likelihood. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Lyapunov exponent
docs.text: A Lyapunov exponent is the average rate at which two nearby paths separate along one direction. A positive exponent means chaos, a negative one contraction, and zero a direction along which paths neither separate nor approach. See Analyse.

docs.title: Main public methods
docs.text: The main public methods of a part are prepare, which checks it against what it works on, and run, which sets what it contributes. Both return the part itself. See How the parts fit.

docs.title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
docs.text: Markov chain Monte Carlo draws samples of a posterior with a random walk whose long-run distribution is the posterior. The No-U-Turn Sampler follows the gradient of the likelihood to move faster. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Mass action
docs.text: The law of mass action makes the rate of a reaction proportional to the product of the amounts of its reactants. Epidemiology calls the same assumption homogeneous mixing. See ReactionNetworkSystem.

docs.title: Member
docs.text: A member is one instance of the element class of a group, such as one cell of a lattice or one agent of a flock. Each member holds its own copy of the states of the class. See GroupElement.

docs.title: Model parameter
docs.text: A model parameter is an argument of a system class, such as the growth rate r, set with set_params. Changing it builds new parts, while a dotted name changes a value of the built parts. See Change it.

docs.title: Neighbourhood
docs.text: A neighbourhood says which members of a space count as neighbours of each member, such as the four nearest sites of a lattice or every point within a radius. Interactions over neighbours read it. See Spaces, neighbourhoods, and times.

docs.title: Nested system
docs.text: A nested system is a system held inside another as one of its parts. Its elements are reached by paths such as village/farmers, and it becomes a partition when its laws fit one form. See Simulate.

docs.title: Observable
docs.text: An observable is a named value computed from the states at every frame, such as the total population. The trajectory records it beside the states. See Simulate.

docs.title: Observer
docs.text: An observer receives the frames of a run as they come. The recorder keeps them as a trajectory, and other observers check invariants or stream the run to a viewer. See Observe.

docs.title: Ordinary differential equation
docs.text: An ordinary differential equation gives the rate of change of each state as a function of the states and time. A system of rate laws in continuous time compiles to one. See Simulate.

docs.title: Orbit diagram
docs.text: An orbit diagram shows the values a state visits after a transient, for every value of a parameter. One value means a steady state, a few a periodic cycle, and many a cycle that does not repeat. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Partition
docs.text: A partition is a part of a system that runs with its own solver during co-simulation. Each nested system whose laws fit one form becomes one. See Simulate.

docs.title: Phase space
docs.text: A phase space pairs every position of a lattice with a value on one or more class axes, such as a velocity. A density on it describes a population, such as the molecules of a gas, by how much of it sits in each cell. See PhaseSpace.

docs.title: Posterior
docs.text: The posterior is the distribution of the parameters given the data and the prior. A posterior method of calibration returns samples of it. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Posterior predictive check
docs.text: A posterior predictive check simulates data from posterior draws and asks whether they look like the observed data. The share of observed points inside the simulated band measures it. See Evaluate.

docs.title: Prior
docs.text: The prior is the distribution of the parameters before the data are seen. A bound (low, high) reads as a uniform prior. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Propensity
docs.text: The propensity of a random event is its rate, the expected number of firings per unit of time. Under mass action it is the rate constant times the product of the reactant amounts. See Simulate.

docs.title: Recipe
docs.text: A recipe is a general system of skcomplex.systems.general, such as a reaction network or a stock and flow model, that a field system subclasses or fills with data. See Build a custom system.

docs.title: Recurrence
docs.text: A recurrence is a pair of times at which the states of a run lie close to each other. The share of recurrences that form diagonal lines, the determinism, is close to 1 for a periodic series. See Analyse.

docs.title: Residual
docs.text: A residual is the difference between a simulated value and an observed one at the same time. Losses and measures of fit are built from residuals. See Evaluate.

docs.title: Role
docs.text: A role is a named slot of an interaction, such as predator or prey, bound to an element by its label. It names the kinds of element and the states it reads. See Check a system.

docs.title: Run settings
docs.text: The run settings are the arguments of simulate, such as until, dt, and random_state. A system class tunes defaults for those a call leaves out. See Simulate.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text: A scenario is a named variant of a system, such as an intervention, run under the same random draws as the baseline. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text: A schedule sets parameters from functions of time at every frame of a run, such as a slow ramp of a birth rate. See Simulate.

docs.title: Section
docs.text: A section reduces a flow to a map by keeping its states at chosen moments. A Poincaré section keeps the moments when a state crosses a value, and a stroboscopic section samples once per period of a periodic force. See Analyse.

docs.title: Sensitivity analysis
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis ranks the inputs of a model by their effect on an output, one at a time or by splitting the variance of the output. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: A solver advances a compiled problem in time, such as the LSODA method for ordinary differential equations or the Gillespie algorithm for jumps. The tags of a system choose the default solver. See Simulate.

docs.title: Space
docs.text: A space places the members of a group and says who neighbours whom, such as a lattice, a network, or continuous space. See Spaces, neighbourhoods, and times.

docs.title: Spec
docs.text: A spec is a small frozen record that describes a value, such as a StateSpec that gives the domain and the order of a state. Parts read specs for their declarations and settings. See How the parts fit.

docs.title: State
docs.text: A state is a number that changes as a system runs, such as the size of a population. Its initial value is the default of its argument. See How the parts fit.

docs.title: Steady state
docs.text: A steady state is a state that a run reaches and keeps, so its rates are zero there. It is a fixed point that attracts nearby runs. See Run experiments.

docs.title: Stiff
docs.text: A stiff system mixes fast and slow time scales, so an explicit solver needs tiny steps to stay stable. Implicit methods such as BDF take large steps instead. See Simulate.

docs.title: Stochastic
docs.text: A stochastic system draws random numbers, so one initial state gives many possible runs. A random_state makes one of them reproducible. See Simulate.

docs.title: Stoichiometry
docs.text: The stoichiometry of a reaction is the number of units of each species it consumes and produces. Its stoichiometric vector is the change of every amount when the reaction fires once. See ReactionInteraction.

docs.title: Surrogate
docs.text: A surrogate is a system learned from data that runs, forecasts, and is analysed like a system written by hand. See Analyse.

docs.title: Sweep
docs.text: A sweep runs a system once per row of a design of parameter values and collects the outputs in one table. See Run experiments.

docs.title: System
docs.text: A system composes elements, interactions, a space, and a time into one model that simulate runs. A system class builds its parts from model parameters. See Systems.

docs.title: System class
docs.text: A system class is a subclass of BaseSystem that builds its parts from model parameters and tunes its run settings. The catalog holds ready-made system classes. See System classes.

docs.title: Tag
docs.text: A tag records a capability of a part, such as its time, its law kinds, the domains of its states, or its randomness. The tags of a system join those of its parts and choose its solver. See Check a system.

docs.title: Time
docs.text: The time of a system says whether it flows continuously, steps in discrete increments, or is solved once without time. See ContinuousTime.

docs.title: Trajectory
docs.text: A trajectory holds the frames of a run, with the times, the states, and the parameters of every frame. simulate returns it. See Simulate.

docs.title: Variational inference
docs.text: Variational inference fits a simple distribution, such as a multivariate normal, to the posterior instead of sampling it. It is fast but can miss a skewed posterior. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Virtual population
docs.text: A virtual population is a set of parameter rows whose runs look like real observations, drawn from priors and kept when their outputs lie in plausible ranges. See Calibrate.

docs.title: Observe
docs.text: This tutorial records the quantities of a run that the states do not hold, watches a run in the Rerun viewer with a layout of its views, and plots trajectories and experiment results with matplotlib. It follows the hare and lynx model of the tutorial Build a custom system.

docs.title: The running example
docs.text:
LotkaVolterraSystem of skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology holds the predator and prey model of Lotka and Volterra with the rates of Carpenter (2018). It starts from the pelt records of 1900, 30.0 thousand hares and 4.0 thousand lynx.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0).get_values('prey.x').round(1)[:6].tolist()

[30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2, 48.8, 18.6]

The hares rise from 30.0 to 81.2 thousand in 1903 and fall to 18.6 thousand in 1905, as in the build tutorial.

docs.title: Observables
docs.text:
An observable is a quantity that a run computes at every frame from the states, such as the total of two populations. An ObservableSpec pairs a label with an expression, a function of the namespace s of the system that returns a symbolic expression. simulate takes the observables in observables, records them in the trajectory under their labels, and logs them to Rerun when an observer runs.

The Lotka and Volterra model conserves a quantity along every cycle, V = b H - d ln H + a L - r ln L for hares H and lynx L. Recording it checks that the solver keeps it constant.

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import log

from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec


def total(s):
    return s.prey.x + s.predators.x


def conserved(s):
    return 0.024 * s.prey.x - 0.80 * log(s.prey.x) + 0.028 * s.predators.x - 0.55 * log(s.predators.x)


observables = [ObservableSpec('total', total), ObservableSpec('V', conserved)]
observed = simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0, observables=observables)
observed.get_values('total').round(1)[:4].tolist(), np.ptp(observed.get_values('V')) < 1e-4

([34.0, 50.8, 76.3, 103.7], True)

The two populations together grow from 34.0 to 103.7 thousand animals in 1903. The quantity V varies by less than 0.0001 over the twenty years, so the solver keeps it constant up to its tolerance. A drift of V would show that the solver loses accuracy over long runs.

An observable must pickle with its system, so its functions are module-level functions. A lambda raises an error.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    simulate(system, until=1, observables=[ObservableSpec('total', lambda s: s.prey.x + s.predators.x)])
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message.splitlines()[1][:80]

- system: The expression of the observable 'total' cannot be pickled: Can't pick

The message says that the expression of the observable 'total' cannot be pickled, and asks for a module-level function or a symbolic expression instead of a lambda or a local function.

docs.title: Observables of a group
docs.text:
A group holds many identical members, and an observable may reduce a variable of every member to one number. The reduction is count, sum, mean, min, max, var, or a function. Here a group of 100 phase oscillators, each turning at its own frequency, records the mean of the phase vector exp(i theta) of the members, and the order parameter, its modulus, is an expression that reads the earlier observable by its label as s.z. An order parameter near 1 means the phases sit together, and near 0 that they spread around the circle.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import I, exp, pi

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec, ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class OscillatorElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        theta: Annotated[float, StateSpec(period=2 * pi)] = 0.0,
        omega: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.theta = theta
        self.omega = omega

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.theta, s.omega)]


def phase_vector(member):
    return exp(I * member.theta)


def order_parameter(s):
    return abs(s.z)


values = {'theta': np.linspace(0, 1, 100), 'omega': np.linspace(0.9, 1.1, 100)}
oscillators = CompositeSystem(elements=[GroupElement('phases', element=OscillatorElement, size=100, values=values)])
observables = [ObservableSpec('z', phase_vector, group='phases'), ObservableSpec('order', order_parameter)]
order = simulate(oscillators, until=50, dt=1.0, observables=observables).get_values('order')
round(float(order[0]), 3), round(float(order[-1]), 3)

(0.958, 0.12)

The oscillators start within one radian of each other and drift apart at their own frequencies, so the order falls from 0.958 to 0.12.

docs.title: Laws that read observables
docs.text:
A law may react to a quantity of the whole system, such as the mean field of all oscillators. It reads an observable through a role bound to the label of the observable, as s.<role>.value. The interaction below pulls every oscillator towards the mean phase, with the means X of cos theta and Y of sin theta as its roles.

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import cos, sin

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import Interaction
from skcomplex.core.specs import RoleSpec


class MeanFieldInteraction(Interaction):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        X: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        Y: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        K: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.target = target
        self.X = X
        self.Y = Y
        self.K = K

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.target.theta, s.K * (s.Y.value * cos(s.target.theta) - s.X.value * sin(s.target.theta)))]


def cosine(member):
    return cos(member.theta)


def sine(member):
    return sin(member.theta)


values = {'theta': np.linspace(0, 6, 100), 'omega': np.linspace(0.9, 1.1, 100)}
coupled = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[GroupElement('phases', element=OscillatorElement, size=100, values=values)],
    interactions=[MeanFieldInteraction('coupling', target='phases', X='X', Y='Y', K=2.0)],
)
observables = [ObservableSpec('X', cosine, group='phases'), ObservableSpec('Y', sine, group='phases')]
synchronised = simulate(coupled, until=20, dt=1.0, observables=observables)
X, Y = synchronised.get_values('X'), synchronised.get_values('Y')
round(float(np.hypot(X[0], Y[0])), 2), round(float(np.hypot(X[-1], Y[-1])), 2)

(0.04, 1.0)

The phases start spread over the whole circle, with an order parameter of 0.04, and the coupling gathers them, so the order parameter, the modulus of (X, Y), ends at 1.0. When the law reads the value depends on where the observable and the law live:

  • A symbolic observable is an expression, or a reduction with a string reduce over an element group. Laws of its own partition read it at the current state. The compiled problem evaluates it before the law, so the value the law reads equals the recorded value at every frame.
  • A law of another partition reads the observable as held at the last synchronisation point. This is how agents and equations exchange macroscopic quantities in a co-simulation.
  • An observable with a Python function as reduce, or one over agents, is read only from another partition. Reading it in its own partition raises an error.

docs.title: Watching a run with Rerun
docs.text:
Rerun is a viewer for data that change in time. RerunObserver logs the frames of a run to it, and simulate takes it in observers. It sends the frames to a viewer it spawns with spawn=True, to a running viewer with connect=True, or to a .rrd file with save_path. The blocks of this page save to a temporary file, so they run without a viewer.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.viz import RerunObserver
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
observer = RerunObserver('pelts', save_path=folder / 'pelts.rrd', interval=5)
simulate(system, until=20, dt=0.1, observers=[observer])
(folder / 'pelts.rrd').exists(), observer.logged_frames_

<skcomplex.core.engine.runtime._trajectories.Trajectory object at 0x752fc80957b0>
(True, 41)

The recording exists, and with interval=5 the observer logged every fifth of the 201 frames, 41 in all. Open it with rerun pelts.rrd. The entity paths follow the system tree, so the hares appear under prey and the lynx under predators, and the parameters under parameters/. Each frame sets the timelines sim_time, the simulated time, and step, the index of the frame.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
A visual draws one element or group of a system in Rerun, and each type of element declares its default visual. The populations of the example are scalar elements, so their visual is a ScalarsVisual that logs every state as a time series. The prepared observer holds the visual of every element in visuals_.

[(type(visual).__name__, visual.path) for visual in observer.visuals_]

[('ScalarsVisual', 'prey'), ('ScalarsVisual', 'predators')]

Both populations are drawn by a ScalarsVisual, one at the path prey and one at predators. The visuals of skcomplex.core.engine.viz are named by a kind, which a VisualSpec gives:

Kind Visual What it draws 'scalars' ScalarsVisual every state component of an element as a time series 'points' PointsVisual a vector state as points, and other states as time series 'agents' AgentsVisual the agents of a group as one batch per frame 'histograms' HistogramVisual histograms of agents or of groups without a space 'image' ImageVisual every state of a lattice group as an image coloured by value 'sites' SiteVisual every state of a non-square lattice group as coloured sites 'cayley' CayleyVisual every state of a lattice group on a group space as a graph 'mesh' MeshVisual every state of a finite element field as a triangle mesh 'cell' CellVisual a state on the edges or faces of a complex 'phase_ring' PhaseRingVisual the wrapped phases of oscillators against their position 'axes' AxisVisual the axes of a tensor state or the arrows of a vector state 'bodies' BodiesVisual bodies at positions computed from the states of an element 'matrix' MatrixVisual a matrix-valued state or parameter as an image 'expectations' ExpectationVisual the local expectations of operator elements and groups 'geometry' GeometryVisual the structure of a rewritten element 'linear_program' LinearProgramVisual the linear program of an element

The default visuals follow the kind of element:

  • Particles appear as 3D points, and populations as time series.
  • Agents on grids and in continuous spaces appear as points coloured by a state, and agents on networks as graph nodes.
  • Reporters appear under reporters/.
  • A group is logged as one batch per state.
  • Points and agents in a continuous space without a given radius take a share of the extent of the view. A group of at most ten points draws the trail of its recent positions, which trail=0 turns off.
  • A one-dimensional lattice also logs a space-time image, one row per logged frame with the oldest at the top, holding at most ImageVisual(history=...) rows.
  • A complex state of a lattice or a mesh appears as two images. Its modulus goes under <path>/<state>/modulus, coloured over the range, and its phase under <path>/<state>/phase, coloured by a cyclic palette over (-π, π]. A complex scalar appears as the series <path>/<state>/real and <path>/<state>/imag.

An element or a group sets its own visual with its argument visual. Below, two atoms joined by a spring move in three dimensions, and the second atom asks for points coloured by its velocity x_d1 with VisualSpec('points', {'position': 'x', 'color_by': 'x_d1'}).

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec, VisualSpec


class AtomElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        x: Annotated[object, StateSpec(vector=True, order=2, role='position')] = 0.0,
        x_d1: object = 0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.x = x
        self.x_d1 = x_d1


speed = VisualSpec('points', {'position': 'x', 'color_by': 'x_d1'})
molecule = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[
        AtomElement('a', x=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]),
        AtomElement('b', visual=speed, x=[1.5, 0.0, 0.0], x_d1=[0.0, 0.5, 0.0]),
    ],
    interactions=[
        RateInteraction('pull', target='a', sources=['b'], rate=lambda s: 4.0 * (s.sources[0].x - s.target.x)),
        RateInteraction('push', target='b', sources=['a'], rate=lambda s: 4.0 * (s.sources[0].x - s.target.x)),
    ],
    space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=3),
)
atoms = RerunObserver('molecule', save_path=folder / 'molecule.rrd')
simulate(molecule, until=5, dt=0.02, observers=[atoms])
[type(visual).__name__ for visual in atoms.visuals_], type(atoms.views_[0]).__name__

<skcomplex.core.engine.runtime._trajectories.Trajectory object at 0x752fc8095bd0>
(['ScalarsVisual', 'PointsVisual'], 'Spatial3DView')

The first atom keeps the default visual of a new type of element, a ScalarsVisual of time series. The second is drawn by a PointsVisual with the colours of its speed, and its 3D spatial view comes first. Every visual subclasses BaseVisual. prepare(problem) finds the element at the entity path path in a compiled problem and sets its views in views_, and run(frame) logs the element at one frame to the recording recording. A new visual implements the hook _log for elements or _log_agents for agents, declares its views with _views, and is given to a VisualSpec as its class.

docs.title: Layouts and blueprints
docs.text:
A Rerun blueprint arranges the views of the viewer. Every visual declares the views that show what it logs, and RerunObserver(blueprint='default') arranges them into a blueprint.
