A blueprint of your own may replace it. Preparing an observer on a compiled problem builds the blueprint without sending it anywhere, so it can be inspected first.

problem = simulate(system, until=0).problem
layout = RerunObserver(blueprint='default').prepare(problem)
[type(view).__name__ for view in layout.views_], [str(view.origin) for view in layout.views_]

(['TimeSeriesView'], ['/'])

The populations are scalars of one type, so they share one time series view, a TimeSeriesView with the origin /. The views follow what is logged:

  • Scalars go in time series views.
  • Points go in 2D or 3D spatial views, by their dimension.
  • Lattices and fields go in one 2D view per state, after the 2D views of their space-time images in one dimension.
  • Meshes go in 3D views.
  • Agents go in a 2D view, or a graph view on a network. Agents without a space get no spatial view.

The default blueprint arranges these views:

  • Spatial views come first and side by side, with time series views below them.
  • Scalar elements of one type share a time series view with at most six series.
  • Parameters are left out unless parameters=True.
  • The side panels are collapsed, the top panel is hidden, and the time panel follows the latest frame.

primary names the view to put first, so the first view shows the behaviour that defines the system. The observer sends the blueprint, kept as blueprint_, with the recording, and writes it next to a saved recording as a .rbl file with the same stem. Below, a blueprint of your own shows the hares alone, with the side panels collapsed.

import rerun.blueprint as rrb

hares_only = rrb.Blueprint(rrb.TimeSeriesView(origin='/prey', name='hares'), collapse_panels=True)
custom = RerunObserver('pelts', save_path=folder / 'hares.rrd', blueprint=hares_only)
simulate(system, until=20, observers=[custom])
sorted(file.name for file in folder.glob('hares.*'))

<skcomplex.core.engine.runtime._trajectories.Trajectory object at 0x752fc8095c80>
['hares.rbl', 'hares.rrd']

The folder holds the recording hares.rrd and its blueprint hares.rbl. Open both with rerun hares.rrd hares.rbl to see the layout.

docs.title: Plots with matplotlib
docs.text:
A figure for a paper or a report is drawn from the arrays of a trajectory or an experiment result. The blocks below use the backend 'Agg' of matplotlib, which draws into files and opens no window. The data are the pelt records of 1900 to 1920, in thousands, as distributed with the case study of Carpenter (2018, Predator-Prey Population Dynamics: the Lotka-Volterra model in Stan) in the file knitr/lotka-volterra/hudson-bay-lynx-hare.csv of the Stan example models. The tutorial Build a custom system traces their source.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

years = np.arange(1900, 1921)
hares = np.array(
    [30.0, 47.2, 70.2, 77.4, 36.3, 20.6, 18.1, 21.4, 22.0, 25.4, 27.1]
    + [40.3, 57.0, 76.6, 52.3, 19.5, 11.2, 7.6, 14.6, 16.2, 24.7]
)
lynx = np.array(
    [4.0, 6.1, 9.8, 35.2, 59.4, 41.7, 19.0, 13.0, 8.3, 9.1, 7.4]
    + [8.0, 12.3, 19.5, 45.7, 51.1, 29.7, 15.8, 9.7, 10.1, 8.6]
)
system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
trajectory = simulate(system, until=20, dt=0.1)
times = 1900 + np.asarray(trajectory.times)

figure, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
left.plot(times, trajectory.get_values('prey.x'), label='hares, model')
left.plot(times, trajectory.get_values('predators.x'), label='lynx, model')
left.plot(years, hares, 'o', label='hares, pelts')
left.plot(years, lynx, 's', label='lynx, pelts')
left.set(xlabel='year', ylabel='thousands', title='Populations')
left.legend()
right.plot(trajectory.get_values('prey.x'), trajectory.get_values('predators.x'))
right.plot(hares, lynx, 'o')
right.set(xlabel='hares (thousands)', ylabel='lynx (thousands)', title='Phase plane')
path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'pelts.png'
figure.savefig(path)
plt.close(figure)
path.exists(), len(left.lines), len(right.lines)

[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc72a6850>]
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc72a6990>]
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc72a6ad0>]
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc72a6c10>]
[Text(0.5, 0, 'year'), Text(0, 0.5, 'thousands'), Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Populations')]
<matplotlib.legend.Legend object at 0x752fc72a6d50>
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc82460d0>]
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc8246350>]
[Text(0.5, 0, 'hares (thousands)'), Text(0, 0.5, 'lynx (thousands)'), Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Phase plane')]
(True, 4, 2)

The left panel draws the model against the records over time, four lines with the two series of points. The right panel draws the phase plane, the lynx against the hares, where the model runs on a closed cycle and the records circle around it. get_values returns the series of a state path and times the times of the frames, which the block shifts to calendar years.

An experiment result gives its arrays in the same way. Below, a sweep of the growth rate of the hares is drawn with the peak of the hares on one axis and the rate on the other, from get_column of the result.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sweep


def hare_peak(trajectory):
    return float(trajectory.get_values('prey.x').max())


rates = np.linspace(0.4, 0.7, 7)
swept = sweep(system, {'r': rates}, until=20, dt=0.5, outputs=[hare_peak])
figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
axes.plot(swept.get_column('r'), swept.get_column('hare_peak'), 'o-')
axes.set(xlabel='growth rate of the hares (per year)', ylabel='highest count of hares (thousands)')
figure.savefig(path.with_name('sweep.png'))
plt.close(figure)
swept.get_column('hare_peak').round(1).tolist()

[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x752fc5da11d0>]
[Text(0.5, 0, 'growth rate of the hares (per year)'), Text(0, 0.5, 'highest count of hares (thousands)')]
[65.0, 70.3, 76.0, 81.5, 87.2, 92.4, 98.6]

The highest count of hares rises with their growth rate, from 65.0 thousand at r = 0.4 to 98.6 thousand at r = 0.7. The page Run experiments runs the other experiments, whose results hold arrays to plot in the same way.

docs.title: Run experiments
docs.text: This tutorial runs the hare and lynx model many times and reads what the runs say together. It sweeps the rates, repeats a stochastic version, compares an intervention with the baseline, ranks the rates by their effect, measures how often the lynx fall to a dangerous level, and finds where the cycles settle. Every experiment is a function of skcomplex.core.experiments that takes a system and returns a frozen result, as the model selection functions of scikit-learn take an estimator.

docs.title: The running example
docs.text:
The model is the predator and prey cycle of the snowshoe hare and the Canada lynx, built in the tutorial Build a custom system. LotkaVolterraSystem of skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology holds it with the rates of Carpenter (2018): the growth rate r of the hares, the rate a at which the lynx remove hares, the rate b at which eating hares feeds the lynx, and the death rate d of the lynx, all per year. The runs start from the pelt records of 1900, 30.0 thousand hares and 4.0 thousand lynx.

from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
[interaction.label for interaction in system.prepare().system_.interactions]

['growth', 'predation', 'death']

The system has the populations prey and predators, each with the state x, and the interactions growth, predation, and death. An experiment names a value in two ways. A name without a dot, such as r, is a model parameter of the system, set on a copy with set_params. A dotted path, such as growth.r or prey.x, is a parameter or an initial state of a part, which keeps its value for the whole run.

docs.title: Sweeps
docs.text:
A sweep runs the system once per row of a design and collects the outputs of every run in one table. Here sweep runs three growth rates of the hares. An output is a state path, whose series the run keeps, or a function of a trajectory that returns a number, named after the function.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sweep


def hare_peak(trajectory):
    return float(trajectory.get_values('prey.x').max())


swept = sweep(system, {'r': [0.45, 0.55, 0.65]}, until=20, dt=1.0, outputs=['predators.x', hare_peak])
[(row['r'], round(row['hare_peak'], 1)) for row in swept.rows]

[(0.45, 69.8), (0.55, 81.2), (0.65, 85.8)]

The highest count of hares over twenty years rises with their growth rate, from 69.8 thousand at r = 0.45 through 81.2 thousand at the estimate of Carpenter to 85.8 thousand at r = 0.65. The result is an ExperimentResult. Its rows hold one mapping per run, with the values of the row, the scenario, the replicate, the seed, and the outputs. A state output appears in a row by its last value, and get_series returns its whole series, one row per run.

swept.get_column('hare_peak').round(1).tolist(), swept.get_series('predators.x').shape

([69.8, 81.2, 85.8], (3, 21))

get_column returns the scalar output of every run, here the three peaks, and get_series the lynx of the three runs at the 21 frames of the years 1900 to 1920.

docs.title: Designs
docs.text:
A grid runs every combination of the values it is given. For several inputs a sampled design covers the space with fewer runs. The rates below are dotted paths, and design='latin_hypercube' draws 8 rows, one in every eighth of the range of each rate. convert_to_frame returns the rows as a pandas data frame.

bounds = {'growth.r': (0.4, 0.7), 'death.d': (0.6, 1.0)}
sampled = sweep(
    system, bounds, design='latin_hypercube', n=8, until=20, dt=1.0, outputs=[hare_peak], random_state=0
)
frame = sampled.convert_to_frame()
frame[['growth.r', 'death.d', 'hare_peak']].round(2).head(3).values.tolist()

[[0.53, 0.79, 77.85], [0.7, 0.75, 86.57], [0.59, 0.65, 76.83]]

The first three rows pair a growth rate and a death rate with the peak of the hares they produce, such as 0.53 and 0.79 with a peak of 77.85 thousand. The designs are these:

  • 'grid', the default, runs every combination of a sequence of values per name, the last name varying fastest.
  • 'random' draws n rows uniformly within a pair (low, high), or from a SciPy distribution given per name.
  • 'latin_hypercube' draws n rows with one in every stratum of every name.
  • 'sobol' takes n points of a scrambled Sobol sequence, best with n a power of 2.

The sweep compiled the model once for all eight rows. Runs that change only dotted paths, initial states, or seeds reuse one compiled problem, while a model parameter such as r builds a new system. A study of thousands of rows should therefore sweep dotted paths.

A sequence of mappings is a design of given rows, which run as they are. The first argument may also be a factory of systems, such as the system class itself, which takes the values of a row as keyword arguments.

records = {'prey': 30.0, 'predators': 4.0, 'r': 0.55, 'a': 0.028, 'b': 0.024, 'd': 0.80}
given = sweep(LotkaVolterraSystem, [records, {**records, 'predators': 8.0}], until=20, dt=1.0, outputs=[hare_peak])
given.get_column('hare_peak').round(1).tolist()

[81.2, 59.9]

Twice as many lynx in 1900 hold the highest count of the hares down from 81.2 to 59.9 thousand.

docs.title: Analyses of every run
docs.text:
An analysis function can run on every trajectory of an experiment. bind_analysis fixes its settings, and every field of its result becomes a column named <function>.<field>. Here spectrum computes the power spectrum of the hares, and the frequency of the highest power gives the period of the cycle. The setting dt gives the spectrum the time between frames, so its frequencies are per year.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import bind_analysis, spectrum

rhythm = bind_analysis(spectrum, variables=['prey.x'], dt=0.5)
cycles = sweep(system, {'r': [0.45, 0.65]}, until=60, dt=0.5, analyses=[rhythm])
[round(float(1 / row['spectrum.frequencies'][row['spectrum.power'][0].argmax()]), 1) for row in cycles.rows]

[12.1, 10.1]

The cycle lasts about 12.1 years at r = 0.45 and 10.1 years at r = 0.65, so faster growth of the hares shortens it, towards the cycle of about ten years in the records. Sixty years give a coarse spectrum. The times between the peaks of the same runs are 11.4 and 10.0 years, and a study of the period would run longer or measure those times.

docs.title: Ensembles
docs.text:
An ensemble repeats the runs of a stochastic system with independent random streams, to show the spread of its outcomes. ensemble refuses the deterministic model, because its runs repeat one another.

from skcomplex.core.errors import TagError
from skcomplex.core.experiments import ensemble

try:
    ensemble(system, replicates=5, until=10)
except TagError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

ensemble needs the randomness stochastic, but LotkaVolterraSystem has the randomness deterministic. Its runs repeat one another, so run it once with `simulate`, or give it a part or a solver that draws.

The message says that ensemble needs the randomness stochastic while LotkaVolterraSystem is deterministic, and suggests running it once with simulate or giving it a part or a solver that draws. The randomness is one of the capability tags of a system, which the page Check a system describes.

On a small island the populations are counted one animal at a time, and chance decides each birth and death. The recipe ReactionNetworkSystem of skcomplex.systems.general.reactions runs the four terms of the model as reactions. In the mode 'jump' each reaction is a random event that changes a count by one animal, drawn by the algorithm of Gillespie. Each row of the table holds the reactants, the products, and the rate constant.

from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem

reactions = {
    'births': ({'prey': 1}, {'prey': 2}, 0.55),
    'hunting': ({'prey': 1, 'predators': 1}, {'predators': 1}, 0.028),
    'feeding': ({'prey': 1, 'predators': 1}, {'prey': 1, 'predators': 2}, 0.024),
    'deaths': ({'predators': 1}, {}, 0.80),
}
island = ReactionNetworkSystem({'prey': 30, 'predators': 4}, reactions, mode='jump')
runs = ensemble(island, replicates=20, until=10, dt=1.0, outputs=['predators.x'], random_state=0)
times, values, seeds = runs.get_ensemble('predators.x')
values.shape, int((values[:, -1] == 0).sum())

((20, 11), 4)

get_ensemble returns the common times, one row of values per run, and the seed of every run. The 20 runs of ten years hold 11 values each, and in 4 of them the lynx have died out by the tenth year. The deterministic model never reaches zero, so the extinctions come from chance alone. get_summary gives the mean, the standard deviation, and the 5%, 50%, and 95% quantiles of every output across the replicates.

summary = runs.get_summary()[0]
round(summary['predators.x.mean'], 1), round(summary['predators.x.q0.05'], 1), round(summary['predators.x.q0.95'], 1)

(6.3, 0.0, 16.2)

After ten years the island holds 6.3 lynx on average, with 0.0 at the 5% quantile and 16.2 at the 95% quantile. A study of the risk of extinction would run hundreds or thousands of replicates.

Every design row and replicate gets its own random stream, spawned from random_state in a fixed order. The results are therefore the same whether the runs go one after another, on threads, or on processes, which the argument executor chooses with 'serial', 'thread', or 'process'. A sweep with replicates greater than one repeats every row in the same way.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A scenario is a named variant of a system, such as an intervention, compared with the baseline under the same random draws. A ScenarioSpec changes values before the run with overrides, changes parameters during the run with schedule, or replaces the system for a change of structure. Here trappers raise the death rate of the lynx from 0.80 to 1.0 from year 10 on, and compare_scenarios runs both scenarios.

from skcomplex.core.components.specs import ScenarioSpec
from skcomplex.core.experiments import compare_scenarios

scenarios = [ScenarioSpec('baseline'), ScenarioSpec('trapping', schedule=[(10.0, 'death.d', 1.0)])]
compared = compare_scenarios(system, scenarios, until=60, dt=0.1, outputs=['prey.x'], warmup=10)
[row['scenario'] for row in compared.rows], compared.get_series('prey.x').mean(axis=1).round(1).tolist()

(['baseline', 'trapping'], [34.4, 41.6])

warmup drops the frames before year 10 from the kept series, so the means cover the years after the trapping starts. The hares average 34.4 thousand without trapping and 41.6 thousand with it. This is the principle of Volterra: the average of the prey over a cycle is d / b, which is 33.3 at d = 0.80 and 41.7 at d = 1.0, so killing the predators raises the average of their prey. A scenario with overrides={'predators.x': 8.0} would start from more lynx instead. Every scenario of a replicate shares one random stream, so the scenarios of a stochastic system differ only through what they change.

docs.title: Sensitivity
docs.text:
Sensitivity analysis ranks the inputs of a model by their effect on one output. Here the output is the count of hares in 1903, the year of the first peak, and each of the four rates varies by a tenth to a fifth around its estimate. sensitivity reads the last value of the output, so the runs stop at year 3.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sensitivity

rates = {'growth.r': (0.45, 0.65), 'predation.a': (0.023, 0.033), 'predation.b': (0.019, 0.029), 'death.d': (0.7, 0.9)}
one_at_a_time = sensitivity(system, rates, output='prey.x', method='oat', until=3, dt=1.0)
one_at_a_time.ranking, {name: round(effect, 1) for name, effect in one_at_a_time.effects.items()}

(['predation.b', 'growth.r', 'death.d', 'predation.a'],
 {'growth.r': 16.1, 'predation.a': -11.4, 'predation.b': -41.0, 'death.d': 15.9})

The method 'oat' moves one input at a time from its lower to its upper bound, with the others at their midpoints, and gives the change of the output. The feeding rate b matters most: raising it lowers the peak by 41.0 thousand hares, because fed lynx multiply faster and eat the hares sooner. The growth rate r raises the peak by 16.1 thousand, the death rate d by 15.9 thousand, and the hunting rate a lowers it by 11.4 thousand.

One move per input misses interactions between inputs. The method 'morris' takes n random paths through a grid of four levels per input and averages the absolute effects of the steps, and 'sobol' splits the variance of the output into shares, with SALib.

screening = sensitivity(system, rates, output='prey.x', method='morris', n=10, until=3, dt=1.0, random_state=0)
variance = sensitivity(system, rates, output='prey.x', method='sobol', n=64, until=3, dt=1.0, random_state=0)
screening.ranking, {name: round(index, 2) for name, index in variance.total_order.items()}

(['predation.b', 'growth.r', 'death.d', 'predation.a'],
 {'growth.r': 0.2, 'predation.a': 0.05, 'predation.b': 0.95, 'death.d': 0.1})

Both methods agree on the ranking b, r, d, a. The total Sobol index of b is 0.95, so the feeding rate alone drives most of the variance of the peak, and the index of r is 0.2. The Morris screening ran 50 runs, 10 paths of 5 steps each. The Sobol analysis ran 384 runs, six for each of the 64 base points, and its indices carry confidence intervals in first_order_conf and total_order_conf. A study would run at least 1024 base points, the default.

docs.title: Basin stability
docs.text:
Basin stability draws many initial states and asks which final behaviour each one ends in. The share of initial states that reach a behaviour measures how stable it is against large disturbances. The cycles of Lotka and Volterra are neutral: every initial state runs on a cycle of its own and no cycle attracts the others. So the classifier below labels an outcome rather than an attractor, whether the lynx fall below one thousand animals during twenty years, a level at which a real population risks dying out. basin_stability draws the initial states uniformly within the bounds.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import basin_stability


def lynx_fate(trajectory):
    lowest = trajectory.get_values('predators.x').min()
    return 'below one thousand' if lowest < 1.0 else 'above one thousand'


starts = {'prey.x': (5.0, 100.0), 'predators.x': (1.0, 40.0)}
basins = basin_stability(system, starts, lynx_fate, n=100, until=20, dt=0.5, random_state=0)
{label: round(share, 2) for label, share in basins.fractions.items()}, round(basins.errors['below one thousand'], 2)

({'above one thousand': 0.96, 'below one thousand': 0.04}, 0.02)

Of 100 initial states, 96 keep the lynx above one thousand and 4 drive them below, with a standard error of 0.02 on each share. The initial states sit in rows and their labels in labels. With vectorized=True all initial states run as the members of one simulation, which is faster for many small runs. A study would draw thousands of initial states.

docs.title: Orbit diagrams
docs.text:
An orbit diagram shows the values a state visits after a transient, for every value of a parameter. A single value means the run settles at a steady state, a few values a periodic cycle, and many values a cycle that does not repeat at the sampled times. With a carrying capacity K the hares grow logistically, and the cycles of the model damp towards a steady state. orbit_diagram runs three capacities for 200 years and keeps the next 20 yearly values of the lynx.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import orbit_diagram

crowded = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80, K=200.0)
diagram = orbit_diagram(
    crowded, 'growth.K', [40.0, 200.0, 2000.0], 'predators.x', transient=200, keep=20, dt=1.0, decimals=1
)
diagram.periods.tolist(), [round(float(points.max() - points.min()), 1) for points in diagram.points]

([1, 1, 18], [0.0, 0.0, 19.3])

periods counts the distinct kept values, rounded to decimals, here one decimal, and points holds them. A capacity of 40 or 200 thousand hares settles the lynx at one value, while at 2000 thousand the lynx take 18 distinct values and still swing over a range of 19.3 thousand after 200 years. A richer habitat damps the cycles more slowly. The same function shows the period doubling of a map, such as the logistic map in the page Analyse.

docs.title: Calibration and evaluation
docs.text:
Fitting the rates to the pelt records is the subject of the page Calibrate, which runs every method of calibrate, from a local least squares fit to Markov chain Monte Carlo. The same page samples virtual populations and fits every individual of a data set on its own, with virtual_population and calibrate_individuals.

Whether a fit can be trusted is the subject of the page Evaluate. It compares the fit with the records, checks the credible intervals of a posterior method with posterior_coverage, and asks with identifiability which rates the records determine.

docs.title: Select a ready-made system
docs.text: This page finds a system of the catalog, reads what it models, and runs it with the settings it was tuned for. The catalog is the set of ready-made systems of skcomplex.systems, each a class built from the public parts of the core.

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text:
This section runs one system of the catalog and reads its description. Every ready-made system is a class named after the system with the suffix System, such as SIRSystem, the epidemic model of Kermack and McKendrick (1927). You import it from its subfield, the package skcomplex.systems.<field>.<subfield>, and simulate runs it with its tuned settings.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem

trajectory = simulate(SIRSystem())
trajectory.get_values('I.x').max().round()

304.0

The number of infected people peaks at 304. simulate returns a trajectory, the recorded run. Its method get_values returns the values of a state, an observable, or a parameter by its dotted path, such as I.x, the state x of the element I, and its attribute names lists every path.

A system class says what it is through plain attributes and methods.

  • The first line of its docstring describes it.
  • field, topics, and references are class attributes.
  • get_params() returns the parameters of its model with their defaults, as for any scikit-learn estimator.
  • get_tags() returns its capability tags, such as its time, its space, the kinds of its laws, and its randomness.
  • get_run_settings() returns the tuned run settings that simulate uses for every argument a call leaves out, such as the end time until and the time between frames dt.
SIRSystem.__doc__.splitlines()[0], SIRSystem.field, SIRSystem.topics, SIRSystem.references

('An epidemic that moves individuals from susceptible to infected to recovered.', 'biology/epidemiology',
 ('compartments', 'ode', 'jump'), ('Kermack and McKendrick 1927',))

The docstring reads "An epidemic that moves individuals from susceptible to infected to recovered." The field path is 'biology/epidemiology', the topics are 'compartments', 'ode', and 'jump', and the reference is Kermack and McKendrick (1927).

system = SIRSystem()
system.get_params(), system.get_tags().laws, system.get_run_settings()['until']

({'beta': 0.0003,
  'gamma': 0.1,
  'infected': 10.0,
  'label': 'system',
  'recovered': 0.0,
  'stochastic': False,
  'susceptible': 990.0},
 frozenset({'rate'}), 160.0)

The parameters are 990 susceptible, 10 infected, and 0 recovered people, the infection rate beta = 0.0003, the recovery rate gamma = 0.1, stochastic=False, and the label. The system holds rate laws, so it runs as differential equations, and its tuned run ends at time 160.

docs.title: Finding a system
docs.text:
This section finds systems by field, by topic, and by what they do. all_systems returns the name and the class of every system that matches its filters. A field path such as 'biology/ecology' selects one subfield.

from skcomplex.systems import all_systems

[name for name, _ in all_systems(field='biology/ecology')][:5]

['AgentBasedLotkaVolterraSystem', 'CometsSystem', 'CommunityFBASystem', 'CompetitionSystem', 'ConsumerResourceSystem']

The first five systems of ecology are AgentBasedLotkaVolterraSystem, CometsSystem, CommunityFBASystem, CompetitionSystem, and ConsumerResourceSystem. A field alone, such as 'chemistry', selects all its subfields.

sorted({cls.field for _, cls in all_systems(field='chemistry')})

['chemistry/kinetics', 'chemistry/pattern_formation']

The systems of chemistry belong to 'chemistry/kinetics' and 'chemistry/pattern_formation'. A topic selects systems across every field.

[name for name, _ in all_systems(topics='oscillation')][:5]

['AdlerEquationSystem', 'AgentBasedLotkaVolterraSystem', 'BrusselatorODESystem', 'BrusselatorSystem',
 'CoupledPendulumsSystem']

The first five oscillators are AdlerEquationSystem, AgentBasedLotkaVolterraSystem, BrusselatorODESystem, BrusselatorSystem, and CoupledPendulumsSystem. Tags select systems by what they do, here the systems of chemistry that draw random numbers.

[name for name, _ in all_systems(field='chemistry', tags={'randomness': 'stochastic'})]

['ChemicalLangevinEquationSystem', 'ChemicalLangevinNetworkSystem']

They are ChemicalLangevinEquationSystem and ChemicalLangevinNetworkSystem. A listing by field and topics reads the sources of the catalog, so it imports only the modules of the systems it returns. A filter by tags builds every selected class with its default parameters, and the tags describe that default. SIRSystem is deterministic by default, and SIRSystem(stochastic=True) is stochastic.

simulate, the analyses, and the experiments take a system instance, never a name. A function that builds several systems, such as a sweep, takes a class or a factory.

docs.title: Fields and subfields
docs.text:
This section lists the field paths of the catalog. Each system has a field path <field>/<subfield>, which all_systems takes as a filter, and you import the system from the subfield package of the same path, such as skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology for biology/epidemiology. The page of each system under Systems shows its import.

Field Subfields physics mechanics, celestial_mechanics, nonlinear_oscillators, synchronization, statistical_mechanics, criticality, soft_matter, active_matter, fluids, waves, pattern_formation, heat, cosmology, climate, oceanography, seismology chemistry kinetics, pattern_formation biology ecology, epidemiology, evolution, neuroscience, systems_biology, physiology, collective_behaviour, oncology economics macroeconomics, markets, finance, econophysics, resources, innovation social opinion_dynamics, segregation, cooperation, spreading, crowds, organizations, language engineering traffic, circuits, control, power_systems, robotics, processes, mechatronics mathematics dynamical_systems, stochastic_processes, networks, fractals, fractional_dynamics computer_science automata, evolutionary_computation, neural_networks

A system lives in the field whose science poses it, and its topics carry its reach into other fields. Three rules keep the catalog apart from the core, and the checks of the package layout enforce them.

  • The core never imports the systems.
  • Every system is built only from the public names of the core.
  • No subfield package imports another. Code that several subfields of one field share lives in the common package of that field, and no field uses the common package of another.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
This section says which systems need an optional install. Most systems run on the default install. A few need a library from an optional extra. Without the extra they stay in the catalog, and preparing or simulating one raises MissingExtraError with the name of the system, the extra, and the install command.

Extra Library Systems Install notes structures Biopython fuzzy_oil_drop, early_stage_folding_intermediate Biopython 1.88 publishes no wheel for macOS on Intel, so the extra builds it from source there with a C compiler. rna ViennaRNA rna_neutral_networks The licence of ViennaRNA allows research and commercial use, forbids redistribution for a fee, and is not OSI approved, so the default install never brings it. trajectories MDTraj none, it reads molecular dynamics trajectories for the systems biology systems MDTraj is under the LGPL.

docs.title: Systems as patterns
docs.text:
This section shows how a ready-made system serves as the pattern of a system of your own. The ready-made systems use the core interface and no other, so the page of every field under Systems shows for each system what a builder needs to copy:

  • its class, with its parameters and tags,
  • its element and interaction types, with their states, parameters, and laws as written,
  • for differential equations and maps, its equations as symbolic(system).equations returns them.

A system of your own follows the same steps. Declare the element and interaction types, and write a class that builds the system from its parameters, as the page System classes shows. The tutorial Check a system shows how to find which parts fit together, and the contributing guide covers adding a system to the catalog.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
This section explains the record of every system the library has surveyed. The inventory, docs/overview/inventory.toml, lists the systems found in the reference books and articles, with their sources and their status: implemented, pending a planned change, or blocked by a missing feature of the core. A system that the core cannot express is recorded as blocked on the OpenSpec change that specifies the missing general feature. It is never worked around inside the system package.

An entry writes the components and the bindings of its system by hand. The time, the space, the laws, and the domains of an implemented system come from get_tags() of its class, so they cannot drift from the code. A check that the documentation build runs compares the inventory with the catalog and the changes.

The systems exist first to exercise the core, and the ready-made systems are a by-product. Every entry lists the core primitives it exercises, such as rates, jumps, groups, lattices, or agents, from a vocabulary that the inventory defines. A primitive that the core lacks names the change that adds it. The priority of an entry is core when it exercises a primitive, or a combination of primitives, that no earlier implemented entry exercises, or when it needs a missing one. It is example when it repeats a covered pattern. So new systems go first where the core is least exercised.

docs.title: Share a system
docs.text: This tutorial turns the hare and lynx model into a system class of the catalog, checks it the way the tests of the catalog do, and writes its inventory entry and its gallery example. It ends with the steps of a contribution to the repository. The page Extend the library explains where a new part goes, and this page follows its placement rule.

docs.title: The system class
docs.text:
A system of the catalog is a subclass of BaseSystem whose name ends in System. It takes its model parameters as arguments, stores each under its own name, and builds its parts in _build_system. Four class variables describe it:

  • field is the field path, a field and a subfield of the catalog, such as 'biology/ecology'.
  • topics are the words that all_systems filters by, such as 'predator-prey'.
  • references are the works the model comes from, each an author and a year.
  • until and dt are the tuned run settings, which simulate reads when a call leaves them out.

The tutorial Build a custom system wrote the model as PeltSystem from core parts. The class below builds it from the same core parts. A class of the catalog would build it from the parts that the systems of ecology share in skcomplex.systems.biology.common, a population element and the growth, predation, and mortality interactions, so that one model has one implementation. Its defaults are the rates of Carpenter (2018) and the pelt records of 1900, and its docstring follows the style of the catalog: a summary, a paragraph on what the model shows, the arguments, and an example.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import DeclaredElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import BaseSystem, CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.specs import DeclaredVariableSpec, StateSpec


class HareLynxSystem(BaseSystem):
    """Snowshoe hares and Canada lynx whose populations cycle through predation.

    The defaults are the posterior means that Carpenter (2018) fitted to the pelt records of the Hudson's Bay Company,
    and the initial populations are the records of 1900, in thousands of pelts. The system has the populations `hares`
    and `lynx`.

    Args:
        hares:
            The initial number of hares, in thousands, such as `30.0`.

        lynx:
            The initial number of lynx, in thousands, such as `4.0`.

        alpha:
            The birth rate of the hares, per year.

        beta:
            The rate at which the lynx remove hares, per thousand lynx and year.

        gamma:
            The death rate of the lynx, per year.

        delta:
            The rate at which eating hares feeds the lynx, per thousand hares and year.

        label:
            The label of the system, which names it when it is nested in another one.

    Examples:
        >>> HareLynxSystem().prepare().system_.elements[0].label
        'hares'
    """

    field = 'biology/ecology'
    topics = ('predator-prey', 'ode', 'oscillation', 'data')
    references = ('Hewitt 1921', 'Carpenter 2018')
    until = 20.0
    dt = 1.0

    def __init__(
        self,
        hares=30.0,
        lynx=4.0,
        *,
        alpha=0.55,
        beta=0.028,
        gamma=0.80,
        delta=0.024,
        label='system',
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.hares = hares
        self.lynx = lynx
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.beta = beta
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.delta = delta

    def _build_system(self):
        hares = DeclaredElement('hares', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(self.hares, StateSpec())})
        lynx = DeclaredElement('lynx', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(self.lynx, StateSpec())})
        alpha, beta, gamma, delta = self.alpha, self.beta, self.gamma, self.delta
        interactions = [
            RateInteraction('births', target='hares', state='x', rate=lambda s: alpha * s.target.x),
            RateInteraction(
                'hunting',
                target='hares',
                state='x',
                sources=['lynx'],
                rate=lambda s: -beta * s.target.x * s.sources[0].x,
            ),
            RateInteraction(
                'feeding',
                target='lynx',
                state='x',
                sources=['hares'],
                rate=lambda s: delta * s.target.x * s.sources[0].x,
            ),
            RateInteraction('deaths', target='lynx', state='x', rate=lambda s: -gamma * s.target.x),
        ]
        return CompositeSystem(self.label, elements=[hares, lynx], interactions=interactions)


HareLynxSystem().get_params()

{'alpha': 0.55, 'beta': 0.028, 'delta': 0.024, 'gamma': 0.8, 'hares': 30.0, 'label': 'system', 'lynx': 4.0}

get_params returns the initial populations, the four rates, and the label by name, as for any estimator of scikit-learn, so set_params, clone, and the experiments of the library change them. The constructor only stores its arguments, which is what makes this work.

docs.title: Checking the class
docs.text:
The catalog tests run every system class through one generic check. It builds the class with its default parameters, simulates it for ten frames while a RerunObserver saves the run, and requires a frame logged for every simulated frame. Then it clones the system and compiles the copy. The block below runs the same check on the new class, saving to a temporary file so that no viewer opens.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from sklearn.base import clone

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.viz import RerunObserver

system = HareLynxSystem()
settings = system.get_run_settings()
observer = RerunObserver('hare_lynx', save_path=Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'run.rrd')
trajectory = simulate(system, until=10 * settings['dt'], observers=[observer], random_state=0)
copy = clone(system)
hares = trajectory.get_values('hares.x').round(1)[:4].tolist()
observer.logged_frames_ == len(trajectory.times), copy is not system, hares

(True, True, [30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2])

The observer logged all eleven frames, the clone is a new object, and the hares rise from 30.0 to 81.2 thousand in 1903, as in the build tutorial. The tuned dt of one year set the length of the run.

A class of the catalog must also run like the same parts put together by hand, and it must say what it is through its capability tags. The block below compares the states of a run with those of LotkaVolterraSystem, which holds the same model with the rates r, a, b, and d, and reads the tags.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

reference = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
difference = simulate(system, until=20).states - simulate(reference, until=20, dt=1.0).states
tags = system.get_tags()
bool(np.abs(difference).max() < 1e-9), sorted(tags.time), tags.randomness, sorted(tags.laws)

(True, ['continuous'], 'deterministic', ['rate'])

The states of the two systems agree to within rounding error, below 1e-9 thousand animals, so the new class adds the data and the names, not a new model. The tags say that the system runs in continuous time, is deterministic, and holds rate laws. The catalog test of the tags reads the same values, and the inventory takes them from the class rather than repeating them.

A class is listed by all_systems when its module lives in the package skcomplex.systems and its body sets field. The listing reads the sources without importing them, so field, topics, and references must be literal values. A class defined anywhere else, such as on this page, stays out of the listing.

from skcomplex.systems import all_systems

listed = [name for name, _ in all_systems(field='biology/ecology')]
'LotkaVolterraSystem' in listed, 'HareLynxSystem' in listed

(True, False)

LotkaVolterraSystem is listed and HareLynxSystem is not. The listing raises a RegistryError for a class of the package whose name lacks the suffix System or whose field is computed at run time.

docs.title: The files of a contribution
docs.text:
A new system adds a module, an export, an inventory entry, and a gallery example. The catalog already holds this model as LotkaVolterraSystem, so the files below show the steps rather than a contribution the catalog needs. A real one adds a system the catalog lacks.

src/skcomplex/systems/biology/ecology/
    _pelts.py                    the class HareLynxSystem
    __init__.py                  imports HareLynxSystem and lists it in __all__
tests/systems/biology/ecology/
    test_pelts.py                the tests of the class, mirroring the source
docs/overview/inventory.toml     the entry hare_lynx under [biology.ecology]
docs/examples/biology/ecology/
    plot_hare_lynx.py            the gallery example

The module holds one system with the parts only it uses. A part that several systems of ecology share goes to skcomplex.systems.biology.common, and a part that several fields share goes to skcomplex.systems.general, as the placement rule of Extend the library says.

docs.title: The inventory entry
docs.text:
The inventory docs/overview/inventory.toml lists every system surveyed from the reference books and articles, with its status. The name of an entry is the class name without System in snake case, so HareLynxSystem is hare_lynx. The entry sits in the table of its field path, and the check of the inventory, which the documentation build runs, compares it with the class.

[biology.ecology]
hare_lynx = { title = "Hare and lynx pelts", sources = ["Hewitt 1921", "Carpenter 2018"], primitives = ["rates", "interactions"], system = { components = ["element"], bindings = ["members"] }, priority = "example", status = "implemented" }

The fields of the entry are these:

  • title names the system in the gallery.
  • sources are keys of the table sources with a section, arXiv identifiers, or citations of an author and a year.
  • primitives are the capabilities of the core the system exercises, from the table primitives.
  • system maps the system to the vocabulary: its components, here single elements, and its bindings, here roles bound to elements.
  • priority is 'core' when the system exercises a set of primitives that no earlier entry exercises, and 'example' otherwise. The rates and interactions of this model repeat those of lotka_volterra.
  • status is 'implemented' once the class exists, or 'pending <change>' while an OpenSpec change builds it.

An implemented entry does not write its time, space, laws, or domains, since the check reads them from get_tags() of the class, as the block above did.

docs.title: The gallery example
docs.text:
Every system of the catalog has one example in the gallery, a script under docs/examples/<field>/<subfield>/plot_<name>.py. After the inventory entry exists, the command PYTHONPATH=docs python -m gallery_tools scaffold writes a scaffold for every system without an example. The finished script sets SYSTEM to the gallery name, runs the system with a RerunObserver and a blueprint, and draws one figure of an analysis whose result the caption predicts.

"""
# Hare and lynx pelts

The hares and the lynx of the Hudson's Bay Company records cycle out of phase, and every peak of the hares is followed
by a peak of the lynx a year later.
"""

# %%
# The system starts from the records of 1900 and runs for twenty years with the rates of Carpenter (2018).

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.viz import RerunObserver
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import HareLynxSystem

SYSTEM = 'hare_lynx'

observer = RerunObserver(SYSTEM, save_path=f'{SYSTEM}.rrd', blueprint='default')
trajectory = simulate(HareLynxSystem(), observers=[observer])

# %%
# The phase plane
# ---------------
# The run is one closed cycle around the equilibrium (gamma / delta, alpha / beta).

fig, axes = plt.subplots()
axes.plot(trajectory.get_values('hares.x'), trajectory.get_values('lynx.x'))
axes.set(xlabel='hares (thousands)', ylabel='lynx (thousands)', title='The phase plane')
plt.show()

The docstring gives the title and a caption of the behaviour the thumbnail must show. The command PYTHONPATH=docs python -m gallery_tools run hare_lynx runs the example and captures its screenshot, which a reviewer compares with the caption.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: A contribution goes to the repository as a pull request. The contributing guide lists the tasks that format the code, run the checks and the tests, and build the documentation, with the convention of commit messages and the guidelines of pull requests. Before the pull request, run the tests of the catalog, pytest tests/systems/test_catalog.py, which apply the checks of this page to the new class, and build the documentation, which runs the check of the inventory and the gallery example.

docs.title: Simulate a system
docs.text: This tutorial runs the predator and prey model of the build tutorial and reads what the run returns. It sets the run settings, chooses a solver and a backend from the tags of the system, makes random runs reproducible, records and replays their draws, and closes with large systems, external simulators, and systems whose parts need different solvers.

docs.title: The first run
docs.text:
The goal of this section is a trajectory of the hares and the lynx from 1900 to 1920, compared with the pelt records. The Hudson's Bay Company bought the pelts of hares and lynx from trappers for two centuries, and the counts rise and fall in cycles of about ten years. The counts below are the pelts of 1900 to 1920, in thousands, as distributed with the case study of Carpenter (2018, Predator-Prey Population Dynamics: the Lotka-Volterra model in Stan) in the file knitr/lotka-volterra/hudson-bay-lynx-hare.csv of the Stan example models. That file cites the lecture notes of Howard (2009) at Texas A&M University, which trace the numbers through the notes of Mahaffy (Math 636, San Diego State University) to Purves, Sadava, Orians, and Heller, Life: The Science of Biology.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

years = np.arange(1900, 1921)
hares = np.array(
    [30.0, 47.2, 70.2, 77.4, 36.3, 20.6, 18.1, 21.4, 22.0, 25.4, 27.1]
    + [40.3, 57.0, 76.6, 52.3, 19.5, 11.2, 7.6, 14.6, 16.2, 24.7]
)
lynx = np.array(
    [4.0, 6.1, 9.8, 35.2, 59.4, 41.7, 19.0, 13.0, 8.3, 9.1, 7.4]
    + [8.0, 12.3, 19.5, 45.7, 51.1, 29.7, 15.8, 9.7, 10.1, 8.6]
)
system = LotkaVolterraSystem(prey=30.0, predators=4.0, r=0.55, a=0.028, b=0.024, d=0.80)
trajectory = simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0)
trajectory.get_values('prey.x').round(1)[:6].tolist()

[30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2, 48.8, 18.6]

simulate checks the system, compiles its laws into one problem, picks a solver, and advances the problem from time 0 to until in frames of dt. Here a frame is one year. The simulated hares rise from 30.0 to 81.2 thousand in 1903 and fall to 18.6 thousand in 1905, as the records do.

fit = np.sqrt(np.mean((trajectory.get_values('prey.x') - hares) ** 2))
round(float(fit), 1), int(years[trajectory.get_values('prey.x').argmax()])

(7.8, 1903)

The root mean square difference to the records is 7.8 thousand pelts, and the simulated hares peak in 1903, the year of the highest count. The system itself does not change in a run, so the same instance runs again with other settings.

docs.title: The trajectory
docs.text:
A Trajectory holds the frames of a run. Every state and parameter has a dotted name, the label of its part and the name of the value, such as prey.x or predation.a.

trajectory.names, trajectory.times[:3].tolist(), trajectory.states.shape, trajectory.parameters.shape

(['prey.x', 'predators.x', 'growth.r', 'predation.a', 'predation.b', 'death.d'], [0.0, 1.0, 2.0], (21, 2), (21, 4))
  • names lists the states prey.x and predators.x, then the parameters growth.r, predation.a, predation.b, and death.d, the parameters of the built parts.
  • times holds the time of every frame, 0, 1, 2, and so on.
  • states holds one row per frame and one column per state, here 21 frames of 2 states.
  • parameters holds one row per frame and one column per parameter, 21 by 4.

get_values(name) returns the column of one name, a state or a parameter. A parameter is recorded at every frame, because a schedule may change it during the run, as the next section shows.

docs.title: Run settings
docs.text:
The arguments of simulate set how a run starts and evolves. Each one left out comes from the tuned run settings of the class of the system, which get_run_settings() returns.

settings = system.get_run_settings()
settings['until'], settings['dt'], len(simulate(system).times)

(50.0, 0.1, 501)

LotkaVolterraSystem tunes until=50.0 and dt=0.1, so a call without them runs fifty years in 501 frames. The settings are these.

  • until sets the end time. A system without a tuned end time, such as a plain CompositeSystem, raises an error that asks for it.
  • dt sets the time between frames. Without a tuned value it is 1 for discrete maps and agents. For other forms it is 0.01, raised to the smallest of 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, and so on, in steps of 1, 2, and 5 times a power of ten, that keeps the run at most 1000 frames long. So a plain composite run with until=1000 takes frames of 1.
  • initial_state replaces initial values of the elements for one run, by dotted name.
  • schedule sets parameters from functions of time at every frame, such as a slow ramp of a control parameter.
  • solver and backend choose how the run steps and evaluates its laws, as the section on solvers shows.
  • random_state makes a stochastic run reproducible.
  • observables adds quantities computed at every frame, invariants names those that must stay constant, and observers stream the run to a viewer, as the tutorial Observe shows.

docs.title: Changing a run
docs.text:
A schedule changes a parameter while the system runs, and initial_state continues a run from where another stopped. Here the first run covers 1900 to 1910, and the second starts from its last frame with predation switched off.

first = simulate(system, until=10, dt=1.0)
last = {name: first.get_values(name)[-1] for name in ('prey.x', 'predators.x')}
second = simulate(system, until=10, dt=1.0, initial_state=last, schedule={'predation.a': lambda t: 0.0})
second.get_values('prey.x')[0] == first.get_values('prey.x')[-1], second.get_values('prey.x').round(1)[-1]

(True, 5735.6)

The second run starts at the 23.4 thousand hares where the first stopped, and its times start again from 0. Without predation the hares grow at the rate 0.55 a year and reach 5735.6 thousand in ten years, the exponential growth the lynx hold back. A ramp works the same way: schedule={'growth.r': lambda t: 0.55 + 0.01 * t} raises the birth rate from 0.55 to 0.75 over twenty years.

A changed model parameter, such as LotkaVolterraSystem(r=0.65) or set_params(r=0.65), builds a new set of parts, which compile again. A schedule changes a value of the built parts, so it names them by their path, such as growth.r.

docs.title: Observables and invariants
docs.text:
An observable is a value computed from the states at every frame. The Lotka and Volterra model keeps the quantity V = b H - d ln H + a L - r ln L constant along every orbit, so it serves as a check of the numerical integration.

from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec


def get_constant(t, values):
    prey, predators = values['prey.x'], values['predators.x']
    return 0.024 * prey - 0.80 * np.log(prey) + 0.028 * predators - 0.55 * np.log(predators)


constant = ObservableSpec('constant', function=get_constant)
observed = simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0, observables=[constant], invariants={'constant': 1e-3})
observed.get_values('constant').round(4)[[0, -1]].tolist()

[-2.6514, -2.6514]

The ObservableSpec reads the dotted names of the states and returns a number, which the trajectory records under its label. The constant is -2.6514 at the start and at the end, and the run raises no error, because it stays within the tolerance of 0.001 that invariants gives it. The section on solvers below shows a run that leaves it.

docs.title: Solver and backend
docs.text:
The tags of a system choose its default solver before anything compiles. A solver advances the compiled problem in time, and a backend turns its laws into numeric functions. This section reads which ones a run used and replaces them.

tags = system.get_tags()
sorted(tags.time), sorted(tags.laws), trajectory.problem.form.value, trajectory.problem.backend

(['continuous'], ['rate'], 'ordinary differential equations', 'numpy')

The model runs in continuous time with rate laws, so it compiles to ordinary differential equations, which run on the NumPy backend. The default solver of this form is ScipyODESolver with the method LSODA of SciPy. It starts with Adams methods and switches to BDF methods while the system is stiff, that is, while it mixes fast and slow time scales, so stiff systems also run with the default solver.

A solver passed by hand must support the tags of the system, and a solver that lacks one raises a TagError that names it, as the tutorial Check a system shows. A fixed-step solver suits a check of accuracy. Forward Euler with a step of 0.1 drifts off the orbit, and the invariant catches it.

from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import EulerSolver, RK4Solver
from skcomplex.core.errors import ConservationError

rk4 = simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0, solver=RK4Solver()).get_values('prey.x').round(1)[:6].tolist()
euler = EulerSolver(dt=0.1)
try:
    simulate(system, until=20, dt=1.0, solver=euler, observables=[constant], invariants={'constant': 1e-3})
except ConservationError as error:
    message = str(error)
rk4, message

([30.0, 46.4, 68.5, 81.2, 48.8, 18.6],
 'The invariant constant changed from -2.65142 to -2.64349 at frame 1, time 1, beyond its tolerance 0.001.')

RK4Solver, the classical Runge-Kutta method of order four, gives the same hares as the default solver. The message says that the invariant changed from -2.65142 to -2.64349 at frame 1, time 1, beyond its tolerance. Forward Euler gains a little on every turn of the cycle, so a smaller step or a solver of higher order fixes it.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
The library has three backends.

  • NumpyBackend evaluates every law with NumPy arrays.
  • NumbaBackend generates one compiled function per form. It adds compiled cell lists for pair interactions and compiled loops for RK4Solver, EulerMaruyamaSolver, GillespieSolver, and IterationSolver.
  • JaxBackend writes discrete maps and ordinary differential equations as pure JAX functions, which JAX traces, compiles, and differentiates. It is the backend of the inner system of a system that trains, and a forward backend that agrees with NumPy within 1e-10 in double precision.

Without a backend, simulate picks Numba when the groups of a system hold at least 1000 members in total. Compiling takes a second or two, which small systems such as the two populations above do not win back. Compiled kernels are cached on disk, under ~/.cache/skcomplex or the cache_dir of NumbaBackend(cache_dir=...), so running the same system again skips compilation.

docs.title: Random runs
docs.text:
The equations follow the mean of many animals. A small population also feels chance: a lynx may die before it finds a hare, and the last predators may vanish. This section runs the model as random events and makes the runs reproducible.

The pelt model is a set of four reactions, and ReactionNetworkSystem of skcomplex.systems.general.reactions runs them as random events with mode='jump'. Each reaction fires one at a time, at random times whose rate is its propensity, the rate constant times the product of the reactant amounts. The amounts become counts of animals, as if the records described a small local population.

from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem

reactions = {
    'births': ({'hares': 1}, {'hares': 2}, 0.55),
    'hunting': ({'hares': 1, 'lynx': 1}, {'lynx': 1}, 0.028),
    'feeding': ({'hares': 1, 'lynx': 1}, {'hares': 1, 'lynx': 2}, 0.024),
    'deaths': ({'lynx': 1}, {}, 0.80),
}
jumps = ReactionNetworkSystem(species={'hares': 30, 'lynx': 4}, reactions=reactions, mode='jump')
runs = [simulate(jumps, until=20, dt=1.0, random_state=seed).get_values('hares.x')[:6].tolist() for seed in (0, 0, 1)]
jumps.get_tags().randomness, runs

('stochastic',
 [[30.0, 41.0, 58.0, 78.0, 44.0, 9.0], [30.0, 41.0, 58.0, 78.0, 44.0, 9.0], [30.0, 49.0, 64.0, 48.0, 35.0, 43.0]])

The tags call the system stochastic, so the default solver is GillespieSolver, the exact algorithm of Gillespie for random events in continuous time. The random_state fixes its random numbers. Two runs with the seed 0 give the same hares, 30, 41, 58, 78, 44, and 9, and the seed 1 gives another path, 30, 49, 64, 48, 35, and 43. A run without a random_state draws a fresh path each time.

A random run answers a question the equations cannot, such as how often the lynx die out within ten years.

ends = [simulate(jumps, until=10, dt=1.0, random_state=seed).get_values('lynx.x')[-1] for seed in range(20)]
sum(end == 0 for end in ends)

2

The lynx die out in 2 of 20 runs. The fraction is a rough estimate, and a real study would run thousands of seeds, as ensemble of the tutorial Run experiments does. The runs stop after ten years for speed. Once the lynx are gone, nothing holds the hares back, and the Gillespie solver fires one event per birth, so a longer run of an extinct path counts millions of events.

The same random_state gives the same path on every backend. A fixed-step solver splits every frame into the same number of equal steps on NumPy and Numba, and the Gillespie solver draws its events in the same order.

from skcomplex.core.engine.backends import NumbaBackend, NumpyBackend

paths = [
    simulate(jumps, until=20, dt=1.0, random_state=0, backend=backend).get_values('hares.x')
    for backend in (NumpyBackend(), NumbaBackend())
]
bool((paths[0] == paths[1]).all())

True

The two paths are equal.

docs.title: Recording and replaying draws
docs.text:
A recorded run keeps every random draw, so the same path can be scored under other parameters. This is the likelihood of a path, which calibration uses as its event loss.

record_draws=True stores in trajectory.draws every named draw by its owner and name, with the step it fell in and the arguments of its distribution, and every firing of a jump law under Gillespie with its time and law. replay=trajectory runs a system with those draws forced to their recorded values. It computes the arguments of each distribution from its own parameters and states, and its trajectory holds the total log-probability of the forced draws as log_probability.

recorded = simulate(jumps, until=20, dt=1.0, random_state=0, record_draws=True)
scores = {}
for birth_rate in (0.45, 0.55, 0.65):
    changed = {**reactions, 'births': ({'hares': 1}, {'hares': 2}, birth_rate)}
    candidate = ReactionNetworkSystem(species={'hares': 30, 'lynx': 4}, reactions=changed, mode='jump')
    replayed = simulate(candidate, until=20, dt=1.0, random_state=0, replay=recorded)
    scores[birth_rate] = round(float(replayed.log_probability), 1)
len(recorded.draws.firing_times), bool((replayed.states == recorded.states).all()), scores

(614, True, {0.45: 1537.1, 0.55: 1538.8, 0.65: 1535.9})

The recorded run fires 614 reactions in twenty years. Every replay follows the same path, and its log-probability is 1537.1 for a birth rate of 0.45, 1538.8 for 0.55, and 1535.9 for 0.65. The rate that drew the path scores highest.

  • The draws of the laws of stochastic maps, such as normal('kick', 0, s), and the named draws that agent rules make through system.draw(name, distribution, **arguments) are recorded. A draw from system.rng is not, so rules draw every random outcome that matters to a likelihood by name.
  • A replayed Gillespie run fires the recorded laws at the recorded times and adds the log propensity of every firing minus the integral of the total propensity, the exact log-likelihood of the path.
  • A replay takes the same random numbers as the recorded run, so replay with its random state, and the draws that are not named, such as the order of agents, stay the same.
  • A run that records or replays uses the NumPy backend unless one is given. A system whose draws differ from those of the trajectory raises an error that names the draw and the step.

docs.title: Large systems
docs.text:
The two populations run in a fraction of a second. A system of many members needs a compiled backend, and the next example, a gas of 50,000 molecules, shows one.

from skcomplex.core.engine.backends import NumbaBackend
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import RK4Solver
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IdealGasSystem

gas = IdealGasSystem(n_molecules=50_000, random_state=0)
trajectory = simulate(gas, until=0.5, dt=0.01, solver=RK4Solver(dt=0.01), backend=NumbaBackend())
trajectory.get_values('gas.x').shape

(51, 50000, 2)

The positions of the molecules form an array of 51 frames, 50,000 molecules, and 2 coordinates.

docs.title: Compiled functions in laws
docs.text:
A law can call a fast function of its own, once per member, with CallSpec(function, arguments). Here a herd of 2000 groups grows at a rate that saturates with its size.

from typing import Annotated

import numba

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import Interaction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import CallSpec, ParameterSpec, RoleSpec, StateSpec


class PopulationElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, n: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.n = n


@numba.njit
def saturating(t, n, r):
    return r * n / (1 + n)


class SaturationInteraction(Interaction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], r: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.target = target
        self.r = r

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.target.n, CallSpec(saturating, (s.target.n, s.r)))]


herds = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[GroupElement('herds', element=PopulationElement, size=2000, values={'n': 1.0})],
    interactions=[SaturationInteraction('growth', target='herds')],
)
round(float(simulate(herds, until=1, dt=0.1).get_values('herds.n')[-1, 0]), 4)

1.5571

Each herd grows from 1 to 1.5571 in one time unit. A function compiled with Numba runs inside the compiled kernels, and the NumPy backend calls it from Python. The group holds 2000 members, so the run picks Numba by itself.

A plain Python function of the values, as in RateLaw(s.target.n, lambda t, values: ...), also works with the Numba backend. It runs in Python, though, and turns off the compiled stepper loops for that kind of law.

docs.title: External simulators
docs.text:
A whole system can run in a third-party simulator while the library keeps its frames, trajectories, schedules, and Rerun visualization. LammpsSolver runs particle systems in LAMMPS, which integrates them with velocity Verlet. Here 100 atoms under the Lennard-Jones potential and a drag start on a square grid.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import PairInteraction, RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import derivative
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import LammpsSolver
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class AtomElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self, label, *, x: Annotated[object, StateSpec(vector=True, order=2, role='position')] = 0.0, x_d1: object = 0.0
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.x = x
        self.x_d1 = x_d1


class LennardJonesInteraction(PairInteraction):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        first,
        second,
        cutoff=1.0,
        position='x',
        *,
        epsilon: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
        sigma: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, first, second, cutoff=cutoff, position=position, potential=self._get_energy)
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.sigma = sigma

    @staticmethod
    def _get_energy(s, r):
        return 4 * s.epsilon * ((s.sigma / r) ** 12 - (s.sigma / r) ** 6)


class DragInteraction(RateInteraction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, target, gamma: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label, target=target, state='x', rate=self._get_rate)
        self.gamma = gamma

    @staticmethod
    def _get_rate(s):
        return -s.gamma * s.target.x.apply_map(lambda item: derivative(item, 1))


def get_pair_coefficients(value):
    return f'{float(value("epsilon")[0])} {float(value("sigma")[0])}'


def get_drag_fix(fix):
    return f'fix {fix.name} {fix.group} viscous {float(fix.value("gamma")[0])}'


side = np.arange(10) * 1.2
grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(side, side), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2)
atoms = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[GroupElement('atoms', element=AtomElement, size=100, values={'x': grid})],
    interactions=[
        LennardJonesInteraction('lj', 'atoms', 'atoms', cutoff=2.5),
        DragInteraction('air', target='atoms', gamma=1.0),
    ],
    space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2),
)
pairs = {LennardJonesInteraction: ('lj/cut', get_pair_coefficients)}
fixes = {DragInteraction: get_drag_fix}
solver = LammpsSolver(dt=0.005, pairs=pairs, fixes=fixes)
trajectory = simulate(atoms, until=1, dt=0.05, solver=solver, random_state=0)
trajectory.get_values('atoms.x').shape

(21, 100, 2)

The positions come back from LAMMPS as 21 frames of 100 atoms in 2 dimensions. Two maps tell the solver how to write the interactions in LAMMPS.

  • pairs maps pair potential classes to native LAMMPS pair styles, with a function that writes their coefficients.
  • fixes maps interaction classes to native fixes, with a function that writes the fix.

Both maps are written for each class of one's own, as above, and the ready-made particle systems come with theirs. A function in fixes reads a seed from the random state of the run with fix.seed(), for a stochastic fix such as fix langevin.

Before the first frame the solver checks the system. It raises one error that lists every element, interaction, and law it cannot run. The library translates a system to LAMMPS as follows.

  • Elements and groups with a vector position of order 2, such as AtomElement, become one atom type per element or group. The velocities of the atoms are the first derivatives of the positions. Their mass is the parameter that the divisor of their interactions names, or 1 without one.
  • Two or three dimensions become dimension 2 with fix enforce2d, or dimension 3.
  • ContinuousSpace(extent, boundary='reflecting') becomes fix wall/reflect at 0 and the extent.
  • ContinuousSpace(extent, boundary='periodic') becomes periodic boundaries of the extent, shared by every group.
  • A class in pairs, such as LennardJonesInteraction, becomes its native pair style, such as pair_style lj/cut.
  • Any other PairInteraction with a potential becomes pair_style lepton, with the potential printed as a Lepton expression.
  • A class in fixes becomes its native fix, such as fix addforce, fix viscous, or fix langevin.
  • Any other interaction that only changes the derivatives of the positions becomes fix external, which the library evaluates at every step.

docs.title: Co-simulation
docs.text:
Some systems hold parts that need different solvers, such as farming agents next to the differential equation of the land they harvest. Such a system is split into partitions at the boundaries of its nested systems, and each partition runs with its own solver.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.economics.resources import HarvestingSystem

trajectory = simulate(HarvestingSystem(farmers=10, effort=0.05), until=50, random_state=0)
round(trajectory.get_values('land/stock.n')[-1]), trajectory.get_agents('village/farmers', 50).values['wealth'].size
trajectory.get_values('village/farmers_count.value')[-1]

(500, 10)
10.0

The land is a differential equation and the village holds agents, so each runs as its own partition. After fifty years the village still counts 10 farmers.

Every nested system whose laws fit one form becomes a partition. A law joins the partition that owns its target, so an interaction of the parent system may contribute to several partitions. A nested system whose own elements mix law kinds raises IncompatibleLawsError, with its path and the suggestion to split it.

The partitions exchange values in these ways.

  • Every partition holds the states of the other partitions as inputs. They keep their values from the last synchronisation point while it advances.
  • A law of one partition reads a reduction of a group of another through a role bound to the group, such as count(s.farmers) or total(s.farmers.wealth). The co-simulation computes every reduction of agents at each synchronisation point and holds it until the next, in the state value of an element next to the group, such as village/farmers_count.value. A reduction of an element group reads the states of the other partition, which keep their values from the last synchronisation point too.
  • Agent rules read the states of other partitions through system.inputs[name], such as system.inputs['land/stock.n'].

The CoSimulationSolver advances the partitions and controls the exchange.

  • It advances every partition with its own solver, chosen per partition through solvers={'land': ScipyODESolver()}.
  • It exchanges inputs every sync_dt. This defaults to the frame duration and must divide it, and it must be a whole number of steps for discrete and agent partitions.
  • The Gauss-Seidel scheme, the default, advances partitions in system order, each reading the values already advanced by those before it. scheme='jacobi' advances all of them from the values at the start of the interval.
  • Splitting adds an error of first order in sync_dt. Halving sync_dt roughly halves it, at the cost of more exchanges. CoSimulationSolver(split=True) splits a system that fits one form, which shows the error against the joint solution.

docs.title: System classes
docs.text: This page changes what a ready-made system builds by subclassing it, and writes a system of your own as a class that takes the parameters of its model. Such a class clones, sweeps, and calibrates like any estimator of scikit-learn.

docs.title: Four kinds of system
docs.text:
This section places every system class in one of four kinds, from the most general to the most specific. Every system derives from BaseSystem.

  • BaseSystem is the base of every system. It holds the main public methods, derives the tags, and builds the parts of a system from its model parameters.
  • CompositeSystem is the composite of elements, interactions, and nested systems, on a space and in a time. It plays the role of Pipeline in scikit-learn: it holds parts and adds no model of its own.
  • General realizations name a structure that several fields share. ReactionNetworkSystem of skcomplex.systems.general.reactions is a reaction network, whose reactions fire at a rate constant times the product of the reactant amounts. The general systems of skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics name structures of states and their evolution. DynamicalSystem holds rates or maps of declared states, NetworkDynamicalSystem holds states on the nodes of a graph, ReactionDiffusionSystem holds fields on a lattice, and StockFlowSystem holds stocks that change through named flows. They are recipes written with the core.
  • Field realizations, such as SIRSystem, give a general system or BaseSystem the parameters and the words of one field. Every ready-made system of the catalog is one.

The kinds mirror the linear models of scikit-learn, where Ridge and Lasso realize one general structure with parameters of their own.

from skcomplex.core.components.systems import BaseSystem, CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import DynamicalSystem
from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem
from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.dynamical_systems import HenonMapSystem

(
    issubclass(SIRSystem, ReactionNetworkSystem),
    issubclass(HenonMapSystem, DynamicalSystem),
    issubclass(ReactionNetworkSystem, BaseSystem),
    issubclass(CompositeSystem, BaseSystem),
)

(True, True, True, True)

All four checks return True. The epidemic is a reaction network, the map of Hénon is a dynamical system, and both general systems and the composite derive from BaseSystem.

docs.title: How a system class builds its parts
docs.text:
This section writes a system as a class whose parameters read like those of its model. A subclass of BaseSystem does two things.

  • Its __init__ takes the parameters of the model and stores each under its own name, and nothing else, as in scikit-learn. So get_params, set_params, and clone work on them.
  • Its hook _build_system returns the CompositeSystem of its parts, written in terms of these parameters.

The example is a tank that drains at a rate proportional to its level, written with the base class Element and the general RateInteraction.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import BaseSystem, CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec


class TankElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, level: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.level = level


class DrainingTankSystem(BaseSystem):
    until = 10.0
    dt = 0.1

    def __init__(self, level=1.0, *, k=0.5, label='system'):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.level = level
        self.k = k

    def _build_system(self):
        drain = RateInteraction('drain', target='tank', state='level', rate=lambda s: -self.k * s.target.level)
        return CompositeSystem(self.label, elements=[TankElement('tank', level=self.level)], interactions=[drain])


tank = DrainingTankSystem(k=0.2)
tank.get_params(), sorted(tank.get_tags().laws)

({'k': 0.2, 'label': 'system', 'level': 1.0}, ['rate'])

get_params returns k=0.2, the label, and level=1.0, and the tags hold one kind of law, 'rate'. The class runs like any system.

round(float(simulate(tank).get_values('tank.level')[-1]), 3)

0.135

The level falls to 0.135 at time 10, which is exp(-0.2 * 10). prepare builds the parts from the current parameters and keeps them as system_. It builds them again only when a parameter changed, so set_params(k=0.4) changes the parts of the next prepare and of the next simulate. The tags come from the parts and are never declared, so they cannot drift from what the system does.

The class attributes until and dt above are tuned run settings. simulate reads them, with solver, observables, initial_state, invariants, schedule, compiler, and backend, for every argument a call leaves out. A system whose settings depend on its parameters overrides get_run_settings instead.

docs.title: Field realizations
docs.text: This section shows how a field realization fills a general system. It takes the parameters of its model under its own names and gives the general system its parts through hooks. SIRSystem subclasses ReactionNetworkSystem. It returns its compartments from _get_species, and its infection and recovery from _get_interactions. Epidemics and enzyme kinetics are both reaction networks with a product propensity, so they share the general realization and differ only in their field realizations. HenonMapSystem subclasses DynamicalSystem in discrete time. It returns its two states from _get_states, its parameters from _get_parameters, and its map from _get_equations, so its module defines no element class.

docs.title: Changing a ready-made system by subclassing it
docs.text:
This section adds a process to a ready-made system and keeps everything else it does. A subclass of SIRSystem that vaccinates susceptible people at the rate nu adds one parameter and one reaction. ReactionInteraction moves people from S to R at that rate.

from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionInteraction
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem


class VaccinatedSIRSystem(SIRSystem):
    until = 100.0

    def __init__(
        self,
        susceptible=990.0,
        infected=10.0,
        recovered=0.0,
        *,
        beta=0.0003,
        gamma=0.1,
        nu=0.02,
        stochastic=False,
        label='system',
    ):
        super().__init__(susceptible, infected, recovered, beta=beta, gamma=gamma, stochastic=stochastic, label=label)
        self.nu = nu

    def _get_interactions(self):
        vaccination = ReactionInteraction(
            'vaccination',
            reactants={('S', 'x'): 1},
            products={('R', 'x'): 1},
            k=self.nu,
            mode='jump' if self.stochastic else 'rate',
        )
        return [*super()._get_interactions(), vaccination]


vaccinated = VaccinatedSIRSystem()
[interaction.label for interaction in vaccinated.prepare().system_.interactions]

['infection', 'recovery', 'vaccination']

The parts hold the interactions infection, recovery, and vaccination. The subclass repeats the arguments of its parent in its __init__, since get_params reads the signature of the class, as in scikit-learn. It overrides one hook and calls the parent for the rest, so the infection, the recovery, the stochastic mode, and the tuned time step keep working.

simulate(SIRSystem()).get_values('I.x').max().round(), simulate(vaccinated).get_values('I.x').max().round()

(304.0, 132.0)

Vaccination lowers the peak of the epidemic from 304 to 132 infected people. The subclass is an estimator like its parent, so every function of the library takes it.

stochastic = vaccinated.set_params(stochastic=True)
