The kernel reads coordinate(name) for the point c that a law updates, integration_variable(name) for the point c' integrated over, and the parameters, so it need not be a function of c - c'. The compiler samples it at the cell centres, and the integral is a product with the dense matrix of the kernel.
  • cumulative_integral(expression, axis, reverse=False) integrates along one axis of a lattice, from the start of the domain to every site, or from every site to the end with reverse=True, counting half of the cell of the site. The light under a canopy is exp(-gamma * cumulative_integral(f * coordinate('h')**2, 1, reverse=True)).
  • convolve acts along the position axes of a phase space at every class, with a kernel of the displacements of the position axes, and it follows the boundary of the position lattice. Seeds disperse over position at every height this way.
  • simulate rejects a kernel that reads a state with the issue kernel-state, and an integral over class axes of a field without a phase space with the issue law-space.

docs.title: Simplex domains
docs.text:
This section holds a density over the frequencies of three strategies, which sum to one. A simplex is the set of points whose coordinates are nonnegative and sum to at most one. A SimplexSpace is a phase space whose class axes are the free frequencies of a simplex, each on [0, 1] with the same number of cells. A uniform density of two on the 2-simplex, a triangle of area one half, has the integral one.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import moment
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace, SimplexSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import AxisSpec, ObservableSpec, StateSpec


class DensityElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, x: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.x = x


def total(s):
    return moment(s.x, 0, axes=('x', 'y'))


axes = [AxisSpec('x', 20, 0.0, 1.0), AxisSpec('y', 20, 0.0, 1.0)]
simplex = SimplexSpace(LatticeSpace((1,)), axes).prepare()
groups = FieldElement('groups', element=DensityElement, space=simplex, values={'x': 2.0 * (simplex.volumes_ > 0)})
observables = [ObservableSpec('total', total, group='groups')]
trajectory = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[groups]), until=0.1, dt=0.1, observables=observables)
round(float(np.asarray(trajectory.get_values('total'))[-1]), 10)

1.0

The observable total returns 1.0, the integral of the density over the triangle. The space weights each cell by the part of it that lies inside the simplex.

  • volumes_ holds the fraction of every cell inside the simplex. Cells below the slanted face are whole, cells along it are partial, which is half a cell in two dimensions, and cells beyond it are empty. apertures_ holds the fraction of every face inside the simplex.
  • Finite-volume fluxes pass only through the open part of every face and change a cell by its volume. So the total is conserved and no density enters the empty cells. A density on a simplex starts at zero in the empty cells.
  • moment, reduce_axes, integral_transform, and cumulative_integral weight every cell by its volume.
  • simulate rejects a local operator of a field on a simplex, such as laplacian or a finite-difference advection, with the issue law-space. SemiLagrangianSolver refuses partial cells, and SSPRKSolver divides its wave speed by the smallest cell volume.

docs.title: Encounters and equilibria
docs.text:
This section moves particles between classes at one position and relaxes them towards a local equilibrium. The function maximum_entropy(expression, axes, order=2) returns the density exp(a + b c + d |c|^2) whose discrete moments equal those of the expression at every position. Newton steps find the coefficients, so a relaxation towards it conserves the moments to round-off. This relaxation is the collision term of the BGK equation.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import maximum_entropy

relax = RateInteraction('r', target='gas', state='x', rate=lambda s: maximum_entropy(s.target.x, axes=('v',)) - s.target.x)
relax.state

x

The block returns 'x', the state of the gas that the relaxation changes. The encounters of the classes at one position are the recipe EncounterInteraction of the general realizations, which writes them as bilinear laws of the core.

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text:
This section adds binary collisions between particles of different velocities, as in the Boltzmann equation. The function collision_integral(f, kernel) of skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils is the binary collision integral over two interval class axes, and a RateInteraction adds it to the rate of a density. The general realization EncounterInteraction with a cross_section and a factor writes the same rate. The pages of the catalog listed at the end build these collisions in full.

  • The cross-section is the kernel B(speed, cosine) of the relative speed and of the cosine of the deflection angle. It returns an expression of the two and numbers, written with Sage functions.
  • The rate is a RateLaw of f and collision_integral(f, kernel), and the call carries its kernel. A kernel that reads a state or a parameter raises a ValidationError.
  • The integral enters the fast spectral method of Mouhot and Pareschi through a singular value decomposition, with a single term for Maxwell molecules.
  • The method uses products of fast Fourier transforms on a grid padded by (3 + sqrt(2)) / 2. It conserves the density exactly, and the momentum and the energy within its spectral accuracy.
  • A factor that multiplies the integral scales the collision frequency, such as a function of the density moment for the local Enskog equation.
  • simulate rejects a collision without two interval class axes with the issue law-space.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
This section steps transport and collisions each with the method that suits it and combines the two. Transport is fast and linear, so a semi-Lagrangian step follows it exactly. Collisions are local and stiff, so a Runge-Kutta step with a smaller step integrates them.

from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import RK4Solver, SemiLagrangianSolver, StrangSplittingSolver

solver = StrangSplittingSolver(SemiLagrangianSolver(dt=0.1), RK4Solver(dt=0.01), dt=0.1)
solver.dt

0.1

The block returns 0.1, the step of the split method. Each solver plays its own part.

  • SemiLagrangianSolver(dt) advances fields whose fluxes are linear drifts a u, with a free of the state and constant along its own axis. It shifts each slice along its characteristic, in the splitting of Cheng and Knorr. It is stable at any Courant number and conserves the total on periodic axes. Other fluxes raise a named error.
  • StrangSplittingSolver(transport, collision, dt) composes a half transport step, a full collision step, and a half transport step. The compiled problem keeps the source rates, problem.sources, apart from the flux differences.
  • RK4Solver, ScipyODESolver, and the other method-of-lines solvers accept phase-space fields as well.

docs.title: Visualizing
docs.text: ImageVisual(slices=..., moments=...) logs the plane that fixes every axis but two, such as slices={'vy': 2}. It also logs the moments over the class axes, as a bar series over a one-dimensional position lattice and as an image over a two-dimensional one.

docs.title: Systems of the catalog
docs.text: BoltzmannEquationSystem, BGKEquationSystem, VlasovEquationSystem, and EnskogSystem in physics.fluids, and BertinDrozGregoireSystem in physics.active_matter, are the kinetic equations of the library. NonlinearPairwiseGroupConflictSystem and TrimorphicMultilevelSelectionSystem in social.cooperation integrate against two-point kernels, the second on the simplex. ForestSizeStructureSystem in biology.ecology shades trees by a cumulative integral over height.

docs.title: Quantum systems
docs.text: This page builds a quantum system, such as a chain of spins, and follows its state in time or finds its spectrum. A quantum system is a set of quantum subsystems whose state is one vector of their joint Hilbert space, the complex vector space whose unit vectors are the possible states.

docs.title: A spectrum from the catalog
docs.text:
This section finds the two lowest energies of a chain of four spins, the Heisenberg chain of the catalog. The analysis operator_measures diagonalises the generator of the system exactly, and n_states sets how many of the lowest eigenvalues it returns.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import operator_measures
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import QuantumHeisenbergSystem

spectrum = operator_measures(QuantumHeisenbergSystem(n_sites=4), n_states=2)
spectrum.energies.round(6).tolist()

[-2.0, -1.0]

The two lowest energies are -2.0 and -1.0, in units of the coupling.

The core names this machinery for its mathematics, linear operator dynamics on tensor products, while the physics systems keep the words of physics. For example, GeneratorLaw takes a Hermitian operator, which physics calls a Hamiltonian.

Every subsystem holds its state psi in the Hilbert space of a HilbertSpec, which names its operators. A subsystem of your own declares the operators it needs. Typical subsystems have these operators.

  • A spin has the components x, y, z and the ladder operators plus and minus of spin j.
  • A qubit has the Pauli matrices.
  • A mode has annihilate, create, and number, truncated at quanta.
  • A particle on the sites of a lattice or a network has its laplacian and its adjacency.

A group of subsystems, such as a GroupElement of spins on 'sites', is the tensor product of the spaces of its members, in member order. The initial state of every subsystem is a basis label, an index, or a vector.

docs.title: Operators and laws
docs.text:
This section writes the generator of a system from the operators of its subsystems. A spin one half is an Element whose state psi lives in the two-dimensional space of a HilbertSpec with the three spin components. Neighbouring spins on a ring of six sites exchange their spin with the coupling J, the Heisenberg exchange J (Sx Sx + Sy Sy + Sz Sz). A NeighborInteraction writes the exchange once for a bond and returns it as a GeneratorLaw. The chain starts in the alternating state up, down, up, down, up, down, and the observable sz records the expectation of Sz at every site.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import CC

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import NeighborInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import GeneratorLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import local_operator
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import HilbertSpec, ObservableSpec, ParameterSpec, RoleSpec, StateSpec

PAULI = {
    'x': (np.array([[0, 0.5], [0.5, 0]]), True),
    'y': (np.array([[0, -0.5j], [0.5j, 0]]), True),
    'z': (np.array([[0.5, 0], [0, -0.5]]), True),
}
SPIN_HALF = HilbertSpec(2, PAULI, basis={'up': 0, 'down': 1})


class SpinElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, psi: Annotated[object, StateSpec(domain=CC)] = 'up', *, hilbert=SPIN_HALF):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.psi = psi
        self.hilbert = hilbert


class ExchangeInteraction(NeighborInteraction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], J: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.target = target
        self.J = J

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        a, b = s.source.psi, s.target.psi
        exchange = sum(local_operator(a, name) * local_operator(b, name) for name in ('x', 'y', 'z'))
        return [GeneratorLaw(s.J * exchange)]


def sz(member):
    return local_operator(member.psi, 'z')


def sites(values):
    return values


chain = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[
        GroupElement(
            'chain', element=SpinElement, space=LatticeSpace(6), on='sites', values={'psi': ['up', 'down'] * 3}
        ),
    ],
    interactions=[ExchangeInteraction('exchange', target='chain')],
)
observables = [ObservableSpec('sz', sz, group='chain', reduce=sites)]
trajectory = simulate(chain, until=2.0, dt=0.5, observables=observables)
trajectory.get_values('sz').shape, round(float(np.ptp(trajectory.get_values('energy'))), 8)

((5, 6), 0.0)

The record of sz has the shape (5, 6), five output times by six sites. The energy varies by 0.0 over the run, so the unitary evolution conserves it exactly.

Laws name the operators of a subsystem with local_operator(s.psi, name), from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils. Operators combine by sums, numbers, and symbolic coefficients of parameters and time. operator_product and dagger keep the order of products and adjoints. Two laws build the dynamics.

  • GeneratorLaw(operator) adds to the generator, with ħ = 1.
  • DissipatorLaw(operator, rate) adds a Lindblad dissipator, a term that lets the system lose energy or coherence to its surroundings, which makes the system open.

A NeighborInteraction is written once for a bond, with s.source and s.target. It acts on every pair of neighbours of the space of the group that its one role binds, here the LatticeSpace of six sites. Compiling checks that the generator is Hermitian, and that the dimension stays within the max_dimension of the operator solver.

A whole-system initial state, such as an entangled vector or 'ground', is given to simulate as initial_state={'<system label>.state': value}.

docs.title: Solvers, observables, and spectra
docs.text:
This section chooses how the state evolves, records the expectations of operators, and diagonalises the generator exactly. simulate compiles a system of quantum elements to the operator form. Its state is stored as complex pairs under <system>.state, a pure state for a closed system and a density matrix for an open one. Its solvers hand every frame to QuTiP.

  • UnitarySolver solves the Schrödinger equation.
  • LindbladSolver, the default, solves the master equation.
  • JumpTrajectoriesSolver draws quantum jumps from the random stream of the run.

An ObservableSpec whose expression is an operator records its expectation. One over a group gives one value per member when its reduce keeps the values, as sites does above. Every quantum run also records its energy, and its purity when it is open. Groups on a lattice stream the space-time image of their local expectations to Rerun.

operator_measures(system, kind=...) analyses quantum systems by its kind.

  • 'spectrum' and 'ground-state' diagonalise the generator exactly, optionally in the sector of a conserved diagonal operator.
  • 'purity' and 'entanglement' read trajectories.

symbolic(system, kind='hamiltonian') prints the Hamiltonian in operator notation.

docs.title: Rewriting systems
docs.text: This page grows a structure generation by generation, as an L-system grows a plant or a substitution tiling grows a fractal. A rewriting system replaces all its parts in parallel at every step, so one generation rewrites every symbol of a word or every tile of a patch at once.

docs.title: A first rewriting system
docs.text:
This section grows the algae of Lindenmayer, a word over the symbols A and B where every A becomes AB and every B becomes A. A WordElement holds the word, and its _get_laws returns one ProductionLaw per rule. The CompositeSystem runs five generations from the axiom A, the word of generation 0.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import WordElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import ProductionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate


class AlgaeElement(WordElement):
    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [ProductionLaw('A', 'AB'), ProductionLaw('B', 'A')]


algae = CompositeSystem(elements=[AlgaeElement('algae', axiom='A')])
trajectory = simulate(algae, until=5)
trajectory.get_values('algae.size').tolist(), trajectory.get_structure('algae', 5).text

([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0, 13.0], 'ABAABABAABAAB')

The lengths of the words are 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 13, the Fibonacci numbers, and the word of generation 5 is ABAABABAABAAB.

There are two kinds of rewritten element.

  • A WordElement is a string of symbols that grows by string productions, in the style of L-systems.
  • A PatchElement is a set of tiles that grows by affine substitutions.

simulate compiles a system of words or patches to the rewriting form, and every step is one generation. simulate(system, until=n) records the generations 0 to n. The structure itself lives next to the state vector. The states are the count of every symbol or prototile that is a word, and the size <element>.size. Trajectory.get_structure(path, frame) returns the recorded structure of a frame, which later generations do not change.

docs.title: Words and productions
docs.text:
This section writes the rules of a word as productions with parameters and conditions. A word or a patch rewrites itself by the rewriting laws it returns from _get_laws, a ProductionLaw for every rule of a word. Strings are words of one-character symbols, and a ModuleSpec gives a symbol parameters, such as the length of a segment. Here an apex A(x) lays down a segment F(x) and a new apex of half the length, as long as x exceeds 0.1. The ratio one half is a parameter of the element.

from typing import Annotated

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import var

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import WordElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import ProductionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ModuleSpec, ParameterSpec

x = var('x')


class ShrinkingElement(WordElement):
    def __init__(self, label, axiom=(), *, alphabet=None, ratio: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.5):
        super().__init__(label, axiom, alphabet=alphabet)
        self.ratio = ratio

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        successor = [ModuleSpec('F', (x,)), ModuleSpec('A', (s.ratio * x,))]
        return [ProductionLaw(ModuleSpec('A', (x,)), successor, condition=x > 0.1)]


plant = CompositeSystem(elements=[ShrinkingElement('plant', axiom=[ModuleSpec('A', (1.0,))], alphabet={'A': 1, 'F': 1})])
simulate(plant, until=5).get_structure('plant', 5).text

F(1) F(0.5) F(0.25) F(0.125) A(0.0625)

After five generations the word is F(1) F(0.5) F(0.25) F(0.125) A(0.0625). The apex stops at 0.0625, since the condition x > 0.1 fails there.

A production can take several forms.

  • Stochastic. Its probabilities sum to one per predecessor and context, and it draws from the random stream of the run.
  • Context-sensitive. It depends on a left or a right context. The context skips the ignore symbols of the word and treats bracketed branches as Prusinkiewicz and Lindenmayer (1990) do. A context-sensitive production takes precedence over context-free productions.
  • Parametric. It binds the parameters of the predecessor to symbols, such as x above. Its condition and the parameters of its successor are expressions of these symbols and of the parameters of the rewritten element. A schedule changes those parameters between generations.

A word element with parameters declares them as annotated arguments of its __init__, as ratio above. A generation that would make a word longer than max_size raises RewritingError before allocating it. The frames before it stay recorded.

docs.title: Word geometries
docs.text:
This section draws a word as a curve and measures it. A GeometrySpec of skcomplex.core.specs draws a word as line segments in two or three dimensions, as the turtle interpretation of L-systems does. The Koch curve replaces every segment by four segments of a third of its length, turning by 60 degrees.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import scaling
from skcomplex.core.components.elements import PatchElement, WordElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import ProductionLaw, SubstitutionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import AffineSpec, GeometrySpec, PrototileSpec


class KochElement(WordElement):
    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [ProductionLaw('F', 'F+F--F+F')]


koch = CompositeSystem(elements=[KochElement('koch', axiom='F', geometry=GeometrySpec(angle=60.0, contraction=1 / 3))])
curve = simulate(koch, until=4).get_structure('koch', 4)
len(curve.get_segments()), round(curve.get_length(), 6)

(256, 3.160494)

After four generations the curve has 256 segments and the length 3.160494, which is (4/3)^4. The symbols of the turtle have fixed meanings.

  • F draws forward, and f moves forward without drawing.
  • + and - turn by the angle.
  • [ and ] push and pop a branch.
  • contraction scales the step at every generation.

docs.title: Patches and measures
docs.text:
This section grows a patch of tiles and measures it as a fractal. A PatchElement holds tiles. Each tile is a PrototileSpec, a segment or a polygon, under an affine placement. A SubstitutionLaw replaces every tile of a prototile by pieces, each placed by an AffineSpec map relative to it. The Cantor set below keeps the outer thirds of every interval.

interval = PrototileSpec('interval', [(0, 0), (1, 0)])
thirds = [('interval', AffineSpec(scale=1 / 3)), ('interval', AffineSpec(scale=1 / 3, translation=(2 / 3, 0)))]


class CantorElement(PatchElement):
    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [SubstitutionLaw('interval', thirds)]


cantor = CompositeSystem(elements=[CantorElement('cantor', prototiles=[interval])])
trajectory = simulate(cantor, until=5)
trajectory.get_values('cantor.size')[-1], round(trajectory.get_values('cantor.length')[-1], 6)

(32.0, 0.131687)

After five generations the patch holds 32 intervals of total length 0.131687, which is (2/3)^5. Structures with a geometry report <element>.length and <element>.area at every frame. They also give get_bounds(), and get_raster(resolution), a boolean grid that the analysis scaling reads. The box-counting dimension counts the boxes of each size that the set touches, and its slope against the size on a log scale estimates the fractal dimension.

grid = trajectory.get_structure('cantor', 5).get_raster(729)
round(scaling(grid, kind='box-counting', scales=[3, 9, 27]).exponent, 2)

0.65

The estimate is 0.65, close to the dimension log 2 / log 3, about 0.63, of the Cantor set.

The geometry visual logs segments and outlines as line strips, and a patch with filled=True as an image of its raster. It draws within the bounds the element declares, or else within the bounds of its first tiles.

docs.title: Static systems
docs.text: This page solves a system of equations that has no time axis, such as a dose-response curve, and sweeps its parameters. A system under a StaticTime has EquationLaws that name their target, the state each equation solves for. A run solves them once and gives one frame.

docs.title: Equations and sweeps
docs.text:
This section computes the surviving fraction of cells after a dose of radiation, by the linear-quadratic model exp(-0.3 D - 0.03 D^2), and sweeps the dose. The Element holds the survival as a state and the dose as a parameter. A function builds the CompositeSystem from the dose, so the experiment sweep can run it once per value.

from types import SimpleNamespace
from typing import Annotated

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import exp

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import EquationLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import StaticTime
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.experiments import sweep
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class DoseElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label: str,
        survival: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        dose: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 2.0,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(label)
        self.survival = survival
        self.dose = dose

    def _get_laws(self, s: SimpleNamespace) -> list[EquationLaw]:
        return [EquationLaw(s.survival == exp(-0.3 * s.dose - 0.03 * s.dose**2), target=s.survival)]


def dose_response(dose: float = 2.0) -> CompositeSystem:
    return CompositeSystem(elements=[DoseElement('cells', dose=dose)], time=StaticTime())


result = sweep(dose_response, {'dose': [0.0, 2.0]}, until=0.0, outputs=['cells.survival'])
[round(float(row['cells.survival']), 4) for row in result.rows]

[1.0, 0.4868]

The survival is 1.0 without a dose and 0.4868 after a dose of 2. Each static run gives one row of the sweep. The equations are solved in one of two ways.

  • The compiler solves the equations with Sage when it finds a unique explicit solution, and problem.equations holds it.
  • Otherwise RootSolver solves them with scipy.optimize.root and their exact Jacobian, from the initial state as the guess. It raises a SolverError that names the equations and the largest residual when the solve does not converge.

Equations combine across the parts of a system.

  • A target on a group gives one unknown per member, and reductions such as total couple the members.
  • The equations of one target from every element and interaction add.
  • A system without equations solves to its initial state, so its observables run on quenched states in one frame.

simulate raises a ValidationError with the code equation-target for an equation with no target, or with a target that is not a state. A law that does not run under static time gives the code law-time.

docs.title: Log-sum-exp
docs.text:
This section reduces over a group without overflow. log_sum_exp(expression, over=None) reduces over the members of a group like total, as log sum_j exp(a_j), without overflow for values of any size. A system-level observable cannot reach a group from another element. So a quantity built on it is an EquationLaw on a scalar element, read by an interaction that binds the group. The random energy system of Derrida, RandomEnergySystem of the catalog, computes its entropy this way, from the energies of all the configurations of its spins.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import RandomEnergySystem

trajectory = simulate(RandomEnergySystem(n_spins=12, temperature=2.0), until=1.0)
round(float(trajectory.get_values('ensemble.entropy')[0]), 4)

0.6309

With 12 spins at temperature 2.0, the entropy per spin is 0.6309.

Quenched disorder, randomness drawn once and then held fixed, is drawn when the system builds its parts. So a disorder average sweeps its random_state as an axis of sweep. The replicates of ensemble share one draw of the disorder and vary only the dynamics.

docs.title: Contact clusters
docs.text:
This section measures the clusters that points form when they touch. The analysis clusters(points, kind=..., radius=...) reads the positions of points, joins those closer than twice the radius, and measures their clusters. A cluster spans along axis when it holds points within the radius of both faces of the space.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters

clusters([[0, 0], [1, 0], [5, 5]], kind='sizes', radius=0.6).sizes.tolist()

[2, 1]

The first two points lie one apart, less than twice the radius 0.6, so they form a cluster of size 2. The third point stands alone.

docs.title: Stochastic maps
docs.text: This page writes discrete-time stochastic processes, such as a random walk or a Markov chain, with update laws that draw random numbers. An update law gives the next value of a state from the values of the current step. The draws come from the random generator of the run, so two runs with the same random_state give the same trajectory.

docs.title: Random draws
docs.text:
This section puts random draws inside update laws and runs a group of random walkers. A draw is a symbolic random value that enters a law like any other expression. uniform(name, low, high), normal(name, mean, deviation), bernoulli(name, p), and categorical(name, weights) build one.

Here each walker of a persistent random walk keeps its direction with probability q and turns back otherwise, with a small normal jitter on every step. An Element subclass returns two UpdateLaw instances, one for the direction d and one for the position x, and a GroupElement makes 500 walkers of it inside a CompositeSystem.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import UpdateLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import bernoulli, normal, where
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class PersistentElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        d: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0,
        x: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        q: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.8,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.d = d
        self.x = x
        self.q = q

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        turn = where(bernoulli('turn', 1 - s.q) > 0, -s.d, s.d)
        return [UpdateLaw(s.d, turn), UpdateLaw(s.x, s.x + turn + normal('jitter', 0, 0.1))]


walkers = CompositeSystem(elements=[GroupElement('walkers', element=PersistentElement, size=500)])
final = simulate(walkers, until=200, dt=1.0, random_state=0).get_values('walkers.x')[-1]
round(float(final.var() / 200), 1)

3.9

After 200 steps the variance of the positions grows by 3.9 per step. A persistent walk whose steps keep their sign with correlation r = 2q - 1 = 0.6 spreads at (1 + r) / (1 - r) = 4 per step for long times, and the sample of 500 walkers comes close to it.

The draws follow these rules.

  • A draw takes a fresh value at every step, and every member of a group draws its own value.
  • The arguments of a draw can be expressions of states and parameters, and they take the values from before the step.
  • Every draw carries a name. Every use of the same name in one element reads the same value within a step, and draws with different names are independent.
  • Two uses of one name with different distributions or arguments fail to compile.
  • Within a step, the draws are taken by element path, then draw name, then member index. So the trajectory does not depend on the order of the laws.
  • The NumPy and Numba backends give equal trajectories for uniform, Bernoulli, and categorical draws.

Only update laws and renewal laws take draws. A draw in a rate, noise, jump, boundary, equation, or crossing law raises IncompatibleLawsError, because noise laws and jump laws give randomness in continuous time. Draws are not states, so the trajectory does not record them. A system that wants to keep a draw assigns it to a state.

docs.title: Markov chains and hidden Markov sources
docs.text:
This section steps a state over a finite alphabet with a transition matrix, and emits an observed symbol from a hidden state. A Markov chain draws its next value from a row of probabilities that its current value selects. In a hidden Markov source, the observer sees only a symbol drawn from a row that the hidden value selects. TransitionLaw(targets, matrix) is the step of a discrete-time Markov chain, and TransitionLaw(targets, matrix, source=source) draws an observed state from the row that a hidden state selects.

Here the weather stays calm with probability 0.9 and turns calm again from a storm with probability 0.4. Calm weather emits the symbol 'a' more often, and a storm emits 'b' more often.

from typing import Annotated

from sage.sets.finite_enumerated_set import FiniteEnumeratedSet

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import TransitionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class SourceElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        hidden: Annotated[str, StateSpec(domain=FiniteEnumeratedSet(['calm', 'storm']))] = 'calm',
        symbol: Annotated[str, StateSpec(domain=FiniteEnumeratedSet(['a', 'b']))] = 'a',
        stay: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.9,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.hidden = hidden
        self.symbol = symbol
        self.stay = stay

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [
            TransitionLaw(s.hidden, [[s.stay, 1 - s.stay], [0.4, 0.6]]),
            TransitionLaw(s.symbol, [[0.7, 0.3], [0.2, 0.8]], source=s.hidden),
        ]


trajectory = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[SourceElement('source')]), until=10000, dt=1.0, random_state=0)
round(float((trajectory.get_values('source.hidden') == 'calm').mean()), 1)

0.8

The weather is calm in a share of 0.8 of the 10000 steps. This is the stationary share of the chain, 0.4 / (0.1 + 0.4).

The two laws follow these rules.

  • The target of a TransitionLaw is a state over a finite alphabet, a FiniteEnumeratedSet of labels or the integers from 0 to n - 1. Its current value selects the row of the transition matrix that the next value is drawn from.
  • A TransitionLaw with a source draws the observed state from the row of an emission matrix that the hidden state selects. It reads the hidden state after the same step, so the two sequences align frame by frame. Its matrix has one row per hidden value and one column per observed value, and it is symbolic only.
  • Both are update laws, so they combine with other update laws.
  • Matrix entries are numbers or expressions of parameters. simulate checks that the entries are nonnegative and that every row sums to 1 at the initial parameter values, and raises an error that names the entry otherwise.

A probability of staying above 1 breaks the first of these checks.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[SourceElement('source', stay=1.5)]), until=10)
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
assert 'below 0' in message
message

The system is not valid, with 1 error(s):
- system: At the initial parameter values, the entry (0, 1) of the transition law of source.hidden_source is -0.5, below 0. Give a matrix with nonnegative entries whose rows sum to 1. Correct the component as the message describes. [value]

The message says that the entry (0, 1) of the transition law is -0.5, below 0, and asks for a matrix with nonnegative entries whose rows sum to 1. The fix is a value of stay between 0 and 1.

docs.title: Ready-made stochastic maps
docs.text:
This section points to the catalog systems that are stochastic maps, so you can start from one of them. They are PersistentRandomWalkSystem, MarkovSourceSystem, HiddenMarkovSourceSystem, and RandomWalkWithMemorySystem of skcomplex.systems.mathematics.stochastic_processes, ChaosGameSystem of skcomplex.systems.mathematics.fractals, ProbabilisticBooleanNetworkSystem of skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology, IntrinsicInstabilitySystem of skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology, and DilutedHopfieldSystem of skcomplex.systems.computer_science.neural_networks.

from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.stochastic_processes import MarkovSourceSystem

MarkovSourceSystem().get_tags().randomness

stochastic

The tag randomness of MarkovSourceSystem reads 'stochastic'.

docs.title: Stocks and flows
docs.text: This page builds stocks that change only through flows, as in system dynamics, checks that what flows is conserved, and finds the feedback loops that drive them. A stock is an amount that accumulates, such as the people of a town or the water in a bath, and a flow is a rate at which an amount enters or leaves a stock. In the library a stock is a state tagged with a quantity, such as StateSpec(quantity='people').

docs.title: Stocks and their flows
docs.text:
This section builds a population whose only changes are births and deaths. A TransferLaw moves an amount of the quantity from one stock to another, and it exchanges the quantity with the environment through a Source and a Sink. The population is an Element with ten people, a birth rate of 3 percent a year and a death rate of 1 percent. The birth rate falls to zero between 100 and 200 people through series(x, points, values), a table function that is piecewise linear between its points and flat outside them.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import Sink, Source, TransferLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import series
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec, ParameterSpec, StateSpec


def birth_rate(s):
    return s.b * s.n * series(s.n, (0, 100, 200), (1.0, 1.0, 0.0))


class PeopleElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        n: Annotated[float, StateSpec(quantity='people')] = 10.0,
        b: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.03,
        d: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.01,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.n = n
        self.b = b
        self.d = d

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [
            TransferLaw(Source(), s.n, birth_rate(s), label='births'),
            TransferLaw(s.n, Sink(), s.d * s.n, label='deaths'),
        ]


crowd = CompositeSystem(elements=[PeopleElement('crowd')])
observed = [ObservableSpec('birth_rate', birth_rate, element='crowd')]
trajectory = simulate(crowd, until=10, dt=1.0, observables=observed)
round(float(trajectory.get_values('crowd.births')[-1]), 3), round(float(trajectory.get_values('crowd.deaths')[-1]), 3)

(0.366, 0.122)

After ten years the births run at 0.366 people a year and the deaths at 0.122. Trajectories record every flow under <element path>.<label>, such as crowd.births. What the amount of a TransferLaw means depends on the laws around it.

  • In a system of rate laws the amount is a rate.
  • In a system of update laws it is moved once per step.
  • With rate=... it is the size of a jump with that propensity.

An intermediate expression, such as the birth rate, is a function of the namespace that the laws call. ObservableSpec(label, function, element=element) records the same function as the observable <element>.<label>, which Rerun logs under the element.

round(float(trajectory.get_values('crowd.birth_rate')[-1]), 3)

0.366

The observable crowd.birth_rate reads 0.366 at ten years, the same value as the flow crowd.births.

docs.title: Conservation
docs.text:
This section checks that the stocks change only through flows and shows how much of each quantity enters from outside. A rate or update law outside flows that changes a tagged state raises ConservationError when the system compiles. The analysis symbolic(system, kind='conservation') returns the net inflow of every quantity from the environment, after checking that the internal flows cancel.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import loops, symbolic
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import ConservationObserver

symbolic(crowd, kind='conservation').inflows

{'people': b_crowd*n_crowd*where(n_crowd < 0.0, 1.0, where(n_crowd < 100.0, 1.0, where(n_crowd < 200.0, -0.01*n_crowd + 2.0, 0.0))) - d_crowd*n_crowd}

The inflow of people is the birth rate times the population, b_crowd*n_crowd times the table of the birth rate, minus the deaths d_crowd*n_crowd. The compiler accumulates this inflow in the hidden state __boundary.<quantity>, and the observer ConservationObserver checks at every frame that each total changed only by it. The analysis loops(trajectory, kind='flow-matrix', frame=frame) gives the transaction-flow matrix of a frame of a trajectory, with one row per flow and one column per holder.

monitored = simulate(crowd, until=10, dt=1.0, observers=[ConservationObserver()])
loops(monitored, kind='flow-matrix').matrix.sum(axis=1).tolist()

[0.0, 0.0]

The rows of the matrix sum to [0.0, 0.0], since every flow leaves one holder and enters another, the environment included.

distributed_delay(value, time, order, conserved=True) is a material delay of any order. It is a chain of hidden stocks in series, and it returns their outflow. With conserved=False it is an information smoothing. It adds hidden stocks <element path>.<kind>_delay<order>_<index> to the rate laws of single elements and interactions, and they start in equilibrium with their input. The DELAY1 and DELAY3 functions of system dynamics are distributed_delay(value, time, 1) and distributed_delay(value, time, 3), and SMOOTH is distributed_delay(value, time, conserved=False).

docs.title: Feedback loops
docs.text:
This section finds the feedback loops of a system and ranks them over a run. A feedback loop is a closed chain of dependencies, through which a change in a state comes back to it. It is reinforcing when the change returns with the same sign and balancing when it returns with the opposite sign. loops(system) derives the signed dependency graph of a system from its laws and lists its feedback loops with their polarity.

feedback = loops(crowd)
[(polarity, ' -> '.join(nodes)) for nodes, polarity in zip(feedback.loops, feedback.polarities, strict=True)]

[('reinforcing', 'crowd.n -> crowd.births'), ('balancing', 'crowd.n -> crowd.deaths')]

The population has a reinforcing loop through its births and a balancing loop through its deaths. loops(trajectory, kind='dominance') ranks the loops by their gains at every frame of a trajectory.

dominance = loops(trajectory, kind='dominance')
dominance.polarities[int(dominance.dominant[-1])]

reinforcing

The reinforcing loop dominates at the last frame, since the births still outrun the deaths at ten years.

An edge of the graph goes from one state to another when the rate of the second depends on the first, with the sign of the entry of the Jacobian. In systems that declare flows, the edges also go through the flows. They go from a state to every flow it drives, and from a flow to its sink with sign + and to its source with sign -.

The graph is that of any system with a vector field or a map, not only of stocks and flows. At one prey and one predator, prey growth closes a reinforcing self-loop, predator death a balancing one, and predation a balancing loop through both populations.

from skcomplex.systems.biology.ecology import LotkaVolterraSystem

predation = loops(LotkaVolterraSystem(), at=[1.0, 1.0])
dict(zip(predation.loops, predation.polarities, strict=True))

{('predators.x',): 'balancing', ('prey.x',): 'reinforcing', ('predators.x', 'prey.x'): 'balancing'}

The loops read ('prey.x',) reinforcing, ('predators.x',) balancing, and ('predators.x', 'prey.x') balancing.

docs.title: Conserved quantities between agents
docs.text:
This section moves money and claims between agents so that the totals stay constant, and lets the run check it. Agents move conserved quantities between each other inside rules. transfer(source, sink, amount, state) moves an amount between two agents at once. A negative holding is an amount owed, and the total holdings stay constant. Here three traders in a GroupElement each hold 10 units of cash, and at every step each one lends a unit to the first trader in exchange for a claim, through a RuleLaw. A run checks that an expression keeps its first value with simulate(system, invariants={name: tolerance}), where the name is an observable of the run, here the total net worth.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RuleLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import transfer
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec, StateSpec


def net_worth(agent):
    return agent.cash + agent.claims - agent.equity


def lend(agent, system):
    borrower = system.get_agents('traders')[0]
    if borrower != agent:
        transfer(agent, borrower, 1.0, 'cash')
        transfer(borrower, agent, 1.0, 'claims')


class TraderElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        cash: Annotated[float, StateSpec(quantity='money')] = 10.0,
        claims: Annotated[float, StateSpec(quantity='claims')] = 0.0,
        equity: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 10.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.cash = cash
        self.claims = claims
        self.equity = equity

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RuleLaw(lend)]


balance = ObservableSpec('net_worth', net_worth, group='traders', reduce='sum')
market = CompositeSystem(elements=[GroupElement('traders', element=TraderElement, size=3)])
traders = simulate(market, until=3, observables=[balance], invariants={'net_worth': 1e-9})
float(traders.get_agents('traders', 3).values['cash'].sum())

30.0

The cash of the three traders still sums to 30.0 after three steps, and the net worth keeps its first value within 1e-9. At every frame the run compares the observable with its value at the first frame. It raises ConservationError, naming the observable and the first frame that breaks it. Removing an agent that still holds a tagged state also raises ConservationError, until its holdings are settled with transfers.

docs.title: Translating systems
docs.text:
This section turns a Vensim or Stella file into a system that runs and that the analyses read. SystemDynamicsTranslator(path) reads a Vensim (.mdl) or XMILE (.xmile, .xml, .stmx) file and writes the source of a system module. PySD reads the file. The translator writes source_ from the abstract model of PySD, and settings_ from the control section of the file. The source is saved and imported like any module. The file below holds a population with births and deaths.

import importlib
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from skcomplex.core.analysis import loops
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.engine.solvers import EulerSolver
from skcomplex.core.engine.translators import SystemDynamicsTranslator

text = """
Population = INTEG(Births - Deaths, 100) ~ People ~ |
Births = Population * Birth Fraction ~ People/Year ~ |
Deaths = Population / Lifetime ~ People/Year ~ |
Birth Fraction = 0.03 ~ 1/Year ~ |
Lifetime = 70 ~ Years ~ |
Doubling Share = Population / 200 ~ Dmnl ~ |
INITIAL TIME = 0 ~ Years ~ |
FINAL TIME = 100 ~ Years ~ |
TIME STEP = 0.25 ~ Years ~ |
SAVEPER = 1 ~ Years ~ |
"""
folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / 'people.mdl').write_text(text)
translator = SystemDynamicsTranslator(folder / 'people.mdl').prepare().run()
(folder / 'translated_people.py').write_text(translator.source_)
sys.path.insert(0, str(folder))
module = importlib.import_module('translated_people')
translator.settings_.until, module.DT

376
2917
(100.0, 0.25)

The run lasts 100 years with steps of 0.25 years, as the control section of the file says. The births and deaths of the population are its only flows, so the module defines two things.

  • The system class PeopleSystem, named after the file, a subclass of StockFlowSystem from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics. Its keyword arguments are the constants, with the values of the file as defaults. It returns the stocks from _get_stocks, the constants from _get_parameters, and the flows from _get_flows. Its tuned run settings are the length of the run, the saving interval, and one observable per auxiliary.
  • The constants START, UNTIL, DT, and SAVE_EVERY.

The class runs like any system, with its constants as model parameters.

system = module.PeopleSystem(birth_fraction=0.04)
trajectory = simulate(system)
trajectory.get_values('people.births')[0], trajectory.get_values('people.doubling_share')[0]

(4.0, 0.5)

With a birth fraction of 0.04, the births start at 4.0 people a year and the doubling share at 0.5, a population of 100 against the 200 of its definition. The loops of the translated system are those of the population above.

loops(system).polarities

['reinforcing', 'balancing']

The block returns ['reinforcing', 'balancing'], the births and the deaths. The class is a subclass of the recipe, and its model parameters are the constants of the file.

from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import StockFlowSystem

issubclass(module.PeopleSystem, StockFlowSystem), list(system.get_params())

(True, ['birth_fraction', 'label', 'lifetime'])

The block returns True and the parameters ['birth_fraction', 'label', 'lifetime']. A file whose stocks also change outside flow variables, or are subscripted, keeps the shape of a custom system. It gets one element class, whose states are the stocks and whose parameters are the constants, and a system class on BaseSystem that builds the element and its interactions.

Time in the module runs from zero, and Time in the file becomes t + START. The parts of the file become these.

  • A flow variable that leaves one stock and enters another is a flow between them. A flow variable of one stock is a flow with the environment, a TransferInteraction with Source() or Sink(). The trajectory reports each flow as <element>.<flow>.
  • The rest of the net rate of a stock is a RateInteraction. When it has the form (goal - stock) / time or (goal - stock) * rate, its rate is (goal - stock) / time of a goal function and a time function.
  • An auxiliary is a private function _name(s, t) of the module that the laws call, and an ObservableSpec under its snake-case name.
  • A lookup is a series of its input through its points. The built-in functions are where, step, ramp, pulse, pulse_train, distributed_delay for the delays and smoothings, delayed, minimum, maximum, clip, and the draws uniform and normal.
  • A system whose stocks are all subscripted over one range is a GroupElement with one member per subscript. SUM over the range is total, and a read of one subscript is a total over that member.

The default solver finds the exact solution. Vensim and Stella integrate with Euler steps by default. A run with solver=EulerSolver(dt=module.DT) and dt=module.DT reproduces their run step by step. A run with the default solver differs from it by the Euler error of the time step of the file.

stepped = simulate(system, until=module.UNTIL, dt=module.DT, solver=EulerSolver(dt=module.DT))
final = stepped.get_values('people.population')[-1]
round(float(final), 3)

1297.726

The Euler run ends with 1297.726 people after 100 years.

One ValidationError lists every construct that does not translate, with its variable. These are GAME, ALLOCATE, the vector functions, TREND, FORECAST, SAMPLE IF TRUE, data read from spreadsheets, macros, variables subscripted over more than one range, systems that mix subscripted and unsubscripted stocks, delays and smoothings whose initial value differs from their input, and DELAY FIXED of anything other than a stock.

The library sets these limits on what a translated module does.

  • The core takes random draws only in update and renewal laws. A module with a random function translates, but raises IncompatibleLawsError when its system is prepared.
  • A run cannot record an auxiliary that reads DELAY FIXED, or a delay that no law reads, so observables leaves it out.
  • A trajectory records the flow of one member from the values of that member. So in a group, a flow variable that reads SUM or one named subscript stays in the rate of its stock, without a flow, and its value stays an observable.

The systems of the catalog built on flows cover several fields.

  • Engineering processes: BathtubSystem, RiceMillingSystem, SolidWasteSystem, FoodReliefSystem, and IrrigationSystem.
  • Markets: CarDealerSystem, CommodityCycleSystem, and BeerGameSystem.
  • Innovation: BassDiffusionSystem.
  • Macroeconomics: StockFlowConsistentEconomySystem.
  • Organizations: SuccessToTheSuccessfulSystem, ShiftingTheBurdenSystem, and EscalationSystem.

docs.title: Case studies
docs.text:
The case studies take one system of the catalog through the whole workflow, from selecting and checking it to simulating, analysing, evaluating or calibrating, experimenting, and drawing a figure. Each study comes from a different field and tests the model against data or a known result, which the page cites. The data enter as short inline arrays, so the pages need no download, and every page runs in under a minute with small budgets and fixed seeds.

  • An epidemic calibrated to case data fits the SIR model to the daily counts of an influenza outbreak in an English boarding school in 1978, reported in the British Medical Journal. It checks the fit and the coverage of the posterior, asks whether the counts determine the two rates, and compares scenarios of earlier isolation.
  • An opinion model swept and analysed sweeps the bounded confidence model of Deffuant et al. over its confidence bound, with an ensemble of runs per value. It counts the opinion clusters against the known result 1 / (2 d) and measures how the final consensus depends on the bound and the convergence rate.
  • A lattice phase transition sweeps the two-dimensional Ising model over temperature on lattices of three sizes. It finds the peak of the susceptibility near the exact critical temperature of Onsager and estimates the critical exponents by finite-size scaling.

The workflow tutorials explain each step on its own, such as Simulate, Calibrate, and Run experiments.

docs.title: An epidemic calibrated to case data
docs.text: This case study fits the epidemic model of Kermack and McKendrick to the daily counts of an influenza outbreak in an English boarding school in 1978. It selects the model from the catalog, checks it, fits its two rates, checks the fit and the posterior, asks whether the data determine the rates, and compares scenarios of earlier isolation.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
In January 1978 influenza spread through a boarding school in England, and 512 of its 763 boys fell ill. The British Medical Journal reported the outbreak (Anonymous, 1978, "Influenza in a boarding school", British Medical Journal 1(6112), News and Notes, pages 586 to 590). The counts below are the boys confined to bed on each day from 22 January to 4 February, and the boys convalescing after their time in bed. They come from the file data/influenza_england_1978_school.RData of the R package outbreaks, in the GitHub repository reconverse/outbreaks. Its documentation, R/influenza_england_1978_school.R, cites the report and says the numbers were read from a figure of it by De Vries et al. (2006, A Course in Mathematical Biology, SIAM), so other sources give slightly different counts.

import numpy as np

days = np.arange(14.0)
in_bed = np.array([3, 8, 26, 76, 225, 298, 258, 233, 189, 128, 68, 29, 14, 4], dtype=float)
convalescent = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 9, 17, 105, 162, 176, 166, 150, 85, 47, 20], dtype=float)
int(days[in_bed.argmax()]), int(in_bed.max())

(5, 298)

Day 0 is 22 January. The number in bed peaks on day 5, 27 January, at 298 boys.

docs.title: Selecting and checking the model
docs.text:
The SIR model of Kermack and McKendrick (1927, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 115, 700) splits a population into the susceptible S, who can catch the disease, the infected I, who spread it, and the recovered R, who are immune. A susceptible boy meets an infected one and falls ill at the rate beta S I, and an infected boy leaves the infected compartment at the rate gamma I:

dS/dt = -beta S I
dI/dt = beta S I - gamma I
dR/dt = gamma I

The catalog holds this model as SIRSystem. The study assumes that the boys in bed are the infected compartment. The school starts with 3 boys in bed and 760 susceptible boys.

from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem

school = SIRSystem(susceptible=760.0, infected=3.0, recovered=0.0)
tags = school.get_tags()
[element.label for element in school.prepare().system_.elements], sorted(tags.laws), tags.randomness

(['S', 'I', 'R'], ['rate'], 'deterministic')

prepare builds the parts and checks that they fit together. The system has the elements S, I, and R, its laws are rates, and it is deterministic, so one run gives the answer and no ensemble is needed. The tags tell simulate which solver fits.

docs.title: A first simulation
docs.text:
The default rates of SIRSystem describe a slow epidemic, so the first run shows how far they are from the school.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

trajectory = simulate(school, until=13, dt=1.0)
trajectory.get_values('I.x').round().tolist()[::4]

[3.0, 5.0, 8.0, 14.0]

With beta = 0.0003 and gamma = 0.1 per day, the number infected creeps from 3 to 5, 8, and 14 boys on days 4, 8, and 12, while the school had 298 in bed on day 5. The rates have to come from the data.

docs.title: Calibrating the rates
docs.text:
calibrate fits the model parameters to observed series. Each series is a pair of times and values under the path of a state, here I.x, the number infected. The bounds keep each rate in a range that a school epidemic allows. The default method 'local' is a least squares fit. The basic reproduction number, the number of boys one sick boy infects in a school of susceptible boys, follows from the fit as R0 = beta N / gamma with N the 763 boys.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import calibrate

data = {'I.x': (days, in_bed)}
bounds = {'beta': (0.0005, 0.005), 'gamma': (0.1, 1.0)}
fit = calibrate(school, data, bounds)
reproduction = fit.estimates['beta'] * 763 / fit.estimates['gamma']
estimates = round(fit.estimates['beta'], 5), round(fit.estimates['gamma'], 3), round(reproduction, 1)
estimates, round(fit.r2, 3), round(fit.rmse, 1)

((0.00223, 0.447, 3.8), 0.974, 16.6)

The fit gives beta = 0.00223 per pair of boys and day and gamma = 0.447 per day, so a boy stays infected for about 1 / gamma = 2.2 days. Each sick boy infected about 3.8 others at the start of the outbreak. The model explains 97.4% of the variance of the counts, with a root mean square error of 16.6 boys.

docs.title: Analysing the fitted run
docs.text:
The analysis function events finds the episodes when a series stays above a threshold. Applied to the fitted run and to the data, it compares when the school had more than 100 boys in bed and for how long.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import events

fitted_run = simulate(fit.system, until=13, dt=1.0)
simulated = events(fitted_run, variables=['I.x'], threshold=100.0)
observed = events(in_bed, threshold=100.0)
(simulated.starts.tolist(), simulated.durations.tolist()), (observed.starts.tolist(), observed.durations.tolist())

(([4.0], [6.0]), ([4.0], [6.0]))

Both the model and the school pass 100 boys in bed on day 4 and stay above it for 6 days.

docs.title: Evaluating the posterior
docs.text:
A least squares fit gives one value per rate. A posterior method gives a distribution over the rates, the posterior, which says how well the data pin each rate down. The method 'variational' fits a normal distribution to the posterior, and the loss 'likelihood' reads the data as the model plus Gaussian noise of unknown size. The result also holds a posterior predictive check: the band of runs drawn from the posterior and the share of observed counts inside it. The block starts again from the counts, so it runs on its own.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import calibrate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem

days = np.arange(14.0)
in_bed = np.array([3, 8, 26, 76, 225, 298, 258, 233, 189, 128, 68, 29, 14, 4], dtype=float)
school = SIRSystem(susceptible=760.0, infected=3.0, recovered=0.0)
data = {'I.x': (days, in_bed)}
bounds = {'beta': (0.0005, 0.005), 'gamma': (0.1, 1.0)}
posterior = calibrate(
    school, data, bounds, method='variational', loss='likelihood', n_samples=200, budget=1000, random_state=0
)
low, high = np.quantile(posterior.samples['gamma'], [0.05, 0.95])
round(posterior.estimates['gamma'], 3), round(float(low), 3), round(float(high), 3), posterior.predictive['coverage']

(0.448, 0.421, 0.478, 1.0)

The posterior median of gamma is 0.448 per day, and 90% of the posterior lies between 0.421 and 0.478. The band from the 5% to the 95% quantile of the posterior runs holds every one of the 14 counts, a coverage of 1.0.

A band that holds the data does not prove that the intervals are honest. posterior_coverage tests the method itself. It draws true rates from the prior, simulates data from them with noise, calibrates each data set, and counts how often the credible interval holds the true value. A calibrated method covers the truth with its 90% interval in about 90% of the data sets. The prior here is narrower than the bounds of the fit, so that every draw makes an outbreak, and the noise of 15 boys matches the error of the fit.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import posterior_coverage
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem

school = SIRSystem(susceptible=760.0, infected=3.0, recovered=0.0)
prior = {'beta': (0.0015, 0.003), 'gamma': (0.3, 0.6)}
check = posterior_coverage(
    school,
    prior,
    np.arange(14.0),
    paths=['I.x'],
    method='variational',
    n=3,
    levels=(0.9,),
    noise=15.0,
    n_samples=200,
    budget=1000,
    random_state=0,
)
check.coverage[0.9]

{'beta': 1.0, 'gamma': 1.0}

The 90% intervals held the true beta and the true gamma in all 3 simulated data sets, a coverage of 1.0 for each. Three data sets show that the check runs, not that the method is calibrated. Each data set costs one calibration of a few seconds. A real study uses 100 data sets or more, and compares the ranks in check.ranks with a uniform distribution, the test of simulation-based calibration (Talts et al., 2018, arXiv:1804.06788).

docs.title: Identifiability of the two rates
docs.text:
A calibration returns estimates even when the data cannot determine them. identifiability tells whether they do. Its default method computes the profile likelihood of each rate. It fixes the rate at values on both sides of the best fit, fits the other rate again, and keeps the values whose likelihood stays within the 95% threshold of a likelihood ratio test. A rate is identifiable when this interval ends inside its bounds on both sides.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import identifiability
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem

days = np.arange(14.0)
in_bed = np.array([3, 8, 26, 76, 225, 298, 258, 233, 189, 128, 68, 29, 14, 4], dtype=float)
school = SIRSystem(susceptible=760.0, infected=3.0, recovered=0.0)
bounds = {'beta': (0.0005, 0.005), 'gamma': (0.1, 1.0)}
profile = identifiability(school, {'I.x': (days, in_bed)}, bounds, n_starts=1, random_state=0)
intervals = {name: tuple(float(f'{value:.3g}') for value in pair) for name, pair in profile.intervals.items()}
profile.verdicts, intervals

({'beta': 'identifiable', 'gamma': 'identifiable'}, {'beta': (0.00215, 0.00231), 'gamma': (0.419, 0.478)})

Both rates are identifiable. The 95% interval of beta runs from 0.00215 to 0.00231, and that of gamma from 0.419 to 0.478, close to the 90% posterior interval above. The outbreak rises and falls within the data, so the rise fixes beta and the decline fixes gamma. A real study takes n_starts=5 or more, so the best fit does not depend on one start.

docs.title: Scenarios of earlier isolation
docs.text:
A scenario changes the system before or during a run. Isolating the sick boys from the others lowers the rate of infection, which the study models as halving beta from a given day. The system takes the fitted rates, rounded. compare_scenarios runs every ScenarioSpec on it. The schedule of a scenario changes the parameter beta of the interaction infection at the given day. An output is a path, kept as a series and as its last value, or a function of the trajectory, here the highest number of boys in bed.

from skcomplex.core.components.specs import ScenarioSpec
from skcomplex.core.experiments import compare_scenarios
from skcomplex.systems.biology.epidemiology import SIRSystem


def peak_in_bed(trajectory):
    return float(trajectory.get_values('I.x').max())


fitted = SIRSystem(susceptible=760.0, infected=3.0, recovered=0.0, beta=0.00223, gamma=0.447)
scenarios = [
    ScenarioSpec(),
    ScenarioSpec('isolation from day 4', schedule=[(4.0, 'infection.beta', 0.00223 / 2)]),
    ScenarioSpec('isolation from day 2', schedule=[(2.0, 'infection.beta', 0.00223 / 2)]),
]
outcomes = compare_scenarios(fitted, scenarios, until=30, dt=1.0, outputs=['I.x', 'R.x', peak_in_bed])
[(row['scenario'], round(row['peak_in_bed']), round(row['R.x'])) for row in outcomes.rows]

[('baseline', 290, 744), ('isolation from day 4', 212, 647), ('isolation from day 2', 117, 594)]

Without isolation the fitted model peaks at 290 boys in bed, and 744 boys catch the virus by day 30. Isolation from day 4 lowers the peak to 212 and the total to 647. Isolation from day 2 lowers them to 117 and 594. Two days earlier cut the peak by another 95 boys. The model predicts more cases in total than the 512 boys the school counted as ill, because it fits only the counts in bed and assumes every boy could catch the virus.

docs.title: Visualising the scenarios
docs.text:
The figure draws the counts and the run of every scenario. It uses the Agg backend of matplotlib, which draws to memory and opens no window.

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

in_bed = np.array([3, 8, 26, 76, 225, 298, 258, 233, 189, 128, 68, 29, 14, 4], dtype=float)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for row, series in zip(outcomes.rows, outcomes.get_series('I.x')):
    ax.plot(np.arange(series.size), series, label=row['scenario'])
ax.plot(np.arange(in_bed.size), in_bed, 'o', color='black', label='in bed, 1978')
ax.set_xlabel('days from 22 January 1978')
ax.set_ylabel('boys')
ax.legend()
plt.close(fig)
[text.get_text() for text in ax.get_legend().get_texts()]

[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x753012924cd0>]
Text(0.5, 0, 'days from 22 January 1978')
Text(0, 0.5, 'boys')
<matplotlib.legend.Legend object at 0x753012924e10>
['baseline', 'isolation from day 4', 'isolation from day 2', 'in bed, 1978']

The legend names the three scenarios and the counts of 1978. A script saves the figure with fig.savefig('school.png'). Outside the Agg backend, plt.show() opens it in a window.

docs.title: What a real study would add
docs.text: The page keeps its budgets small, so it runs in under a minute. A real study would run the variational fit for a few thousand steps or use method='mcmc' with four chains, check the coverage on 100 or more simulated data sets, and fit the convalescent counts as a fourth compartment. The pages Calibrate and Run experiments describe each method and its settings.

docs.title: A lattice phase transition
docs.text: This case study locates the phase transition of the two-dimensional Ising model and estimates its critical exponents from small lattices. It checks the model from the catalog, sweeps it over temperature on lattices of three sizes, finds the peak of the susceptibility near the exact critical temperature of Onsager, and estimates the exponents by finite-size scaling.

docs.title: The model and the exact result
docs.text:
The Ising model places a spin s = +1 or s = -1 on every site of a square lattice. Neighbouring spins prefer to point the same way, with the energy -J s s' per pair. At low temperature most spins align and the lattice is magnetised. At high temperature thermal noise breaks the order. The magnetization m, the mean spin, measures the order. Onsager (1944, "Crystal statistics. I. A two-dimensional model with an order-disorder transition", Physical Review 65, 117) solved the model exactly. The order vanishes at the critical temperature:

T_c = 2 J / (k_B ln(1 + sqrt(2))) = 2.269 J / k_B

The temperatures below are in units of J / k_B. Near T_c the order parameter and the susceptibility follow power laws with exponents known from the exact solution: beta = 1/8 for the magnetization, gamma = 7/4 for the susceptibility, and nu = 1 for the correlation length, the distance over which spins are correlated.

docs.title: Selecting and checking the model
docs.text:
The catalog holds the model as IsingSystem. One unit of time is one sweep, an attempt to flip every spin once by the Metropolis rule. An ObservableSpec records the magnetization at every sweep, the mean of the variable spin over the group spins.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem

magnetization = ObservableSpec('magnetization', group='spins', variable='spin', reduce='mean')
lattice = IsingSystem(16, temperature=1.8, initial='up')
tags = lattice.get_tags()
order = []
for temperature in (1.8, 3.0):
    lattice.set_params(temperature=temperature)
    run = simulate(lattice, until=500, observables=[magnetization], random_state=0)
    order.append(round(float(np.abs(run.get_values('magnetization')[100:]).mean()), 2))
sorted(tags.space), tags.randomness, order

(['lattice'], 'stochastic', [0.96, 0.17])

The spins live on a lattice and the updates are random. On a lattice of 16 by 16 spins that starts with every spin up, the mean of |m| after 100 sweeps stays at 0.96 at T = 1.8, below T_c, and falls to 0.17 at T = 3.0, above it.

docs.title: Sweeping the temperature
docs.text:
The susceptibility measures how strongly the magnetization fluctuates. For a lattice of N = L^2 spins it is chi = N (<m^2> - <|m|>^2) / T, where the brackets are means over the sweeps of a run. It peaks at the transition, and on a finite lattice the peak sits a little above T_c and moves towards it as the lattice grows. sweep runs a grid of the side size and the temperature, two replicates per pair. An output function returns the moments of |m| of a run after 300 sweeps of warm-up.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sweep
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec
from skcomplex.systems.physics.statistical_mechanics import IsingSystem

magnetization = ObservableSpec('magnetization', group='spins', variable='spin', reduce='mean')


def moments(trajectory):
    values = np.abs(trajectory.get_values('magnetization')[300:])
    return {'m': values.mean(), 'm2': (values**2).mean(), 'm4': (values**4).mean()}


sizes = np.array([8, 16, 32])
temperatures = np.round(np.arange(1.9, 2.95, 0.1), 2)
swept = sweep(
    IsingSystem(initial='up'),
    {'size': sizes, 'temperature': temperatures},
    replicates=2,
    until=1500,
    observables=[magnetization],
    outputs=[moments],
    random_state=0,
)
shape = (sizes.size, temperatures.size, 2)
m, m2, m4 = (swept.get_column(f'moments.{name}').reshape(shape) for name in ('m', 'm2', 'm4'))
chi_runs = sizes[:, None, None] ** 2 * (m2 - m**2) / temperatures[:, None]
chi = chi_runs.mean(axis=2)
peaks = temperatures[chi.argmax(axis=1)]
tc = 2 / np.log(1 + np.sqrt(2))
peaks.tolist(), round(float(tc), 3), bool(abs(peaks[-1] - tc) < 0.3)

([2.5, 2.4, 2.3], 2.269, True)

The grid runs the last name fastest, so the rows reshape into sizes, temperatures, and replicates. The susceptibility peaks at T = 2.5, 2.4, and 2.3 for the sides 8, 16, and 32. The peak moves towards T_c = 2.269 as the lattice grows, and on the lattice of 32 by 32 spins it lies within the tolerance 0.3 of the exact value. The grid steps by 0.1, so the peak cannot be located more finely than that.

docs.title: Critical exponents by finite-size scaling
docs.text:
Finite-size scaling, the theory of how a transition looks on a finite lattice, predicts that the susceptibility curves of all sizes fall onto one curve when they are rescaled. The curve chi_L(T) L^(-gamma / nu) is plotted against (T - T_c) L^(1 / nu). data_collapse fits the exponents that make the rescaled curves overlap best. With kind='crossings' it finds where the curves of consecutive sizes cross, here the Binder cumulant U = 1 - <m^4> / (3 <m^2>^2), whose curves cross near T_c independently of the size. scaling fits power laws. With kind='allometric' it fits the growth of the peak of the susceptibility with the side, chi_max ~ L^(gamma / nu), and with kind='power' the decay of the magnetization below T_c, m ~ (T_c - T)^beta.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import data_collapse, scaling

binder = 1 - m4.mean(axis=2) / (3 * m2.mean(axis=2) ** 2)
crossings = data_collapse(dict(zip(sizes, binder)), kind='crossings', parameters=temperatures).crossings
collapse = data_collapse(
    dict(zip(sizes, chi)), parameters=temperatures, critical=tc, nu=1.0, exponent=1.75, fit=('nu', 'exponent')
)
growth = scaling(dict(zip(sizes, chi_runs.max(axis=1))), kind='allometric', resamples=200)
below = temperatures < tc
decay = scaling(m[-1].mean(axis=1)[below], kind='power', parameters=temperatures[below], critical=tc)
(
    crossings.round(2).tolist(),
    round(collapse.nu, 2),
    round(collapse.exponent, 2),
    round(growth.exponent, 2),
    round(float(decay.exponent[0]), 2),
)

([2.28, 2.22], 0.98, 1.81, 1.79, 0.1)

The Binder cumulants of the sides 8 and 16 cross at 2.28, and those of 16 and 32 at 2.22, on both sides of the exact 2.269. The collapse gives nu = 0.98 against the exact 1, and gamma / nu = 1.81 against the exact 7/4 = 1.75. The growth of the peak of the susceptibility gives 1.79. The magnetization of the lattice of 32 by 32 spins gives beta = 0.10 against the exact 1/8 = 0.125. The fit uses the temperatures below T_c, where a small lattice still keeps some magnetization close to the transition, so the estimate of beta is the least accurate of the four.

docs.title: Visualising the collapse
docs.text:
The figure draws the rescaled susceptibility of the three sizes against the rescaled temperature with the fitted exponents. It uses the Agg backend of matplotlib, which draws to memory and opens no window.

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for size, curve in zip(sizes, chi):
    rescaled = (temperatures - tc) * size ** (1 / collapse.nu)
    ax.plot(rescaled, curve * size ** (-collapse.exponent), 'o-', label=f'L = {size}')
ax.set_xlabel('(T - T_c) L^(1 / nu)')
ax.set_ylabel('chi L^(-gamma / nu)')
ax.legend()
plt.close(fig)
[text.get_text() for text in ax.get_legend().get_texts()]

Text(0.5, 0, '(T - T_c) L^(1 / nu)')
Text(0, 0.5, 'chi L^(-gamma / nu)')
<matplotlib.legend.Legend object at 0x753001525d10>
['L = 8', 'L = 16', 'L = 32']

The legend names the three sizes. A script saves the figure with fig.savefig('collapse.png'). Outside the Agg backend, plt.show() opens it in a window.

docs.title: What a real study would add
docs.text: The page keeps its budgets small, so it runs in under a minute. A real study would use lattices up to 128 by 128 spins or more, a grid of steps of 0.01 near T_c, runs of 10^5 sweeps or more with error bars from blocks of sweeps, and a cluster algorithm such as that of Wolff (1989, Physical Review Letters 62, 361), since local rules such as Metropolis slow down near T_c. The page Run experiments describes sweep, and the page Analyse the analysis functions.

docs.title: An opinion model swept and analysed
docs.text: This case study takes the bounded confidence model of Deffuant et al. from the catalog and asks how many opinion groups it forms. It checks the model, runs it once, counts the clusters of opinions, sweeps the confidence bound with an ensemble of runs per value, compares the counts with the known result 1 / (2 d), and measures which parameter the final consensus depends on.

docs.title: The model and the known result
docs.text:
Deffuant, Neau, Amblard, and Weisbuch (2000, "Mixing beliefs among interacting agents", Advances in Complex Systems 3, 87) proposed the model. Each agent holds an opinion between 0 and 1. At each encounter two random agents compare their opinions x and y. If they differ by less than the confidence bound d, both move towards each other by the fraction mu of the difference, the convergence rate:

x <- x + mu (y - x)
y <- y + mu (x - y)

Agents whose opinions lie further apart than d ignore each other. From uniform initial opinions the population settles into clusters, groups of agents with the same opinion. Deffuant et al. found by simulation that the number of clusters is close to the integer part of 1 / (2 d), and that mu changes how fast the opinions settle but not where they settle. The study checks both statements.

docs.title: Selecting and checking the model
docs.text:
The catalog holds the model as DeffuantSystem. Its parameters are the number of agents, the bound confidence, the rate convergence, and the seed random_state of the initial opinions. The study uses 100 agents.

from skcomplex.systems.social.opinion_dynamics import DeffuantSystem

opinions_model = DeffuantSystem(100, confidence=0.2, convergence=0.5)
tags = opinions_model.get_tags()
[element.label for element in opinions_model.prepare().system_.elements], sorted(tags.time), tags.randomness

(['people'], ['discrete'], 'stochastic')

prepare builds the parts and checks that they fit together. The model has one element, the group people that holds the agents. Time is discrete, since the model steps through rounds of encounters, and the model is stochastic, since the pairs meet at random. A run therefore needs a seed, and a study needs several runs per setting.

docs.title: One run and its clusters
docs.text:
simulate runs the model for its tuned number of steps, 50 rounds of encounters. The agents of a group are read at a frame with get_agents, which returns their states.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

trajectory = simulate(opinions_model, random_state=0)
final = trajectory.get_agents('people', len(trajectory.times) - 1).values['opinion']
initial = trajectory.get_agents('people', 0).values['opinion']
round(float(initial.std()), 3), round(float(final.std()), 3)

(0.303, 0.257)

The standard deviation of the opinions falls only from 0.303, close to the value 1 / sqrt(12) = 0.289 of uniform opinions, to 0.257. The agents have not come to one opinion. They have split into groups far apart.

The analysis function clusters finds the groups. With a radius, it reads an array of points, one row per point, and joins the points closer than twice the radius. Here a point is the opinion of one agent, and the radius 0.005 joins opinions that differ by less than 0.01.

from skcomplex.core.analysis import clusters

groups = clusters(final[:, None], kind='sizes', radius=0.005)
groups.sizes.tolist()

[53, 47]

The 100 agents end in two clusters, of 53 and 47 agents. At d = 0.2 the known result gives 1 / (2 d) = 2.5, so two or three clusters.

docs.title: Sweeping the confidence bound
docs.text:
sweep runs the model over a grid of values of a model parameter. With replicates it repeats every value with different random encounters, an ensemble of runs per value. An output may be a function of the trajectory, here the number of clusters of at least five agents, so that a few stragglers between the large clusters do not count.
