The initial opinions of every run are those of the seed random_state=0 of the system.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sweep


def large_clusters(trajectory):
    opinions = trajectory.get_agents('people', len(trajectory.times) - 1).values['opinion']
    sizes = clusters(opinions[:, None], kind='sizes', radius=0.005).sizes
    return int(np.sum(sizes >= 5))


bounds = np.array([0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5])
swept = sweep(
    DeffuantSystem(100), {'confidence': bounds}, replicates=4, outputs=[large_clusters], random_state=0
)
counts = swept.get_column('large_clusters').reshape(len(bounds), 4)
counts.mean(axis=1).tolist(), np.floor(1 / (2 * bounds)).tolist()

([4.25, 3.5, 2.25, 2.0, 1.75, 1.0, 1.0], [5.0, 3.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])

The rows of the result run over the bounds, with the four replicates of a bound next to each other, so the column reshapes into one row per bound. The mean count falls from 4.25 clusters at d = 0.1 to one cluster, a consensus, at d = 0.4 and above. The integer part of 1 / (2 d) gives 5, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, and 1 clusters. The simulated means lie within one cluster of these values at every bound, as the known result predicts.

docs.title: Sensitivity of the final consensus
docs.text:
The variance of the opinions measures the final consensus. It is zero when every agent holds the same opinion and grows as the opinions split into clusters far apart. An ObservableSpec computes it at every frame, as it reduces the variable opinion of the group people with 'var'. sensitivity then varies the bound and the convergence rate within their bounds and measures the effect of each on the last value of the observable. The method 'morris' runs Morris trajectories, each of which changes one input at a time. Its index mu_star is the mean absolute change of the output per change of an input, and ranks the inputs.

from skcomplex.core.experiments import sensitivity
from skcomplex.core.specs import ObservableSpec

spread = ObservableSpec('spread', group='people', variable='opinion', reduce='var')
ranges = {'confidence': (0.1, 0.5), 'convergence': (0.1, 0.5)}
effects = sensitivity(
    DeffuantSystem(100), ranges, output='spread', method='morris', n=10, until=100, observables=[spread], random_state=0
)
effects.ranking, {name: round(value, 4) for name, value in effects.mu_star.items()}

(['confidence', 'convergence'], {'confidence': 0.1109, 'convergence': 0.0035})

The bound ranks first, with mu_star equal to 0.1109, and the convergence rate has 0.0035, about 30 times smaller. The runs last 100 rounds, so that slow convergence rates also settle. This matches the finding of Deffuant et al. that the bound decides the final state and the convergence rate only how fast it is reached.

docs.title: Visualising the sweep
docs.text:
The figure draws the mean number of clusters per bound, with the spread of the ensemble, against the known result. It uses the Agg backend of matplotlib, which draws to memory and opens no window.

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.errorbar(bounds, counts.mean(axis=1), yerr=counts.std(axis=1), marker='o', capsize=3, label='simulated')
grid = np.linspace(0.08, 0.52, 200)
ax.plot(grid, np.floor(1 / (2 * grid)), color='black', linestyle='--', label='floor(1 / (2 d))')
ax.set_xlabel('confidence bound d')
ax.set_ylabel('clusters of at least five agents')
ax.legend()
plt.close(fig)
[text.get_text() for text in ax.get_legend().get_texts()]

<ErrorbarContainer object of 3 artists>
[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x7530027982d0>]
Text(0.5, 0, 'confidence bound d')
Text(0, 0.5, 'clusters of at least five agents')
<matplotlib.legend.Legend object at 0x753002799a90>
['floor(1 / (2 d))', 'simulated']

The legend names the known result and the simulated counts. A script saves the figure with fig.savefig('clusters.png'). Outside the Agg backend, plt.show() opens it in a window.

docs.title: What a real study would add
docs.text: The page keeps its budgets small, so it runs in under a minute. A real study would use 1000 agents or more, a finer grid of bounds, 20 or more replicates per bound with different initial opinions, and the method 'sobol' of sensitivity with 1024 base points, which also measures how the two inputs interact. The page Run experiments describes each experiment and its settings.

docs.title: How the parts fit
docs.text: This page explains the parts that every system is made of and how a run turns them into numbers. It ends with a predator and its prey on a lattice, built one part at a time.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
An element holds states, the numbers that change as the system runs, such as the size of a population. An interaction reads states through its roles and returns laws that change them. A law is one equation or rule for one state, such as a rate or the next value at a step. A space places the members of a group and says who neighbours whom. A time says whether the system flows, steps, or is solved once. A system composes all of them.

classDiagram
    direction LR
    class CompositeSystem {
        elements
        interactions
        space
        time
    }
    class GroupElement {
        element
        values
    }
    class Element {
        states
        parameters
    }
    class Interaction {
        roles
        parameters
    }
    class Law {
        target state
        expression
    }
    CompositeSystem o-- Element : holds
    CompositeSystem o-- GroupElement : holds
    CompositeSystem o-- Interaction : holds
    CompositeSystem o-- Space : lives on
    CompositeSystem o-- Time : runs in
    GroupElement o-- Element : members of one class
    Space <-- GroupElement : sits on
    Interaction --> Element : reads through roles
    Interaction ..> Law : returns
    Element ..> Law : may return
    Law --> Element : changes a state of

None of these words belongs to one field. A population, a chemical species, a bank account, and a cell of a lattice are all elements, and an epidemic, a reaction, and a payment are all interactions.

docs.title: A run
docs.text:
simulate takes a system to a trajectory in four stages.

flowchart LR
    A[System] -->|prepare checks the parts and collects their laws| B[Laws]
    B -->|the compiler lowers the laws| C[Problem]
    C -->|a solver advances it on a backend| D[Frames]
    D -->|observers record them| E[Trajectory]

prepare checks every part and binds every role to an element. The compiler reads the laws of the parts and builds a problem of one mathematical form, such as a system of ordinary differential equations. A solver advances the problem from frame to frame, and a backend, NumPy by default, evaluates its functions. Observers receive the frames, and the recorder keeps them as the trajectory that simulate returns.

docs.title: A system step by step
docs.text: Prey grow and predators hunt them on every site of a lattice, and prey move between neighbouring sites. Each step below adds one part and runs what it has so far.

docs.title: The elements
docs.text:
An element class declares its states as arguments of its __init__, each annotated with a StateSpec. The default of each argument is the initial value of the state. A GroupElement holds one member of that class on every site.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import oo
from sage.sets.real_set import RealSet

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec

AMOUNT = StateSpec(domain=RealSet.closed_open(0, oo))


class HabitatElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        prey: Annotated[float, AMOUNT] = 1.0,
        predators: Annotated[float, AMOUNT] = 0.5,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.prey = prey
        self.predators = predators


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
habitats = GroupElement('habitats', element=HabitatElement, on='sites', values={'prey': rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, 25)})
habitats.values['prey'][:3].round(2).tolist()

[1.14, 0.77, 0.54]

docs.title: The interactions
docs.text:
Two RateInteraction parts give the local equations of Lotka and Volterra. Prey grow at rate one and are eaten in proportion to the predators, and predators grow in proportion to the prey and die at rate one. Each interaction names the states its role reads.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import CouplingInteraction, RateInteraction

births = RateInteraction(
    'births', target='habitats', state='prey', rate=lambda s: s.target.prey * (1.0 - s.target.predators)
)
hunting = RateInteraction(
    'hunting', target='habitats', state='predators', rate=lambda s: s.target.predators * (s.target.prey - 1.0)
)
births.get_requirements().roles['target'].states

('prey',)

A CouplingInteraction moves prey between neighbouring sites. Each site gains the difference between the prey of each neighbour and its own, so prey flow from crowded sites to empty ones.

dispersal = CouplingInteraction('dispersal', target='habitats', read='prey', write='prey', mode='edges')
dispersal.get_requirements().roles['target'].states

('prey',)

docs.title: The space
docs.text:
A LatticeSpace of five by five sites holds the 25 members of the group. Its periodic boundary joins opposite edges, so every site has the same number of neighbours.

from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace

grid = LatticeSpace((5, 5), boundary='periodic')
grid.prepare().size_

25

docs.title: The time
docs.text:
The populations change at every instant, so the system runs in ContinuousTime.

from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousTime

time = ContinuousTime()

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
A CompositeSystem holds the parts. Its tags come from them: rate laws in continuous time.

from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem

ecosystem = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[habitats], interactions=[births, hunting, dispersal], space=grid, time=time
)
sorted(ecosystem.get_tags().laws), sorted(ecosystem.get_tags().time)

(['rate'], ['continuous'])

docs.title: The run
docs.text:
simulate prepares the system, chooses a solver from its tags, and returns the trajectory. The mean prey over the lattice rises and falls in the cycles of Lotka and Volterra.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

trajectory = simulate(ecosystem, until=10, dt=1.0)
trajectory.get_values('habitats.prey').mean(axis=1).round(2).tolist()

[0.99, 1.56, 1.65, 0.89, 0.53, 0.54, 0.78, 1.27, 1.74, 1.27, 0.64]

docs.title: The main public methods
docs.text:
Every part has two main public methods, and both return the part itself. prepare checks the part against what it works on, such as the space of its system. run sets what the part contributes: the laws of an element, an interaction, or a system in laws_, and the value of a law in value_. A part runs only after it is prepared. Every part also has get_params, set_params, and get_tags, as scikit-learn estimators do. simulate is a function, since it is what is done to a system and not a part of it.

A law runs on its own too, so it can be checked before it joins a system. This rate law gives its rate at x = 10.

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import var

from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RateLaw

x = var('x')
RateLaw(x, 0.5 * x).prepare('growth').run({'x': 10.0}).value_

5.0

docs.title: Laws and the default solver
docs.text:
The laws of a system give its tags, and the tags decide the default solver.

Laws Form Default solver RateLaw ordinary differential equations ScipyODESolver with LSODA RateLaw and NoiseLaw stochastic differential equations EulerMaruyamaSolver JumpLaw jump process GillespieSolver UpdateLaw discrete map IterationSolver

A run also records observables, named values computed from the states at every frame, and checks the invariants it is given.

docs.title: Where the parts live
docs.text: Family Import from Reference Elements skcomplex.core.components.elements Elements Interactions skcomplex.core.components.interactions Laws skcomplex.core.components.laws Spaces, neighbourhoods, and times skcomplex.core.components.spaces Systems skcomplex.core.components.systems Specs skcomplex.core.specs Simulation skcomplex.core.engine.runtime Shared recipes skcomplex.systems.general General realizations

docs.title: Choosing parts
docs.text:
This guide leads from the features of a problem to the parts of the core that model it. Four questions, asked in order, fix the time, the element, the space, and the interactions, and a CompositeSystem then holds the parts. How the parts fit explains each family, and every leaf below links the reference section of its part.

flowchart TD
    A[A problem] --> B{Does the state flow or step?}
    B --> C{Is it one amount, a vector, or many members?}
    C --> D{Where do the members sit?}
    D --> E{How do they act?}
    E --> F[CompositeSystem]

A problem with one amount skips the third question, since one amount needs no space.

docs.title: Does the state flow or step?
docs.text:
This question fixes the time of the system, which decides the kinds of laws it may hold. A state that changes at every instant, such as a temperature or the size of a large population, flows. A state that changes once per round, such as a yearly census or the move of a player, steps. A problem that asks for a balance or an optimum, and not for a path, has no time at all.

flowchart TD
    A{Does the state flow or step?} -->|it changes at every instant| B[ContinuousTime]
    A -->|it changes once per round| C[DiscreteTime]
    A -->|the answer is a balance or an optimum| D[StaticTime]
Leaf Part Typical laws it changes at every instant ContinuousTime rates, noises, and random events it changes once per round DiscreteTime updates, local rules, and agent rules the answer is a balance or an optimum StaticTime equations and objectives solved once

CompositeSystem takes the time as time=.... Without one, a system of rate laws runs in continuous time.

docs.title: Is it one amount, a vector, or many members?
docs.text:
This question fixes the element, the part that holds the states. One amount, or a few named numbers, sits in one element. A vector, such as the position of a body, is one state with several components. Many alike units, such as the people of an epidemic on a network or the cells of a grid, are the members of a group, and a quantity that has a value at every point of a space is a field.

flowchart TD
    A{Is it one amount, a vector, or many members?} -->|one amount or a few named numbers| B{Is the model a class of its own?}
    B -->|no, the numbers are data| C[DeclaredElement]
    B -->|yes| D[Element]
    A -->|a vector, such as a position| E[Element with a vector StateSpec]
    A -->|many alike members| F[GroupElement]
    A -->|a value at every site of a space| G[FieldElement]
    A -->|a word or a pattern of tiles| H[WordElement or PatchElement]
Leaf Part the numbers are data DeclaredElement the model is a class of its own Element a vector, such as a position Element with StateSpec(vector=True), or the recipe PointElement many alike members GroupElement a value at every site of a space FieldElement a word or a pattern of tiles WordElement or PatchElement

An amount that cannot be negative, such as a count or a sum of money, has the recipe NonnegativeElement.

docs.title: Where do the members sit?
docs.text:
This question fixes the space of a group or a field, which places its members and says who neighbours whom. Members on a grid of cells sit on a lattice. Members joined by contacts, roads, or trades sit on the nodes of a network. Members that move freely, such as particles or animals, sit in continuous space.

flowchart TD
    A{Where do the members sit?} -->|on a grid of cells| B[LatticeSpace]
    A -->|on the nodes of a network| C[NetworkSpace]
    A -->|anywhere, moving freely| D[ContinuousSpace]
    A -->|on an irregular domain| E[MeshSpace]
    A -->|over a position and a trait| F[PhaseSpace]
    B --> G[BallNeighborhood]
    C --> H[AdjacencyNeighborhood]
    D --> I[RadiusNeighborhood]
Leaf Space Who neighbours whom on a grid of cells LatticeSpace BallNeighborhood, the cells within a radius on the nodes of a network NetworkSpace AdjacencyNeighborhood, the nodes joined by an edge anywhere, moving freely ContinuousSpace RadiusNeighborhood, the members within a distance on an irregular domain MeshSpace the cells of the mesh over a position and a trait PhaseSpace the classes at the same position

A GroupElement takes the space as space=... and on='sites', and a group on the links of a network takes on='edges'.

docs.title: How do they act?
docs.text:
This question fixes the interactions, the parts that read states and return the laws that change them. Members that change at rates act through rate laws in continuous time. Members that set their next values once per step act through maps. Agents that look around, decide, and act one after another follow agent rules.

flowchart TD
    A{How do they act?} -->|by rates| B{What changes the state?}
    B -->|its own rate| C[RateInteraction]
    B -->|amounts that move between holders| D[TransferInteraction]
    B -->|its neighbours| E[CouplingInteraction]
    B -->|random events| F[JumpInteraction]
    B -->|forces of close members| G[PairInteraction]
    A -->|by maps| H{What sets the next value?}
    H -->|a function of the state| I[MapInteraction]
    H -->|the pattern of the cells around| J[LocalRuleInteraction]
    H -->|an aggregate of the neighbours| K[CouplingInteraction with form map]
    A -->|by agent rules| L{Who acts with whom?}
    L -->|each agent alone| M[Interaction that returns RuleLaw]
    L -->|members in random groups| N[GroupingInteraction]
Leaf Part its own rate RateInteraction amounts that move between holders TransferInteraction its neighbours CouplingInteraction random events JumpInteraction, or TransitionInteraction for a few discrete states forces of close members PairInteraction a function of the state MapInteraction the pattern of the cells around LocalRuleInteraction an aggregate of the neighbours CouplingInteraction with form='map' each agent alone an Interaction that returns a RuleLaw members in random groups GroupingInteraction

The shared recipes of General realizations cover the agent rules that several fields use, such as MovementInteraction and ChoiceInteraction, and reactions at a product propensity with ReactionInteraction.

docs.title: A worked path
docs.text:
This section follows the four questions for one problem and builds the parts they lead to. A population of people lives on a friendship network, and each day every person moves their opinion halfway towards the mean opinion of their friends.

  1. The opinions change once a day, so the state steps, and the time is DiscreteTime.
  2. There are many alike people, so the element is a GroupElement.
  3. The people sit on the nodes of a network, so the space is a NetworkSpace.
  4. Each person reads the mean of their neighbours and sets the next value, so the interaction is a CouplingInteraction with form='map'.

The network is a path of three people with the opinions 0, 3, and 9. The member class is a DeclaredElement with one state x, and combine sets the next opinion to the mean of the own opinion and that of the friends.

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import DeclaredElement, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import CouplingInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import DiscreteTime, NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import DeclaredVariableSpec, StateSpec

opinions = {'variables': {'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(0.0, StateSpec())}, 'x': [0.0, 3.0, 9.0]}
friends = NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(3))
people = GroupElement('people', element=DeclaredElement, space=friends, on='sites', values=opinions)
averaging = CouplingInteraction(
    'averaging',
    target='people',
    function=lambda s: s.other.x,
    reduce='mean',
    form='map',
    combine=lambda s, mean: (s.member.x + mean) / 2,
)
society = CompositeSystem(elements=[people], interactions=[averaging], time=DiscreteTime())
trajectory = simulate(society, until=20)
trajectory.get_values('people.x')[[0, 1, 20]].round(3).tolist()

[[0.0, 3.0, 9.0], [1.5, 3.75, 6.0], [3.75, 3.75, 3.75]]

After one day the opinions read 1.5, 3.75, and 6.0, and after twenty days all three agree on 3.75. The middle person has two friends, so the consensus weighs each opinion by the number of friends, (0 + 2 * 3 + 9) / 4. The tags confirm the choices of the four questions.

tags = society.get_tags()
sorted(tags.time), sorted(tags.space), sorted(tags.laws)

(['discrete'], ['network'], ['update'])

The time is ['discrete'], the space ['network'], and the laws ['update'], the next values that the map sets once per step.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text: An element holds the states of a system, the numbers that change as the system runs. An interaction reads these states and returns laws that change them, a space places the members of a group, and a system composes elements, interactions, and a space into one model. How the parts fit shows the families together, and the elements parts page compares every element class and holds its fact sheet.

docs.title: DeclaredElement
docs.text:
A DeclaredElement takes its states and parameters as data, so it needs no class of its own. Each variable is a DeclaredVariableSpec with an initial value and a spec. Here one compartment holds 100 infected people, and a RateInteraction makes them recover at a rate of 0.1 a day.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import DeclaredElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import DeclaredVariableSpec, StateSpec

infected = DeclaredElement('infected', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(100.0, StateSpec())})
recovery = RateInteraction('recovery', target='infected', state='x', rate=lambda s: -0.1 * s.target.x)
epidemic = CompositeSystem(elements=[infected], interactions=[recovery])
simulate(epidemic, until=10, dt=5.0).get_values('infected.x').round(1).tolist()

[100.0, 60.7, 36.8]

The infected fall from 100 to 60.7 after five days and to 36.8 after ten, the exponential decay 100 exp(-0.1 t).

The same class holds the balance of a bank account. Interest at 5 percent a year grows it continuously.

account = DeclaredElement('account', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(250.0, StateSpec())})
interest = RateInteraction('interest', target='account', state='x', rate=lambda s: 0.05 * s.target.x)
savings = CompositeSystem(elements=[account], interactions=[interest])
simulate(savings, until=1, dt=1.0).get_values('account.x').round(2).tolist()

[250.0, 262.82]

The balance reaches 262.82 after one year, which is 250 exp(0.05).

How the engine runs it. The element returns no laws of its own. The compiler reads each declared variable as it reads a state that a subclass annotates, so the rate laws of the interactions above form an ordinary differential equation that ScipyODESolver integrates. A state of order 2 also gets a companion state for its first derivative, named x_d1, which get_value reads and set_params changes.

mass = DeclaredElement('mass', variables={'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(1.0, StateSpec(order=2))})
mass.get_value('x'), mass.set_params(x_d1=0.5).get_value('x_d1')

(1.0, 0.5)

How it combines. It fills any role whose domains include those of its states. Its usual partners are RateInteraction for flows, TransferInteraction for amounts that move between compartments, and JumpInteraction for random events. Systems that learn their variables while they build, such as a network read from a table of reactions, build one DeclaredElement per entry.

Limits and errors. The element holds one value per variable, not a member per site, so a lattice or a network needs a GroupElement. Every name must be an identifier that no argument of the constructor takes, and prepare raises a ValidationError otherwise.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    DeclaredElement('cell', variables={'2x': DeclaredVariableSpec(1.0, StateSpec())}).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Element 'cell' declares '2x'. Use an identifier that no argument takes.

The message reads "Element 'cell' declares '2x'. Use an identifier that no argument takes." The fix is a name such as x2.

A field realization. A field names the element in its own words and derives the variables from its arguments. The subclass overrides the hook _declare_variables, which DeclaredElement reads in place of variables.

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import oo
from sage.sets.real_set import RealSet


class CompartmentElement(DeclaredElement):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, people=0.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.people = people

    def _declare_variables(self):
        return {'x': DeclaredVariableSpec(self.people, StateSpec(domain=RealSet.closed_open(0, oo)))}


CompartmentElement('susceptible', people=990.0).get_value('x')

990.0

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: Element
docs.text:
An Element is the base of an element class of your own. The class declares each state and parameter as an argument of its __init__, annotated with StateSpec or ParameterSpec, and may return laws of its own from _get_laws. Here a population grows at a rate proportional to its size.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class GrowthElement(Element):
    law_classes = (RateLaw,)

    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        x: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0,
        r: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.5,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.x = x
        self.r = r

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        return [RateLaw(namespace.x, namespace.r * namespace.x)]


rabbits = GrowthElement('rabbits', x=40.0, r=0.5)
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[rabbits]), until=1, dt=1.0).get_values('rabbits.x').round(1).tolist()

[40.0, 65.9]

The same class is a bank deposit that earns interest at 5 percent.

deposit = GrowthElement('deposit', x=250.0, r=0.05)
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[deposit]), until=1, dt=1.0).get_values('deposit.x').round(2).tolist()

[250.0, 262.82]

How the engine runs it. prepare reads the annotations to find the states, parameters, and their specs. At compile time the element returns its laws for a namespace whose attributes are the symbols of its variables, and the class attribute law_classes names their kinds, so get_tags knows them before a run.

sorted(rabbits.get_tags().laws), sorted(rabbits.get_tags().domains)

(['rate'], ['real'])

How it combines. An element with laws of its own runs alone, and interactions add laws to its states. As the member class of a GroupElement or a FieldElement it runs on every site of a space. An element whose laws are agent rules is an agent, and one that declares ports joins others through a ConnectionInteraction.

Limits and errors. A spec must be valid for its state. An order of 0, for example, is neither a whole number of at least 1 nor a fraction in (0, 1), and prepare raises a ValidationError.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError


class BrokenElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, x: Annotated[float, StateSpec(order=0)] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.x = x


try:
    BrokenElement('broken').prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The order 0 is neither an integer of at least 1 nor a real number in (0, 1).

The message says that the order 0 is neither a whole number of at least 1 nor a real number in (0, 1). The fix is StateSpec(order=1), the default, for a state with a first derivative.

A field realization. The catalog writes its elements as subclasses that rename the states for one field, such as a capacitor whose state is a voltage.

class CapacitorElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        v: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        C: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1e-3,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.v = v
        self.C = C


CapacitorElement('c1', v=5.0).get_params()

{'C': 0.001, 'label': 'c1', 'v': 5.0, 'visual': None}

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: GroupElement
docs.text:
A GroupElement holds many members of one element class, with one row per member in every state. Here three herds of grazing animals start at different sizes.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class StockElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        x: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        r: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.1,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.x = x
        self.r = r


herds = GroupElement('herds', element=StockElement, size=3, values={'x': [40.0, 25.0, 60.0]})
herds.prepare().size_

3

The same class holds the assets of a portfolio, each with its own yearly return.

holdings = {'x': [100.0, 50.0], 'r': [0.05, 0.02]}
assets = GroupElement('assets', element=StockElement, size=2, values=holdings)
returns = RateInteraction('returns', target='assets', state='x', rate=lambda s: s.target.r * s.target.x)
portfolio = CompositeSystem(elements=[assets], interactions=[returns])
simulate(portfolio, until=1, dt=1.0).get_values('assets.x').round(2).tolist()

[[100.0, 50.0], [105.13, 51.01]]

How the engine runs it. The laws of the member class and of the interactions are written for one member. The compiler runs them for every member at once as arrays, so a group of a thousand members costs one vectorised call per evaluation.

How it combines. With on='sites' the members sit on the sites of a lattice or the nodes of a network, and with on='edges' or on='hyperedges' on the links of a network. Neighbour interactions, such as CouplingInteraction, then read the members around each member. With variable=True, laws add and remove members during a run.

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import NetworkSpace

lines = GroupElement('lines', element=StockElement, space=NetworkSpace(nx.cycle_graph(5)), on='edges')
lines.prepare().size_

5

Limits and errors. Every member shares the class of the group. Each value holds one row per member or one value for all, and prepare raises a ValidationError for any other count.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    GroupElement('herds', element=StockElement, size=3, values={'x': [40.0, 25.0]}).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Group 'herds' has 2 values of x for 3 members. Give one value per member, or one value shared by every member.

The message says that the group has 2 values of x for 3 members. The fix is three values, or one value shared by every member.

A field realization. A field fixes the member class and the space of its group in a subclass, such as the sites of a forest.

class ForestElement(GroupElement):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, size=100):
        super().__init__(label, element=StockElement, size=size, visual=visual)


ForestElement('forest', size=4).prepare().size_

4

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: FieldElement
docs.text:
A FieldElement holds one member on every site of a space and gives its states the operators of space, such as the Laplacian, and boundary conditions. Here heat spreads through a plate of 10 by 20 sites with insulated edges.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.laws.utils import laplacian
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class DiffusionElement(Element):
    law_classes = (RateLaw,)

    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=None,
        *,
        u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        D: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.u = u
        self.D = D

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        return [RateLaw(namespace.u, namespace.D * laplacian(namespace.u))]


walls = {'u': 'zero-flux'}
plate = FieldElement('plate', element=DiffusionElement, space=LatticeSpace((10, 20)), boundary=walls)
plate.prepare().size_

200

The same law spreads a pollutant along a channel of three reaches until each reach holds the same amount.

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate

channel = NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(3))
river = FieldElement('river', element=DiffusionElement, space=channel, values={'u': [9.0, 0.0, 0.0]})
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[river]), until=10, dt=10.0).get_values('river.u').round(2).tolist()

[[9.0, 0.0, 0.0], [3.0, 3.0, 3.0]]

How the engine runs it. The compiler turns each operator of space into a stencil of the space: the Laplacian of a lattice reads the neighbours of each site, and that of a network reads the edges. The boundary conditions replace the values beyond the edges of a lattice. The result is one large system of ordinary differential equations, which a solver for stiff fields can integrate.

How it combines. It is a GroupElement with one member per site, so every interaction of groups applies. ConservationInteraction and GradientInteraction read its operators directly.

Limits and errors. A field needs a space with sites, and it cannot add or remove members. Its values follow the rules of a group, one per site or one for all.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    FieldElement('river', element=DiffusionElement, space=channel, values={'u': [9.0, 0.0]}).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Group 'river' has 2 values of u for 3 members. Give one value per member, or one value shared by every member.

The message says that the group has 2 values of u for 3 members. The fix is three values, one per reach.

A field realization. A field names the field and fixes its member class, such as the temperature of a rod.

class RodElement(FieldElement):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, sites=50):
        super().__init__(label, element=DiffusionElement, space=LatticeSpace((sites,)), visual=visual)


RodElement('rod', sites=8).prepare().size_

8

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: WordElement
docs.text:
A WordElement holds a word of symbols that productions rewrite at every generation. In the algae of Lindenmayer A becomes AB and B becomes A, so the length of the word runs through the Fibonacci numbers.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import WordElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import ProductionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate


class AlgaeElement(WordElement):
    law_classes = (ProductionLaw,)

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        return [ProductionLaw('A', 'AB'), ProductionLaw('B', 'A')]


trajectory = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[AlgaeElement('algae', axiom='A')]), until=5)
trajectory.get_values('algae.size').tolist()

[1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0, 13.0]

The Thue and Morse sequence of symbolic dynamics comes from the same class, with 0 becoming 01 and 1 becoming 10.

class MorseElement(WordElement):
    law_classes = (ProductionLaw,)

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        return [ProductionLaw('0', '01'), ProductionLaw('1', '10')]


simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[MorseElement('morse', axiom='0')]), until=3).get_values('morse.size').tolist()

[1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]

How the engine runs it. Each generation applies every production to every matching symbol at once. The rewriting solver advances one generation per unit of time and records the size of the word as the state size.

How it combines. Its productions are its own laws, so it usually runs alone. A geometry draws the word as line segments, as a turtle does, for plants and fractal curves.

Limits and errors. The word grows at every generation, so max_size bounds it. A symbol outside alphabet, or a word that would grow past max_size, raises a RewritingError during the run.

from skcomplex.core.errors import RewritingError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[AlgaeElement('algae', axiom='A', max_size=4)]), until=5)
except RewritingError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Word 'algae' would reach 5 symbols at generation 3, above its maximum size 4. Raise max_size or run fewer generations.

The message says that the word would reach 5 symbols at generation 3, above its maximum size 4. The fix is a larger max_size or fewer generations.

A field realization. The subclasses above are already field realizations, the algae of biology and the sequence of symbolic dynamics.

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: PatchElement
docs.text:
A PatchElement holds tiles, placed copies of basic shapes, that substitutions replace by smaller pieces at every generation. Keeping the outer thirds of every interval builds the Cantor set.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import PatchElement
from skcomplex.core.components.laws import SubstitutionLaw
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.core.specs import AffineSpec, PrototileSpec


class CantorElement(PatchElement):
    law_classes = (SubstitutionLaw,)

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        thirds = [AffineSpec(scale=1 / 3), AffineSpec(scale=1 / 3, translation=(2 / 3, 0))]
        return [SubstitutionLaw('interval', [('interval', third) for third in thirds])]


cantor = CantorElement('cantor', prototiles=[PrototileSpec('interval', [(0, 0), (1, 0)])])
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[cantor]), until=3).get_values('cantor.size').tolist()

[1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]

Replacing every triangle by its three corner triangles builds the Sierpinski triangle of geometry.

class SierpinskiElement(PatchElement):
    law_classes = (SubstitutionLaw,)

    def _get_laws(self, namespace):
        corners = [(0, 0), (1 / 2, 0), (1 / 4, 1 / 2)]
        pieces = [('triangle', AffineSpec(scale=1 / 2, translation=corner)) for corner in corners]
        return [SubstitutionLaw('triangle', pieces)]


triangle = SierpinskiElement('sierpinski', prototiles=[PrototileSpec('triangle', [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1 / 2, 1)])])
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[triangle]), until=3).get_values('sierpinski.size').tolist()

[1.0, 3.0, 9.0, 27.0]

How the engine runs it. Each generation applies every substitution to every tile of its prototile at once, and the rewriting solver records the number of tiles as the state size.

How it combines. Its substitutions are its own laws, so it usually runs alone, and its tiles are drawn as polygons.

Limits and errors. Every tile must name a prototile of the patch, and prepare raises a RewritingError otherwise.

from skcomplex.core.errors import RewritingError

try:
    interval = PrototileSpec('interval', [(0, 0), (1, 0)])
    PatchElement('patch', tiles=[('square', None)], prototiles=[interval]).prepare()
except RewritingError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The patch patch has a tile of the unknown prototile 'square'.

The message names the unknown prototile square. The fix is a tile of the prototile interval.

A field realization. The two subclasses above are realizations of mathematics, and a tiling of physics, such as the Penrose tiling of a quasicrystal, is written the same way.

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: BaseElement
docs.text:
BaseElement is the abstract base of every element. A new kind of element that stores its members in a way of its own, as GroupElement does, derives from it. Every other element derives from Element.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import BaseElement, Element, GroupElement

issubclass(Element, BaseElement), issubclass(GroupElement, BaseElement)

(True, True)

See its fact sheet and its API entry.

docs.title: General realizations
docs.text:
skcomplex.systems.general holds the recipes that systems of several fields share, such as a nonnegative amount, a reaction, an agent that moves, or a market that matches buyers with sellers. A recipe is a part written with the public parts of the core alone, so each one is also an example of how to build a part of your own. The core never imports these recipes, and every field imports them freely. How the parts fit shows the parts of the core that the recipes are written with, and the section Where a part goes at the end of this page gives the rule that decides whether a new part is a recipe.

The package has one subpackage per concept, and every recipe is imported from its subpackage.

Subpackage Concept Recipes elements amounts and bodies NonnegativeElement, PointElement flows chaotic flows LorenzElement reactions reactions at a product propensity ReactionInteraction, ReactionNetworkSystem kinetics encounters of distributions EncounterInteraction dynamics systems given as equations DynamicalSystem, NetworkDynamicalSystem, ReactionDiffusionSystem, StockFlowSystem agents agent rules MovementInteraction, ChoiceInteraction, ImitationInteraction, EvolutionInteraction, BirthDeathInteraction matching markets that pair two groups MatchingInteraction, its rule specs, and MatchSpec

docs.title: NonnegativeElement
docs.text:
A NonnegativeElement holds one number x that stays at zero or above, such as a count of people or the moles of a chemical species. It is an Element whose one state carries the domain [0, +oo), and it returns no laws of its own. Here 100 infected people recover at a rate of 0.1 a day through a RateInteraction.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import NonnegativeElement

infected = NonnegativeElement('infected', x=100.0)
recovery = RateInteraction('recovery', target='infected', state='x', rate=lambda s: -0.1 * s.target.x)
epidemic = CompositeSystem(elements=[infected], interactions=[recovery])
simulate(epidemic, until=10, dt=5.0).get_values('infected.x').round(1).tolist()

[100.0, 60.7, 36.8]

The infected fall from 100 to 60.7 after five days and to 36.8 after ten.

The same element holds the moles of a chemical species in a reactor. A species that decays at the rate 0.5 loses about two thirds of its amount in two seconds.

species = NonnegativeElement('A', x=2.0)
decay = RateInteraction('decay', target='A', state='x', rate=lambda s: -0.5 * s.target.x)
simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[species], interactions=[decay]), until=2, dt=1.0).get_values('A.x').round(3).tolist()

[2.0, 1.213, 0.736]

The amount falls from 2.0 to 1.213 and then to 0.736, which is 2 exp(-1).

How the engine runs it. The element adds no laws. The compiler reads its state as it reads any annotated state, and the laws of the interactions that target it form the equations a solver integrates.

How it combines. It is the species of ReactionInteraction and ReactionNetworkSystem, and a GroupElement of it on the sites of a lattice is the distribution that EncounterInteraction reads.

Limits and errors. It holds one number. A system that tracks several numbers per member declares its own Element. The check of the domain runs when the system compiles, so a negative initial value raises a ValidationError from simulate.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[NonnegativeElement('A', x=-1.0)]), until=1, dt=1.0)
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The system is not valid, with 1 error(s):
- A: A.x = -1.0 is not in its domain [0, +oo). Correct the component as the message describes. [value]

The message names the value A.x = -1.0 and the domain [0, +oo) that does not hold it. The fix is an initial value of zero or above.

A field realization. Biology names it a compartment of an epidemic and declares the same state again, so the docstring of the subclass can say that x counts people.

from typing import Annotated

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import oo
from sage.sets.real_set import RealSet

from skcomplex.core.specs import StateSpec


class CompartmentElement(NonnegativeElement):
    def __init__(self, label, visual=None, *, x: Annotated[float, StateSpec(domain=RealSet.closed_open(0, oo))] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual, x=x)


CompartmentElement('susceptible', x=990.0).get_params()

{'label': 'susceptible', 'visual': None, 'x': 990.0}

See its API entry.

docs.title: PointElement
docs.text:
A PointElement is a body that moves in a continuous space by its acceleration. Its state x is a vector of order 2, the position, and the companion state x_d1 holds the velocity. Here a ball leaves the origin at the velocity (1, 2) and falls under a gravity of 1, which a RateInteraction gives as the second derivative of x.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import PointElement

ball = PointElement('ball', x=[0.0, 0.0], x_d1=[1.0, 2.0])
gravity = RateInteraction('gravity', target='ball', state='x', rate=lambda s: [0.0, -1.0])
flight = CompositeSystem(elements=[ball], interactions=[gravity], space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2))
simulate(flight, until=2.0, dt=1.0).get_values('ball.x').round(3).tolist()

[[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.5], [2.0, 2.0]]

The ball reaches (1, 1.5) after one second and (2, 2) after two, the parabola (t, 2t - t^2 / 2).

A star that drifts through a cluster at a constant velocity is the same element with no force on it.

star = PointElement('star', x_d1=[1.0, 0.0])
drift = CompositeSystem(elements=[star], space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2))
simulate(drift, until=2.0, dt=1.0).get_values('star.x')[-1].tolist()

[2.0, 0.0]

The star stands at (2, 0) after two units of time.

How the engine runs it. The laws on x give its second derivative, and the compiler adds the first-order equations of the pair x and x_d1. A backend for molecular dynamics, such as LAMMPS, reads the velocity of a point from the declared state x_d1, and the boundary of the space acts on x.

How it combines. It lives in a ContinuousSpace. A PairInteraction adds forces between points, such as those of a gas or of a flock.

Limits and errors. Its state is a vector, so the system needs a space with a dimension, and simulate raises a SpaceError without one.

from skcomplex.core.errors import SpaceError

try:
    simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[PointElement('p', x_d1=[1.0, 0.0])]), until=2.0, dt=1.0)
except SpaceError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The system is not valid, with 1 error(s):
- p: p.x is a vector or a tensor, so the system that holds it or one of its parents must have a space. Give the system a space whose kind the component supports. [space-missing]

The message says that p.x is a vector, so the system that holds it must have a space. The fix is space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2).

A field realization. Physics names the point an atom and fixes its start at rest.

class AtomElement(PointElement):
    def __init__(self, label, x=0.0, visual=None):
        super().__init__(label, x=x, x_d1=0.0, visual=visual)


AtomElement('argon', x=[1.0, 2.0]).get_params()

{'label': 'argon', 'visual': None, 'x': [1.0, 2.0]}

See its API entry.

docs.title: LorenzElement
docs.text:
A LorenzElement follows the Lorenz flow x' = sigma (y - x), y' = x (rho - z) - y, z' = x y - beta z, which Lorenz derived from convection in the atmosphere. It is an Element that returns three RateLaw laws. For sigma = 10, rho = 28, and beta = 8/3 its runs never settle and never repeat.

from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.flows import LorenzElement

trajectory = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[LorenzElement('lorenz')]), until=1.0, dt=0.5)
trajectory.get_values('lorenz.x').round(3).tolist()

[1.0, 1.198, -9.379]

The state x moves from 1.0 to 1.198 and swings to -9.379 after one unit of time.

Below the critical value of rho the same flow describes a water wheel that settles into a steady rotation. With rho = 10 the state z settles at rho - 1.

wheel = simulate(CompositeSystem(elements=[LorenzElement('wheel', rho=10.0)]), until=20.0, dt=10.0)
wheel.get_values('wheel.z').round(3).tolist()

[1.0, 9.023, 9.0]

The state z passes 9.023 at time 10 and rests at 9.0 at time 20.

How the engine runs it. The three rates form an ordinary differential equation that ScipyODESolver integrates.

How it combines. It runs alone as a model, or it drives a response system through an interaction that reads its states, as in studies of chaotic synchronization.

Limits and errors. Its parameters are sigma, rho, and beta, and set_params raises a ValueError for any other name.

try:
    LorenzElement('lorenz').set_params(r=1.0)
except ValueError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Invalid parameter 'r' for estimator LorenzElement(label='lorenz'). Valid parameters are: ['beta', 'label', 'rho', 'sigma', 'visual', 'x', 'y', 'z'].

The message lists the valid parameters beta, label, rho, sigma, visual, x, y, and z. The fix is rho=....

A field realization. LorenzSystem of mathematics wraps the element in a system class that takes the parameters of the model, and the chaotic synchronization of physics drives a response system with it.

from skcomplex.systems.mathematics.dynamical_systems import LorenzSystem

LorenzSystem(rho=20.0).prepare().system_.elements[0].rho

20.0

The system builds one LorenzElement with rho = 20.0.

See its API entry.

docs.title: ReactionInteraction
docs.text:
A ReactionInteraction moves units from its reactants to its products, at a propensity that is the rate constant k times the product of the reactant amounts, each raised to its coefficient. It is a JumpInteraction whose changes are the stoichiometric vector, the number of units each reaction takes from or gives to every species. A species is a pair of the path of an element and a state name. Here an epidemic runs as two reactions, infection S + I -> 2 I and recovery I -> R.

from skcomplex.core.components.interactions import JumpInteraction
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import NonnegativeElement
from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionInteraction

infection = ReactionInteraction('infection', reactants={('S', 'x'): 1, ('I', 'x'): 1}, products={('I', 'x'): 2}, k=5e-4)
recovery = ReactionInteraction('recovery', reactants={('I', 'x'): 1}, products={('R', 'x'): 1}, k=0.1)
people = [NonnegativeElement('S', x=990), NonnegativeElement('I', x=10), NonnegativeElement('R')]
sir = CompositeSystem(elements=people, interactions=[infection, recovery])
trajectory = simulate(sir, until=50, dt=10.0)
infected = trajectory.get_values('I.x').round(1).tolist()
infected, float(trajectory.states[-1].sum()), issubclass(ReactionInteraction, JumpInteraction)

([10.0, 294.4, 400.3, 175.0, 68.6, 26.4], 1000.0000000000003, True)

The infected rise from 10 to 400.3 at day 20 and fall to 26.4 at day 50, while the population stays at 1000. The last value confirms that the class is a JumpInteraction.

In chemistry the same class is the law of mass action. Two species bind into a complex, A + B -> C.

binding = ReactionInteraction('binding', reactants={('A', 'x'): 1, ('B', 'x'): 1}, products={('C', 'x'): 1}, k=0.01)
species = [NonnegativeElement('A', x=100.0), NonnegativeElement('B', x=50.0), NonnegativeElement('C')]
reactor = CompositeSystem(elements=species, interactions=[binding])
simulate(reactor, until=10, dt=5.0).get_values('C.x').round(2).tolist()

[0.0, 47.86, 49.83]

The complex reaches 47.86 after five seconds and 49.83 after ten, close to the 50 units of B, the reactant that runs out.

How the engine runs it. The argument mode chooses the laws. With 'rate' the reaction is a RateLaw per species, the rate equation. With 'jump' it is a JumpLaw that fires at the propensity and moves the units of the coefficients, which the algorithm of Gillespie runs. With 'langevin' it adds to the rate a NoiseLaw whose amplitude is the square root of the propensity. The tags follow the mode.

jumps = binding.set_params(mode='jump')
sorted(jumps.get_tags().laws), jumps.get_tags().randomness

(['jump'], 'stochastic')

The laws are ['jump'] and the randomness is 'stochastic'.

How it combines. Its species are usually NonnegativeElement parts. With target, a species may be the name of a state of the target alone, and a target that is a group or a field reacts in every member. modifiers enter the propensity without changing, as a catalyst does, and propensity replaces the product form, such as a saturating rate of enzyme kinetics.

Limits and errors. The propensity is a product of amounts unless propensity says otherwise, and a reaction needs at least one reactant or product. prepare raises a ValidationError for an empty reaction.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    ReactionInteraction('nothing', k=1.0).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Reaction 'nothing' has neither reactants nor products. Give at least one of them.

The message reads "Reaction 'nothing' has neither reactants nor products. Give at least one of them." The fix is a reactant, such as reactants={('A', 'x'): 1} for a decay.

A field realization. Epidemiology binds the species under roles of its own names. The subclass declares the roles with RoleSpec and returns the stoichiometry from the hooks _get_reactants and _get_products.

from typing import Annotated

from skcomplex.core.specs import RoleSpec


class InfectionInteraction(ReactionInteraction):
    def __init__(
        self, label, *, susceptible: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], infected: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], k=5e-4
    ):
        super().__init__(label, k=k)
        self.susceptible = susceptible
        self.infected = infected

    def _get_reactants(self):
        return {(self.susceptible, 'x'): 1, (self.infected, 'x'): 1}

    def _get_products(self):
        return {(self.infected, 'x'): 2}


spread = InfectionInteraction('infection', susceptible='S', infected='I')
compartments = [NonnegativeElement('S', x=990), NonnegativeElement('I', x=10)]
outbreak = CompositeSystem(elements=compartments, interactions=[spread])
simulate(outbreak, until=10, dt=10.0).get_values('I.x').round(1).tolist()

[10.0, 599.9]

Without recovery the infected reach 599.9 after ten days.

See its API entry.

docs.title: ReactionNetworkSystem
docs.text:
A ReactionNetworkSystem writes a whole network of reactions as a table, with no element or interaction to write. It takes the initial amount of every species and maps the label of every reaction to its reactants, its products, and its rate constant. Here A and B convert into each other.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem

isomerization = ReactionNetworkSystem(
    species={'A': 10.0, 'B': 0.0},
    reactions={'forth': ({'A': 1}, {'B': 1}, 0.3), 'back': ({'B': 1}, {'A': 1}, 0.1)},
)
round(float(simulate(isomerization, until=50.0, dt=1.0).get_values('A.x')[-1]), 3)

2.5

The amount of A relaxes to 2.5, which is 0.1 / (0.3 + 0.1) of the total.

An epidemic of susceptible, infected, and recovered people is the same table with other names.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.reactions import ReactionNetworkSystem

sir = ReactionNetworkSystem(
    species={'S': 990.0, 'I': 10.0, 'R': 0.0},
    reactions={'infection': ({'S': 1, 'I': 1}, {'I': 2}, 5e-4), 'recovery': ({'I': 1}, {'R': 1}, 0.1)},
)
simulate(sir, until=50, dt=10.0).get_values('I.x').round(1).tolist()

[10.0, 294.4, 400.3, 175.0, 68.6, 26.4]

The infected follow the curve of the epidemic of the previous section, 10, 294.4, 400.3, 175.0, 68.6, and 26.4 every ten days.

How the engine runs it. prepare builds a CompositeSystem with one NonnegativeElement per species, named after it with its amount in x, and one ReactionInteraction per reaction. The mode writes the reactions as rate equations, 'rate', as random events of single units, 'jump', or as chemical Langevin equations, 'langevin'.

sir.set_params(mode='jump').get_tags().randomness

stochastic

The jump mode makes the system 'stochastic'.

How it combines. It is a BaseSystem, so simulate, calibrate, and the analyses take it as they take any system. A field system subclasses it and gives its parts through hooks:

  • _get_species returns the initial amount of every species by name.
  • _get_reactions returns the reaction table.
  • _get_mode returns the mode.
  • _get_interactions returns the reactions as interactions, for a realization whose reactions bind roles of their own names, such as the susceptible and infected roles of an infection.

Limits and errors. Every propensity is a product of amounts. A reaction with another propensity goes through _get_interactions. An unknown mode raises a ValidationError from prepare.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    sir.set_params(mode='fast').prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

Reaction 'infection' has the mode 'fast'. Use one of rate, jump, langevin.

The message reads "Reaction 'infection' has the mode 'fast'. Use one of rate, jump, langevin."

A field realization. A field system takes the parameters of its model under its own names. SIRSystem of biology takes beta and gamma this way. Epidemics and enzyme kinetics are both reaction networks with a product propensity, which epidemiology calls homogeneous mixing and chemistry the law of mass action, so they share the general system and differ in their realizations.

class OutbreakSystem(ReactionNetworkSystem):
    def __init__(self, *, beta=5e-4, gamma=0.1, label='system'):
        super().__init__(label=label)
        self.beta = beta
        self.gamma = gamma

    def _get_species(self):
        return {'S': 990.0, 'I': 10.0, 'R': 0.0}

    def _get_reactions(self):
        return {'infection': ({'S': 1, 'I': 1}, {'I': 2}, self.beta), 'recovery': ({'I': 1}, {'R': 1}, self.gamma)}


simulate(OutbreakSystem(gamma=0.2), until=50, dt=25.0).get_values('I.x').round(1).tolist()

[10.0, 132.1, 4.1]

With a faster recovery of 0.2 a day the infected number 132.1 at day 25 and 4.1 at day 50, so the outbreak stays smaller.

See its API entry.

docs.title: EncounterInteraction
docs.text:
An EncounterInteraction models the meetings of members of two distributions in a kinetic system. A distribution is a GroupElement of NonnegativeElement with one member per class of a trait, such as the levels of an opinion. A candidate at class h meets the field at class k at the rate rate[h, k], and a conservative encounter moves it to class i with the probability kernel[h, k, i]. Here candidates at three opinion levels meet a field that pulls every one of them to the first level.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.elements import NonnegativeElement
from skcomplex.systems.general.kinetics import EncounterInteraction

kernel = np.zeros((3, 1, 3))
kernel[:, :, 0] = 1.0
gather = EncounterInteraction(
    'gather', candidate='candidates', field='field', rate=lambda s: 1.0, kernel=lambda s: kernel
)
system = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[
        GroupElement('candidates', element=NonnegativeElement, size=3, on='sites', values={'x': [0.2, 0.3, 0.5]}),
        GroupElement('field', element=NonnegativeElement, size=1, values={'x': 1.0}),
    ],
    interactions=[gather],
    space=LatticeSpace(3, boundary='fixed'),
)
np.round(simulate(system, until=4.0, dt=0.5).get_values('candidates.x')[-1], 2).tolist()

[0.99, 0.01, 0.01]

After four units of time 0.99 of the candidates hold the first level.

In immunology a destructive encounter removes the tumour cells that immune cells meet. A tumour density of 1 meets an immune density of 0.4 at the rate 0.5, so it decays at the rate 0.2.

killing = EncounterInteraction('killing', candidate='tumour', field='immune', rate=lambda s: 0.5, outcome='destructive')
cells = CompositeSystem(
    elements=[
        GroupElement('tumour', element=NonnegativeElement, size=1, on='sites', values={'x': 1.0}),
        GroupElement('immune', element=NonnegativeElement, size=1, values={'x': 0.4}),
    ],
    interactions=[killing],
    space=LatticeSpace(1, boundary='fixed'),
)
simulate(cells, until=10.0, dt=5.0).get_values('tumour.x').round(3).tolist()

[[1.0], [0.368], [0.135]]

The tumour falls to 0.368 at time 5 and to 0.135 at time 10, which is exp(-2).

How the engine runs it. The interaction lowers to a BilinearLaw, a rate that is a sum of products of the two densities, which the compiler evaluates as arrays over the classes. A proliferative outcome adds a candidate at class i, and with a cross_section the rate is the collision integral of kinetic theory, evaluated by a fast spectral method.

How it combines. The candidates sit on the sites of a LatticeSpace of classes, or on a PhaseSpace, where encounters pair classes at the same position. Without a field the encounter is a linear redistribution between classes.

Limits and errors. The bilinear law needs a lattice of classes. A conservative encounter moves candidates by a kernel, so prepare raises a ValidationError without one.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    EncounterInteraction('exchange', candidate='candidates', rate=lambda s: 1.0).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The conservative encounter 'exchange' moves candidates by a kernel. Give `kernel`.

The message reads "The conservative encounter 'exchange' moves candidates by a kernel. Give kernel."

See its API entry.

docs.title: DynamicalSystem
docs.text:
A DynamicalSystem is a set of states and the equations that evolve them, rates in continuous time or next values in discrete time. It takes its data by name and writes one DeclaredElement with one RateInteraction or MapInteraction per state. The populations of Wilson and Cowan in neuroscience are rates.

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import exp

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import DynamicalSystem

populations = DynamicalSystem(
    states={'e': 0.1, 'i': 0.05},
    equations={
        'e': lambda s: -s.target.e + 1 / (1 + exp(-(2 * s.target.e - 3 * s.target.i))),
        'i': lambda s: -s.target.i + 1 / (1 + exp(-(2 * s.target.e - s.target.i))),
    },
    element='populations',
)
round(float(simulate(populations, until=20.0, dt=1.0).get_values('populations.e')[-1]), 3)

0.272

The excitatory activity e is 0.272 at time 20.

The multiplier and accelerator model of economics is a map. In discrete time every equation reads the states at the start of the step, so previous takes the income of the last year.

economy = DynamicalSystem(
    states={'y': 1.0, 'previous': 1.0},
    equations={
        'y': lambda s: (
            s.target.g + s.target.c * (1 + s.target.v) * s.target.y - s.target.c * s.target.v * s.target.previous
        ),
        'previous': lambda s: s.target.y,
    },
    parameters={'g': 1.0, 'c': 0.5, 'v': 0.5},
    time='discrete',
    element='economy',
)
simulate(economy, until=3).get_values('economy.y').round(3).tolist()

[1.0, 1.5, 1.875, 2.031]

The income runs through 1.0, 1.5, 1.875, and 2.031, a damped oscillation around the level g / (1 - c), which is 2.

How the engine runs it. In continuous time the rates form an ordinary differential equation, or a stochastic one with noises, whose amplitudes are read in the Itô or Stratonovich convention. In discrete time the maps set the next values once per step. An equation is a function of a namespace whose target holds the states and parameters and whose t holds the time.

How it combines. It is a BaseSystem, so every workflow takes it. A subclass takes the parameters of its model under its own names and returns its data from the hooks _get_states, _get_equations, _get_parameters, _get_noises, _get_time, and _get_element_label. The hook _get_variables gives the specs of the states and the parameters, such as a domain or the order of a Caputo derivative.

Limits and errors. All states live in one element, so a model with many members uses NetworkDynamicalSystem or ReactionDiffusionSystem. A noise needs continuous time, and prepare raises a ValidationError otherwise.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

noisy = DynamicalSystem(
    states={'y': 1.0}, equations={'y': lambda s: s.target.y}, noises={'y': lambda s: 0.1}, time='discrete'
)
try:
    noisy.prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

DynamicalSystem has noise amplitudes in discrete time. Noise amplitudes need continuous time.

The message reads "DynamicalSystem has noise amplitudes in discrete time. Noise amplitudes need continuous time." The fix is time='continuous', or no noise.

A field realization. Ecology writes the logistic growth of a population with its own parameters.

class LogisticSystem(DynamicalSystem):
    def __init__(self, *, r=1.0, K=100.0, label='system'):
        super().__init__(label=label)
        self.r = r
        self.K = K

    def _get_states(self):
        return {'n': 10.0}

    def _get_equations(self):
        return {'n': lambda s: s.target.r * s.target.n * (1 - s.target.n / s.target.K)}

    def _get_parameters(self):
        return {'r': self.r, 'K': self.K}


round(float(simulate(LogisticSystem(), until=10.0, dt=10.0).get_values('state.n')[-1]), 2)

99.96

The population approaches its capacity of 100 and reaches 99.96 at time 10.

See its API entry.

docs.title: NetworkDynamicalSystem
docs.text:
A NetworkDynamicalSystem puts the states on every node of a graph and adds to the rate of every coupled state the sum over the neighbours sum_j A_ij g(x_i, x_j). Cells of a tissue exchange ions through gap junctions this way.

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import NetworkDynamicalSystem

cells = NetworkDynamicalSystem(
    nx.cycle_graph(4),
    states={'v': [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]},
    equations={'v': lambda s: -s.target.v / s.target.tau},
    coupling={'v': lambda s: s.member.g * (s.other.v - s.member.v)},
    parameters={'tau': 10.0, 'g': 0.5},
    element='cells',
)
simulate(cells, until=5.0, dt=1.0).get_values('cells.v')[-1].round(3).tolist()

[0.154, 0.152, 0.15, 0.152]

After five units of time the voltages are 0.154, 0.152, 0.15, and 0.152. The charge of the first cell has spread over the ring and decays.

Heat that flows between three rooms in a row is diffusion on a path graph, with no local equation.

rooms = NetworkDynamicalSystem(
    nx.path_graph(3),
    states={'u': [3.0, 0.0, 0.0]},
    equations={'u': lambda s: 0 * s.target.u},
    coupling={'u': lambda s: s.other.u - s.member.u},
    element='rooms',
)
simulate(rooms, until=10.0, dt=10.0).get_values('rooms.u')[-1].round(3).tolist()

[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]

The rooms reach the same temperature, 1.0 each, and the total stays 3.

How the engine runs it. The states are those of a DeclaredElement that is the member of a FieldElement on the NetworkSpace of the graph. The equations are RateInteraction parts, and the coupling is a CouplingInteraction that reads node i as s.member and its neighbour as s.other. The system runs in continuous time.

How it combines. A subclass returns the graph from _get_graph and the couplings from _get_coupling, besides the hooks of DynamicalSystem. A local equation may also read the graph Laplacian, as network diffusion does.

Limits and errors. Every node holds the same states. A system without a graph raises a ValidationError from prepare.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    NetworkDynamicalSystem(states={'v': 1.0}, equations={'v': lambda s: -s.target.v}).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

NetworkDynamicalSystem has no graph. Give a NetworkX graph whose nodes hold the states.

The message reads "NetworkDynamicalSystem has no graph. Give a NetworkX graph whose nodes hold the states."

See its API entry.

docs.title: ReactionDiffusionSystem
docs.text:
A ReactionDiffusionSystem puts the states as fields on the sites of a lattice, with local kinetics and the diffusion D laplacian(u) of every field that has a diffusivity D. The front of Fisher and Kolmogorov in ecology invades an empty line.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import ReactionDiffusionSystem

initial = np.zeros(50)
initial[:5] = 1.0
front = ReactionDiffusionSystem(
    states={'u': initial},
    equations={'u': lambda s: s.target.r * s.target.u * (1 - s.target.u)},
    diffusivities={'u': 1.0},
    shape=50,
    boundary='reflecting',
    parameters={'r': 1.0},
)
density = simulate(front, until=10.0, dt=5.0).get_values('medium.u')[-1]
int((density > 0.5).sum())

20

After ten units of time 20 sites hold more than half the capacity.

A pollutant that spreads along a channel and decays at the rate 0.1 is the same system with linear kinetics.

spill = np.zeros(20)
spill[10] = 1.0
channel = ReactionDiffusionSystem(
    states={'u': spill},
    equations={'u': lambda s: -s.target.k * s.target.u},
    diffusivities={'u': 0.5},
    shape=20,
    boundary='reflecting',
    parameters={'k': 0.1},
)
round(float(simulate(channel, until=5.0, dt=5.0).get_values('medium.u')[-1].sum()), 3)

0.607

The total falls to 0.607, which is exp(-0.5), since diffusion keeps the total and only the decay removes it.

How the engine runs it. The states are those of a DeclaredElement that is the member of a FieldElement on a LatticeSpace. The diffusion of every field is a separate RateInteraction, so a split solver can treat it apart from the kinetics, and the compiler turns the Laplacian into a stencil of the lattice.

How it combines. A subclass returns the diffusivities from _get_diffusivities, the lattice from _get_space, and the boundary of every field from _get_boundaries, besides the hooks of DynamicalSystem. A chemistry system whose kinetics are reactions returns them from _get_equation_interactions, as the Gray-Scott system of pattern formation does.

Limits and errors. Every diffusivity must name a declared state, and prepare raises a ValidationError otherwise.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

broken = ReactionDiffusionSystem(
    states={'u': 0.0}, equations={'u': lambda s: 0 * s.target.u}, diffusivities={'w': 1.0}, shape=5
)
try:
    broken.prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

ReactionDiffusionSystem has a diffusivity for the state 'w', which it does not declare. The declared states are ['u'].

The message says that the system has a diffusivity for the state 'w', which it does not declare, and lists the declared states ['u'].

See its API entry.

docs.title: StockFlowSystem
docs.text:
A StockFlowSystem is a set of stocks that change only through named flows, each from a stock or a source to a stock or a sink. The trajectory reports every flow. The arms race of Richardson is two stocks of arms that grow with the arms of the other nation.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import StockFlowSystem

race = StockFlowSystem(
    stocks={'a': 1.0, 'b': 1.0},
    flows={
        'arming_a': (None, 'a', lambda s: s.source.k * s.source.b),
        'arming_b': (None, 'b', lambda s: s.source.k * s.source.a),
    },
    parameters={'k': 0.1},
    element='nations',
)
trajectory = simulate(race, until=10.0, dt=5.0)
trajectory.get_values('nations.a').round(3).tolist(), trajectory.get_values('nations.arming_a').round(3).tolist()

([1.0, 1.649, 2.718], [0.1, 0.165, 0.272])

The arms of each nation grow as exp(0.1 t), to 2.718 at time 10, and the flow arming_a grows with them.

The bathtub of engineering fills from a tap at a rate of 1 and drains at half its content.

from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.dynamics import StockFlowSystem

tub = StockFlowSystem(
    stocks={'water': 0.0},
    flows={'tap': (None, 'water', 1.0), 'drain': ('water', None, lambda s: 0.5 * s.source.water)},
    element='tub',
)
simulate(tub, until=10.0, dt=5.0).get_values('tub.water').round(3).tolist()

[0.0, 1.836, 1.987]

The water rises to 1.836 at time 5 and to 1.987 at time 10, towards the level 2 where the drain matches the tap.

How the engine runs it. The stocks and parameters are the variables of one DeclaredElement. Every flow is a TransferInteraction from the element to itself, so a flow between two stocks keeps their total, and the trajectory reports it as <element>.<flow>. None stands for the environment, and a labelled Source or Sink of skcomplex.core.components.laws in its place names it.

How it combines. A subclass returns its data from the hooks _get_stocks, _get_flows, _get_parameters, _get_element_label, and _get_variables. The translator of system dynamics files reads models into this system.

Limits and errors. Every flow must leave or enter a declared stock, and prepare raises a ValidationError otherwise.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    StockFlowSystem(stocks={'water': 0.0}, flows={'tap': (None, 'bath', 1.0)}).prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The flow 'tap' of StockFlowSystem names the stock 'bath', which it does not declare. The declared stocks are ['water'].

The message says that the flow 'tap' names the stock 'bath', which the system does not declare, and lists the declared stocks ['water'].

See its API entry.

docs.title: MovementInteraction
docs.text:
A MovementInteraction moves the agents of a group by steps at every step of discrete time. It returns a RuleLaw, an agent rule that the agent solver runs on every agent. Here two sheep start in the middle of a pasture of 5 by 5 cells and each takes one step to a neighbouring cell.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.agents import MovementInteraction

sheep = GroupElement('sheep', element=Element, size=2, location=[(2, 2), (2, 2)])
walk = MovementInteraction('walk', target='sheep', step='neighbor')
pasture = CompositeSystem(elements=[sheep], interactions=[walk], space=LatticeSpace((5, 5), metric='manhattan'))
trajectory = simulate(pasture, until=1, random_state=0)
[int(abs(cell - 2).sum()) for cell in trajectory.get_agents('sheep', 1).locations]

[1, 1]

Each sheep stands one cell away from the middle.

Divers swim in a box of three dimensions by Gaussian steps, the random walk of physics.

from skcomplex.core.components.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.components.spaces import ContinuousSpace
from skcomplex.core.components.systems import CompositeSystem
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.general.agents import MovementInteraction

divers = GroupElement('divers', element=Element, size=4)
swim = MovementInteraction('swim', target='divers', step='gaussian', scale=0.1)
space = ContinuousSpace(extent=(10.0, 5.0, 2.0), boundary='periodic')
system = CompositeSystem(elements=[divers], interactions=[swim], space=space)
trajectory = simulate(system, until=5, random_state=0)
trajectory.get_agents('divers', 5).locations.shape

(4, 3)

The trajectory holds one location of three coordinates for each of the four divers.

How the engine runs it. MesaSolver runs the rule once per step for every agent for which condition holds, in the order of schedule. The step chooses where an agent goes:

  • 'neighbor': a random cell or node next to its own, on a lattice or a network.
  • 'gaussian': its position plus a normal vector of deviation scale, in a continuous space.
  • 'levy': a random direction and a Pareto length, in a continuous space.
  • 'best': the next cell with the highest score(agent, cell, system).
  • a function step(agent, system) that returns the destination, or None to stay.

An agent takes a step with the probability probability and then with the probability accept(agent, destination, system). An exclusive movement never enters a cell held by another agent, and every step charges its cost.

How it combines. It moves the members of a GroupElement on a LatticeSpace, a NetworkSpace, or a ContinuousSpace of two or three sides, and it changes where agents stand, while a TopologyInteraction changes the space itself. In three dimensions, placement, steps, radius queries, the minimum image of a periodic box, and the locations of a trajectory use every side, and system.dimensions returns every side. The solver rejects a continuous space with any other number of sides, or without an extent, before the first frame, and the compile report holds the issue location-dimension for an initial location whose length differs from the dimension of its space. AgentsVisual draws agents in three dimensions as Points3D.

Limits and errors. It runs in discrete time with the agent solver. The step 'best' maximizes a score, so prepare raises a ValidationError without one.

from skcomplex.core.errors import ValidationError

try:
    MovementInteraction('forage', target='divers', step='best').prepare()
except ValidationError as error:
    message = str(error)
message

The step `best` of 'forage' maximizes a score. Pass `score(agent, cell, system)`.

The message reads "The step best of 'forage' maximizes a score. Pass score(agent, cell, system)." The fix is a score, such as the food in a cell.

A field realization. ZoneCouplingInteraction of biology and the boids of Boids3dSystem move agents by forces of their own. A short realization fixes the step of a foraging animal.
